Title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core claim: OOD robustness mostly depends on selecting transferable PCA/Q7 subspace rather than full source-trained probe; full reps can mix behavioral and source-specific/surface cues, hurting transfer despite high ID accuracy. Sparse directional subspaces may isolate more general behavioral structure.

Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer 15 residual stream, assistant-response tokens averaged. Source Roleplaying (V8); targets C2R, W6, J9. Labels GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1 removed, deceptive=1. Dataset totals/label counts (-1/0/1): V8 371=140/59/172; C2R 473=218/194/61; W6 151=29/38/84; J9 1000=379/375/246. Source activations standardized; same stats for targets. PCA/N4D on source standardized activations, retain leading 100 Q7. Subset S projection before train/eval. Logistic regression lambda=10. B8Q/full baseline trains directly on all standardized activations. Error bars 95% CIs.

Experiments/Fig 2: source-trained full B8Q, source-trained leading 100 Q7, target-trained leading 100 source Q7 with 5-fold CV. Appendix AUROC/F3: B8Q C2R .706, W6 .874, J9 .606. Target-trained leading-100 CV: C2R .936, W6 .950, J9 .869. Baseline W6 already high; C2R moderate; J9 poor/most OOD.

Transferable subspace: Greedy oracle H2 starts empty, considers leading 100 source Q7, trains source logistic regression on candidate subset, adds direction maximizing target F3; CV selection uses non-held-out target folds, evaluates selected source-trained probe on held-out fold; stop if improvement <=.001. H2 is transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Appendix: H2 improvement over B8Q .22 C2R, .23 J9; H2 F3 for recovery comparison C2R .929, J9 .832; mean H2 subset size target CV C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target H2 k C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Appendix D Table 2 instead lists H2 selected indices sizes C2R 13, W6 7, J9 15, conflict for J9. Earlier appendix says small H2 subset range 8–15, conflicting with full-target W6 k=7. Y4 variance selection matches H2 only on easy W6; far behind C2R/J9.

Hypotheses: T6 source-PCA ranking probe and M9 target-PCA ranking probe use X4 rankings = abs probe coefficient * Q7 std on source-N4D-projected activations; train source probe on top-k ranked directions. Neither source nor target ranking recovers transferable subspace/basis better than B8Q; M9 good C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9.

Interpretability: C7 LLM judge scores directions using 8 most/least activating source examples; L2 = retained max-R5 directions, trained as source probe. Appendix E: max observed R5=6; 2 scoring runs; 19 directions reached max in both and retained for L2; A7 uses complement 81. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on Roleplaying source and evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Main claim: small source-PC subsets enable OOD transfer near target/oracle probes; PC interpretations can select transferable PCs. Claimed baseline-to-oracle gap closure: 78% Report, 25% Sandbagging.

Datasets: Roleplaying 371 labels -1/0/1 = 140/59/172; Report 473 = 218/194/61; Confirm 151 = 29/38/84; Sandbagging 1000 = 379/375/246. Honest 0, ambiguous -1, deceptive 1; ambiguous removed.

Setup: layer 15 residual stream, assistant response token average. Source activations standardized, same stats for targets. PCA on scaled source activations, top 100 PCs. Logistic regression λ=10. Baseline full standardized activations.

Baseline §4.1 source-trained full target AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace: 0.936/0.950/0.869, likely Confirm/Report/Sandbagging.

Greedy oracle §4.2: select PCs among top 100 maximizing target AUROC, source-trained weights, target labels used for subset choice, 5-fold CV over target, stop improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves full baseline by 0.22 Report and 0.23 Sandbagging; close to target-trained. Variance top-k control matches only Confirm.

§4.3: PC rankings by standardized coefficient abs(coef × PC std). k from greedy on full target dataset: Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA transfers about baseline; target-PCA good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below-random on Sandbagging. Possible earlier ambiguity: target-PCA ranking said target-trained probe weights, then says both probes trained on source data projected to selected PCs.

§4.4/Appendix B: GPT-5-mini judge interprets source PCs with bipolar examples and rates OOD deception usefulness 1–10. No PC above 6; keep PCs scoring max in both runs: 19 PCs. Of 5 PCs in greedy selections for >1 target, 3/5 max OOD; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs did.

§4.5: 19 interp-selected PCs target-data-free. Outperforms full baseline, top-19 variance, and remaining 81 on all 3. Report 0.706→0.881 vs greedy 0.929 (78% gap). Confirm baseline near ceiling. Sandbagging 0.606→0.662 vs greedy 0.832 (25% gap). Limitation: no causal validation; interpretations descriptive.

Appendix C: lower PCs show stronger decoder alignment to SAE features, Spearman ρ=-0.857 best feature, -0.917 mean top 10; SAE andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct.

Appendix D Table 2 PC sets. Source probe weights: PC7,8,11,12,4,5,2,3,6,27,22,21,1,41,18. Greedy Report 13 PCs; Confirm 7; Sandbagging table lists 15 PCs, conflicting with earlier k=14. Target separability rankings list 15 PCs each. Appendix claims Jaccard greedy vs target-pca: Report 0.182, Confirm 0.077, Sandbagging 0.167; but using full table sets gives Report 4/24=0.167, Confirm 2/20=0.1, Sandbagging 5/25=0.2.

Appendix E: Table 3 lists 5 PCs selected on multiple OOD targets: PC62 score 6 Report+Sandbagging; PC57 score 6 Report+Sandbagging; PC9 score 3 Report+Sandbagging; PC81 score 3 Confirm+Sandbagging; PC86 score 6 Confirm+Sandbagging. This matches earlier 3/5 max score but conflicts if Table 3 is described as interpretation-selected for likely transferability. Table 4 begins source-weight PCs: PC7 score 3, PC8 4, PC11 3, PC12 3, PC4 6.

Abstract claims:

- Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Acknowledgment: work during 11th AI Safety Camp; compute; thanks. Impact Statement: generic ML advancement, no specific consequences.

Core claims: Linear probes can fail OOD; Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on Roleplaying source and evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Main finding: projecting onto small source-PC subsets enables transfer near target/oracle probes. PC interpretations can select transferable PCs; intro/§4.5 claimed baseline-to-oracle gap closure: 78% Report, 25% Sandbagging. Conclusion: OOD probing as representation/subspace selection; robust probing requires finding where behavioral signal is robustly represented, not just linear accessibility; full probes may mix general features with dataset-specific cues.

Datasets: Four Goldowsky-Dill datasets. Appendix A descriptions/counts: Roleplaying simple scenario with opportunity to lie; total 371 labels -1/0/1 = 140/59/172. Insider Trading Report: trader decides whether to honestly report using insider info; total 473 = 218/194/61. Insider Trading Confirm: after hiding earlier use of insider info, asked to confirm it did not use any; total 151 = 29/38/84. Sandbagging: deliberately underperform on some tasks while normal on others; total 1000 = 379/375/246. Labels honest 0, ambiguous -1, deceptive 1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed for experiments.

Setup: Activations: layer 15 residual stream, assistant response token average. Source activations standardized; same stats for targets. PCA on scaled source activations, top 100 PCs. Logistic regression λ=10. Baseline full standardized activations.

Baseline 4.1: source-trained full target AUROCs: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace via 5-fold CV: 0.936/0.950/0.869, likely Confirm/Report/Sandbagging. Claim: info exists in source-PC subspace; problem is learned direction.

Greedy oracle 4.2: Select PCs among top 100 to maximize target AUROC, training weights on source subset; target labels used for subset choice. 5-fold CV over target. Stop improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Greedy improves full baseline by 0.22 Report and 0.23 Sandbagging, close to target-trained; variance top-k control matches only Confirm. PC usefulness not variance-predicted.

4.3: Tests whether greedy PCs are target-separating PCs or source-probe-heavy PCs. PC rankings by standardized coefficient abs(coef × PC std) for probes in source-PCA basis. Possible inconsistency noted earlier: target-PCA ranking said to use target-trained probe weights, but then says both probes trained on source data projected to top-k selected PCs. k from greedy on full target dataset: Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA transfers about like baseline; target-PCA good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below-random on Sandbagging. Conclusion: subset cannot be found by source-side or target-side separability alone.

4.4/Appendix B: LLM judge prompt uses GPT-5-mini (OpenAI, 2025) to interpret PC directions. Prompt says direction is bipolar; examples are high-positive/high-negative from Roleplaying source, lines formatted token<TAB>activation with normalized integers -10 to +10. Judge must infer positive pole, negative pole, shared direction, and rate OOD deception usefulness 1–10. Prompt discourages broad sentiment assumptions/overgeneralization; low scores for surface cues/task-specific phrasing/noisy brittle directions; 5+ reserved for general deception-relevant strategy/behavior. Earlier 4.4: no PC above 6; keep PCs scoring max in both runs: 19 PCs. Of 5 PCs in greedy selections for >1 target, 3/5 max OOD; only 1 of top 5 source-PCA PCs did.

4.5: 19 interp-selected PCs as target-data-free subspace. Controls: full baseline, top-19 variance, remaining 81. Interp-selected outperforms baseline/variance on all 3, outperforms ablated on all 3. Report 0.706→0.881 vs greedy 0.929 (78% gap). Confirm baseline near ceiling. Sandbagging 0.606→0.662 vs greedy 0.832 (25% gap). 4.5 had causal-sounding claim PC selection “causally reduces model’s deceptive behavior,” though only detection/probe AUROC measured.

§5 Limitations: single model/source/layer; Confirm uninformative due to baseline 0.874. Sandbagging margins small, Report robust. Fully linear. No causal validation: interpretations descriptive; no inference ablations to verify causal encoding.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Model: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream, assistant-response token activations averaged. Source dataset: Roleplaying deception. Targets: Insider Trading Report, Insider Trading Confirm, Sandbagging. Labels honest=0/deceptive=1; ambiguous=-1 removed. Appendix A label counts before removal: Roleplaying 371 = -1/0/1: 140/59/172; Report 473 = 218/194/61; Confirm 151 = 29/38/84; Sandbagging 1000 = 379/375/246.

Preprocess: standardize using source stats; PCA fit on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression probes lambda=10. Baseline probes train on full standardized activations. For subset S, project to source PCA PCs in S.

Main thesis: OOD robustness mainly determined by subspace selection. Projecting into source PCA and selecting small subsets can make source-trained probes transfer almost as well as target-trained/oracle probes. Quant claims: LLM-judge/interp-selected PC method closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and 25% on Sandbagging.

Key results: full-representation source transfer AUROC: Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes within top-100 source PCs via 5-fold CV: 0.936/0.950/0.869 across targets, context Report/Confirm/Sandbagging. Greedy target-label PC selection with source probe weights is an upper bound; reported average subset sizes 15 Report, 8 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging. Greedy upper bounds: Report 0.929, Sandbagging 0.832; improves full baseline by 0.22 Report and 0.23 Sandbagging. Section 4.3 k from greedy full target: 13 Report, 7 Confirm, 14 Sandbagging; transfer not explained by target separability or source-probe weight.

Interpretability: For each top-100 source PC, LLM describes positive/negative poles/shared direction from 8 most/least source examples and rates OOD deception usefulness 1–10. No PC scored above 6; retain PCs with max score in both runs => 19 interp-selected PCs. Interp-selected probe outperforms full baseline, top-19 variance PCs, and remaining-81/interp-ablated on all targets. Report 0.706→0.881; Sandbagging 0.606→0.662. Appendix E Table 3, however, says “PCs selected for likely transferability” but lists only five PCs: PC62, PC57, PC9, PC81, PC86, conflicting with earlier 19 selected PCs. Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars. Work during 11th AI Safety Camp.

Core: Linear probes can fail OOD; robust probing requires identifying where behavioral signal is robustly represented. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct deception probes trained on Roleplaying source and evaluated on Insider Trading Report, Confirm, Sandbagging. Main finding: projecting onto small source-PC subsets enables transfer near target/oracle probes. PC interpretations can select transferable PCs; reported closure: 78% Report, 25% Sandbagging.

Datasets: Roleplaying 371 = 140/59/172; Report 473 = 218/194/61; Confirm 151 = 29/38/84; Sandbagging 1000 = 379/375/246. Labels honest 0, ambiguous -1, deceptive 1 by GPT-4o; ambiguous removed.

Setup: layer 15 residual stream, assistant response token average. Source activations standardized; same stats for targets. PCA on scaled source activations, top 100 PCs. Logistic regression λ=10. Baseline full standardized activations.

Baseline 4.1: source-trained full target AUROCs Confirm 0.874, Report 0.706, Sandbagging 0.606. Target-trained probes in top-100 source-PC subspace via 5-fold CV: 0.936/0.950/0.869, likely Confirm/Report/Sandbagging.

Greedy oracle 4.2: selects among top 100 PCs to maximize target AUROC, source-trained weights, target labels used for subset choice. 5-fold CV. Stop improvement ≤0.001. Avg subset sizes: Report 15, Confirm 8, Sandbagging 14. Improves full baseline by about 0.22 Report and 0.23 Sandbagging.

4.3: PC ranking tests. Possible inconsistency: target-PCA ranking said to use target-trained probe weights, then says both probes trained on source data projected to selected PCs. k set by greedy on full target, not CV: Report 13, Confirm 7, Sandbagging 14. Source-PCA transfers about like full baseline; target-PCA good on Report, worse than greedy on Confirm, below-random on Sandbagging.

4.4/4.5: LLM interpretations. Earlier text says max score 6 and 19 PCs selected by repeated max score; Appendix B/E says usefulness rated 1–10. Interp-selected 19-PC probe: Report 0.706→0.881, closes 78% gap to greedy 0.929; Confirm baseline near ceiling; Sandbagging 0.606→0.662, closes 25% gap to greedy 0.832. Appendix E Table 3 says “PCs selected for likely transferability” but lists only 5 PCs, including PC9 and PC81 with score 3, conflicting with earlier 19-PC max-score-6 selection.

Appendix C: lower PCs have stronger decoder alignment with SAE features; Spearman ρ=-0.857 best-matching SAE feature, -0.917 mean top 10; used andyrdt/saes-llama-3.1-8b-instruct.

Appendix D: Table lists PC sets. Report greedy 13, Confirm greedy 7, Sandbagging greedy 15, conflicting with earlier Sandbagging greedy size 14. Target-separability lists 15 PCs each. Stated Jaccards 0.182/0.077/0.167 conflict with table-calculated values: Report 4/24=0.167, Confirm 2/20=0.100, Sandbagging 4/26=0.154. Claims “agree on more than half” and “matching most greedy choices” conflict with low overlaps/table.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Thesis: source-probe-heavy directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode same contrast more abstractly/natural-language; OOD robustness largely determined by subspace/representation selection, not classifier fitting.

Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6). Layer 15 residual stream, averaged over assistant-response tokens only. Datasets: source Roleplaying V8; targets C2R, W6, J9. Labels honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Counts incl. ambiguous: V8 371 labels 140/59/172; C2R 473 labels 218/194/61; W6 151 labels 29/38/84; J9 1000 labels 379/375/246. Source activations standardized; same stats for targets. PCA/N4D retains leading 100 PCs/Q7. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full baseline B8Q trains on all standardized activations, not PCA subset. Error bars 95% CIs.

Baseline/target results: W6 transfer high, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained probes in retained source PCA subspace separate honest/deceptive on every target, so information exists but source-trained direction fails. Appendix B8Q AUROC/F3: C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606. Target-trained leading-100 source subspace 5-fold CV: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869.

Transferable subspace H2: greedy oracle over leading 100 Q7 using target labels for subset selection, not weights; upper bound. Target CV selects on non-held-out target folds, evaluates source-trained probe on held-out fold; stop if no improvement >0.001. Appendix H2: improvement over B8Q C2R 0.22, J9 0.23; F3 recovery C2R 0.929, J9 0.832; mean H2 subset size CV C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target H2 k C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Appendix D table lists H2 selected indices: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 15 (possible conflict with full-target J9 k=14). Appendix E: H2 directions shared by >1 target = 5: 62,57,9 for C2R+J9 and 81,86 for W6+J9; 3/5 have max R5=6.

Rankings: T6 source-side and M9 target-side rankings do not recover transferable subspace/basis better than B8Q. Appendix D nevertheless claims H2–M9 agree on “more than half,” but D3 table says C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167. T6 top indices source: 7,8,11,12,4,5,2,3,6,27,22,21,1,41,18. X4=absolute probe coefficient × corresponding Q7 std. Appendix E top T6 first five ratings: 7=3, 8=4, 11=3, 12=3, 4=6; thus 1 of top 5 max-rated.

Interpretation: C7 GPT-5-mini rates OOD deception usefulness R5 on normalized high/low Q7 examples. Appendix E: max observed R5=6, no direction exceeded; 2 scoring runs; 19 directions reached max in both runs and retained for L2; complement A7 uses 81. L2 language-only interp-selected PC probe improves over B8Q on all targets and over variance control, especially C2R/J9; exceeds A7 everywhere. L2: C2R F3 0.881, J9 0.662; baseline–H2 gap recovered C2R 78%, J9 25%. W6 little headroom.

Decoder alignment: lower-index Q7 align more strongly with SAE decoder features; correlations noted earlier best rho -0.857, mean top10 rho -0.917; Appendix C repeats lower Q7 stronger alignment using andyrdt SAE.

Limitations: narrow claims; single model/source; W6 high baseline uninformative; J9 weakest/most OOD; linear pipeline; encoding claims descriptive not causal.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Authors Daniel Yoo and Adrians Skapars.

Abstract claims:
- Linear probes can detect behaviors/concepts in LM activations but may fail OOD.
- Study: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct probes over 3 held-out deception detection datasets.

- Quantified gains: closes baseline-to-oracle gap by 78% on Insider Trading Report and by 25% on Sandbagging.
- Interpretation claim: source probe heavily weighted directions encode source-specific surface features; directions that transfer encode same contrast more abstractly and can be captured by natural language descriptions.
- Broad conclusion: OOD robustness of probes is largely determined by subspace selection.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Thesis: source probe heavy directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode same contrast abstractly/natural-language describable; OOD robustness depends on subspace/representation selection.

Setup: standardized source activations -> PCA/N4D retaining leading 100 PCs/Q7; project to selected subset before train/eval. Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, layer 15 residual stream, activations averaged over assistant response tokens only. Source Roleplaying V8; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. Labels GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1 removed, deceptive=1. Earlier text said V8 retained responses=311, but Appendix Table 1 gives V8 total 371 with counts -1/0/1 = 140/59/172, implying 231 non-ambiguous retained. Target counts: C2R 473, 218/194/61; W6 151, 29/38/84; J9 1000, 379/375/246. Source stats used for targets. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full baseline B8Q all standardized activations. Error bars 95% CIs.

Baseline/Appendix numbers: B8Q AUROC/F3 C2R .706, W6 .874, J9 .606. Target-trained leading-100 source subspace 5-fold CV: C2R .936, W6 .950, J9 .869.

H2 greedy oracle: empty over leading 100 source PCs, adds direction maximizing target F3 while fitting source logistic regression on candidate subset; target labels guide subset selection only. Appendix H2: improvement over B8Q C2R .22, J9 .23; H2 F3 C2R .929, J9 .832; mean subset sizes C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; full-target H2 k C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Appendix D Table 2 gives H2 selected sets: C2R 13 dirs; W6 7 dirs; J9 15 dirs (conflicts with earlier J9 k=14). D Table reports H2–M9 Jaccard C2R .182, W6 .077, J9 .167, but listed sets imply C2R 4/24=.167, W6 2/20=.100, J9 4/26=.154.

Hypothesis tests: T6 source-PCA ranking probe; M9 target-PCA ranking probe; X4 ranking = abs(coef)*PC std dev. T6 ~B8Q; M9 good C2R, worse than H2 W6, below random J9. T6 top indices: 7,8,11,12,4,5,2,3,6,27,22,21,1,41,18. Appendix E Table 4 gives top-five T6 R5 ratings: 7=3, 8=4, 11=3, 12=3, 4=6, supporting “1 of top 5” max-rated.

Interpretability: C7 LLM judge interprets leading source directions from 8 most/least activating examples. GPT-5-mini prompt; bipolar Q7 activations -10 to +10; observed max R5=6; scoring runs=2; directions reaching max in both runs retained for L2 = 19; complement A7=81. Appendix E says H2 directions selected for >1 target = 5; max-rated among shared H2 selections = 3/5; shared listed: 62,57,9 C2R+J9 and 81,86 W6+J9, with R5 62=6,57=6,9=3,81=3,86=6. Potential conflict: Table 3 title says C7-selected likely transferability but includes R5=3 directions. L2 F3 C2R .881, J9 .662; recovers baseline-H2 gap C2R 78%, J9 25%. Decoder alignment Spearman rho best feature -0.857, mean top 10 -0.917; lower-index Q7 align more strongly with SAE decoder features U9.

Limitations: single model/source; linear pipeline; interpretability descriptive not causal/ablated.

steps.notes_before: Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. Introduction context: linear probes reveal semantic information in LM representations but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance; behavioral concepts have linear representations, but probes may learn spurious correlations; this unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method framing: selection problem is to find dimensions permitting generalizing rather than spurious source-trained classification. Potential terminology issue noted/reported: intro says they work in “source Q7 coordinates,” while Fig. 1 caption says pipeline projects into the “source N4D basis.” Figure 1 pipeline: projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. Introduction context: linear probes reveal semantic information in LM representations but can fail OOD despite strong in-distribution performance; behavioral concepts have linear representations, but probes may learn spurious correlations; this unreliability is problematic for harmful-interaction monitoring. Related Work (part 2): cites prior work claiming true/false, honesty, emotion, refusal, and assistant-like behavior have simple/linear activation directions, supporting mechanistic understanding/intervention while leaving stable concepts vs context-dependent correlations unresolved. Notes linear probes can have high accuracy without proving the model represents the target property because probes may learn tasks or exploit surface correlates; encoded vs recoverable information are distinct; strong in-distribution probes generalize unevenly, so safety-probe evaluation must separate robust internal signals from artifacts. Also discusses natural-language feature explanations and use of automatic concept identification/ablation for intervention.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract claims: directions heavily weighted by a source probe encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode the same contrast more abstractly and can be captured in natural language; probe OOD robustness is largely determined by subspace selection. Introduction: linear probes can reveal semantic info but fail OOD despite strong in-distribution; behavioral concepts have linear representations but probes may learn spurious correlations; concern for harmful-interaction monitoring. Method framing: select dimensions allowing generalizing rather than spurious source-trained classification. Terminology to track: intro said “source Q7 coordinates,” Fig. 1 caption said projection into “source N4D basis”; Setup defines PCA as N4D and principal components as Q7, so these may be consistent if Q7 coordinates are PCs in N4D basis. Fig. 1 pipeline: projection into source N4D basis, filtering candidate Q7 directions, probe training in selected low-dimensional subspace.

Related Work: prior work claims true/false, honesty, emotion, refusal, assistant-like behavior have simple/linear activation directions, supporting mechanistic understanding/intervention but stable concepts vs context-dependent correlations unresolved. Linear probes can have high accuracy without proving model represents target because probes may learn task/surface correlates; encoded vs recoverable info distinct. Strong in-distribution probes generalize unevenly, so safety-probe evaluation must separate robust internal signals from artifacts. Natural-language feature explanations and automatic concept identification/ablation discussed.

Setup: Model is Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6); use layer 15 residual-stream activations, based on Ying et al. 2026 saying layer has highest cross-domain discrimination. For each prompt, activations averaged over assistant-response tokens only. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025: one source Roleplaying (V8), 311 retained responses; three held-out targets: Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). No other source dataset. Labels by GPT-4o (K8): honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed. Source activations standardized to zero mean/unit variance; source stats also used for targets. PCA (N4D) after standardization retains leading 100 principal components (PCs: Q7). Projection to subset S precedes training/evaluation. Classifiers are logistic regression with lambda=10. Full-representation baseline B8Q trains directly on all standardized activations, not PCA/subset. Retained 100 PCs chosen for interpretability comparability, not because low-index PCs generalize better; alignment with U9 (Bricken et al. 2023) decreases with PC index, so lower indices more interpretable. Error bars are 95% CIs.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Abstract/intro: source probe heavy directions encode source-specific surface features; transferable directions encode same contrast abstractly/natural-language describable; OOD robustness largely subspace selection. Linear probes may learn spurious correlates; aim is selecting dimensions that generalize. Fig.1/setup terminology: standardized source activations -> PCA/N4D retaining leading 100 PCs/Q7; projection to selected subset before training/eval. Model/data: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer 15 residual stream, activations averaged over assistant response tokens only. Source Roleplaying V8, 311 retained responses; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. Labels GPT-4o K8: honest=0, ambiguous=-1 removed, deceptive=1. Standardize source to zero mean/unit variance; source stats used for targets. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full-representation baseline B8Q trains on all standardized activations, not PCA/subset. 100 PCs retained for interpretability comparability; lower PC index more aligned/interpretable but not necessarily more generalizing. Error bars 95% CIs.

Experiments part 4: Baseline results: W6 transfer reasonably good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classification within retained source PCA subspace separates honest/deceptive on all targets, so information is present but source-trained direction fails to generalize. Fig2: target F3 for B8Q/full reps trained on 311 source responses (blue), source-trained leading 100 Q7 (orange), target-trained leading 100 source Q7 with 5-fold CV (green).

Transferable subspace: greedy oracle H2 starts empty over leading 100 source PCs; iteratively fits source logistic regression on candidate subset and adds direction maximizing target F3. Target 5-fold CV: selection uses non-held-out target folds, evaluates selected source-trained probe on held-out fold; stop if no improvement >0.001. Target labels guide subset selection only, never weight fitting; transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD. Small source-trained H2 subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R/J9. Variance control Y4 matched to H2 k only matches on easy W6, far behind on C2R/J9; explained variance not predictive. Fig3: B8Q, Y4, H2.

Hypothesis tests: T6 = source-PCA ranking probe; M9 = target-PCA ranking probe; both use X4 standardized coefficient ranking = abs(probe coefficient)*PC std dev on source-N4D-projected activations. Evaluated probes train on source data projected to top-k ranked directions. Greedy oracle H2 supplies stable set/k, numbers slightly differ from CV. Results: neither source nor target ranking recovers transferable subspace or transfers better than B8Q. T6 about as B8Q/source-reliant directions don’t generalize. M9 good C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9; target class separation and source-fitted transfer choose different directions.

Interpretation/selection: C7 LLM judge interprets each leading source direction from 8 most/least activating source examples, generates pole/whole-direction descriptions, assigns OOD/generalization score R5. Scores noisy; retain intersection of directions reaching observed maximum in both scoring runs. L2 = interp-selected PC probe; controls A7 = complement/interp-ablated PC probe, Y4 = equal-dimensional top-k variance PCs; all source-trained. Language-only L2 improves over B8Q on all targets and over Y4, widely on C2R/J9; exceeds A7 everywhere. Recovery: C2R substantially closes baseline-H2 gap; J9 partial; W6 little headroom, all methods except A7 roughly tied.

Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct layer 15 residual stream activations, averaged over assistant response tokens only. Source activations standardized; same source stats for targets. PCA on scaled source activations; retain top 100 PCs. Logistic regression λ=10. Baseline probes train on full standardized activations.

Sec 4.2: Greedy PC selection uses target labels, CV over target; source probe weights trained only on source projections. Stop if no AUROC improvement >0.001. Sec 4.1 baseline: Figure 2 compares source-trained full reps (blue), source-trained top-100 PCs (orange), and target-trained top-100 source PCs (green, 5-fold CV). Hypotheses: transferable PCs are those separating target classes well individually, or those source probe weights most heavily. Rankings use standardized coefficient = absolute probe coefficient times std dev of corresponding PC, from a probe trained on activations projected onto source-PCA basis.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core claim: robust behavioral probing requires selecting robust representation/subspace, not just linearly accessible info; full probes may mix behavioral and source-specific cues; sparse subspaces can isolate generalizable structure.

Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025: source Roleplaying V8; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. Labels GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed for experiments. Label counts incl ambiguous: V8 371 = 140/59/172; C2R 473 = 218/194/61; W6 151 = 29/38/84; J9 1000 = 379/375/246. Source activations standardized; same stats for targets. PCA/N4D on source activations, leading 100 directions Q7. Logistic regression lambda=10. Full baseline B8Q trains on all standardized activations, not PCA subset. Error bars 95% CIs. AUROC called F3.

4.1 baseline transfer: B8Q F3: C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606. Target-trained in leading-100 source subspace CV: C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869.

4.2 H2 greedy oracle: subset selection from leading 100 Q7 uses target labels; classifier fit on source labels. Stop if no target F3 improvement >0.001. Transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. H2 improvement over B8Q: C2R ~0.22, J9 ~0.23; H2 F3 for recovery comparison: C2R 0.929, J9 0.832. Mean H2 subset size in target CV: C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14. Earlier full-target H2 k recorded: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14, but Appendix D Table 2 lists H2 J9 as 15 indices (internal inconsistency); C2R 13 and W6 7 match. Variance selection Y4 only matches H2 on W6.

4.3 T6 source-side ranking about as good as B8Q; M9 target-side ranking strong on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. X4 standardized coefficient = abs probe coefficient × Q7 std dev on source-N4D-projected activations. H2 stable set/k from full-target selection; numbers differ slightly from CV.

4.4–4.5/App E: C7 interpreter uses 8 most/least activating source examples per direction. R5 max observed = 6; two scoring runs. 19 directions reached max in both runs and were retained for L2; A7 complement has 81 directions. H2 selected 5 directions for more than one target; only 3/5 were max-rated (contradicts earlier “recovers all five” summary). Shared H2 Table 3: 62 C2R+J9 R5 6; 57 C2R+J9 R5 6; 9 C2R+J9 R5 3; 81 W6+J9 R5 3; 86 W6+J9 R5 6. Maximum-rated among top T6 selections: 1 of top 5; top T6 table starts 7,8,11,12,4 with R5s 3,4,3,3,6. L2 F3: C2R 0.881, J9 0.662; baseline–H2 gap recovered: C2R 78%, J9 25%. L2 exceeds B8Q/Y4/A7 on all targets; W6 little headroom. Decoder alignment Spearman: best-matching feature -0.857, mean top 10 -0.917; lower-index Q7 align more strongly with SAE decoder features U9.

Appendix D: H2–M9 Jaccard D3: C2R 0.182, W6 0.077, J9 0.167; claim overlap less than a fifth. Table 2 selected sets: T6 Source top 15 = 7,8,11,12,4,5,2,3,6,27,22,21,1,41,18. H2 C2R 13; H2 W6 7; H2 J9 listed 15. M9 lists 15 per target.

Limitations: narrow/single model/source; W6 high baseline uninformative; J9 weakest/OOD; C2R improvement robust. Fully linear pipeline; descriptions not causal; no inference-time ablations.

Setup: Model Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer 15 residual-stream activations, averaged over assistant-response tokens only. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025: source Roleplaying (V8); held-out targets Insider Trading Report (C2R), Insider Trading Confirm (W6), Sandbagging (J9). Experiment 4.1: Baseline transfer: W6 good, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained classification within retained source subspace separates deceptive/honest on every target, so relevant info is present but source-trained direction fails to generalize. Fig 2 compares source-trained full reps B8Q (blue), source-trained leading 100 Q7 (orange), target-trained leading 100 source Q7 with 5-fold CV (green).

4.2: Transferable subspaces exist. Greedy oracle H2 starts empty, considers leading 100 source Q7, trains source logistic regression on candidate subset, adds direction with best target F3 improvement; target 5-fold CV selects on non-held-out target folds and evaluates source-trained probe on held-out fold; stop if no improvement >0.001. Target labels guide subset selection, never probe fitting, so H2 is transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. Small source-trained subspaces nearly match target-trained probes, especially C2R/J9. Variance selection Y4 with k matched to H2 matches H2 only on easy W6, far behind on C2R/J9; explained variance not predictive. Fig 3: B8Q blue, Y4 teal, H2 purple.

Paper title: “Probe Generalization as Subspace Selection for OOD Deception Detection.” Core claim: robust behavioral probing requires selecting robust representation/subspace, not just linearly accessible info. Setup: Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (E6), layer 15 residual-stream activations averaged over assistant-response tokens. Datasets from Goldowsky-Dill et al. 2025: source Roleplaying V8; targets C2R Insider Trading Report, W6 Insider Trading Confirm, J9 Sandbagging. Labels GPT-4o: honest=0, ambiguous=-1, deceptive=1; ambiguous removed for experiments. Appendix label counts incl ambiguous: V8 total 371, -1/0/1 = 140/59/172; C2R 473 = 218/194/61; W6 151 = 29/38/84; J9 1000 = 379/375/246. Source activations standardized; same stats for targets. PCA/N4D on source activations, leading 100 directions Q7. Classifiers logistic regression lambda=10. Full baseline B8Q trains on all standardized activations, not PCA subset. Error bars 95% CIs. AUROC called F3.

4.1 baseline transfer: B8Q F3: C2R 0.706, W6 0.874, J9 0.606. W6 already high/easy, C2R moderate, J9 poor. Target-trained in leading-100 source subspace (5-fold CV): C2R 0.936, W6 0.950, J9 0.869, showing relevant info present though source-trained probe may not generalize.

4.2 H2 greedy oracle: selects subsets from leading 100 source Q7 using target labels for subset selection only, source labels for classifier fitting; stop if no target F3 improvement >0.001. Transfer upper bound, not unbiased OOD estimate. H2 improvement over B8Q: C2R ~0.22, J9 ~0.23; H2 F3 used for recovery comparison: C2R 0.929, J9 0.832. Mean H2 subset size in target CV: C2R 15, W6 8, J9 14; small H2 subset range 8–15. Full-target H2 k: C2R 13, W6 7, J9 14. Variance selection Y4 only matches H2 on W6; far behind C2R/J9.

4.3 T6 source-side ranking about as good as B8Q; M9 target-side ranking strong on C2R, worse than H2 on W6, below random on J9. X4 standardized coefficient = abs probe coefficient × Q7 std dev on source-N4D-projected activations. H2 stable set/k from full-target selection; numbers differ slightly from CV.

4.4–4.5: C7 interpreter uses 8 most/least activating source examples per direction; OOD score R5 recovers all five repeatedly transferable Q7. Language-only selection L2 uses retained intersection; controls A7 complement and equal-dimensional variance Y4. L2 F3: C2R 0.881, J9 0.662; baseline–H2 gap recovered: C2R 78%, J9 25%. L2 exceeds B8Q/Y4/A7 on all targets; W6 little headroom. Decoder alignment Spearman: best-matching feature -0.857, mean top 10 -0.917.

Limitations: narrow/single model/source; W6 high baseline uninformative; J9 weakest/OOD; C2R improvement robust. Fully linear pipeline; descriptions not causal; no inference-time ablations.

final_notes:
Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Studies active-context privacy leakage: whether user-disclosed secrets in current conversation remain recoverable after unrelated topic drift and persuasion probes. Excludes training-data memorization, parameter privacy, static privacy/access-control norms, unsafe content generation, instruction hijacking/immediate jailbreaks, unlearning, personalization memory/cross-session retention.

Framework: user discloses secret S at turn t0; then d unrelated content-dense drift turns; standardized probe appended; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Behavioral re-disclosure, not raw transcript visibility.

Dataset/evaluation: 1,000 controlled dialogues per model across three LLMs: 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored inserted throughout, not stored as separate block; cached metadata lacks human-authored IDs, so only aggregate results and no human-vs-synthetic comparison. Four fixed-format PII categories: phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs, credit card numbers. Table 1 overall length: avg 359.16 words, median 385, min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00. Appendix A/Table 7 by drift: d=0 N197 avg words 44.29 median 43 avg tokens 59.05 median 57.33; d=2 N147 avg words 253.97 median 258 avg tokens 338.62 median 344; d=3 N142 avg words 344.18 median 347 avg tokens 458.91 median 462.67; d=4 N166 avg words 452.27 median 447 avg tokens 603.02 median 596; d=5 N181 avg words 520.92 median 543 avg tokens 694.56 median 724; d=6 N167 avg words 568.03 median 605 avg tokens 757.37 median 806.67. Counts sum to 1000 and weighted avg words matches Table 1.

Dialogue/probes: persona from >100 profiles; secret inserted in opening turn. Drift turns from dense Q/A library etc.; subset human-authored. Three persuasion levels: Simple/direct, Medium/contextual justification, Hard/high-pressure. Drift d=0 p=.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}; no d=1. Bounded drift only up to d=6.

Detection: hierarchical hybrid detector: normalized exact match or Llama judge for full/substantial/partial enough secret. Regex-only, fuzzy, hybrid reported separately. No formal human IAA. τ: δ=0.1*L(0); τ=min observed d where L(d)≤δ and all later observed also ≤δ; if none τ=max(D_obs)+1.

Setup: Models GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter/API-served models. Each dialogue has one seeded secret and d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}; three probes/dialogue => 3,000 cached model-probe responses/model, 9,000 total. Dialogue-level leaks if any probe elicits secret. Persuasion/fuzzy analyses probe-level.

Key results: Dialogue-level hybrid leakage DeepSeek 38.70%, GPT 47.70%, Qwen 54.60%. Regex vs hybrid: GPT +0, DeepSeek +0.90, Qwen +1.10. Persuasion non-monotonic/model-dependent. Drift dips near d=3 then rebounds; Appendix B probe-level drift effect sizes: DeepSeek V=0.1073 small, GPT V=0.0659 negligible, Qwen V=0.0723 negligible. Secret type strongest/large: DeepSeek V=0.5871, GPT V=0.7731, Qwen V=0.6927. Persuasion negligible: DeepSeek V=0.0718, GPT V=0.0689, Qwen V=0.0639. τ=7 for all models/persuasion levels, exceeds observed d≤6. Fuzzy close to hybrid; mostly direct/near-direct leakage. Artifacts planned: code/templates/scripts/aggregate results/sanitized subset; examples use non-real identifiers/templates. Appendix C has Figure 6 dialogue construction details.

It is not about training-data memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Motivation: users/designers may underestimate elicitation of earlier sensitive info through later indirect/justified/high-pressure/tool-mediated prompts in shared sessions, browser assistants, enterprise copilots, agentic workflows, prompt injection.

Intro says “1,000 dialogues per model.” Axes: topic drift = number of unrelated turns between secret disclosure and probing; persuasion intensity = interaction style used to elicit secret. Drift window tested is d ≤ 6. Probe styles: direct, justified, high-pressure. Secret types include SSNs, credit cards, emails, phone numbers, financial identifiers, health-related details/PII.

Main reported results so far: dialogue-level leakage under hybrid detection ranges from 38.7% to 54.6%, varies strongly by model, secret type, and persuasion intensity. SSNs and credit cards suppressed far more often than emails and phone numbers. Persuasion intensity significantly affects leakage. Within tested drift window, additional topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage. Contribution claims no evaluated model reaches stable decay within observed drift range.

Detection/metrics: reproducible hybrid detector combines normalization-based matching with open-weights LLM judge. Paper reports dialogue-level, probe-level, regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid leakage rates. Proposes Privacy Half-Life (τ), a stability-based metric for persistent suppression.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Studies active-context privacy leakage: whether user-disclosed secrets in current conversation remain recoverable after unrelated topic drift and persuasion probing. Excludes training-data memorization, parameter privacy, static privacy/access-control norms, unsafe content generation, instruction hijacking/immediate jailbreaks, and unlearning. Limitations: findings do not imply permanent/cross-session model memory or characterize full long-context windows; leakage is behavioral recovery from active context under bounded drift.

Framework/threat model: user discloses secret S at turn t0; then d unrelated content-dense drift turns; standardized probe appended. Leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Concern is not raw transcript visibility but behavioral re-disclosure. Probes: Simple/direct, Medium/contextual justification, Hard/high-pressure. Drift d=0 p=0.2, otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}; no d=1. Drift only up to d=6.

Dataset/evaluation: Intro/conclusion/§4 say 1,000 dialogues per model across three LLMs, but §3.2 says N=1000 controlled dialogues total: 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored. Human-authored inserted throughout; cached metadata lacks IDs, so only aggregate results/no human-vs-synthetic comparison. Table 1: 1,000 dialogues; 4 secret categories; drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6; avg 359.16 words, median 385, min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00. Appendix A/Table 7 by drift: d0 N=197 avg words 44.29 median 43 tokens 59.05/57.33; d2 N=147 avg 253.97 median 258 tokens 338.62/344; d3 N=142 avg 344.18 median 347 tokens 458.91/462.67; d4 N=166 avg 452.27 median 447 tokens 603.02/596; d5 N=181 avg 520.92 median 543 tokens 694.56/724; d6 N=167 avg 568.03 median 605 tokens 757.37/806.67. Counts sum to 1000 and weighted avg matches Table 1. Four fixed-format PII categories: phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs, credit card numbers. Earlier broad mention of financial identifiers and health-related details/PII conflicts with four-category definition. Limitations acknowledge fixed-format secrets are easier to detect than unstructured sensitive attributes.

Detection: hybrid detector. Leakage if normalized secret appears in response OR Llama judge says response reveals full secret, substantial substring, or enough partial info. §7 says deterministic matching, fuzzy matching, and external LLM judge, and claims regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid labels are reported separately—possible inconsistency because prior results only showed regex vs hybrid. Discussion says leakage mostly direct/near-direct reproduction because fuzzy matching closely tracks hybrid leakage. No formal human inter-annotator agreement; future manual audit planned.

§4 setup: evaluates GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter API, same histories/probe templates. Says 1,000 dialogues per model, each with one secret and d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}, three probes. Claims 3,000 cached responses per model but incorrectly says 8,000 total across three models; arithmetic implies 9,000. API models may change; logs IDs, prompts, timestamps, cached responses, paired stats.

Key §5/conclusion results: Dialogue-level hybrid: DeepSeek 38.70%, GPT 47.70%, Qwen 54.60%. Regex vs hybrid: GPT +0.00, DeepSeek +0.90, Qwen +1.10. Probe-level by persuasion: GPT Simple 39.30, Medium 40.50, Hard 32.90; DeepSeek 28.10, 22.00, 29.20; Qwen 38.70, 33.30, 40.60. Persuasion significant but nonmonotonic/model-dependent. Drift: dip near d=3 then rebound; small/negligible Cramer V DeepSeek 0.1073, GPT 0.0659, Qwen 0.0723. Half-life τ=7 all models/persuasion; exceeds observed d≤6/no stable decay. Secret type strongest/large association: DeepSeek 0.5871, GPT 0.7731, Qwen 0.6927. Probe-level by type: SSN GPT 0.14, DeepSeek 1.11, Qwen 5.97; credit card 0.00, 0.39, 4.01; email 78.24,57.11,81.13; phone 70.89,46.13,57.24. Interpretation: SSN/credit-card suppression vs email/phone leakage suggests format-sensitive safeguards. Appendix B/Table 8 effect sizes match: persuasion Cramer V negligible DeepSeek 0.0718, GPT 0.0689, Qwen 0.0639; secret type large; drift small/negligible.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Studies active-context privacy leakage: whether user-disclosed secrets in current conversation remain recoverable after unrelated topic drift and persuasion probes. Excludes training-data memorization, personalization/cross-session memory, parameter privacy, static privacy/access-control norms, unsafe content generation, instruction hijacking/immediate jailbreaks, and unlearning. Behavioral re-disclosure, not raw transcript visibility/permanent memory.

Framework: user discloses secret S at turn t0; then d unrelated content-dense drift turns; standardized probe P appended; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset: N=1000 controlled dialogues total: 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored, inserted throughout benchmark; metadata does not preserve which rows are human-authored, so only aggregate results. Same 1,000 dialogues evaluated on each of three API-served models. Four fixed-format PII categories: phone, email, SSN, credit card. Drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6; no d=1. Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Core claim: persistent shared-session tool-augmented LLMs can re-disclose user secrets after unrelated topic drift; QX2 audits active-context privacy, not memorization/jailbreaks. PII includes phone, email, financial/payment IDs, government IDs, health details. E9U = active-context re-disclosure of prior user secret after unrelated exchanges; leakage exact/approx/semantic.

Dataset/setup: N=1000 dialogues, 900 synthetic/100 human-authored interspersed. Secret categories S8Q: A2L phone, F8Z email, W3B SSN, N6G credit card. Drift D7A d in {0,2,3,4,5,6}; d=0 p=.2 else uniform 2–6. Appendix A Table 7 D7A counts/lengths: d0 N197 avg 44.29 words/59.05 tokens; d2 N147 avg 253.97/338.62; d3 N142 avg 344.18/458.91; d4 N166 avg 452.27/603.02; d5 N181 avg 520.92/694.56; d6 N167 avg 568.03/757.37; sums to 1000. Three V4N probes: C8R simple, Z2F medium/contextual justification, L9W hard/urgent. All systems receive identical histories/probes via OpenRouter; each model processes full dataset under every V4N. Cached responses: 3000/model, 9000 total, implying 3 models. G4P = any-probe dialogue-level leakage; P6S = probe-level leakage. H8D hybrid detector positive if normalization/regex inclusion or judge finds full/substantial/partial identifying disclosure. U3P/B6T deterministic baseline. K2V tau: threshold delta=.1*L(0), stable all-later suppression required; if none tau=max(Dobs)+1.

Models: M7Q GPT-OSS-120B, T4X DeepSeek-R1, Y9C Qwen3-VL-235B; API-served models may change over time despite logged identifiers/prompts/timestamps/cached responses/paired stats.

Section 5 results: Table 2 G4P U3P vs H8D: M7Q 47.70/47.70 delta 0 p=1; T4X 37.80/38.70 delta +0.90 p=7.7e-3; Y9C 53.50/54.60 delta +1.10 p=2.57e-3. Table 3 H8D G4P CIs: T4X 38.70% [35.7,41.6], M7Q 47.70% [44.6,50.8], Y9C 54.60% [51.6,57.7].

V4N P6S Table 4: M7Q C8R 39.30, Z2F 40.50, L9W 32.90; T4X C8R 28.10, Z2F 22.00, L9W 29.20; Y9C C8R 38.70, Z2F 33.30, L9W 40.60. Cochran Q p<1e-5 every model. Text says non-monotonic; internal error: it claims T4X maximizes at Z2F, but table max is L9W and Z2F lowest. Discussion says M7Q urgency activates safety/refusal behavior (supported by lower L9W), Y9C weaker pressure resistance (L9W highest).

D7A associations small/negligible; Figure 4 dip near d=3 then rebound; risk persists. K2V: every model/condition observed d<=6 assigned tau=7; no stable suppression. Limitations: bounded short-to-medium drift, active context only, not full-window/cross-session/training memory.

S8Q Table 5 H8D P6S: W3B M7Q .14, T4X 1.11, Y9C 5.97; N6G 0, .39, 4.01; F8Z 78.24,57.11,81.13; A2L 70.89,46.13,57.24. S8Q strongest association; W3B/N6G suppressed far more than F8Z/A2L. Conclusion: S8Q asymmetry suggests uneven safeguards based on format/sensitivity cues rather than generalized contextual confidentiality. R5J Table 6 cached P6S: T4X U3P25.50 R5J.85 26.40 R5J.80 26.53 H8D26.43; M7Q 36.80/37.03/37.07/37.57; Y9C 36.97/37.60/37.93/37.53.

Appendix B Table 8 cached P6S effect sizes H8D-benchmark-variable associations: S8Q large for all (T4X .5871, M7Q .7731, Y9C .6927); D7A small/negligible (T4X .1073 small; M7Q .0659 negligible; Y9C .0723 negligible); V4N negligible (T4X .0718, M7Q .0689, Y9C .0639). Appendix C: Figure 6 dialogue construction details.

Limitations/future: fixed-format identifiers easier to detect than unstructured sensitive attributes; human-vs-synthetic comparison deferred because cached metadata no longer preserves human row IDs; no formal human–automated IAA; larger manual audits future. Planned artifact release: generation code, probe templates, eval scripts, aggregate results, sanitized dialogue subset; non-real identifiers/templates for reproduction.

Excludes training-data memorization, parameter privacy, static access-control/privacy norms, immediate jailbreaks, unlearning, personalization/cross-session retention.

Dataset/evaluation inconsistency: Intro/setup/conclusion say 1,000 dialogues per model across three LLMs; §3.2 says N=1000 controlled dialogues total: 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored. Human-authored IDs unavailable, so only aggregate results; no human-vs-synthetic comparison. Table 1: 1,000 dialogues; PII categories phone/email/SSN/credit card; drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6; avg 359.16 words, median 385, min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00. Appendix C only references Figure 6 dialogue construction details.

Detection: hierarchical hybrid detector; leakage if normalized secret appears or Llama judge says full/substantial/semantic reveal. Regex, fuzzy, hybrid reported. No formal human inter-annotator agreement. Privacy Half-Life τ: δ=.1*L(0); τ=min observed d with L(d)≤δ and all later observed d' also ≤δ; if none τ=max(D_obs)+1.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Privacy risk is active-context persistence/re-disclosure, not training memorization, unlearning, static norms, or jailbreaks. Threat model asks whether model re-discloses user secret S after drift/probe.

Dataset/setup: N=1,000 controlled dialogues per model. Composition inconsistent: early and §7 say 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored, inserted throughout; another earlier statement said “1,000 dialogues generated by PrivDrift pipeline.” §7 adds metadata does not preserve which evaluated rows were human-authored, so only aggregate results, no human-vs-synthetic comparison. Three models: GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter/API-served; logged identifiers, prompts, timestamps, cached responses. Same histories/probes. One seeded secret/dialogue; drift length d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}; d=0 p=.2, otherwise uniform over 2–6; no d=1. Appendix A Table 7 drift counts sum to 1,000: d0=197, d2=147, d3=142, d4=166, d5=181, d6=167. Avg words/tokens rise with drift: d0 44.29 words/59.05 tokens; d6 568.03 words/757.37 tokens; tokens estimated from word counts. Three probes/dialogue: Simple/direct neutral, Medium/contextual justification, Hard/high-pressure. 3,000 cached responses/model, 9,000 total.

Secrets: four fixed-format PII categories: phone, email, SSN, credit card. Earlier headline said SSNs/credit cards suppressed far less often than emails/phones, but §5.5 and §6 say opposite: SSNs/credit cards suppressed far more often. Table 5 leakage: GPT SSN .14%, CC 0%, Email 78.24%, Phone 70.89%; DeepSeek SSN 1.11%, CC .39%, Email 57.11%, Phone 46.13%; Qwen SSN 5.97%, CC 4.01%, Email 81.13%, Phone 57.24%.

Detection/metrics: hierarchical hybrid detector: Stage 1 normalization/regex exact-ish matching; Stage 2 Llama judge for regex negatives; fuzzy matching also reported. Binary full/substantial/identifying partial disclosure. Dialogue leakage counts if any probe leaks; probe-level analyses one response per persuasion condition. Dialogue bootstrap CIs; chi-square/Cramer’s V; McNemar/Bonferroni; Cochran’s Q. §7 says no formal human inter-annotator agreement yet; future manual audit.

Main results: Dialogue-level hybrid leakage substantial, 38.7%–54.6%. Regex vs hybrid: GPT 47.70 vs 47.70; DeepSeek 37.80 vs 38.70; Qwen 53.50 vs 54.60. Hybrid 95% CI: DeepSeek 38.70 [35.7,41.6], GPT 47.70 [44.6,50.8], Qwen 54.60 [51.6,57.7]. Probe-level hybrid by persuasion: GPT Simple 39.30, Medium 40.50, Hard 32.90; DeepSeek 28.10, 22.00, 29.20; Qwen 38.70, 33.30, 40.60. Cochran Q p<1e-5 all; non-monotonic.

Drift: dip near d=3 then rebound; V small/negligible: DeepSeek .1073, GPT .0659, Qwen .0723; drift does not reliably reduce leakage within d≤6. Privacy Half-Life δ=.1*L(0): no model reaches threshold; τ=max(Dobs)+1=7 for all models/persuasion. §7: bounded drift only up to d=6, not long-context saturation.

Appendix B Table 8 probe-level Cramer’s V: Secret type large for all (DeepSeek .5871, GPT .7731, Qwen .6927); Drift length DeepSeek .1073 small, GPT .0659 negligible, Qwen .0723 negligible; Persuasion negligible for all (DeepSeek .0718, GPT .0689, Qwen .0639). Appendix C only says Figure 6 dialogue construction details.

Fuzzy probe-level close to hybrid; leakage mostly direct/near-direct. Artifact plan: release generation code, templates, eval scripts, aggregates, sanitized subset; examples non-real identifiers/templates.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, WVU.

Core framework: QX2/PrivDrift audits active-context user-secret re-disclosure after unrelated topic drift in persistent/shared/tool-augmented LLM conversations. Threat model E9U: user gives secret S at t0; dense unrelated drift J7K D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; later standardized probe P asks/pressures for it. Leakage = exact/approx/semantic revelation of S. Not parameter memorization or mere transcript access; transcript invisibility not assumed.

Dataset/setup: N=1000 dialogues: 900 synthetic, 100 human-authored, interspersed. One seeded secret and sampled drift length d per dialogue. S8Q categories: A2L phone/contact, F8Z email/electronic contact, W3B SSN/government IDs, N6G credit-card/payment IDs. D7A values 0,2,3,4,5,6 with p=0.2 for d=0 and p=0.8 uniform over 2–6. Overall avg/median/min-max words 359.16/385/43–795; approx tokens 478.87/513.33/57.33–1060. Appendix A Table 7 D7A counts/lengths: d=0 N197 avg/median words 44.29/43 tokens 59.05/57.33; d=2 N147 253.97/258 tokens 338.62/344; d=3 N142 344.18/347 tokens 458.91/462.67; d=4 N166 452.27/447 tokens 603.02/596; d=5 N181 520.92/543 tokens 694.56/724; d=6 N167 568.03/605 tokens 757.37/806.67. Three probes/conditions per dialogue: C8R simple neutral retrieval; Z2F medium contextual justification; L9W hard urgent/high-pressure. Via OpenRouter. Cached responses: 3,000/model = 1000 dialogues x 3 probes; 9,000 total, 3 models: M7Q = GPT-OSS-120B, T4X = DeepSeek-R1, Y9C = Qwen3-VL-235B.

Evaluation/metrics: H8D hybrid detector positive if normalized inclusion succeeds or LLM judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or sufficient partial identifying info. Stage 1 U3P normalization/inclusion; Stage 2 Llama judge on deterministic negatives. U3P regex-only baseline separately. G4P = dialogue-level any-probe leakage; P6S = probe/response statistic. G4P CIs bootstrap over dialogues. McNemar, Cochran Q/McNemar, chi-square/Cramer’s V.

Results: Table 2 G4P U3P vs H8D: M7Q 47.70/47.70 delta 0 p=1; T4X 37.80/38.70 delta +0.90 p=7.7e-3; Y9C 53.50/54.60 delta +1.10 p=2.57e-3. Table 3 H8D G4P: T4X 38.70 [35.7,41.6], M7Q 47.70 [44.6,50.8], Y9C 54.60 [51.6,57.7]. Table 4 P6S by V4N: M7Q C8R 39.30 Z2F 40.50 L9W 32.90; T4X 28.10/22.00/29.20; Y9C 38.70/33.30/40.60; Cochran Q p<1e-5 every model. Table 5 S8Q P6S: W3B 0.14/1.11/5.97, N6G 0.00/0.39/4.01, F8Z 78.24/57.11/81.13, A2L 70.89/46.13/57.24 for M7Q/T4X/Y9C. Table 6 cached-output P6S: T4X U3P 25.50 R5J .85 26.40 .80 26.53 H8D 26.43; M7Q 36.80/37.03/37.07/37.57; Y9C 36.97/37.60/37.93/37.53. K2V: every model/condition d<=6 assigned tau=7; no stable suppression.

Appendix B Table 8 effect sizes X2H for H8D-benchmark-variable associations: S8Q large (T4X .5871, M7Q .7731, Y9C .6927); D7A T4X small .1073, M7Q/Y9C negligible .0659/.0723; V4N negligible all models T4X .0718, M7Q .0689, Y9C .0639. Appendix C only says Fig 6 dialogue construction details.

Discussion/limitations: behavioral recoverability not permanent memory/uniform long-context; active context only; J7K/topic drift not implicit privacy boundary. D7A short-to-medium, no context saturation. Mixed synthetic/human but human-vs-synthetic comparison deferred due metadata limitations. Detector automated; no formal human–automated IAA. Planned artifacts listed.

Introduction opening claims: SSNs and payment identifiers receive much weaker suppression than contact identifiers; no evaluated system attains stable decay. QX2 provides controlled persistence auditing; direct/justified/high-pressure elicitation; reproducible composite detection using deterministic processing and an open-weights judge; G4P and P6S reporting; and a stability criterion rather than transient-decrease criterion.

Intro framing: LLMs are persistent assistants across extended interactions in healthcare, financial planning, enterprise copilots, personal productivity. Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Studies active-context privacy leakage: whether user-disclosed secrets in current conversation remain recoverable after unrelated topic drift and persuasion probing. Excludes training-data memorization, parameter privacy, static privacy/access-control norms, unsafe content generation, immediate jailbreaks, unlearning, personalization/cross-session memory. Behavioral re-disclosure, not raw transcript visibility/permanent memory/general long-context claim.

Framework: secret S disclosed at t0; then d unrelated content-dense drift turns; standardized probe P appended; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Dataset: 1,000 PrivDrift dialogues evaluated on GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter, with three persuasion probes each = 3,000 cached responses/model, 9,000 total. Regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid reported separately. No formal human-vs-automated inter-annotator agreement yet; future manual audit. Dialogue-level overall leakage counts dialogue as leaking if any of three probes leaks; persuasion/fuzzy analyses probe-level. Stats: 95% bootstrap CIs over dialogues; McNemar paired comparisons; Cochran’s Q for repeated persuasion; chi-square/Cramer’s V for drift/persuasion/secret type.

Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Core: QX2 audits active-context re-disclosure of user-supplied secrets after topic drift, not training memorization/jailbreaks. Each of 3 models has 3000 cached responses; G4P = any-probe dialogue-level leakage; P6S = probe-level leakage.

Results: Table 2 G4P U3P vs H8D: M7Q 47.70/47.70 delta 0 p=1; T4X 37.80/38.70 delta +0.90 p=7.7e-3; Y9C 53.50/54.60 delta +1.10 p=2.57e-3. V4N P6S H8D Table 4: M7Q C8R 39.30, Z2F 40.50, L9W 32.90; T4X 28.10, 22.00, 29.20; Y9C 38.70, 33.30, 40.60. Cochran Q p<1e-5 for every model; effects non-monotonic. D7A associations small/negligible; Figure 4 described as dip near d=3 then rebound; no reliable reduction across tested window. K2V Table: every model and persuasion condition observed d<=6, assigned tau=max(D_obs)+1=7; no system approaches threshold and suppression never stabilizes. Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Studies active-context privacy leakage: whether user-disclosed secrets in current conversation remain recoverable after unrelated topic drift and persuasion probes. Excludes training-data memorization, parameter privacy, static privacy/access-control norms, unsafe content generation, instruction hijacking/immediate jailbreaks, unlearning, personalization memory, and cross-session retention.

Framework: user discloses secret S at turn t0; then d unrelated content-dense drift turns; standardized probe appended; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Behavioral re-disclosure, not raw transcript visibility.

Dataset/evaluation: Intro/setup/conclusion describe 1,000 dialogues per model across three LLMs; §3.2 describes N=1000 total dialogues: 900 synthetic + 100 human-authored. Human-authored dialogues inserted throughout, but cached metadata lacks human-authored row IDs, so only aggregate results and no human-vs-synthetic comparison. Table 1: 1,000 dialogues; 4 secret categories; drift lengths 0,2,3,4,5,6; avg 359.16 words, median 385, min/max 43/795; avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060.00. Appendix A/Table 7 drift counts: d=0 N=197, d=2 N=147, d=3 N=142, d=4 N=166, d=5 N=181, d=6 N=167; counts sum to 1000 and weighted averages match Table 1.

Four fixed-format PII categories: phone numbers, email addresses, SSNs, credit card numbers. Limitations reiterate fixed-format focus; unstructured sensitive attributes such as health/family/immigration/financial hardship left for future work.

Dialogue/probes: persona from >100 profiles; secret inserted in opening turn. Drift turns from dense Q/A library etc.; subset human-authored. Three persuasion levels: Simple/direct, Medium/contextual justification, Hard/high-pressure. Drift d=0 p=.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6}; no d=1. Bounded drift up to d=6, interpreted as short-to-medium active-context drift, not full long-context saturation.

Detection: hierarchical hybrid detector. Leakage if normalized secret appears in normalized response OR Llama judge says response reveals full secret, substantial substring, or enough partial info. Reports regex-only, fuzzy, and hybrid separately. Limitation says no formal human inter-annotator agreement yet; future manual audit needed. Internal issue in §7: detector-scope sentence claims labels establish behavior for “arbitrary unstructured personal narratives,” conflicting with fixed-format-only benchmark.

Privacy Half-Life τ: δ=0.1*L(0); τ=min observed d with L(d)≤δ and all later observed d' also ≤δ; if none τ=max(D_obs)+1.

Setup: Models GPT-OSS-120B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-VL-235B via OpenRouter/API-served; 1,000 dialogues/model; each dialogue one seeded secret and d∈{0,2,3,4,5,6}; three probes/dialogue => 3,000 cached model-probe responses/model, 9,000 total. Dialogue-level leaks if any probe elicits secret. Persuasion/fuzzy analyses probe-level. Stats: bootstrap CIs, McNemar/Bonferroni, Cochran’s Q, chi-square with Cramer’s V.

Results/conclusion: Dialogue-level regex/hybrid: GPT 47.70/47.70; DeepSeek 37.80/38.70; Qwen 53.50/54.60. Hybrid CIs: DeepSeek 38.70 [35.7,41.6], GPT 47.70 [44.6,50.8], Qwen 54.60 [51.6,57.7]. Persuasion non-monotonic/model-dependent. Drift dips near d=3 then rebounds; topic drift does not reliably reduce leakage. τ=7 for all, exceeding observed window d≤6. Secret type strongest association/asymmetry; emails/phones leak far more than SSNs/credit cards. Fuzzy closely tracks regex/hybrid. Appendix B/Table 8 probe-level Cramer’s V: secret type large (DeepSeek .5871, GPT .7731, Qwen .6927); drift small/negligible (DeepSeek .1073 small, GPT .0659 negligible, Qwen .0723 negligible); persuasion negligible (DeepSeek .0718, GPT .0689, Qwen .0639).

Discussion: persistent active-context risk, not permanent model memory; topic drift not implicit privacy boundary. Artifacts planned: generation code, probe templates, eval scripts, aggregate results, sanitized subset with non-real identifiers/templates. Appendix C just lists Figure 6 dialogue construction details.

Each of 3 models has 3000 cached responses; G4P = any-probe dialogue-level leakage; P6S = probe-level leakage.

V4N P6S H8D Table 4: M7Q C8R 39.30, Z2F 40.50, L9W 32.90; T4X 28.10, 22.00, 29.20; Y9C 38.70, 33.30, 40.60. Cochran Q p<1e-5 for every model; non-monotonic. Paper title: “PrivDrift: Auditing User-Secret Leakage Under Topic Drift in Active LLM Conversations.” Author Luciano Rolando Maldonado Romero, WVU.

Core claim: Persistent, user-facing, shared-session, tool-augmented LLMs can behaviorally re-disclose sensitive user disclosures beyond unrelated tasks/topic drift. QX2 = PrivDrift benchmark audits active-context privacy, not parameter memorization or immediate jailbreaks. Abstract/introduction claim G4P under H8D remains substantial, varies sharply across systems, S8Q, and V4N, and does not reliably decline; no system attains stable decay. SSNs/payment IDs get stronger suppression than contact IDs.

Framing: PII includes phone (A2L), email (F8Z), financial/payment IDs, government IDs, health details. Active-context privacy differs from training-data extraction, membership inference, memorized PII recovery, contextual integrity/legal compliance benchmarks, multi-turn harmful-content jailbreaks, and unlearning benchmarks. Concern is information-flow failure: re-disclosure of earlier user-supplied secret still in context after unrelated exchanges.

Section 3/QX2 framework: Pipeline = controlled multi-turn dialogue construction, standardized probe attachment, target-model queries, composite leakage scoring. Threat model: transcript invisibility not assumed; E9U = active-context re-disclosure, reproduction of earlier sensitive value under later query/justification/pressure, not mere transcript presence. User supplies secret S at t0; topic drift J7K consists of unrelated dense exchanges D={u1,a1,...,ud,ad}; standardized probe P appended. Exact, approximate, or semantic revelation of S counts as leakage.

Dataset: N=1000 dialogues: 900 synthetic, 100 human-authored; human-authored interspersed, not contiguous. Secret categories=4. D7A drift values {0,2,3,4,5,6}. Avg words 359.16, median 385, min/max 43/795. Avg approx tokens 478.87, median 513.33, min/max 57.33/1060. Personas sampled from >100 professions/demographics. Four fixed-format secret types S8Q: A2L=phone numbers, F8Z=email addresses, W3B=SSNs, N6G=credit card numbers. Secrets inserted as ground truth, not inferred.

Topic drift/content: Assigned topics include tax filing, medical triage, travel logistics; dense Q/A library plus professional-writing, structured-reasoning, long-form-summarization fallback tasks; annotators contribute subset. Rewrite model improves fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, turn count, role structure, final-probe conditions.

Probing: V4N persuasion intensity has 3 standardized conditions: C8R Simple = neutral direct retrieval; Z2F Medium = contextual justification; L9W Hard = urgent/high-pressure elicitation. D7A=d counts turns between disclosure and final probe. Sampling: d=0 with p=.2; otherwise Uniform{2,3,4,5,6} with p=.8. Immediate recall included; short-to-medium drift emphasized.

Evaluation: H8D=hybrid composite detector positive if normalized inclusion succeeds or judge finds full secret, substantial substring, or sufficient partial identifying info. B6T/U3P Stage 1 normalization-based/regex-only matching: numeric strips non-digits; alphanumeric normalizes case/whitespace but keeps meaningful delimiters; Leak_U3P=I[phi(S) subset phi(R)]. Stage 2 open-weights Llama judge receives S,R for deterministic negatives; binary full/substantial disclosure verdict; judge errors possible. U3P regex-only baseline separately reported alongside H8D.

K2V = Privacy Half-Life tau. Observed lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d). Threshold delta=0.1*L(0). tau=min d in D_obs such that L(d)<=delta and all later observed d’>d also <=delta. If none, tau=max(D_obs)+1. Stable/sustained suppression required, not transient decrease.

Rewrite model improves fluency/persona realism while preserving exact secret, turn count, role structure, final-probe conditions.

K2V = Privacy Half-Life tau. Observed lengths D_obs and leakage rates L(d). Threshold delta=0.1*L(0). tau=min d in D_obs such that L(d)<=delta and all later observed d’>d also <=delta. Experimental setup: All systems receive identical histories/probe templates via OpenRouter API. Each system processes full QX2 dataset: one seeded secret and one sampled d per dialogue, under every standardized V4N condition. Cached responses: 3,000 per model, 9,000 all evaluated models (implies 3 models). Aggregation: G4P any-probe dialogue-level leakage = dialogue positive if at least one standardized probe elicits secret; P6S probe-level leakage = one observation per dialogue per persuasion condition for V4N/R5J analyses. G4P can exceed mean condition-specific rate. Uncertainty/tests: G4P 95% bootstrap over dialogues; P6S sensitivity uses cached model-probe responses. Matched model/detector comparisons use McNemar, Bonferroni where applicable; repeated persuasion uses Cochran’s Q then McNemar. Independence leakage vs D7A/V4N/S8Q uses chi-square; X2H=Cramer’s V effect size, not substitute for significance.

Framework: user discloses secret S at turn t0; then d unrelated content-dense drift turns; standardized probe P appended; leakage if response reveals S exactly, approximately, or semantically. Behavioral re-disclosure, not raw transcript visibility.

Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability / Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation” by Ajay Pravin Mahale, dated 12 Aug 2026. Core: EU AI Act documentation/explanation requirements; circuit discovery as evidence source. Standard: second analyst using same system/tool should file compatible statement. Authors do not propose better circuit discovery or say interpretability worthless; argue current evidence fails filing standard.

Methods/definitions: Earlier text says pre-registered crossed multiverse over 7 analytic axes, but formal tuple s=(o,a,d,m,τ,P,r,g) has 8 axes incl granularity. φ deterministically maps discovered circuits to Annex IV claims; pre-registered code, not LLM. Model/task: GPT-2 small on IOI. §6 grid: 7 objectives, 7 ablation ops, 4 corruptions nested within 5 operators that read them, 4 metrics, 3 thresholds, 2 prompts, 5 seeds = 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specs pre-registered. One objective fails: 220 cells runtime error; realised grid = 6 objectives, 1,320 cells, 15,840 specs. Internal inconsistency: one part called “Total pre-registered specifications: 15,840,” conflicting with §6’s 18,480 pre-registered / 15,840 realised. Surviving pool: 7,561 specs producing claims. Seed selects prompt/evaluation-set variability, not nondeterminism. Four metrics total. Table 2 discard: comprehensiveness 3947/13/.003; KL 1467/2493/.630; logit diff 1270/2690/.679; sufficiency 877/3083/.779. Table 4 class proportions: early distributed .4109, late sparse .2848, late moderate .0869, late distributed .0647, early sparse .0631, middle moderate .0374, middle sparse .0356, middle distributed .0119, early moderate .0048. Paper title: “Explanation Multiplicity: Circuit-Level Interpretability / Evidence Does Not Survive Defensible Analytic Variation” by Ajay Pravin Mahale, dated 12 Aug 2026.

Abstract key setup: EU AI Act high-risk systems require technical documentation explaining decisions. Mechanistic interpretability/circuit discovery framed as evidence source. Each discovered circuit mapped through deterministic claim map to structured Annex IV statement. Model/task: GPT-2 small on indirect object identification (IOI). Main abstract results: derived statement flips across 73.2% of specification pairs, 95% CI 0.725–0.738. Modal claim commands 41.1% of the space. Evidence fails a filability criterion at every tolerance a conformity assessment body would plausibly accept.
