Section 8 Dropout RBMs: joint uses a hidden bias, b visible bias; internal error found: conditionals swap biases. Section 9: Gaussian dropout Table 10: MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04, Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR-10 Bernoulli 12.6±0.1, Gaussian 12.5±0.1. Conclusion: dropout increases training time 2–3×. Appendix heuristics: wider layers, LR 10–100×, momentum 0.95–0.99, max-norm c 3–4, hidden p 0.5–0.8, real input p≈0.8.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The dimensionality entry says “65536” while the parenthetical description says “256 × 256 color.”
errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 image has 65,536 pixels only if it is single-channel; a color image would have three channels, i.e. 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions. The number and description in the same table conflict.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained network, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network. The 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline in Table 7 is 20.7%, so the prose comparison misstates the baseline.

errors.claim: The conditional hidden distribution uses P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i), and the visible conditional uses P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + ∑_j W_ij h_j).
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where a is multiplied by h and b is multiplied by v.
errors.explanation: Given the joint distribution, a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The conditionals swap these biases: hidden units should use a_j, and visible units should use b_i.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 2014. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by retention p (T6R) to approximate averaging/geometric mean. Internal issue: exact claim that every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear activations/approximate averaging.

Methods/practical guide: gates r~Bernoulli(p); backprop through sampled subnetwork; mask per case/minibatch. Input dropout often p=.8, hidden commonly p=.5; Appendix: hidden typical p=.5–.8, real-valued/image/speech inputs typically p=.8, input optimum closer to 1 than .5. For optimal standard-net layer size n, good dropout layer at least n/p units. Dropout LR typically 10–100× standard; standard momentum .9, dropout .95–.99. V9C/max-norm bounds incoming weights, typical c=3–4. Pretraining unchanged; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p.

§6 claims dropout improves over non-dropout on every tested dataset: MNIST/H4Z, TIMIT/N8Q, CIFAR-10/J3V, CIFAR-100/W6R, SVHN/A2F, ImageNet/K9D, Reuters/M5X, Alternative Splicing/Z7P. Table 1: K9D listed 65536 “256×256 color” (conflict: color 256×256 should be 196608). Results: H4Z best dropout 0.79. A2F best ConvNet+L8J 2.47. J3V/W6R ConvNet+L8J 11.68/38.57. K9D 2012 Avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. N8Q Table 7: G6W-pretrained 8 layers 20.7; mcRBM-G6W 5 layers 20.5; G6W-pretrained+dropout 4/8 layers both 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout error 20.5 but table says 20.7. M5X best NN no dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Z7P bits higher better: NN+dropout 567 vs Bayesian NN 623. Table 9 dropout+V9C 1.05 best listed.

§7: H4Z autoencoder 256 F3N: dropout p=.5 learns edges/strokes/spots vs no dropout co-adapted. Dropout yields sparsity mean activations ~0.7 vs 2.0. Retention: fixed architecture underfits at low p; flat .4≤p≤.8; p=.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected width 1.7%; best near .6, default .5 near optimal. Data size: two smallest H4Z subsets show no dropout improvement. X9M averaging matches T6R around k=50 and slightly better within one SD; Appendix B.1 says X9M samples k thinned nets per test case and as k→∞ approaches true model average.

§8 B8T/dropout RBM: mixture over hidden subsets; r_j~Bernoulli(p), dropped h_j forced 0 by g. Ordinary RBM joint exp(v^TWh + a^T h + b^T v), so a=hidden bias, b=visible bias. Internal error in §8.1: conditionals written with swapped biases. CD-1 with sampled r. B8T p=.5 coarser/fewer dead units; sparser.

§9–10: Marginalized input dropout linear regression objective ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||²; with wtilde=pw penalty coefficient (1-p)/p. Gaussian dropout/D4K uses multiplier N(1,σ²), σ²=(1-p)/p; no test scaling. Table 10 D4K slightly better than P7V on H4Z/J3V.

§11 conclusion: claims QX2 SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z; training typically 2–3× standard same architecture; gradients noisy/not gradients of final inference architecture.

Appendix: H4Z validation 10k, endpoint 1M updates; sweep 2/3/4 layers ×1024/2048, hidden p=.5 input p=.8, momentum .95, V9C c=2. A2F/J3V/W6R conv settings retained p=(.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), V9C c=4, momentum .95. N8Q: 21-frame windows, input p=.8 hidden p=.5, V9C c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1 decay ε0(1+t/T)^-1, G6W pretraining U2L CD-1, Gaussian-U2L input variance fixed 1, best dropout G6W-finetune LR ~.01, V9C during finetuning no improvement. M5X subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 disjoint classes, equal train/test (>200k train). Z7P: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, four tissue types; C4Y formula; dropout net two 1024-unit layers, hidden p=.5 input p=.7, V9C/high decaying LRs, same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958, submitted 11/13, published 6/14. Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Univ. of Toronto. Editor: Yoshua Bengio.

Abstract claims: Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates averaged predictions. Dropout substantially reduces overfitting and gives major improvements; experiments in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology achieve state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Abstract/Intro key claims: Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. Test time uses one unthinned network with reduced/scaled weights to approximate averaged predictions; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. New thinned network sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any specific member rarely/never trained. Dropout claimed to lower generalization error vs other regularizers across varied classification tasks, with major improvements/state-of-art in vision, speech, document classification, biology. Extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models incl. Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than current individual fitness; reduces complex co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness solution. Conspiracy analogy: multiple smaller co-adaptations more likely robust than one large one.

§3 related work (current): Dropout/noise in hidden-unit states gives regularization interpretation extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010), which use input corruption and clean-input reconstruction. Dropout differs/extends via effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging interpretation, supervised + unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron architectures incl. Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling permits higher noise than usually best for DAEs. Reported noise levels: DAEs typical best 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; dropout often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution minimizes expected loss; adversarial feature-removal alternatives Globerson & Roweis 2006 and Dekel et al. 2010 choose removals subject to fixed max number, not probability distribution, and have no hidden units. Analytical marginalization of dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise regularizers incl. dropout as “blankout noise” investigated by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to models without hidden layers. Chen et al. 2012 marginalized denoising autoencoders; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden outputs, e.g. “Any activation f is admissible, including f(x)=1/(1+exp(-x)),” and test-time computation by scaled weights: “At inference, no units are removed and W_test^(l)=p W^(l).”
errors.explanation: With nonlinear activations such as sigmoid, the expected output under random dropout masks is generally E[f(W(r*y)+b)], which is not equal to f(pWy+b). The scaling makes expected inputs/preactivations match in simple cases, not every hidden unit’s expected nonlinear output.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/p, matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 equations define dropout with nonlinear units: z_i = w_i(r*y)+b and y_i=f(z_i), with f allowed to be sigmoid. The earlier noted inference rule scales weights by p, which matches expected inputs/preactivations, not generally expected post-nonlinear outputs: E[f(W(r*y)+b)] generally differs from f(pWy+b).
errors.explanation: Multiplying pretrained weights by 1/p makes the expected preactivation under Bernoulli masking match the pretrained preactivation, but for nonlinear units it does not generally make the expected unit output match the pretraining output. This repeats/extends the earlier internal inconsistency between exact “expected output” claims and the nonlinear dropout equations.

errors.claim: K9D (ILSVRC-2012) dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image has three color channels, so the dimensionality implied by the parenthetical is 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608, not 65,536.
errors.explanation: The numeric dimensionality conflicts with the stated image size and color format in the same table. 65,536 would correspond to 256 × 256 grayscale, not color.

errors.claim: “L8J substitution further reduces error” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports “Conv Net + max pooling + QX2 in all layers” as 12.61 on J3V and 37.20 on W6R, while “Conv Net + L8J” is 11.68 on J3V and 38.57 on W6R.
errors.explanation: L8J reduces J3V error from 12.61 to 11.68, but increases W6R error from 37.20 to 38.57. The prose overstates the improvement as applying generally.

errors.claim: Prose comparison: the 8-layer net had a pre-QX2 error of 20.5%.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% figure belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained NN. The 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline in the table is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2 on Z7P, while QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 lists “Neural Network with QX2 | 567” and “Bayesian Neural Network | 623,” with the text stating higher C4Y values are preferred.
errors.explanation: If Bayesian neural nets outperform QX2, then QX2 does not exceed every other method in Table 8. The claim is only consistent if “every other method” excludes the Bayesian neural network, but it does not say that.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)”
errors.evidence: The joint distribution is defined as \(\exp(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+\mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+\mathbf b^\top\mathbf v)\), so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the biases: hidden units should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), while visible units should use the visible bias \(b_i\). As written, the formulas conflict with the paper’s own joint distribution and parameter dimensions.

errors.claim: “QX2 methods achieve state of the art on A2F, K9D, W6R and H4Z”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes on Alternative Splicing: “Table 8 higher better: early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. Internal ambiguity/error: text says Bayesian nets outperform dropout but dropout exceeds every other method, although Bayesian is higher.”
errors.explanation: If A2F refers to the Alternative Splicing dataset, the paper’s own reported table shows Bayesian NN scoring 623, higher than NN+dropout’s 567, so dropout is not state of the art there.

Paper: JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958, “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting.” Dropout/QX2 trains random thinned nets with Bernoulli masks; test uses full net with weights scaled by p as approximate averaging/geometric mean. Prior internal issues: scaled test/pretraining output-matching rationale is false for nonlinear units except at preactivation/input level.

§6 setup claims dropout improves over non-dropout NNs on every dataset. Dataset sizes include ImageNet as 65536 “256×256 color” (inconsistent: 256×256 color implies 196608). Vision results: MNIST best DBM+dropout 0.79; SVHN dropout all layers/maxout 2.55/2.47; CIFAR dropout all layers 12.61/37.20, maxout 11.68/38.57. Internal error: prose says maxout further reduces CIFAR error, but CIFAR-100 worsens vs dropout all layers. ImageNet dropout convnets ~16% top-5. TIMIT Table 7: pretrained 8 layers 20.7; mcRBM 5 layers 20.5; pretrained 4 or 8 + dropout 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout is 20.5. Reuters/M5X: subset 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 categories, equal train/test >200k train examples; NN 31.05 vs dropout 29.62. Alternative Splicing/Z7P: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue softmaxes with inc/exc/nc states, C4Y metric; Table 8 higher better: early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN+dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. Internal ambiguity/error: text says Bayesian nets outperform dropout but dropout exceeds every other method, although Bayesian is higher. §11 claims QX2 achieves SOTA on A2F, K9D, W6R, H4Z; conflicts with K9D/Z7P table where Bayesian NN 623 > dropout 567.

§7: QX2 autoencoder features more meaningful/localized; induces sparsity hidden mean ~0.7 vs no-QX2 ~2.0. Retention p: fixed architecture underfits at low p; error flat 0.4≤p≤0.8, rises near p=1; fixed expected retained width helps at p=0.1. Dataset size: two smallest MNIST/H4Z subsets no QX2 improvement; gain rises then falls. X9M matches standard after ~50 samples then slightly better within one SD.

§8 RBM dropout: dropped h_j forced 0; CD-1. Joint uses exp(vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv), so a hidden biases, b visible biases. Internal error §8.1: conditional formulas swap biases. RBM dropout features coarser/fewer dead units/sparser.

§9–10: marginalized linear regression dropout gives ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||²; with w~=p w penalty (1-p)/p. Gaussian dropout matched to Bernoulli moments; Table 10 Gaussian slightly better than Bernoulli on H4Z/J3V. Inverted form mean activations unchanged/no test scaling.

Appendix: layer ≥n/p units if standard net has n; dropout LR 10–100× standard, momentum 0.95–0.99, max-norm c 3–4. H4Z/MNIST validation 10k, endpoint 1M updates, p hidden .5 input .8. A2F/SVHN validation 6000; conv filters 96/128/256; retentions (.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5). J3V/W6R CIFAR 50k/10k, 5k validation then combined. N8Q/TIMIT: 680 speakers; 21-frame windows, input p=.8 hidden p=.5, c=4, momentum .95, high LR .1, decay ε0(1+t/T)^-1, RBM pretraining CD-1, Gaussian-RBM input variance fixed 1, best dropout RBM-finetune LR ~.01; max-norm during RBM finetune no improvement.

Abstract: dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, samples exponentially many shared-parameter thinned nets, reduces co-adaptation; at test time a single unthinned net with reduced/scaled weights approximates averaged predictions; reduces overfitting and improves supervised vision, speech, document classification, computational biology, often SOTA.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is best regularization for fixed model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing models’ predictions. An n-unit network represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer parameters; each presentation of each training case samples/trains a new thinned member, so any particular member is trained rarely/never. Motivation: nonlinear nets overfit limited-data noise; standard regularizers include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties. Model combination usually helps but separately training many large nets is costly and inference by averaging many nets is too slow; diversity requires different architectures/training data and lots of compute/data. Practical inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of evaluating exponentially many members; MC model averaging over sampled thinned nets is a more expensive alternative. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout can extend beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines; Restricted Boltzmann Machines admit a Dropout RBM variant.

§2 Motivation: Biological analogy. Sexual reproduction seems disadvantageous for preserving complex co-adapted gene sets because recombination can break them, whereas asexual reproduction preserves them; nevertheless advanced organisms mostly evolved sexually. Livnat et al. (2010) explanation: long-run selection may favor genes’ ability to work with random partners (“mix-ability”) over immediate individual fitness; this discourages large fragile co-adaptations and lowers barriers for useful new genes. Paper analogizes dropout-trained hidden units to genes: because each unit must work with randomly selected partners, it should learn independently useful robust features rather than depend on other hidden units to fix its errors, though units in a layer still learn different functions. Replicating each unit many times is rejected as a poor robustness solution, like replica codes for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: many small conspiracies are more robust under non-stationarity than one large 50-person conspiracy; complex co-adaptations may fit training data but fail on novel test data more readily than multiple simpler co-adaptations.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014), Srivastava et al.

Core dropout: train by independently retaining units with probability p; fresh thinned net per case; backprop only through sampled subnetwork. Test approximation: full net with outgoing weights multiplied by p, W_test^(l)=pW^(l), approximating model average/geometric mean. “Inverted dropout”: multiply retained activations by 1/p at train time, no test scaling; pretrained weights scaled by 1/p before dropout.

Key results/internal issues: MNIST best permutation-invariant DBM+dropout 0.79; p=0.5 hidden, p=0.8 input. SVHN Table 3: Conv Net+max-pooling 3.95; +dropout FC 3.02; stochastic pooling 2.80; +dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47. Possible internal issue: text says non-dropout conv nets best 3.95, but table has stochastic pooling 2.80 apparently no dropout. CIFAR Table 4: dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet: Conv Net+dropout ILSVRC-2010 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout test top-5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7: NN 23.4; dropout NN 21.8; DBN-pretrained 8-layer baseline 20.7; mcRBM-DBN 20.5; DBN-pretrained+dropout 4/8 both 19.7. Internal error: text says 8-layer reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but table’s 8-layer baseline is 20.7; 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM. Reuters: NN 31.05; dropout 29.62; internal arithmetic error: text calls 14.3% relative reduction, actually ~4.6%. Alt Splicing Table 8 Code Quality: NN dropout 567, Bayesian NN 623. Table 9 MNIST regularizers: Dropout+Max-norm 1.05 lowest.

Sec 7–10/conclusion: MNIST autoencoders with dropout p=0.5 similar reconstruction but more meaningful/sparser features. Fixed 784-2048-2048-2048-10, no input dropout, best p broad 0.4–0.8; keeping pn fixed helps small p, best near p=0.6. Data-size MNIST: dropout no help for 100/500, gain rises then declines. MC model averaging: k≈50 sampled nets matches weight scaling; larger k slightly better within one SD. Dropout RBM: hidden masks Bernoulli(p), dropped hidden units 0; CD-1. Internal formula inconsistency: RBM conditionals swap a/b biases versus energy definition. Marginalized dropout linear regression gives L2-like regularizer ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||². Gaussian dropout N(1,σ²), no test scaling; match Bernoulli inverted variance σ²=(1-p)/p. Table 10: Gaussian slightly better than Bernoulli on MNIST/CIFAR. Conclusion claims dropout improves object/digit/speech/document/biology tasks and SOTA on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST; drawback training 2–3× longer.

Model combination usually improves performance, but averaging many separately trained large nets is too expensive; diversity would require different architectures or training data subsets, both difficult/costly, and test-time use of many large nets can be infeasible.

Dropout is presented as addressing overfitting and efficient approximate combination of exponentially many architectures. “Dropout” means temporarily removing units (hidden and visible) plus incoming/outgoing connections. Each unit retained independently with fixed probability p; p can be validated or set to 0.5, said close to optimal for many networks/tasks. For input units, optimal retention probability is usually closer to 1 than 0.5.

Figure 1: standard neural net with 2 hidden layers and example thinned net after applying dropout; crossed units dropped.

Figure 2: At training, a unit is present with probability p and connected to next-layer units with weights w. At test, unit always present and weights are multiplied by p; caption states test-time output is the same as expected output at training time.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958), authors Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims so far: Dropout addresses overfitting in large deep nets by randomly dropping units (hidden and visible) and their incoming/outgoing connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p can be validated or set to 0.5, said close to optimal for many networks/tasks; for input units optimal p is usually closer to 1. Training samples from an exponential number of “thinned” networks with shared weights; a net with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned nets. Total parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. For each presentation of each training case, a new thinned net is sampled and trained, so each thinned net is trained rarely if at all.

Test-time approximation: Explicitly averaging exponentially many thinned models is infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit was retained with probability p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time (Figure 2). This is said to make any hidden unit’s expected output under training-time dropout equal to its actual output at test time, and approximates combining 2^n shared-weight networks into one. Abstract/introduction characterize this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean / model averaging; Figure 2 caption similarly says test-time output is same as expected training-time output.

Motivation/context: Deep nets with multiple nonlinear hidden layers are expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing anti-overfitting methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Ideal Bayesian averaging over all parameter settings is too expensive except small/simple models. Model combination improves performance but training/testing many large nets is costly; diversity by different architectures/data subsets is difficult.

Claims of results: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging yields significantly lower generalization error across many classification problems vs other regularization methods. Abstract claims improvements in vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art on many benchmarks.

Scope/structure: Dropout is not limited to feed-forward nets; can apply to graphical models such as Boltzmann Machines. Training algorithm Sec. 5.1: Train with SGD like standard nets; for each training case in a mini-batch sample a thinned network by dropping units. Forward/backprop only on that thinned net. grade.reason: The reviewer's fourth reported error directly identifies the claimed 14.3% relative reduction as arithmetically inconsistent with the reported 31.05% and 29.62% error rates (actual ~4.6% reduction).

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The dimensionality entry says “65536” while the parenthetical description says “256 × 256 color.”
errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 image has 65,536 pixels only if it is single-channel; a color image would have three channels, i.e. 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions. The number and description in the same table conflict.

errors.claim: “Bag-of-words document classification on a subset of M5X improves with QX2 by a 14.3% relative reduction.”
errors.evidence: The same part reports error rates: “Without QX2 | 31.05%” and “With QX2 | 29.62%.”
errors.explanation: The relative reduction from 31.05% to 29.62% is (31.05−29.62)/31.05 ≈ 4.6%, not 14.3%.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) … 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) … 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-QX2 error belongs to a 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained network, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network, which is listed as 20.7%.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\, \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right)”
errors.evidence: The same section defines the joint exponent as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: The conditional distributions swap the biases: hidden-unit probabilities should use the hidden bias \(a_j\), while visible-unit probabilities should use the visible bias \(b_i\), according to the joint distribution just given.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 1 in the notes lists “CIFAR/J3V 3072 train 60K test 10K.”
errors.explanation: The appendix says J3V has 50,000 training images, while the earlier dataset table recorded 60,000 training images for J3V/CIFAR. These cannot both be the stated training-set size.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 2014. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by p/T6R to approximate model averaging/geometric mean. Prior internal issue: exact claim every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear activations/approximate averaging. Inverted dropout retained activations ×1/p during training and unchanged test weights equivalent to standard retention+test scaling with rescaled layerwise LRs/inits.

Methods/practical guide: input dropout often 20%, hidden 50%; high momentum, large decaying LR, V9C max-norm. Pretraining unchanged; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p. §1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than current individual fitness; reduces complex co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

Logistic/deep nets: closed-form marginalization difficult; Gaussian approximations for logistic inputs/gradients; assumptions weaken with layers, not directly applicable to deep nets.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The dimensionality entry says “65536” while the parenthetical description says “256 × 256 color.”
errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 image has 65,536 pixels only if it is single-channel; a color image would have three channels, i.e. 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions. The number and description in the same table conflict.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained network, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network. The 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline in Table 7 is 20.7%, so the prose comparison misstates the baseline.

errors.claim: The conditional hidden distribution uses P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i), and the visible conditional uses P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + ∑_j W_ij h_j).
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where a is multiplied by h and b is multiplied by v.
errors.explanation: Given the joint distribution, a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The conditionals swap these biases: hidden units should use a_j, and visible units should use b_i.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 2014. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by retention p (T6R) to approximate averaging/geometric mean. Prior internal issue: exact claim that every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear activations/approximate averaging.

Practical guide: masks r~Bernoulli(p); backprop sampled subnetwork. Input dropout often p=.8, hidden commonly p=.5; Appendix says hidden typical p=.5–.8, real-valued inputs/image patches/speech frames p=.8, default p=.5, input optimum closer to 1 than .5. For layer whose optimal standard-net size is n, dropout layer should have at least n/p units. Dropout LR typically 10–100× standard LR; standard momentum .9, dropout .95–.99. V9C/max-norm typical c=3–4. Pretraining unchanged; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p.

§6 results: claims dropout improves over non-dropout on every tested dataset: MNIST/H4Z, TIMIT/N8Q, CIFAR-10/J3V, CIFAR-100/W6R, SVHN/A2F, ImageNet/K9D, Reuters/M5X, Alternative Splicing/Z7P. Retention: fixed architecture underfits low p; flat 0.4≤p≤0.8; p=.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected width 1.7%; best near .6, default .5 near optimal. Abstract claims: Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates averaged predictions. Dropout substantially reduces overfitting and gives major improvements; experiments in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology achieve state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: The conditional hidden distribution uses P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i), and the visible conditional uses P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + ∑_j W_ij h_j).
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where a is multiplied by h and b is multiplied by v.
errors.explanation: Given the joint distribution, a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The conditionals swap these biases: hidden units should use a_j, and visible units should use b_i.

Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by retention p (T6R) to approximate averaging/geometric mean. Prior internal issue: exact claim that every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear activations/approximate averaging.

Methods: gates r~Bernoulli(p); backprop through sampled subnetwork; input dropout often 20%, hidden 50%. W_test=pW. Mini-batch cases have own sampled net. Works best with high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm V9C. Pretraining unchanged; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p.

§6 datasets: claims dropout improves over non-dropout on every tested dataset: MNIST/H4Z, TIMIT/N8Q, CIFAR-10/J3V, CIFAR-100/W6R, SVHN/A2F, ImageNet/K9D, Reuters/M5X, Alternative Splicing/Z7P. Table 1: K9D listed 65536 “256×256 color” (conflict: color 256×256 should be 196608). Results: MNIST best dropout 0.79. SVHN best ConvNet+L8J 2.47. CIFAR ConvNet+L8J 11.68/38.57. ImageNet 2012 Avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7: G6W-pretrained 8 layers 20.7; mcRBM-G6W 5 layers 20.5; G6W-pretrained+dropout 4/8 layers both 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-QX2 error 20.5 but table says 20.7. Reuters best NN no dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Alternative Splicing bits higher better: NN+dropout 567 vs Bayesian NN 623. Table 9 standard regularizers: dropout+V9C 1.05 best listed.

§7: Autoencoder 256 F3N units: dropout p=.5 learns edges/strokes/spots vs no dropout co-adapted. Dropout yields sparsity: mean activations about 0.7 vs 2.0. Retention: fixed architecture underfits at low p; flat 0.4≤p≤0.8; p=.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected width 1.7%; best near .6, default .5 near optimal. Data size: two smallest MNIST subsets show no dropout improvement. X9M averaging matches T6R around k=50 and slightly better within one SD; T6R good approximation.

§8 B8T/dropout RBM: mixture over hidden subsets; r_j~Bernoulli(p), dropped h_j forced 0 by g. Joint ordinary U2L/RBM defined exp(v^TWh + a^T h + b^T v), so a=hidden bias, b=visible bias. Internal error in §8.1: conditionals written with swapped biases (hidden uses b_j, visible uses a_i). Learning: sample r, train retained hidden units, different r per case, CD-1. Features: B8T p=.5 coarser than ordinary U2L, fewer dead units. Sparsity: B8T without extra sparsity regularizer learns much sparser representations; Fig13 many near-zero/few high activations vs U2L many away from zero.

§9 Marginalizing QX2: deterministic marginalized models need no random bits and allow gradients. For linear regression, marginalizing input dropout gives objective E||y-(R*X)w||² = ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||², Γ=(diag(XᵀX))^{1/2}. With wtilde=pw, equivalent penalty coefficient is (1-p)/p on ||Γ wtilde||²: smaller near p=1, larger for more deletion. Logistic/deep nets: exact closed forms hard; Wang/Manning approximate Gaussian marginalization improves logistic regression, assumptions weaken in deeper layers and not directly applicable to deep nets.

grade.reason: None of the reported errors mention the MNIST training/validation recombination or the incorrect 55,000 vs 60,000 image count, so the planted error was not identified.

errors.claim: “The weights obtained from pretraining should be scaled up by a factor of 1/(1-p). This makes sure that for each unit, the expected output from it under random dropout will be the same as the output during pretraining.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Sec. 4 definition in notes: “Each unit retained independently with probability p”; “r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p)”; and test-time scaling uses “W_test^(l)=p W^(l)” so a hidden unit’s expected output under dropout matches the deterministic output.
errors.explanation: If p is the retention probability as formally defined earlier, scaling pretrained weights by 1/(1-p) would make expected output p/(1-p) times the pretrained output, not equal to it. The factor needed would be 1/p. This part appears to use p as the drop probability, conflicting with the earlier formal definition.

errors.claim: ImageNet dimensionality is “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: For other color image datasets, the table uses 3072 for “32 × 32 color,” which equals 32×32×3. But 256×256 color would be 256×256×3 = 196608, not 65536.
errors.explanation: Within the table’s own dimensionality convention for color images, ImageNet’s listed dimensionality omits the color channels or mismatches the parenthetical description.

errors.claim: “Similarly, for an 8-layer net the error reduces from 20.5% to 19.7%.”
errors.location: this part, Sec. 6.2 Results on TIMIT
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “DBN-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010)” with phone error rate 20.7, while 20.5 belongs to “mcRBM-DBN-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The text says the 8-layer pretrained net starts at 20.5%, but the table says the 8-layer pretrained net is 20.7%; 20.5% is a different 5-layer mcRBM-DBN model.

errors.claim: “P(hj = 1|rj, v) = 1(rj = 1) σ(bj + ∑i Wij vi)” and “P(vi = 1|h) = σ(ai + ∑j Wij hj)”
errors.evidence: The same section defines the RBM energy/probability term as “exp(vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv)” and states “θ = {W, a, b}”; thus a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the earlier definition in the same section, the hidden conditional should use hidden bias a_j, and the visible conditional should use visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, creating an internal inconsistency.

errors.claim: “We created a subset of this data set consisting of 402,738 articles ... comprising of 50 categories”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record Reuters as an “800K subset, 50 topics.” This part says the full corpus contains more than 800,000 documents, but the actual subset used contains 402,738 articles.
errors.explanation: If the earlier reported Reuters experimental dataset/subset size was about 800K, it conflicts with Appendix B.5’s statement that the constructed subset used for experiments has 402,738 articles.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Dropout randomly drops units during training. Formal Sec. 4: r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), p=retention probability; test time no dropout, use W_test=pW. Input optimal p closer to 1; hidden often ~0.5. Sec. 5.2 says pretrained weights scaled by 1/(1-p) so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output; conflicts with p=retention probability, which would require 1/p.

Experiments intro: dropout improved generalization on all datasets. Table 1 datasets include ImageNet dimension 65536 (256×256 color), inconsistent with color convention. Key results: MNIST best DBM+dropout 0.79; maxout dropout+max-norm 0.94. Regularizer comparison MNIST ReLU 784-1024-1024-2048-10: max-norm 1.35, dropout+L2 1.25, dropout+max-norm 1.05. SVHN: no-dropout conv 3.95; dropout fc 3.02; all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47. CIFAR: dropout fc 14.32/41.26; all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 conv nets val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4. TIMIT inconsistency: text says 8-layer reduces 20.5 to 19.7, but Table 7 says 8-layer DBN pretrained 20.7; 20.5 is mcRBM-DBN 5-layer. Reuters inconsistency: earlier notes indicate Reuters subset about 800K/50 topics, but Appendix B.5 says full RCV1 corpus >800,000 docs/103 classes and constructed subset is 402,738 articles, 2000-word vocab, 50 categories, split equally train/test. Reuters errors: no-dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62. Alt Splicing bits: dropout NN 567, Bayesian NN 623.

Sec. 7: dropout features more localized; sparse activations. Fixed architecture p: error flat 0.4≤p≤0.8; keeping pn fixed improves small-p; p≈0.6 best. Data-size MNIST: no improvement 100/500, gain grows then declines. MC averaging: k≈50 matches weight scaling; MC later slightly better within one SD.

Sec. 8 RBM: P(h,v)=1/Z exp(vᵀWh+aᵀh+bᵀv), so a hidden bias, b visible bias. Sec. 8.1 conditionals swap a/b. Sec. 9/10: marginalizing dropout linear regression gives ||y-pXw||² + p(1-p)||Γw||²; with w~=pw, regularization constant (1-p)/p. Gaussian dropout multiply by N(1,σ²), no test scaling; Bernoulli train scaling rb=1/p w.p. p else 0, variance (1-p)/p.

Conclusion/App A: claims state-of-art on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST. Typically 2–3× longer to train. Heuristics: dropout layer at least n/p units; hidden p 0.5–0.8, real input p≈0.8.

Appendix B: MNIST details as noted. SVHN: approx 600k train/26k test; p=(0.9,0.75,0.75,0.5,0.5,0.5). CIFAR: 50k/10k, 5k validation recombined; architecture/dropout same as SVHN except smaller input-layer LR. TIMIT Appendix: p input .8 hidden .5; c=4; momentum .95 LR .1; DBN finetune dropout LR ~.01, max-norm no improvement. Core claims: Dropout prevents overfitting by randomly dropping units (hidden and visible/input) and their incoming/outgoing connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p can be validated or set to 0.5, close to optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit optimal p usually closer to 1. Related-work section states dropping 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units was often optimal. With n units there are 2^n possible thinned nets; parameters remain O(n^2) or less. For each training case presentation, a new thinned net is sampled, so each thinned net is rarely/never trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging is infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit was retained with probability p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time. Sec. 4 formalizes: at test time W_test^(l)=p W^(l), no dropout. This makes a hidden unit’s expected output under dropout equal to actual output at test time and approximates combining exponentially many shared-weight networks. Abstract/intro/Fig. 2 characterize this as approximate model averaging / equally weighted geometric mean.

Motivation/context: Deep nets overfit with limited data. Existing anti-overfitting methods include early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing. Bayesian averaging over all parameter settings is too expensive except small/simple models. Model combination helps but training/testing many large nets is costly. Sec. 2 motivates via sexual reproduction and “conspiracies”: units should be useful without relying on fragile co-adaptations. Hidden units will still learn different things; copying units is poor.

Related work: Dropout is like adding noise to hidden units. Denoising Autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free input; dropout extends this to hidden layers, supervised learning, and model averaging. DAE noise around 5% typically best, but dropout’s test-time weight scaling enables higher noise. Deterministic counterparts can be obtained by marginalizing noise in simple cases. van der Maaten et al. studied deterministic regularizers incl. blankout/dropout noise for inputs and no hidden layers; Wang & Manning speed up dropout by marginalizing noise; Chen et al. marginalization for DAEs. Globerson/Roweis and Dekel et al. considered adversarial dropped units with fixed maximum number, not hidden-unit models.

Formal model (Sec. 4): Standard net with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, z/y inputs/outputs, W/b weights/biases; feedforward z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)\tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Applied at each layer; derivatives backprop through sampled sub-network.

Results/scope claims: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging significantly lowers generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; state of the art on many benchmarks. Also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. Boltzmann Machines; later Sec. 8 compares dropout RBM with standard RBM. Paper structure includes Sec. 5 training algorithm, Sec. 6 experiments, Sec. 7 effects/hyperparameters, Sec. 8 RBM, Sec. 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guide.

errors.claim: “The weights obtained from pretraining should be scaled up by a factor of 1/(1-p). This makes sure that for each unit, the expected output from it under random dropout will be the same as the output during pretraining.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Sec. 4 definition in notes: “Each unit retained independently with probability p”; “r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p)”; and test-time scaling uses “W_test^(l)=p W^(l)” so a hidden unit’s expected output under dropout matches the deterministic output.
errors.explanation: If p is the retention probability as formally defined earlier, scaling pretrained weights by 1/(1-p) would make expected output p/(1-p) times the pretrained output, not equal to it. The factor needed would be 1/p. This part appears to use p as the drop probability, conflicting with the earlier formal definition.

steps.notes_before:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014). Core: dropout randomly drops units/connections during training to prevent co-adaptation. Formal Sec. 4: r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), where p is retention probability; thinned outputs r*y. Test time: no dropout, use W_test^(l)=p W^(l), approximating model averaging/geometric mean; expected output under dropout matches deterministic scaled network. Input optimal p closer to 1; hidden p often ~0.5; related work says dropping 20% input and 50% hidden often optimal.

Training Sec. 5.1: train with SGD like standard nets; for each training case in a minibatch sample a thinned network; forward/backprop only on that thinned net; cases not using a parameter contribute zero gradient for it. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 useful. Especially useful: max-norm regularization, constraining incoming weight vector to each hidden unit ||w||_2 ≤ c, implemented by projection to ball radius c; c tuned on validation. Dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum boosts performance over dropout alone; max-norm permits huge learning rates without blow-up, dropout noise explores, decay settles.

Sec. 5.2 unsupervised pretraining: nets can be pretrained with stacks of RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; then finetuned with dropout. Pretraining unchanged. It states pretrained weights should be scaled up by 1/(1-p) so expected output under dropout equals pretraining output. This conflicts with earlier formal p=retention probability, which would require scale 1/p; note for possible later clarification. Authors say high finetuning LRs wiped out pretrained info, smaller LRs retained it and improved generalization vs no dropout finetuning.

Experiments Sec. 6 intro: trained dropout neural nets for classification across domains; claims dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs non-dropout nets. Datasets listed: MNIST handwritten digits; TIMIT clean speech; CIFAR-10/100 tiny natural images; SVHN house number images; ImageNet natural images; Reuters-RCV1 newswire articles; Alternative Splicing RNA features for predicting alternative gene splicing. Purpose: show dropout is general, not domain-specific. Detailed descriptions/results in Appendix B.

errors.claim: “We created a subset of this data set consisting of 402,738 articles ... comprising of 50 categories”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record Reuters as an “800K subset, 50 topics.” This part says the full corpus contains more than 800,000 documents, but the actual subset used contains 402,738 articles.
errors.explanation: If the earlier reported Reuters experimental dataset/subset size was about 800K, it conflicts with Appendix B.5’s statement that the constructed subset used for experiments has 402,738 articles.

grade.reason: The reviewer's first reported error directly identifies the incorrect 1/(1-p) scaling and explains that with retention probability p the correct reciprocal is 1/p, matching the planted error's contradiction.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: “Before QX2 finetuning, pretrained weights are multiplied by 1/(1-p), matching each unit’s expected random-removal output to its pretraining output.”
errors.evidence: Earlier §4 defined dropout gates as r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), with a unit present with probability p; at testing outgoing weights are scaled to pW. Thus if pretrained weights W are used under dropout during finetuning, the expected contribution is pW, and matching the original pretrained output would require scaling weights by 1/p, not 1/(1-p).
errors.explanation: The claim uses 1/(1-p), treating 1-p as the retention probability, but the paper’s earlier definition makes p the retention probability. This contradicts the dropout notation and test-time scaling rule already stated.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right)” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L distribution is defined as exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, hidden conditionals should use the hidden bias a_j and visible conditionals should use the visible bias b_i. The displayed conditional equations swap a and b, and also imply mismatched dimensions when using b_j for hidden units and a_i for visible units.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014), Srivastava et al.

Core dropout: train by independently dropping units with retention p; fresh thinned net per case. Test: full net with outgoing weights multiplied by p, approximating model average/geometric mean. Equivalent inverted scaling: train-time scale by 1/p, no test scaling. p often 0.5 hidden, input closer to 1. Max-norm constrains incoming hidden weights ||w||≤c. Pretraining unchanged; scale pretrained weights up by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

Internal errors found earlier: ImageNet table 65536 conflicts with “256×256 color” if color means 3 channels. MNIST text says maxout “worsened” to 0.94 though lower/better than ReLU 0.95. SVHN text says 3.95 best non-dropout conv net but table has stochastic pooling 2.80. TIMIT text says 8-layer reduces from 20.5 to 19.7 but table says 8-layer baseline 20.7, while 20.5 is 5-layer mcRBM. Sec. 8 conditional equations swap biases, using bj for hidden and ai for visible despite definition a hidden, b visible.

Selected results: MNIST Table 2 dropout ReLU 1.25, ReLU+maxnorm 0.95, maxout 0.94, DBN+dropout 0.92, DBM+dropout 0.79. Table 9 same ReLU architecture: L2 1.62; L2+L1 1.60; L2+KL 1.55; max-norm 1.35; dropout+L2 1.25; dropout+max-norm 1.05. CIFAR best dropout all layers 12.61/37.20, maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet ILSVRC-2010 ConvNet+dropout 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. Reuters NN 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Alt splicing Code Quality: NN 440, regression PCA 463, SVM PCA 487, dropout NN 567, Bayesian NN 623.

Sec. 7/8/9: dropout reduces co-adaptation; hidden dropout p=0.5 gives edge/stroke-like autoencoder features and sparser activations. Dropout-rate MNIST best broad 0.4≤p≤0.8; default 0.5 close. Dataset-size gains peak at intermediate sizes; none for 100/500 cases. MC averaging over k dropout nets: k≈50 as good as weight scaling; more MC slightly better within one std. Dropout RBM: v∈{0,1}D, h∈{0,1}F, P∝exp(vᵀWh + aᵀh + bᵀv); rj~Bernoulli(p), dropped hj=0; CD-1. Linear regression input dropout gives ridge-like penalty (1-p)/p after rescaling. Formal model: Standard feedforward net y^(0)=x; z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then feeds forward/backprops only through sampled subnetwork.

Gradients averaged over cases; if a case does not use a parameter, it contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weight vector at each hidden unit ||w||_2 ≤ c; if w leaves ball radius c, project to surface; c tuned on validation. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm permits huge learning rates without weight blowup, dropout noise explores weight space, decay settles.

Pretraining Sec. 5.2: Nets can be pretrained with stacked RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining can exploit unlabeled data and improve over random init in some cases. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so expected unit output under dropout equals output during pretraining. Initially concern dropout would wipe pretrained info; it did when finetuning learning rates comparable to best random-init rates, but smaller learning rates retained info and improved final generalization vs no dropout during finetuning.

Results/scope: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging significantly lowers generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; state of the art on many benchmarks. Sec. 6 says trained dropout neural nets for classification on diverse domains and found dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout neural nets. Datasets listed: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Table 1 briefly describes datasets; Appendix B has detailed experiment/data descriptions. Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. Boltzmann Machines; Sec. 8 compares dropout RBM with standard RBM. Sec. 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide.

grade.reason: The reviewer's second reported error directly identifies the MNIST/maxout claim as wrong and cites Table 2 showing 0.95 for the largest ReLU versus 0.94 for maxout, demonstrating maxout is an improvement not a worsening.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: “Natural-image scale is represented by (K9D: ImageNet)” with dimensionality “65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: A 256 × 256 color image would have 256 × 256 × 3 = 196608 dimensions, not 65536; 65536 corresponds only to 256 × 256 grayscale/single-channel.
errors.explanation: The dimensionality stated in the same table conflicts with the parenthetical description of the image size and color channels.

errors.claim: “substitution of another activation class (L8J: maxout) worsens them”
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports “QX2 NN + V9C | F3N | 2 layers, 8192 units | 0.95” and then “QX2 NN + V9C (Goodfellow et al., 2013) | L8J | 2 layers, (5 × 240) units | 0.94.”
errors.explanation: On the paper’s own error metric, lower is better, and the maxout/L8J result 0.94 is better than the preceding F3N result 0.95, so it does not worsen the result shown in the table.

errors.claim: Prose comparison: “8-layer net” pre-QX2 error = 20.5%.
errors.location: this part, N8Q prose comparison table
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and lists 20.5 only for “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010).”
errors.explanation: The stated pre-dropout comparison for the 8-layer net uses 20.5%, but the 8-layer row in the table is 20.7%; 20.5% belongs to a different 5-layer mcRBM-pretrained model.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\,\sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).” and “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L/RBM distribution was defined just above as exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, conflicting with the preceding joint distribution and with their implied dimensions.

errors.claim: “Each collection contains 50,000 training and 10,000 test images” for J3V and W6R.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 1: “CIFAR 3072 60K/10K.”
errors.explanation: J3V/W6R are the two CIFAR collections, described here as 50,000 training images each, but the earlier dataset table recorded CIFAR as having 60,000 training images and 10,000 test images.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training; sampled thinned nets share weights; test usually uses unthinned net with weights scaled by p (approx averaging/geometric mean). New thinned net per case. Claimed broad gains across vision/speech/document/bio/RBMs.

§2–5: Dropout reduces co-adaptation; typical optimal input removal 20%, hidden removal 50%. Feedforward gates r~Bernoulli(p); backprop through sampled subnetwork. Internal issue: exact claim that each hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear equations/only approximate averaging. Training: high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm/V9C ||w||≤c; each mini-batch case has own sampled net. Pretraining unchanged; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p.

§6: dropout improves generalization over non-dropout nets on every tested dataset. Table 1: MNIST/H4Z 784 60K/10K; SVHN/A2F 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR/J3V+W6R 3072 60K/10K—conflicts with App B.3 saying J3V/W6R each 50K train/10K test; ImageNet 65536 (256×256 color), 1.2M/150K—internal dimensionality inconsistency with color. MNIST best DBM+dropout 0.79; issue: text says maxout worsens but table has maxout 0.94 better than ReLU 0.95. SVHN best maxout 2.47. CIFAR dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet avg 5 nets 16.4 top-5. TIMIT issue: prose says 8-layer pre-dropout 20.5 but table says 20.7; 20.5 is mcRBM. Reuters best 31.05 without, 29.62 with. Splicing: higher C4Y better; NN+dropout 567, Bayesian NN 623; text says BNN beats dropout, dropout beats all others. Regularizers on same MNIST F3N: best dropout+V9C 1.05.

§7–10: Dropout autoencoder features localized vs non-dropout co-adapted. Induces sparsity: hidden mean ~0.7 vs ~2.0. Retention MNIST: fixed architecture underfits at low p; flat 0.4≤p≤0.8; p=0.1 error fixed 2.7%, fixed expected width 1.7%; best ~p=0.6, default 0.5. Data-size: two smallest no dropout improvement; gain grows then shrinks. Sampling model average X9M matches scaled-weight T6R around 50 samples and slightly better within 1 std. Dropout RBM/B8T: mixture of shared-weight RBMs/U2L; each mini-batch case gets different r; CD-1. Internal issue: conditionals swap biases: hidden conditional uses b_j and visible uses a_i, conflicting with joint/dimensions. B8T p=.5 features coarser, few dead units, much sparser than U2L. Marginalizing dropout/QX2 linear regression gives ridge-like penalty ((1-p)/p)||Γw~||²; logistic/deep Gaussian approximations. Gaussian dropout matches Bernoulli mean/variance; H4Z P7V 1.08±0.04 vs D4K 0.95±0.04; J3V P7V 12.6±0.1 vs D4K 12.5±0.1; inverted dropout r_b=1/p w.p. p else 0.

§11/App: Training typically 2–3× standard net. Practical guide: dropout layer at least n/p units; LR 10–100×; momentum 0.95–0.99; V9C c 3–4 typical; hidden p 0.5–0.8, real-valued inputs/images/speech p≈0.8. A2F: validation 6000; conv 96/128/256 5×5, pool 3×3 stride2, FC 2048×2, F3N, retention (.9,.75,.75,.5,.5,.5), c=4. J3V/W6R: App says 50K train/10K test, 5K validation. Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958, submitted 11/13, published 6/14. Authors: Nitish Srivastava, Geoffrey Hinton, Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, Ruslan Salakhutdinov; Univ. of Toronto. Editor: Yoshua Bengio.

Abstract claims: Large, parameter-rich deep neural nets are powerful but suffer from overfitting; slow test-time use prevents easy combination of independently trained large models. Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units and their connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates the averaged predictions of these networks. Compared with other regularizers, dropout substantially reduces overfitting and gives major improvements; experiments in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology achieve state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks. §1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than current individual fitness; reduces complex co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

§5 learning dropout/QX2 nets: Dropout alone gives gains; further boost from high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight max-norm constraint (here labeled V9C). Max-norm: for incoming hidden-unit weight vector w impose ||w||_2 ≤ c; if outside radius-c ball, project to surface; c tuned on validation. Claimed max-norm often improves SGD even without dropout and was used in collaborative filtering. Optimization account: max-norm allows huge learning rates without explosion; dropout noise explores hard-to-reach regions; decaying rates reduce exploration toward minimum. SGD differs only by sampled thinned net per case: each mini-batch case has own sampled forward/backward network; gradients averaged; unused parameter gets zero contribution. Momentum, annealed rates, and Y5F remain useful.

§5.2 unsupervised pretraining: Pretraining itself unchanged. For dropout finetuning after pretraining, use smaller finetuning learning rates; rates as large as best random-init rates erased pretrained info in initial experiments. Before dropout finetuning, pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p to match expected random-removal output to pretraining output. Unlabeled pretraining can improve over random init in some cases; can use stacked U2L/DBNs, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs, all admitting dropout finetuning.
