errors.evidence: The ordinary U2L/RBM distribution was defined just above as exp( v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v ), so a is the hidden-unit bias vector and b is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the model definition, the hidden conditional should use the hidden bias a_j and the visible conditional should use the visible bias b_i. The displayed conditionals swap a and b, conflicting with the preceding joint distribution and with their implied dimensions.

Formal model: Standard feedforward net y^(0)=x; z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then feeds forward/backprops only through sampled subnetwork.

Training algorithm Sec. 5.1: Train with SGD like standard nets; for each training case in a mini-batch sample a thinned network by dropping units. Forward/backprop only on that thinned net. Gradients averaged over cases; if a case does not use a parameter, it contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weight vector at each hidden unit ||w||_2 ≤ c; if w leaves ball radius c, project to surface; c tuned on validation. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm permits huge learning rates without weight blowup, dropout noise explores weight space, decay settles.

Pretraining Sec. 5.2: Nets can be pretrained with stacked RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining can exploit unlabeled data and improve over random init in some cases. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so expected unit output under dropout equals output during pretraining. Initially concern dropout would wipe pretrained info; it did when finetuning learning rates comparable to best random-init rates, but smaller learning rates retained info and improved final generalization vs no dropout during finetuning.

Results/scope: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging significantly lowers generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; state of the art on many benchmarks. Sec. 6 says trained dropout neural nets for classification on diverse domains and found dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout neural nets. Datasets listed: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Table 1 briefly describes datasets; Appendix B has detailed experiment/data descriptions. grade.reason: The reviewer's fourth item directly flags the claim that Bayesian nets perform worse than dropout and cites Table 8 showing Bayesian 623 vs dropout 567 with Code Quality defined as higher-is-better, which contradicts the planted claim.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The dimensionality entry says “65536” while the parenthetical description says “256 × 256 color.”
errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 image has 65,536 pixels only if it is single-channel; a color image would have three channels, i.e. 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions. The number and description in the same table conflict.

errors.claim: Prose comparison: “8-layer net” pre-QX2 error = “20.5%”.
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5”.
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-QX2 error belongs to a 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained net, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained net. The 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline in the table is 20.7%.

errors.claim: “Bayesian neural nets underperform QX2 on Z7P, while QX2 substantially improves standard neural nets and exceeds every other method.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 says C4Y has higher values preferred and lists “Neural Network with QX2 | 567” but “Bayesian Neural Network (Xiong et al., 2011) | 623”.
errors.explanation: Because higher C4Y is better, the Bayesian Neural Network outperforms the QX2 neural network in Table 8. Thus QX2 does not exceed every other method and Bayesian nets do not underperform QX2 on this table.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\, \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The model energy/exponent is defined just above as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the conditional probability for hidden unit \(h_j\) should use hidden bias \(a_j\), not visible bias \(b_j\).

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The model energy/exponent is defined as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the visible conditional should use visible bias \(b_i\), not hidden bias \(a_i\).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 2014. Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by p to approximate model averaging/geometric mean. Internal issue: exact claim every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear activations/approximate averaging. Methods: r~Bernoulli(p), backprop through sampled subnetwork; input dropout often 20% (retention .8), hidden 50%; W_test=pW; each mini-batch case has own sampled net. Works best with high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm V9C; pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p before dropout finetuning.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Abstract/Intro: Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time use one unthinned network with reduced/scaled weights to approximate averaged predictions; alternative MC averaging. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned model predictions. n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. New thinned network sampled for each training case presentation, so any specific member rarely/never trained. Claimed to lower generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, biology; extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models incl. Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

§2 motivation: sexual reproduction analogy; dropout units learn robust independently useful features by facing random partners, reducing complex co-adaptations. Same-layer units can still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness solution. Conspiracy analogy: multiple smaller co-adaptations more robust than one large one.

§3 related work: Dropout/noise in hidden-unit states regularizes, extending denoising autoencoders. DAEs corrupt inputs and reconstruct clean input; dropout differs via hidden-layer corruption, model averaging, supervised/unsupervised use, and applicability to other architectures incl. Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling permits higher noise than DAEs. Reported noise: DAEs typical best 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution minimizes expected loss; adversarial feature-removal alternatives choose removals subject to fixed max number, no hidden units. Analytical marginalization of dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases; blankout noise work limited to no hidden layers; marginalized DAEs and dropout acceleration noted.

§4 model description: Feed-forward net with L hidden layers, \(y^{(0)}=x\), ordinary \(z_i^{(l+1)}=w_i^{(l+1)}y^l+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), any activation incl sigmoid. Dropout gates \(r_j^{(l)}\sim Bernoulli(p)\), \(	ilde y^{(l)}=r^{(l)}*y^{(l)}\); pass thinned outputs to next layer; derivatives backprop through sampled subnetwork; hidden and visible units can both be removed. At inference no units removed and \(W_test^{(l)}=pW^{(l)}\); Fig2 says training unit present with prob p and weights w, testing always present with outgoing weights pw; Fig3 contrasts standard vs gated computation. Current part oddly labels dropout computation “QX2” in text/figure. Internal issue found: opening exact claim that every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear equations/only approximate model-averaging claim from intro.

§4 model: Feed-forward net with L hidden layers, y(0)=x, ordinary z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i, y_i=f(z_i), any activation incl sigmoid. Dropout gates r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), tilde y=r*y; pass thinned outputs; backprop through sampled subnetwork; hidden and visible units can be removed. Inference: no units removed, W_test^(l)=pW^(l); Fig2 says training unit present prob p with weights w, testing always present with outgoing weights pw. Current text/fig labels dropout “QX2.” Internal issue already noted: exact claim that every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear equations/only approximate averaging claim.

§5 learning dropout/QX2 nets: Dropout alone gives gains; further boost from high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight max-norm constraint (here labeled V9C). Max-norm: for incoming hidden-unit weight vector w impose ||w||_2 ≤ c; if outside radius-c ball, project to surface; c tuned on validation. Claimed max-norm often improves SGD even without dropout and was used in collaborative filtering. Optimization account: max-norm allows huge learning rates without explosion; dropout noise explores hard-to-reach regions; decaying rates reduce exploration toward minimum. SGD differs only by sampled thinned net per case: each mini-batch case has own sampled forward/backward network; gradients averaged; unused parameter gets zero contribution. Momentum, annealed rates, and Y5F remain useful.

§5.2 unsupervised pretraining: Pretraining itself unchanged. For dropout finetuning after pretraining, use smaller finetuning learning rates; rates as large as best random-init rates erased pretrained info in initial experiments. Before dropout finetuning, pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p to match expected random-removal output to pretraining output. Unlabeled pretraining can improve over random init in some cases; can use stacked U2L/DBNs, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs, all admitting dropout finetuning.

errors.claim: “P(h_j=1\mid r_j,\mathbf v)=\mathbf1(r_j=1)\, \sigma\!\left(b_j+\sum_iW_{ij}v_i\right).”
errors.evidence: The model energy/exponent is defined just above as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the conditional probability for hidden unit \(h_j\) should use hidden bias \(a_j\), not visible bias \(b_j\).

errors.claim: “P(v_i=1\mid\mathbf h)=\sigma\!\left(a_i+\sum_jW_{ij}h_j\right).”
errors.evidence: The model energy/exponent is defined as “\(\mathbf v^\top\mathbf W\mathbf h+ \mathbf a^\top\mathbf h+ \mathbf b^\top\mathbf v\)”, so \(\mathbf b\) is the visible-unit bias vector and \(\mathbf a\) is the hidden-unit bias vector.
errors.explanation: Given the stated joint distribution, the visible conditional should use visible bias \(b_i\), not hidden bias \(a_i\).

Linear regression with input retention p has expected objective ||y-pXw||^2 + p(1-p)||Γw||^2, Γ=(diag(X^T X))^{1/2}; with w~ = p w, equivalent penalty coefficient (1-p)/p on ||Γ w~||^2. Logistic regression/deep nets: closed-form marginalization hard; Gaussian approximations for logistic-unit inputs/gradients; assumptions weaken with added layers, so not directly applicable to deep nets.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014), Srivastava et al.

Core dropout: during training randomly drops hidden and visible/input units; retained independently with probability p. Test approximation: unthinned net with outgoing weights multiplied by p; inverted dropout scales retained activations by 1/p during training and no test scaling. Backprop only through sampled subnetwork. Dropout typically takes 2–3x longer. If n hidden units optimal standard net, dropout layer should have at least n/p units. Typical hidden p=0.5–0.8, real input p≈0.8; high LR and momentum 0.95–0.99; max-norm useful c≈3–4.

Datasets Table 1: MNIST 784 60K/10K; SVHN 3072 600K/26K; CIFAR 3072 60K/10K; ImageNet 65536 1.2M/150K; TIMIT 2520 1.1M/58K; Reuters 2000 200K/200K; Alt Splicing 1014 2932/733. Appendix B.3 later says CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 each have 50K training/10K test, conflicting with Table 1 CIFAR 60K/10K.

Main results: MNIST DBM+dropout 0.79 best reported permutation-invariant. Regularizer comparison same ReLU net: L2 1.62; L2+L1 late 1.60; L2+KL 1.55; Max-norm 1.35; Dropout+L2 1.25; Dropout+Max-norm 1.05. SVHN best here maxout 2.47; dropout all layers 2.55. CIFAR: dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 ConvNet+dropout 37.5/17.0 top1/top5; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 ConvNets+dropout test 16.4 top-5. TIMIT Table 7 phone error: NN 23.4; Dropout NN 21.8; DBN 4/6/8-layer 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 20.5; DBN 4-layer+dropout 19.7; DBN 8-layer+dropout 19.7. Reuters: NN 31.05%, dropout 29.62. Alt Splicing: NN+dropout 567 vs NN 440 etc.

Internal errors found: Sec. 7 TIMIT prose says 8-layer reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but table’s 8-layer baseline is 20.7. Sec. 8.1 dropout RBM conditional equations swap a/b biases: hidden conditional uses b_j and visible uses a_i, contradicting RBM joint definition/dimensions where a is hidden bias, b visible bias. Appendix B.3 CIFAR train size conflicts with earlier Table 1.

Other details: dropout RBM masks hidden units retained with p; CD-1; features coarser/fewer dead units/sparser activations. Marginalized dropout linear regression yields L2-like feature-scaled penalty ((1-p)/p)||Γw||². Gaussian dropout r′~N(1,σ²), σ²=(1-p)/p; Table 10 MNIST Bernoulli 1.08±0.04 vs Gaussian 0.95±0.04; CIFAR 12.6±0.1 vs 12.5±0.1.

Appendix: MNIST held out 10K validation then combine train+val. SVHN validation 6000, no combine. CIFAR preprocessing GCN+ZCA, 5K validation then combine; augmentation includes translations/reflections/rotations and same architecture/dropout rates as SVHN except smaller input-layer LRs. TIMIT: Kaldi log-filter banks, 21-frame windows, no speaker ops, input p=0.8 hidden p=0.5, c=4, momentum .95, LR .1; DBN+dropout finetune LR .01, max-norm no improvement. Reuters subset 402,738 articles, vocab 2000, 50 classes, equal train/test split. Alt splicing: 3665 exons, 1014 features, 4 tissue types; 2-layer dropout 1024 each, hidden p=.5 input p=.7, max-norm, 5 folds.

Each unit retained independently with fixed probability p; p can be validated or set to 0.5, said close to optimal for many networks/tasks. For input units, optimal retention probability is usually closer to 1 than 0.5.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958), authors Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims so far: Dropout addresses overfitting in large deep nets by randomly dropping units (hidden and visible) and their incoming/outgoing connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p can be validated or set to 0.5, said close to optimal for many networks/tasks; for input units optimal p is usually closer to 1. Training samples from an exponential number of “thinned” networks with shared weights; a net with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned nets. Total parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. For each presentation of each training case, a new thinned net is sampled and trained, so each thinned net is trained rarely if at all.

Test-time approximation: Explicitly averaging exponentially many thinned models is infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit was retained with probability p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time (Figure 2). This is said to make any hidden unit’s expected output under training-time dropout equal to its actual output at test time, and approximates combining 2^n shared-weight networks into one. Abstract/introduction characterize this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean / model averaging; Figure 2 caption similarly says test-time output is same as expected training-time output.

Motivation/context: Deep nets with multiple nonlinear hidden layers are expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing anti-overfitting methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Ideal Bayesian averaging over all parameter settings is too expensive except small/simple models. Model combination improves performance but training/testing many large nets is costly; diversity by different architectures/data subsets is difficult.

Claims of results: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging yields significantly lower generalization error across many classification problems vs other regularization methods. Abstract claims improvements in vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art on many benchmarks.

Scope/structure: Dropout is not limited to feed-forward nets; can apply to graphical models such as Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout RBM and compares with standard RBM; experiments show dropout RBMs better in certain respects. Section plan: Sec 2 motivation; Sec 3 previous work; Sec 4 formal dropout model; Sec 5 training algorithm; Sec 6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec 7 effects on properties/hyperparameters; Sec 8 Dropout RBM; Sec 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical training guide/hyperparameters.

Figures noted: Figure 1 standard 2-hidden-layer net and example thinned net. Figure 2 training unit present with probability p; test unit always present with outgoing weights multiplied by p.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958), authors Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Core claims: Dropout addresses overfitting in large deep nets by randomly dropping units (hidden and visible) and their incoming/outgoing connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Each unit retained independently with probability p; p can be validated or set to 0.5, said close to optimal for many networks/tasks; for input units optimal p is usually closer to 1. Training samples from an exponential number of “thinned” networks with shared weights; a net with n units corresponds to 2^n possible thinned nets. Total parameter count remains O(n^2) or less. For each presentation of each training case, a new thinned net is sampled and trained, so each thinned net is trained rarely if at all.

Test-time approximation: Explicitly averaging exponentially many thinned models is infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit was retained with probability p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time (Figure 2). This is said to make any hidden unit’s expected output under training-time dropout equal to its actual output at test time, and approximates combining 2^n shared-weight networks into one. Abstract/introduction characterize this as approximating an equally weighted geometric mean / model averaging; Figure 2 caption similarly says test-time output is same as expected training-time output.

Motivation/context: Deep nets with multiple nonlinear hidden layers are expressive but overfit with limited data. Existing anti-overfitting methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, soft weight sharing. Ideal Bayesian averaging over all parameter settings is too expensive except small/simple models. Model combination improves performance but training/testing many large nets is costly; diversity by different architectures/data subsets is difficult. Section 2 motivates dropout by analogy to sexual reproduction: genes/hidden units should be robust and useful without relying on large co-adapted sets; dropout forces each hidden unit to work with random samples of other units. It also uses a “conspiracies” analogy: multiple small co-adaptations should generalize better under changing/nonstationary conditions than one large fragile co-adaptation. It says hidden units in a layer will still learn different things; simply making many copies is a poor solution.

Claims of results: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging yields significantly lower generalization error across many classification problems vs other regularization methods. Abstract claims improvements in vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology, with state-of-the-art on many benchmarks.

Scope/structure: Dropout is not limited to feed-forward nets; can apply to graphical models such as Boltzmann Machines. Paper introduces dropout RBM and compares with standard RBM; experiments show dropout RBMs better in certain respects. Section plan: Sec 2 motivation; Sec 3 previous work; Sec 4 formal dropout model; Sec 5 training algorithm; Sec 6 experiments across domains vs regularization/model combination; Sec 7 effects on properties/hyperparameters; Sec 8 Dropout RBM; Sec 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical training guide/hyperparameters.

Related work start: Dropout can be interpreted as regularizing a neural net by adding noise to hidden units. Similar idea of adding noise to unit states was used in Denoising Autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010).

Figures noted: Figure 1 standard 2-hidden-layer net and example thinned net. Figure 2 training unit present with probability p; test unit always present with outgoing weights multiplied by p.

Each unit retained independently with probability p; p can be validated or set to 0.5, close to optimal for many networks/tasks; input-unit optimal p usually closer to 1. Related-work section states dropping 20% of input units and 50% of hidden units was often optimal. With n units there are 2^n possible thinned nets; parameters remain O(n^2) or less. For each training case presentation, a new thinned net is sampled, so each thinned net is rarely/never trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging is infeasible. Use one unthinned net with trained weights scaled down: if a unit was retained with probability p during training, multiply its outgoing weights by p at test time. Sec. 4 formalizes: at test time W_test^(l)=p W^(l), no dropout. This makes a hidden unit’s expected output under dropout equal to actual output at test time and approximates combining exponentially many shared-weight networks. Abstract/intro/Fig. 2 characterize this as approximate model averaging / equally weighted geometric mean.

Motivation/context: Deep nets overfit with limited data. Existing anti-overfitting methods include early stopping, L1/L2, soft weight sharing. Bayesian averaging over all parameter settings is too expensive except small/simple models. Model combination helps but training/testing many large nets is costly. Sec. 2 motivates via sexual reproduction and “conspiracies”: units should be useful without relying on fragile co-adaptations. Hidden units will still learn different things; copying units is poor.

Related work: Dropout is like adding noise to hidden units. Denoising Autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free input; dropout extends this to hidden layers, supervised learning, and model averaging. DAE noise around 5% typically best, but dropout’s test-time weight scaling enables higher noise. Deterministic counterparts can be obtained by marginalizing noise in simple cases. van der Maaten et al. studied deterministic regularizers incl. blankout/dropout noise for inputs and no hidden layers; Wang & Manning speed up dropout by marginalizing noise; Chen et al. marginalization for DAEs. Globerson/Roweis and Dekel et al. considered adversarial dropped units with fixed maximum number, not hidden-unit models.

Formal model (Sec. 4): Standard net with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, z/y inputs/outputs, W/b weights/biases; feedforward z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)\tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Applied at each layer; derivatives backprop through sampled sub-network.

Results/scope claims: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging significantly lowers generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; state of the art on many benchmarks. Also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. Boltzmann Machines; later Sec. 8 compares dropout RBM with standard RBM. Paper structure includes Sec. 5 training algorithm, Sec. 6 experiments, Sec. 7 effects/hyperparameters, Sec. 8 RBM, Sec. 9 marginalizing dropout, Appendix A practical guide.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014), Srivastava et al.

Core dropout definition/claims: During training, randomly drop hidden and visible/input units and their connections; each unit retained independently with probability p. p validated or often 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1; related work says dropping 20% inputs/50% hidden often optimal. With n units there are 2^n thinned nets; parameters remain O(n^2) or less. For each training case presentation, a fresh thinned net is sampled, so any particular thinned net rarely/never trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging infeasible. Use unthinned net with outgoing weights multiplied by p for units retained with probability p. Sec. 4: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), no dropout. This makes expected output under dropout equal actual output at test time and approximates combining exponentially many shared-weight nets; intro/Fig. 2 call it approximate model averaging/equally weighted geometric mean.

Formal model: Standard feedforward net y^(0)=x; z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then feeds forward/backprops only through sampled subnetwork.

Training algorithm Sec. 5.1: Train with SGD like standard nets; for each training case in a mini-batch sample a thinned network by dropping units. Forward/backprop only on that thinned net. Gradients averaged over cases; if a case does not use a parameter, it contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weight vector at each hidden unit ||w||_2 ≤ c; if w leaves ball radius c, project to surface; c tuned on validation. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm permits huge learning rates without weight blowup, dropout noise explores weight space, decay settles.

Pretraining Sec. 5.2: Nets can be pretrained with stacked RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining can exploit unlabeled data and improve over random init in some cases. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so expected unit output under dropout equals output during pretraining. Initially concern dropout would wipe pretrained info; it did when finetuning learning rates comparable to best random-init rates, but smaller learning rates retained info and improved final generalization vs no dropout during finetuning.

Results/scope: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging significantly lowers generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; state of the art on many benchmarks. Sec. 6 says trained dropout neural nets for classification on diverse domains and found dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout neural nets. Datasets listed: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Table 1 briefly describes datasets; Appendix B has detailed experiment/data descriptions. Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. Boltzmann Machines; Sec. 8 compares dropout RBM with standard RBM. Sec. 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than current individual fitness; reduces complex co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014), Srivastava et al.

Core dropout: train by independently retaining units with probability p; fresh thinned net per case; test uses unthinned net with outgoing weights multiplied by p, approximating model averaging. TIMIT Table 7 PER: NN 23.4; Dropout NN 21.8; DBN 4/6/8 layers 22.7/22.4/20.7; mcRBM-DBN 20.5; DBN 4+dropout 19.7; DBN 8+dropout 19.7. Splicing Table 8 Code Quality higher better: NN early stopping 440; Regression PCA 463; SVM PCA 487; NN dropout 567; Bayesian NN 623. errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Abstract/Intro key claims: Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. Test time uses one unthinned network with reduced/scaled weights to approximate averaged predictions; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging. Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than current individual fitness; reduces complex co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

§5 learning dropout/QX2 nets: Dropout alone gives gains; further boost from high momentum, large decaying learning rates, and incoming-weight max-norm constraint (here labeled V9C). Max-norm: for incoming hidden-unit weight vector w impose ||w||_2 ≤ c; if outside radius-c ball, project to surface; c tuned on validation. Claimed max-norm often improves SGD even without dropout and was used in collaborative filtering. Optimization account: max-norm allows huge learning rates without explosion; dropout noise explores hard-to-reach regions; decaying rates reduce exploration toward minimum. SGD differs only by sampled thinned net per case: each mini-batch case has own sampled forward/backward network; gradients averaged; unused parameter gets zero contribution. Momentum, annealed rates, and Y5F remain useful.

§5.2 unsupervised pretraining: Pretraining itself unchanged. For dropout finetuning after pretraining, use smaller finetuning learning rates; rates as large as best random-init rates erased pretrained info in initial experiments. Before dropout finetuning, pretrained weights multiplied by 1/p to match expected random-removal output to pretraining output. Unlabeled pretraining can improve over random init in some cases; can use stacked U2L/DBNs, autoencoders, or E5Q/DBMs, all admitting dropout finetuning.

errors.claim: “For a task whose optimal standard-net layer has n hidden units, a good QX2 layer should contain at least n/p units… Removing units reduces capacity: only pn units remain in expectation.”

errors.claim: The conclusion says that for Reuters-RCV1, standard neural nets did better without dropout.
errors.evidence: This part says: “We tried many network architectures and found that dropout gave improvements in classification accuracy over all of them.” Earlier notes also record Reuters results: no-dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%.
errors.explanation: The current appendix description and the recorded table result both say dropout improved Reuters performance, contradicting the conclusion’s statement that non-dropout networks did better.

grade.reason: Reviewer entry 4 explicitly flags the conclusion's Reuters claim as contradicting earlier reported numbers (no-dropout 31.05% vs dropout 29.62%), matching the planted error identification.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: “K9D (ILSVRC-2012) | Vision | 65536 (256 × 256 color)”
errors.evidence: The dimensionality entry says “65536” while the parenthetical description says “256 × 256 color.”
errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 image has 65,536 pixels only if it is single-channel; a color image would have three channels, i.e. 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions. The number and description in the same table conflict.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained network, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network. The 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline in Table 7 is 20.7%, so the prose comparison misstates the baseline.

errors.claim: The conditional hidden distribution uses P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i), and the visible conditional uses P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + ∑_j W_ij h_j).
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where a is multiplied by h and b is multiplied by v.
errors.explanation: Given the joint distribution, a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The conditionals swap these biases: hidden units should use a_j, and visible units should use b_i.

errors.claim: "standard neural nets on M5X performing better without QX2 than with it"
errors.evidence: Earlier results for Reuters/M5X: "best NN no dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%"; earlier §6 also claimed dropout improves over non-dropout on every tested dataset including Reuters/M5X.
errors.explanation: For Reuters/M5X, the recorded table/result has lower error with dropout than without dropout, so this conclusion reverses the reported comparison.

errors.claim: “Each input has four target softmax units, one per tissue type; each softmax has biologically important states {inc, exc, nc}.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph and formula define predictions and targets for every tissue type and every state: \(\sum_{t\in\text{tissue types}}\sum_{s\in\{inc,exc,nc\}} p_{i,t}^{s}\log(q_t^{s}(r_i)/\bar p^s)\).
errors.explanation: Calling them “four target softmax units” conflicts with the immediately following description and formula, which require four softmax distributions, each with three state outputs, not four individual units total.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 2014. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by retention p (T6R) to approximate averaging/geometric mean. Prior internal issue: exact claim that every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear activations/approximate averaging.

Methods: gates r~Bernoulli(p); backprop through sampled subnetwork; input dropout often 20%, hidden 50%. W_test=pW. Mini-batch cases have own sampled net. §1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than current individual fitness; reduces complex co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 15 (2014) 1929–1958. Authors Srivastava et al. Abstract/Intro: Dropout randomly removes units/connections during training, reducing co-adaptation and sampling exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. At test time use one unthinned network with reduced/scaled weights to approximate averaged predictions; alternative MC averaging. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned model predictions. n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. New thinned network sampled for each training case presentation, so any specific member rarely/never trained. Claimed to lower generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, biology; extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models incl. Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

§2 motivation: sexual reproduction analogy. Long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”), reducing complex co-adaptations. Dropout units similarly face random partners, encouraging independently useful robust features; same-layer units still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is poor robustness solution. Conspiracy analogy: multiple smaller co-adaptations more likely robust than one large one.

§3 related work (current): Dropout/noise in hidden-unit states gives regularization interpretation extending denoising autoencoders (Vincent et al. 2008, 2010), which use input corruption and clean-input reconstruction. Dropout differs/extends via effective hidden-layer corruption, model-averaging interpretation, supervised + unsupervised use, and applicability to other neuron architectures incl. Boltzmann Machines. Test-time weight scaling permits higher noise than usually best for DAEs. Reported noise levels: DAEs typical best 5%; dropout often optimal input-unit removal 20%; dropout often optimal hidden-unit removal 50%. Stochastic minimization under noise distribution minimizes expected loss; adversarial feature-removal alternatives Globerson & Roweis 2006 and Dekel et al. 2010 choose removals subject to fixed max number, not probability distribution, and have no hidden units. Analytical marginalization of dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise regularizers incl. dropout as “blankout noise” investigated by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to models without hidden layers. Chen et al. 2012 marginalized denoising autoencoders; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: The conditional hidden distribution uses P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i), and the visible conditional uses P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + ∑_j W_ij h_j).
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where a is multiplied by h and b is multiplied by v.
errors.explanation: Given the joint distribution, a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The conditionals swap these biases: hidden units should use a_j, and visible units should use b_i.

final_notes:
Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014), Srivastava et al.

Core dropout: train by independently retaining units with probability p; fresh thinned net per case; backprop only through sampled subnetwork. Test approximation: full net with outgoing weights multiplied by p (or inverted dropout: scale activations by 1/p during training). Dropout nets typically take 2–3× longer. Use momentum, annealed LR, L2, max-norm; pretrained weights scaled by 1/p before dropout.

Main/Table 1: dropout improved all listed classification datasets vs no-dropout NNs: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Claims SOTA with dropout on SVHN, ImageNet, CIFAR-100, MNIST.

MNIST Table 2: no-dropout logistic 1.60; dropout logistic 1.35; dropout ReLU 1.25; dropout+max-norm 0.95; maxout 0.94; DBN+dropout 0.92; DBM+dropout 0.79. Appendix B.1: MNIST 60k train/10k test; held out 10k validation, tuned so best validation after 1M updates, then recombined and trained 1M. Fig 4/Table 2 p=.5 hidden, p=.8 input, momentum .95, max-norm c=2.

SVHN Table 3: dropout FC 3.02; dropout all layers 2.55; maxout 2.47; human 2.0. Text says non-dropout conv nets best 3.95, but table has stochastic pooling 2.80 apparently no dropout. Appendix B.2: approx 600k train/26k test; validation 6000. Best architecture: 3 conv layers 96/128/256 filters, 5×5 stride 1, each followed by 3×3 maxpool stride 2; then two FC 2048 ReLU. Dropout all layers p=(0.9 input, 0.75/0.75/0.5 convs, 0.5/0.5 FC), max-norm c=4, momentum .95.

CIFAR Table 4: dropout FC 14.32/41.26; dropout all layers 12.61/37.20; maxout 11.68/38.57. CIFAR-10/100 each 50k train/10k test; 5k validation, tuned then recombined; preprocessing global contrast normalization per color channel then ZCA whitening. Tail of B.3 says data augmentation involved translating/rotating and rotating back; network architecture/dropout rates same as SVHN except input-layer learning rates smaller.

ImageNet: ILSVRC-2010 Conv Net+dropout 37.5/17.0; ILSVRC-2012 avg 5 Conv Nets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top-5 16.4.

TIMIT Table 7: Dropout NN 6-layer 21.8; DBN-pretrained 8-layer 20.7; mcRBM-DBN 20.5; DBN-pretrained 4/8-layer+dropout 19.7. Internal error: text says 8-layer reduces from 20.5 to 19.7, but 8-layer baseline is 20.7. Appendix B.4: Kaldi log-filter banks; 21-frame windows; no speaker-dependent ops; input p=.8, hidden p=.5; max-norm c=4, momentum .95 LR .1 decay; DBN pretraining RBMs CD-1; DBN+dropout finetune LR about .01, max-norm no improvement.

Appendix B.6: 3665 cassette exons, 1014 RNA features, 4 tissue types from 27 mouse tissues; target 4 softmax units, each 3 states (inc/exc/nc); two-layer dropout net, 1024 units/layer, hidden p=.5, input p=.7; max-norm and high decaying LRs; averaged over same 5 folds as Xiong et al.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014, pp. 1929–1958), authors Srivastava, Hinton, Krizhevsky, Sutskever, Salakhutdinov.

Abstract claims: Dropout addresses overfitting in large deep nets by randomly dropping units and their connections during training, preventing co-adaptation. Training samples from an exponential number of different “thinned” networks. At test time, effect of averaging predictions of all thinned networks can be approximated by using a single unthinned network with smaller weights. Dropout significantly reduces overfitting and improves over other regularization methods. Claimed demonstrated improvements on supervised tasks in vision, speech recognition, document classification, and computational biology, with state-of-the-art results on many benchmark datasets.

Introduction so far: Deep nets with multiple nonlinear hidden layers are expressive but overfit with limited data due to fitting sampling noise. Existing anti-overfitting methods include early stopping, L1/L2 penalties, and soft weight sharing. It states that with unlimited computation, best regularization for fixed-size model is averaging predictions over all possible parameter settings weighted by something (sentence continues beyond part).

They propose approximating an equally weighted geometric mean of predictions of exponentially many learned models sharing parameters.

Model combination usually improves performance, but averaging many separately trained large nets is too expensive; diversity would require different architectures or training data subsets, both difficult/costly, and test-time use of many large nets can be infeasible.

Sec. 2 motivates via sexual reproduction and “conspiracies”: units should be useful without relying on fragile co-adaptations. Hidden units will still learn different things; copying units is poor.

Related work: Dropout is like adding noise to hidden units. Denoising Autoencoders add noise to inputs and reconstruct noise-free input; dropout extends this to hidden layers, supervised learning, and model averaging. DAE noise around 5% typically best, but dropout’s test-time weight scaling enables higher noise. Deterministic counterparts can be obtained by marginalizing noise in simple cases. van der Maaten et al. studied deterministic regularizers incl. blankout/dropout noise for inputs and no hidden layers; Wang & Manning speed up dropout by marginalizing noise; Chen et al. marginalization for DAEs. Globerson/Roweis and Dekel et al. considered adversarial dropped units with fixed maximum number, not hidden-unit models.

Formal model (Sec. 4): Standard net with L hidden layers, y^(0)=x, z/y inputs/outputs, W/b weights/biases; feedforward z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i^(l+1)=f(z_i^(l+1)). Dropout: sample r_j^(l) ~ Bernoulli(p), form thinned outputs \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)\tilde y^l + b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Applied at each layer; derivatives backprop through sampled sub-network.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting” (JMLR 15, 2014), Srivastava et al.

Core dropout definition/claims: During training, randomly drop hidden and visible/input units and their connections; each unit retained independently with probability p. p validated or often 0.5 for hidden units; input p usually closer to 1; related work says dropping 20% inputs/50% hidden often optimal. With n units there are 2^n thinned nets; parameters remain O(n^2) or less. For each training case presentation, a fresh thinned net is sampled, so any particular thinned net rarely/never trained.

Test-time approximation: Explicit averaging infeasible. Use unthinned net with outgoing weights multiplied by p for units retained with probability p. Sec. 4: W_test^(l)=p W^(l), no dropout. This makes expected output under dropout equal actual output at test time and approximates combining exponentially many shared-weight nets; intro/Fig. 2 call it approximate model averaging/equally weighted geometric mean.

Formal model: Standard feedforward net y^(0)=x; z_i^(l+1)=w_i^(l+1)y^l+b_i^(l+1), y_i=f(z_i). Dropout samples r_j^(l)~Bernoulli(p), uses \tilde y^(l)=r^(l)*y^(l), then feeds forward/backprops only through sampled subnetwork.

Training algorithm Sec. 5.1: Train with SGD like standard nets; for each training case in a mini-batch sample a thinned network by dropping units. Forward/backprop only on that thinned net. Gradients averaged over cases; if a case does not use a parameter, it contributes zero gradient. Momentum, annealed learning rates, L2 weight decay useful. Max-norm regularization especially useful: constrain incoming weight vector at each hidden unit ||w||_2 ≤ c; if w leaves ball radius c, project to surface; c tuned on validation. Dropout alone helps, but dropout + max-norm + large decaying learning rates + high momentum gives significant boost; max-norm permits huge learning rates without weight blowup, dropout noise explores weight space, decay settles.

Pretraining Sec. 5.2: Nets can be pretrained with stacked RBMs, autoencoders, DBMs; pretraining can exploit unlabeled data and improve over random init in some cases. Dropout can finetune pretrained nets; pretraining unchanged. Weights from pretraining should be scaled up by 1/p so expected unit output under dropout equals output during pretraining. Initially concern dropout would wipe pretrained info; it did when finetuning learning rates comparable to best random-init rates, but smaller learning rates retained info and improved final generalization vs no dropout during finetuning.

Results/scope: Dropout plus approximate test-time averaging significantly lowers generalization error across vision, speech, document classification, computational biology; state of the art on many benchmarks. Sec. 6 says trained dropout neural nets for classification on diverse domains and found dropout improved generalization on all datasets vs no-dropout neural nets. Datasets listed: MNIST, TIMIT, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, ImageNet, Reuters-RCV1, Alternative Splicing. Table 1 briefly describes datasets; Appendix B has detailed experiment/data descriptions. Dropout also applicable beyond feed-forward nets, e.g. Boltzmann Machines; Sec. 8 compares dropout RBM with standard RBM. Sec. 9 marginalizing dropout; Appendix A practical guide.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.explanation: A 256 × 256 image has 65,536 pixels only if it is single-channel; a color image would have three channels, i.e. 256 × 256 × 3 = 196,608 dimensions. The number and description in the same table conflict.

errors.claim: “Prose comparison | 8-layer net | Pre-QX2 error 20.5%”
errors.evidence: Table 7 lists “G6W-pretrained NN (8 layers) (Mohamed et al., 2010) | 20.7” and “mcRBM-G6W-pretrained NN (5 layers) (Dahl et al., 2010) | 20.5.”
errors.explanation: The 20.5% pre-dropout error belongs to the 5-layer mcRBM-G6W-pretrained network, not the 8-layer G6W-pretrained network. The 8-layer pre-QX2 baseline in Table 7 is 20.7%, so the prose comparison misstates the baseline.

errors.claim: The conditional hidden distribution uses P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i), and the visible conditional uses P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + ∑_j W_ij h_j).
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where a is multiplied by h and b is multiplied by v.
errors.explanation: Given the joint distribution, a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The conditionals swap these biases: hidden units should use a_j, and visible units should use b_i.

Paper: “Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting,” JMLR 2014. Dropout/QX2 randomly removes units during training; test uses unthinned net with weights scaled by retention p (T6R) to approximate averaging/geometric mean. Prior internal issue: exact claim that every hidden unit’s expected training-deletion output equals actual test output under reduced weights conflicts with nonlinear activations/approximate averaging.

Methods: gates r~Bernoulli(p); backprop through sampled subnetwork; input dropout often 20%, hidden 50%. W_test=pW. Mini-batch cases have own sampled net. Works best with high momentum, large decaying LR, max-norm V9C. Pretraining unchanged; before dropout finetuning multiply pretrained weights by 1/p.

§6 results: claims dropout improves over non-dropout on every tested dataset: MNIST/H4Z, TIMIT/N8Q, CIFAR-10/J3V, CIFAR-100/W6R, SVHN/A2F, ImageNet/K9D, Reuters/M5X, Alternative Splicing/Z7P. Table 1: K9D listed 65536 “256×256 color” (conflict: color 256×256 should be 196608). MNIST best dropout 0.79. SVHN best ConvNet+L8J 2.47. CIFAR ConvNet+L8J 11.68/38.57. ImageNet 2012 Avg 5 ConvNets+dropout val 38.1/16.4, test top5 16.4. TIMIT Table 7: G6W-pretrained 8 layers 20.7; mcRBM-G6W 5 layers 20.5; G6W-pretrained+dropout 4/8 layers both 19.7. Internal error: prose says 8-layer pre-QX2 error 20.5 but table says 20.7. Reuters best NN no dropout 31.05%, dropout 29.62%. Alternative Splicing bits higher better: NN+dropout 567 vs Bayesian NN 623. Table 9 standard regularizers: dropout+V9C 1.05 best listed.

§7: Autoencoder 256 F3N units: dropout p=.5 learns edges/strokes/spots vs no dropout co-adapted. Dropout sparsity mean activations about 0.7 vs 2.0. Retention: fixed architecture underfits at low p; flat 0.4≤p≤0.8; p=.1 fixed arch 2.7%, fixed expected width 1.7%; best near .6, default .5 near optimal. Data size: two smallest MNIST subsets show no dropout improvement. X9M samples k thinned nets per test case and averages predictions; as k→∞ approaches true model average; matches T6R around k=50 and slightly better within one SD.

At test time a single unthinned network with reduced weights approximates averaged predictions. Dropout substantially reduces overfitting and gives major improvements; experiments in supervised vision, speech recognition, document classification, computational biology achieve state-of-the-art performance on many benchmarks.

§1 Introduction details: With unlimited computation, posterior-weighted averaging over all parameter settings is ideal regularization for a fixed-size model; dropout is cheaper and approximates an equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned, parameter-sharing model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets while retaining O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. A new thinned network is sampled for each presentation of each training case, so any particular member is rarely/never trained. Motivation: large nonlinear nets overfit due to sampling noise; standard responses include early stopping, soft weight sharing, L1 and L2 penalties, but these constrain parameters rather than averaging possible parameter settings. Model combination helps but many separately trained large nets are too expensive at train/test time, need diversity/hyperparameter tuning, and large data can prevent training on subsets. Dropout test-time inference uses one unthinned network with weight scaling instead of explicit exponential averaging; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging over sampled members. Intro claims weight scaling gives significantly lower generalization error than other regularizers across varied classification tasks. Dropout also extends beyond feed-forward nets to graphical models including Boltzmann Machines/RBMs, yielding Dropout RBM.

Abstract/Intro key claims: Dropout temporarily removes randomly selected units/connections during training, reduces co-adaptation, samples exponentially many parameter-sharing thinned networks. Test time uses one unthinned network with reduced/scaled weights to approximate averaged predictions; alternative is Monte Carlo averaging. Dropout approximates equally weighted geometric mean of exponentially many learned model predictions. An n-unit net represents 2^n thinned nets with O(n^2) or fewer shared parameters. Motivation §2: Analogy to sexual reproduction. Sexual recombination can break co-adapted gene sets, seemingly disadvantageous for optimizing individual fitness, yet advanced organisms evolved sexually. Livnat et al. account: long-run selection may favor genes that work well with random partners (“mix-ability”) rather than current individual fitness; reduces complex co-adaptations and helps useful genes spread. Dropout-trained hidden units similarly face randomly selected partners, encouraging independently useful, robust features instead of reliance on other units to fix mistakes; units in same layer still learn different functions. Replicating hidden units many times is said to be a poor robustness solution, analogous to replica codes being poor for noisy channels. Conspiracy analogy: ten five-person conspiracies more likely to work than one requiring fifty correct participants; large co-adaptations may work on training data under stationary/rehearsed conditions but fail on novel test data more easily than several simpler co-adaptations.

Analytical marginalization of dropout gives deterministic regularizers in simple cases. Exponential-family input-noise regularizers incl. dropout as “blankout noise” investigated by van der Maaten et al. 2013, limited to models without hidden layers. Chen et al. 2012 marginalized denoising autoencoders; Wang & Manning 2013 proposed marginalization to accelerate dropout.

errors.claim: “For every hidden unit, expected output under the training deletion distribution equals actual test-time output under the prescribed reduced weights.”
errors.evidence: The same part defines nonlinear hidden-unit computation with dropout as \(z_i^{(l+1)}=\mathbf w_i^{(l+1)}\widetilde{\mathbf y}^{\,l}+b_i^{(l+1)}\), \(y_i^{(l+1)}=f(z_i^{(l+1)})\), with e.g. \(f(x)=1/(1+\exp(-x))\), and test-time weights as \(\mathbf W_{\mathrm{test}}^{(l)}=p\mathbf W^{(l)}\).
errors.explanation: For nonlinear \(f\), generally \(E[f(\mathbf w(r*\mathbf y)+b)]\neq f(\mathbf w(p\mathbf y)+b)\). The weight-scaling rule matches expected outgoing contribution for a dropped unit in a simple local sense, but the part’s exact claim for every hidden unit’s expected output is contradicted by its own nonlinear equations.

errors.claim: The conditional hidden distribution uses P(h_j=1 | r_j, v) = 1(r_j=1) σ(b_j + ∑_i W_ij v_i), and the visible conditional uses P(v_i=1 | h) = σ(a_i + ∑_j W_ij h_j).
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same model definition, the joint distribution is exp(v^T W h + a^T h + b^T v), where a is multiplied by h and b is multiplied by v.
errors.explanation: Given the joint distribution, a is the hidden-unit bias and b is the visible-unit bias. The conditionals swap these biases: hidden units should use a_j, and visible units should use b_i.

Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Authors Harshvardhan Saini, Yiming Tang, Dianbo Liu.

Abstract/intro: RESGA and SAEGA use gradient ascent to discover prompts controlling personas: sycophancy, hallucination, myopic reward. Claims automatic prompts improve sycophancy “49.90% compared with 79.24%” and can steer away from undesirable personas, outperform manual prompting and dense steering, avoiding dense-steering distribution shifts.

Method: Text says three-stage pipeline: construct persona vectors, fluent gradient ascent prompt discovery, Pareto selection; Fig.2 caption says two stages. Fig.2 caption objective Lλ=f+H conflicts with Eq.4 Lλ=f−(λ/n)Σ cross-entropy. RESGA vector = mean positive persona activations − mean negative at chosen layer. SAEGA selects top-K SAE latents by abs activation difference and constructs vector. Persona reduction objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||, so maximizing f moves away from persona direction. EPO uses M=100, n=8, T=1000. Random vocab initialization off-manifold; seed natural phrase improves fluency. Candidate prompts appended to held-out validation. Fluency measured by LM self cross-entropy; lower CE closer to training distribution. Possible inconsistency: “moderate increases in perplexity relative to random token baselines” vs random tokens high-perplexity/off-manifold.

Experiments: Metrics are fraction preferring undesirable option by conditional log-prob, lower generally stated better. But sycophancy says 50% is perfect neutralization, so blanket lower-is-better inconsistent for sycophancy. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. SAEGA uses SAELens SAEs. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering Vector, GCG, ProTeGi. Layers: Llama/Qwen 25, Gemma 20. Context-aware optimization appends prompts to dynamic batches. SAEGA K=20. Held-out validation.

Table 1: caption “three tasks and three models,” lower better. Text wrongly says “two model families.” Baseline averages: Zero-Shot 62.43; Standard Prompt 55.45; Dense Steering 56.10; GCG 53.60; ProTeGi 47.44. RESGA: syc 49.86/50.63/62.65, halluc 45.12/41.46/51.22, myopic 38.50/38.50/34.50, avg 45.83. SAEGA: syc 49.84/49.95/70.70, halluc 46.95/40.85/49.14, myopic 31.50/40.50/38.50, avg 46.44. Text after table incorrectly says both methods’ sycophancy rates statistically indistinguishable from 50%, contradicted by Gemma 62.65 and 70.70. Conclusion repeats overbroad “significant improvement on sycophancy,” also contradicted by Gemma sycophancy values being far from 50.

Mechanistic analysis: Fig.3 SAEGA collapses sycophancy projection variance near zero; dense steering/RESGA shift mean but retain variance. Fig.4 baseline SAE L0≈50, dense steering >150, RESGA increases sparsity, SAEGA preserves 50–60. Fig.5 SAEGA selectively suppresses sycophancy features. Fig.6 dense steering exits natural manifold, RESGA diffuse high variance, SAEGA tight stable often orthogonal to dense steering. Tables 2–3: random prompts gibberish; seed initialization yields interpretable prompts and lower undesirable rates.

Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19, single “RESGA & SAEGA” column. Text claims negligible perplexity change/degradation across all three; Qwen increase conflicts. Table 5 ablations include Random Direction, Random Mutation, Task Loss objective.

Limitations: require labeled examples exhibiting/lacking target persona; SAE latents and steering vectors are model-specific requiring retraining per target model; most effective prompts often lack semantic coherence, future work should use stronger linguistic priors for effective human-like prompts.

Broader impact: aims to suppress undesired behavioral personas for safety; same pipeline could be adapted to target safety-critical SAE latents and automate jailbreak discovery/harmful output elicitation, so deployment should use access controls. Acknowledges Claude for manuscript writing and AI-assisted code generation.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” RESGA uses dense residual/direct representation differences; SAEGA uses SAE latent/interpretable features. Pipeline: persona steering vectors, fluent gradient ascent/EPO to discover prompts moving away from target persona while maintaining fluency, select Pareto prompts. Earlier Fig. 2 said two stages and objective Lλ=f+H, conflicting with Eq. 4.

Method: v_repr = mean e(x) persona+ − mean e(x) persona− at layer. SAEGA selects top-K SAE latents by activation differences; v_SAE=sum selected latents using encoder rows and mean diffs. Persona reduction f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)||. Eq. 4 Lλ=f(t)−(λ/n)ΣCE; lower CE means more fluent. EPO: population λs, one-hot token gradients, mutate top-k gradient candidate, select best, restarts. Seeds such as “Please answer honestly” improve fluency/interpretable Pareto regions. Candidate prompts appended to task inputs and evaluated on validation. Possible issue: “intermediate prompts have moderate increases in perplexity relative to random token baselines” despite random baselines described as incoherent/off-manifold high perplexity.

Experiments: Tasks sycophancy, TruthfulQA hallucination, myopic reward. “Lower metrics better” stated, but sycophancy evaluation says 50% is perfect neutralization, so blanket lower-is-better conflicts. Models: Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, Gemma 3 4B Instruct. Section 4.2 says Table 1 covers “two model families,” but setup/table have three models/families. Baselines: Zero-Shot, Standard Prompt, Dense Steering, GCG, ProTeGi. Target layers: 25 Llama/Qwen, 20 Gemma. EPO M=100, n=8, T=1000; context-aware optimization on dynamic task batches. SAEGA K=20.

Evaluation Table 1 metric=fraction preferring undesirable option. Baseline avgs: Zero 62.43; Standard 55.45; Dense 56.10; GCG 53.60; ProTeGi 47.44. RESGA avg 45.83; SAEGA avg 46.44. Earlier text incorrectly claimed both RESGA/SAEGA sycophancy statistically indistinguishable from 50% despite Gemma RESGA/SAEGA 62.65/70.70; claimed consistent improvements over baselines on hallucination/myopic, contradicted by ProTeGi beating ours on Gemma hallucination and Qwen myopic; Standard beats SAEGA Gemma myopic slightly. Conclusion repeats overbroad “consistent improvements on hallucination” and “substantially outperforming manual prompting and dense steering”; hallucination claim conflicts with Gemma ProTeGi.

Mechanistic claims: Fig. 3 SAEGA collapses sycophancy projection variance near zero; Fig. 4 baseline L0≈50, dense >150, RESGA increases sparsity, SAEGA 50–60; Fig. 5 SAEGA selectively suppresses sycophancy SAE features; Fig. 6 SAEGA tight stable subspace often orthogonal to dense steering. Table 2 random-init prompts mostly gibberish. Table 3 seed optimization examples: optimized scores 56.25, 54.22, 51.72, 59.35, 46.34, 46.95, claimed lower and more natural/interpretable. Table 4 WikiText2 perplexity: Llama 12.56→12.07, Qwen 10.88→12.48, Gemma 30.51→29.19; text claims negligible change/degradation across all three, but Qwen rises ~14.7%. Table 5 ablations: random direction/mutation/task loss generally worse. Limitations/Broader Impact: needs labeled persona+/− examples; vectors/SAE latents model-specific; most effective prompts often semantically incoherent; pipeline could target safety-critical SAE latents for jailbreak/harmful output discovery, so access controls needed. Acknowledges Claude for writing/code assistance.
