final_notes:
Paper title: “Bridging Mechanistic Interpretability and Prompt Engineering with Gradient Ascent for Interpretable Persona Control.” Core methods: QX2=RESGA dense residual-stream optimization; V7P=SAEGA sparse SAE-latent optimization; J4Z/N8C=gradient-ascent/token-search for fluent prompts. Earlier naming conflict: N8C previously noted as prior EPO, but Algorithm 1 labels paper’s optimizer N8C. H2F=GCG/direct output-logit optimization; Z6Q=ProTeGi; P8D=Dense Steering Vector.

Method details: three-stage procedure, but Fig. 2 caption called it “Two-stage discovery” and used Lλ(t)=f(t)+H(t), conflicting with Eq. 4 Lλ(t)=f(t)−cross-entropy term. Persona vectors: SAE relevance positive-minus-negative activation; top-K absolute differences; V7P direction uses SAE encoder rows/latents; QX2 dense direction=mean positive activation−mean negative activation. Objective f(t)=−<e(t),v>/||e(t)|| using last-token target-layer activation; maximize to reduce persona. Fluency term subtracts λ/n summed next-token CE; lower self-CE=more in-distribution. Context-aware optimization appends task-specific questions at every evolutionary step and uses combined sequence’s final internal state.

Experiments: tasks B2R=Sycophancy, U9K=Hallucination/TruthfulQA MC error, D6V=Myopic Reward; lower metrics better. Models: C7N=Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, W4X=Qwen 2.5 7B Instruct, F9S=Gemma 3 4B Instruct; V7P uses SAE-Lens. Implementation: layers C7N25/W4X25/F9S20; N8C population 100, length 8, iterations 1000; SAE L0≈50; K=20; B2R random/perfect neutralization error=50%; neutral B2R-axis projection=0.0; baseline active SAE features/token≈50; P8D >150; V7P 50–60.

Table 1 averages: X5L62.43, R3W55.45, P8D56.10, H2F53.60, Z6Q47.44, QX245.83, V7P46.44. QX2/V7P per setting: B2R C7N 49.86/49.84, W4X 50.63/49.95, F9S 62.65/70.70; U9K C7N 45.12/46.95, W4X 41.46/40.85, F9S 51.22/49.14; D6V C7N 38.50/31.50, W4X 38.50/40.50, F9S 34.50/38.50. Internal errors found earlier: claims that both methods reach B2R neutralization conflict with F9S; claims of consistent U9K/D6V improvement over baselines conflict with baseline-better entries; “two model families” conflicts with three models/families; V7P “statistically indistinguishable from random choice” conflicts with F9S B2R=70.70; “negligible perplexity change across all three” conflicts/questionable with W4X 10.88→12.48.

Qualitative/interpretability: V7P sparse/semantically grounded, P8D off-manifold, QX2 intermediate. Table 2 random-initialized prompts mostly incoherent. Table 3 seed-initialized N8C lowers seed scores. Table 4 T9B perplexity: C7N 12.56→12.07; W4X 10.88→12.48; F9S 30.51→29.19. Y2H=token priming via induction heads; G6T=semantic/vocabulary shift via ΔLogits. B2R V7P suppresses “Yes/True/Agree” and upweights “However/But”; D6V QX2/V7P upweight “Future/Long/Wait.” Ablations Table 5: K3Y random direction, E8U random mutation, M5A task-loss objective. Conclusion/limitations: future directions include semi-supervised labeled-data reduction, cross-model transfer, multi-persona steering; limitations say QX2/V7P require labeled positive/negative persona examples, model-specific SAE latents/steering vectors, and most effective prompts lack semantic coherence.

Optimizing f alone often yields unnatural/nonsensical strings. Lower self-cross-entropy means closer to training distribution; higher means off-manifold. No hard threshold; analyze whole frontier.

Algorithm 1 is labeled “N8C” in this part: inputs objective f, LM m, prompt length n, population M, fluency weights λ_i; initialize M prompts randomly/seeds; each iteration compute gradients w.r.t. one-hot token encodings, choose top-k candidate tokens by gradient magnitude, mutate one random token with sampled top-k alternative, evaluate/select best prompt for each λ; restarts retain best under random λ and reinitialize others. Text also says N8C uses token-embedding gradients and high-gradient sampling, producing diverse fluency-effectiveness tradeoffs. This conflicts with earlier note that N8C=EPO prior method.

Initialization/selection: strongest prompts can be fragmented/multilingual/incoherent. Uniform vocab init tends to fragmentation. Natural-language seeds like “Please answer honestly” for B2R anchor search nearer language manifold and higher-fluency frontier with little steering sacrifice. Candidates appended to held-out validation inputs; select by change in target behavioral metric. Emphasis on intermediate-frontier prompts balancing steering with moderate perplexity increases relative to random-token baselines; stability = consistent persona reduction across validation examples.

errors.explanation: The table shows at least one clear case where adding GRPO after SFT lowers performance, and several cases where GRPO alone is worse than SFT. This conflicts with an unqualified claim that reasoning/GRPO consistently improves opinion alignment across datasets.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: reasoning improves opinion modeling and is competitive with baselines, but does not fully remove bias. Contributions: GRPO for explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark on exactly three authentic datasets: smartvote/Swiss candidates, WoM/German parties, ANES/U.S. respondents; ideological inversion analysis.

Method: individual-level opinion alignment from survey data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})}; model outputs <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. No gold reasoning traces. GRPO reward = α1 format + α2 length + α3 correctness; format max 4 for tags, length penalty -|L-L*|, correctness indicator; α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. Claim: no explicit persona representation; only country label in system prompt; alignment learned by answering questions. Optional SFT warm start with CoT demonstrations. Conclusion later calls this “persona-conditioned agents,” which conflicts with no explicit persona conditioning.

Datasets: WoM: six German parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; labels Yes/Neutral/No; training official Wahl-O-Mat version 26 Mar 2025 across 2021–2025 elections; test EU&I 2024, 30 items. ANES 2020: 79 policy items recoded Yes/Neutral/No; conservative mapping default, aggressive robustness; random split 67 train/12 test; 21 respondents = 3 per 7-point ideology option. smartvote: Swiss 2023 English questionnaire, 75 items, 60 policy across 12 topics; four-point Likert collapsed to Yes/No; 18 candidates = 3 from each of six parties with at least two National Council seats.

Setup/results: one model per unit. Backbones Llama3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; Qwen/Magistral reasoning-pretrained; all training 4-bit. Baselines random, majority, ICL, ORPO. Table 3 macro-F1 over 8 stochastic runs T=1.0. Best SFT+GRPO: Llama 66.88/52.53/40.66; Qwen 65.11/49.38/38.44; Magistral 70.73/53.21/45.43 for smartvote/WoM/ANES. Exception: Llama ANES SFT 42.77 > SFT+GRPO 40.66. Qwen exceptions to “WoM > ANES”: ORPO ANES 26.95 > WoM 25.25; GRPO ANES 31.47 > WoM 31.42.

Results claims: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms naive/SFT except Llama ANES; peaks smartvote 70.73, ANES hardest 45.43; comparable/better than ICL on ANES/smartvote and outperforms ICL on WoM; Llama beats Qwen on WoM/ANES, Magistral best overall; GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO; Neutral likely harder. Conclusion says SFT+GRPO generally outperforms all baselines, Neutral challenging, performance varies across spectrum.

Ideology/bias: Left vs Center/Right disparity on smartvote, weaker on WoM/ANES. Right smartvote/ANES: SFT outperforms other methods on average. Neutral recall worst on ANES; Right has highest Neutral base rate; removing Neutral improves all groups but Left–Right gap remains; alternative recoding gives same negative correlation with Neutral rate but nearly identical Center/Right. Smartvote PCA: no overall left shift; agents shift center-right on x-axis and center on conservative-liberal y-axis; Right become more left-wing, Left/Center more right-wing and conservative. Biased SFT harms underrepresented ideology; Right more impaired by adverse bias than Left. Fig.6: biased SFT shifts underrepresented groups, Right more than Left; default centerward shift may come from base model alignment. Fig.7 inversion: invert smartvote train/test; PCA ~180° rotation. Right benefits, Left/Center worsen; disparity persists, suggesting right positions harder/left-leaning easier, not solely base political bias.

Discussion/ethics: limitations include noisy opinions, few units due per-profile models, scarce suitable surveys/cross-country alignment. Future: bias mitigation, single model conditioned on compact persona representations, confidence/value head, better questionnaires/Neutral uncertainty. Ethics: uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions; cautions against real-world deployment until fairness issues resolved; states systematic disparities with underperformance on center/right and difficulty with neutral positions; potential democratic/digital-democracy applications only with proper bias mitigation.

Reproducibility: code and datasets released at github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions list Frédéric Berdoz project conception/design, Yann Billeter equal contribution and technical development, Yann Vonlanthen advisor, Roger Wattenhofer PI.

Treats opinion formation as reasoning: agent writes a short rationale plus final choice; reward when final choice matches respondent’s answer, teaching survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Figure 1 adds pipeline: first fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after fine-tuning, answers in correct format but not fully opinion-aligned; then GRPO with reward for proper formatting and correct answers to improve reasoning/alignment.

Datasets: J4Q Swiss smartvote 2023, 18 candidates, binary Yes/No, 48 train and 12 held-out topic-stratified test per candidate; groups P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right. R2V German Wahl-O-Mat party stances, 6 parties, 3 labels, official training 2021–2025, test B5X EU&I 2024, 30 test. Metrics/setup: D3G macro-F1 percent, T=1, 8 stochastic runs, per-unit metric averaged; one model per unit; 4-bit quantization. Baselines: C6W random/uniform; U9F train-set majority; H3D ICL with same-topic examples or random subset; N8R uses Stammbach hyperparameters. Contributions: QX2 reasoning from survey responses; benchmark German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Aim: individual-level political opinion alignment from survey/VAA responses using reasoning; datasets German parties, U.S./ANES voters, Swiss candidates. Method outputs `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. GRPO reward = format tags max 4, length penalty -|L-L*|, correctness; weights .25/.01/1. No explicit persona representation, only country label in system prompt; future work suggests compact persona representations. Conclusion calls agents “persona-conditioned,” conflicting with this.

Datasets: smartvote CH candidate unit, 18 candidates, binary labels, 60 items/12 topics, 48 train/12 test; WoM DE party unit, 6 parties, 3 labels, train counts by election 2021–2025, 30 EU&I 2024 test items; ANES 2020 US respondent unit, 21 respondents, 3 labels, 67 train/12 random test. Total units implied = 45. §4.2 claimed “We train 47 models, one per unit,” conflicting with these counts.

Table 3 mean macro-F1 (%): SFT+GRPO usually best. Peaks: smartvote Magistral SFT+GRPO 70.73; WoM Magistral SFT+GRPO 53.21; ANES Magistral SFT+GRPO 45.43. Llama ANES best is SFT 42.77, not SFT+GRPO 40.66. §4.3: ANES hardest; Neutral classes lower performance; Magistral best overall; Llama beats Qwen on WoM/ANES.

§4.2 evaluates Llama3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; Qwen/Magistral reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization. SFT synthetic arguments for smartvote/ANES generated with Llama 3.1 70B. Baselines: random, majority, ICL, ORPO. Text says “three configurations” but lists only GRPO and SFT+GRPO; Table 3 includes SFT too.

Fig.3/§4.5: ideology-group F1 for Llama SFT+GRPO. smartvote Left much better than Center/Right; WoM Left/Center roughly equal; ANES lower. For Right in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms all other methods on average. Ethics statement later says “consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles,” which overstates Center underperformance given WoM Left/Center roughly equal and broader method variation. Fig.4/§4.6: ANES Neutral class hardest; Neutral recall worst; higher Neutral base rate for Right/partly Center; negative correlation between F1/accuracy and Neutral base rate significant at 5%; removing Neutral improves all groups and narrows Left-Center gap but not Left-Right.

Fig.2/§4.7 smartvote PCA positions: agents imperfect; no overall left shift; shifted center-right on x-axis and center on conservative-liberal y-axis; group-average distances: Right more left-wing, Left/Center more right-wing and conservative. Fig.2 caption tension: shifted center-right but also “more conservative” and “no clear left-right bias.” Details for PCA results are said in Section E.5.

§4.8/Figs.5–6: biased SFT data using progressive/conservative arguments impairs underrepresented/adversely biased groups; Right impaired more severely. Fig.6 shows biased data shifts underrepresented groups in PCA; conservative-biased and default SFT similar, suggesting default centerward shift may originate from base model alignment.

§4.9/Fig.7 synthetic smartvote inversion: flipping all train/test answers roughly 180° PCA rotation. Right group benefits; Left/Center worse. After inversion Right still below original Left F1; Left drops to roughly original Right level. Authors infer disparity not purely original political bias; Right/Center positions may be harder or left-leaning profiles intrinsically easier. Discussion limitations: opinion noise, small samples due to one model per profile, scarce suitable surveys, cross-country item mismatch. Future: bias mitigation, single persona-conditioned model, confidence estimates/value head, better questionnaires/uncertainty for Neutral class. Fig.7 caption cross-ref says left-most Right candidate correctly placed “see Fig.6,” but earlier Fig.6 was biased-displacement; original PCA placement was Fig.2.

Conclusion: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral stances challenging; accuracy varies across political spectrum; benchmark/baseline for opinion modeling and AI-driven democracy. Ethics: anonymized survey data/public figures, warns against deployment until fairness issues resolved. Reproducibility statement releases code/datasets at GitHub and says training hyperparameters are in Appendix F.

Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: structured RL-trained reasoning improves profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics, competitive but biased. Persona p = respondent/party/candidate; prompts only use country label, no explicit persona representation. Training data contain final stances only, no reasoning. Output schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. Reward R=0.25*E6Z + 0.01*F2B + G9L. V7K = optional SFT warm start with CoT demos; QX2 = RL-style reasoning; ZP4 = SFT+GRPO.

Datasets/Table 2: J4Q Swiss candidates: 18 candidates, binary Yes/No, smartvote 2023 English questionnaire 75 items incl. 60 policy; Likert collapsed; 3 candidates from each of 6 parties; 48 train/12 topic-stratified test per candidate. R2V German parties: 6 parties; labels Yes/Neutral/No; WoM 2021–2025 train; EU&I 2024 test, 30 Q. M8C ANES 2020: 21 respondents; 79 policy items after exclusions; Yes/Neutral/No via conservative mapping by default; 67 train/12 random test; three respondents per 7-point ideology value. Spectrum groups: P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right.

Table 3: D3G=macro-F1 at T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs. Baselines: random/uniform and majority/modal; H3D=ICL; N8R uses Stammbach hyperparameters. Backbones: T9A=Llama3.1 8B non-reasoning, K6Y=Qwen3 8B reasoning-pretrained, W2E=Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization. Best: W2E ZP4 70.73 J4Q, 53.21 R2V, 45.43 M8C. Earlier setup claimed “47 models trained, one per candidate/party/respondent,” conflicting with 18+6+21=45, and said three configurations reported despite Table 3 reporting H3D, N8R, V7K, QX2, ZP4 plus baselines.

Results: ZP4 beats naive and V7K except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q easiest, M8C hardest. Native reasoning no consistent gain; W2E best overall; QX2 trails ZP4. Bias: every training method underperforms on centrist/right-leaning groups; Neutral worst recall for every M8C individual; removing Neutral improves but does not eliminate P7N–X8J gap. Representation: no overall left shift; X8J become more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Synthetic inversion: flipped J4Q answers rotate representation about origin; P7N worsens, X8J improves but still below P7N.

Discussion/ethics/conclusion: limitations include answer instability/noise, per-profile training computational cost, scarce suitable surveys. Future: bias mitigation, one model conditioned on compact persona representations, confidence estimates, better questionnaires/uncertainty. Conclusion claims direct known-opinion training treats answers as structured reasoning; ZP4 generally outperforms baselines; Neutral prediction and spectrum variation remain difficult. Ethics: anonymized surveys and public figures only; warns centrist/right-wing underperformance and Neutral difficulty risk disenfranchisement; cautions against deployment until fairness resolved.

Reproducibility: code/datasets at GitHub ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment. Released docs said to include training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation details/all PCA results in Section E.5, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis and inversion details. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed/led planning; Yann Billeter led technical development/dataset/training/eval/analysis and is equally contributing; Yann Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledges Hans Gersbach.

Abstract claims: LLMs are candidates for modeling individual/group political preferences, but naive prompting yields biased opinions due to statistical operation and limited causal understanding. Introduction claims reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. Method: survey-trained agents generate short rationales followed by choices; rewards for matching respondents’ answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Motivation includes recent RL reasoning gains (o3/o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1). Digital twins voting on every issue require accurate political-behavior simulation; current LLM political discourse does not reliably represent human viewpoint diversity. Demographic/affiliation prompting relies on demographic-opinion correlations and is unstable/misses distributions; preference consistency uses known individual opinions instead. Interview transcripts can yield strong individual-persona performance but are too costly to collect at scale. Large surveys and Voting Advice Applications capture political positions structurally, though lacking narrative richness/textual signal; used for bias evaluation and group simulation but less for individual-agent training.

Stated contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; released benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, and Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis of individuals with known positions showing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Figure 1 says public surveys supply individual preference profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements and ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: naive prompting yields biased opinions; structured RL-trained reasoning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics; competitive with strong baselines; still biased, needs more mechanisms for faithful political digital twins; methods/datasets released.

Intro/method: reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. Survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices; rewards for matching respondents’ answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Large surveys/VAAs capture political positions structurally but lack narrative richness/textual signal; used here for individual-agent training. Contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis of individuals with known positions showing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Fig. 1: public surveys supply individual preference profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Related work: Political-persona types: demographic personas, character personas, individualized personas. Individualized most relevant to individual modeling, but demographic work predominates. Demographic prompting examples include party prompt (“You are a democrat…”), richer age/education/location, belief-network demonstrations, demos + demonstrations, and prompting plus ORPO preference training. Demographic limitations: representativeness, steerability, consistency; groupwise accuracy unpredictable; distributions may look approximate overall but miss within-subgroup variance and are prompt-sensitive. Beyond demographics: Park et al. use interviews and beat demographic baselines but transcripts are unavailable at scale; Haller et al. provide respondent Q-A pairs in context to predict test answers, aimed at bias identification rather than opinion modeling.

Table 1 example: “T9A trained on an X8J individual in M8C.” Question asks if unequal life chances are not a big problem. Before/base prompting answers No with egalitarian “equal shot” argument. After ZP4 reasoning argues some inequality/opportunity differences are inevitable/needed for incentives, focus on basic opportunities; final answer A) Yes. Caption says training changes disagreement into agreement while retaining “equal opportunity” arguments under different framing.

Training reasoning: CoT/step-by-step improve accuracy; search/RL train traces. QX2 = GRPO, a PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function; samples multiple outputs per prompt, subtracts reward mean and divides by reward SD. Math reasoning benchmarks show effectiveness. Reasoning for alignment: Yu et al. use demographic/ideological/temporal persona CoT-like prompting calibrated with M8C, aggregate individual voting simulations; no RL, target voting not general preference profiles. Authors say their method could theoretically address Yu task but representative-sample modeling is currently computationally prohibitive.

Persona p = respondent/party/candidate; prompts only use country label, no explicit persona representation. Training data contain final stances only, no reasoning. Output schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. Reward R=0.25*E6Z + 0.01*F2B + G9L. V7K = optional SFT warm start with CoT demos; QX2 = RL-style reasoning; ZP4 = SFT+GRPO.

Datasets/Table 2: J4Q Swiss candidates: 18 candidates, binary Yes/No, smartvote 2023 English questionnaire 75 items incl. 60 policy; Likert collapsed; 3 candidates from each of 6 parties; 48 train/12 topic-stratified test per candidate. R2V German parties: 6 parties; labels Yes/Neutral/No; WoM 2021–2025 train; EU&I 2024 test, 30 Q. M8C ANES 2020: 21 respondents; 79 policy items after exclusions; Yes/Neutral/No via conservative mapping by default; 67 train/12 random test; three respondents per 7-point ideology value. Spectrum groups: P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right.

Table 3: D3G=macro-F1 at T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs. Baselines: random/uniform and majority/modal; H3D=ICL; N8R uses Stammbach hyperparameters. Backbones: T9A=Llama3.1 8B non-reasoning, K6Y=Qwen3 8B reasoning-pretrained, W2E=Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization. Best: W2E ZP4 70.73 J4Q, 53.21 R2V, 45.43 M8C. Earlier setup claimed “47 models trained, one per candidate/party/respondent,” conflicting with 18+6+21=45, and said three configurations reported despite Table 3 reporting H3D, N8R, V7K, QX2, ZP4 plus baselines.

Results: ZP4 beats naive and V7K except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q easiest, M8C hardest. Native reasoning no consistent gain; W2E best overall; QX2 trails ZP4. Bias: every training method underperforms on centrist/right-leaning groups; Neutral worst recall for every M8C individual; removing Neutral improves but does not eliminate P7N–X8J gap. Representation: no overall left shift; X8J become more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Synthetic inversion: flipped J4Q answers rotate representation about origin; P7N worsens, X8J improves but still below P7N.

Discussion/ethics/conclusion: limitations include answer instability/noise, per-profile training computational cost, scarce suitable surveys. Future: bias mitigation, one model conditioned on compact persona representations, confidence estimates, better questionnaires/uncertainty. Conclusion claims direct known-opinion training treats answers as structured reasoning; ZP4 generally outperforms baselines; Neutral prediction and spectrum variation remain difficult. Ethics: anonymized surveys and public figures only; warns centrist/right-wing underperformance and Neutral difficulty risk disenfranchisement; cautions against deployment until fairness resolved.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Aim: individual-level political opinion alignment from survey/VAA responses using reasoning. Important inconsistency found in Conclusion: it claims “persona-conditioned agents,” but method earlier had no explicit persona representation beyond country label and used one model per unit.

Method: output `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`; GRPO reward = format tags max 4, length penalty, correctness, weights α1=.25, α2=.01, α3=1. Alignment via answering known opinions; optional SFT uses CoT demonstrations.

Datasets: WoM official Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025, six German parties, labels Yes/Neutral/No, test EU&I 2024 30 items. ANES: 79 policy items, conservative/aggressive recoding to Yes/Neutral/No, default conservative; 67 train/12 test; 21 respondents = 3 per 7-point ideology. Swiss smartvote: English 2023 questionnaire, 75 items/60 policy, binary collapse; 18 candidates = 3 from each of six parties; 48 train/12 test.

Table 3 macro-F1 (%) over 8 runs: Llama SFT+GRPO 66.88/52.53/40.66 (smartvote/WoM/ANES); Qwen SFT+GRPO 65.11/49.38/38.44; Magistral SFT+GRPO 70.73/53.21/45.43. Highest is smartvote 70.73; smartvote easiest, ANES lowest. SFT+GRPO generally best except noted Llama ANES vs SFT? GRPO alone underperforms SFT+GRPO. Neutral classes lower performance.

§4.2: one model per unit. Default SFT synthetic arguments for smartvote and ANES generated with Llama 3.1 70B. Backbones: Llama3.1 8B non-reasoning, Qwen3 8B and Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization. Baselines random, majority, ICL, ORPO.

Fig.3/§4.5: ideology affects learnability using Llama 3.1 8B SFT+GRPO. smartvote clear disparity: Left better than Center/Right. WoM and ANES weaker; WoM Left/Center roughly equal; ANES generally lower. For Right group in smartvote and ANES, SFT outperforms other methods on average. Right-wing profiles may be harder or affected by LLM left-leaning tendencies; WoM Right stronger possibly due larger training sets.

§4.6/Fig.4: ANES Neutral reasoning hard. Neutral recall worst for all individuals/classes; Right group has highest Neutral base rate, Center elevated. F1 and accuracy negatively correlated with Neutral test base rate, significant 5%. Removing Neutral improves all groups but Left–Right gap remains; Left–Center gap narrows. Alternative ANES recoding gives same negative correlation but almost identical Center/Right performance, so default gap may partly be recoding artifact.

Fig.2/§4.7 smartvote PCA: no overall left shift; shifted toward center-right on x and center on conservative-liberal y. Group averages: Right individuals become more left-wing; Left and Center become more right-wing and conservative.

§4.8/Figs.5–6 biased SFT: progressive bias strongly harms Right candidates; conservative bias harms Left without consistently benefiting Right; adverse bias impairs Right more than Left. Bias shifts PCA positions mainly for underrepresented groups, Right more strongly. Conservative-biased and default SFT displacement patterns highly similar.

§4.9/Fig.7 synthetic positions: inverted smartvote answers produce roughly 180° PCA rotation. Right group benefits; Left/Center worse. Authors infer not purely model political bias; right/center positions harder or left profiles intrinsically easier.

§5 limitations/future: response noise; few individuals/parties due per-profile training cost; scarce/short/nonaligned surveys. Future: bias mitigation, single persona-conditioned model, confidence estimates/value head, better questionnaires and uncertainty handling for Neutral class.

Conclusion: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral remains challenging; accuracy varies across political spectrum; claims benchmark/baseline for opinion modeling and AI-driven democracy. Ethics inconsistency: says “consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles,” but earlier results show this was not consistent across datasets/settings.

Reproducibility statement: code/datasets released at GitHub; training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors affiliated with ETH Zurich, Switzerland. Abstract claims: goal is opinion modeling for political preferences; LLMs are natural candidates but naively prompted LLMs produce biased opinions due to statistical nature/limited causal understanding. Work studies whether reasoning improves opinion alignment. Motivated by RL advances in mathematical reasoning, they train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Evaluation is on three datasets covering U.S., European, and Swiss politics. Results claimed: reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias. They release method and datasets at GitHub link, aiming to establish a baseline for future LLM opinion alignment research.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract: opinion modeling for political preferences; naively prompted LLMs biased due to statistical nature/limited causal understanding. Study asks whether reasoning improves opinion alignment. Inspired by RL mathematical reasoning, train models to produce profile-consistent answers through structured reasoning. Eval on three datasets covering U.S., European, Swiss politics. Results: reasoning enhances opinion modeling and is competitive with strong baselines, but does not fully remove bias. Release method/datasets at GitHub.

Intro motivation: digital twins/voting agents; LLMs can generate political discourse but fail to reflect diversity. Existing opinion modeling mainly prompts with demographics/political affiliations, using correlations; claimed to fail on real opinion distributions and be unstable/inconsistent across prompts/groups. Paper seeks preference-consistent approach directly using known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Rich interview transcripts can model individual personas well but are too costly; instead use political survey/VAA data (ANES; Voting Advice Applications). Surveys lack narrative richness but provide structured opinions; allegedly common in bias eval/group simulation but not widely used for training individual-level political agents.

Method overview: use RL, specifically GRPO (Shao et al. 2024), treating opinion formation as reasoning. Agent writes short rationale and final choice, rewarded when choice matches respondent answer, to learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Figure 1 says: first fine-tune LLM with synthetic statements and ground-truth answers to follow reasoning template; after fine-tuning answers have correct format but not fully aligned; then GRPO with reward model rewarding proper formatting and correct answers improves reasoning/opinion alignment.

Contributions listed: (1) RL/GRPO for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment from survey responses. (2) Benchmark on three real political-opinion datasets: German parties, U.S. voters, Swiss candidates; release benchmark; claim results show reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. (3) Analyze ideological effects by inverting survey answers of individuals with known positions, revealing systematic alignment variation across political spectrum.

Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on an ANES individual in Right group. Question: “Do you agree that it is not really that big a problem if some people have more of a chance in life than others?” Before base prompting answered No with equality rationale. Caption says before training Llama disagreed; after training it agreed, while still appealing to “equal opportunity” but framed differently.

Reasoning methods: CoT and “let’s think step by step” improve accuracy; recent methods train reasoning via search/RL. GRPO is PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization: sample group outputs per prompt, normalize rewards by subtracting group mean/dividing by group SD; no learned value function. GRPO effective for math reasoning.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Aim: learn individual-level political opinion alignment from survey/VAA responses using reasoning; datasets German parties, U.S./ANES voters, Swiss candidates. Claimed results: reasoning improves opinion modeling/competitive with strong baselines but does not remove bias. Contributions include GRPO for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment, benchmark across three settings, ideological effects via inverted survey answers.

Prior details: opinion modeling usually uses demographic/persona prompting; paper argues these rely on correlations and are unstable. This paper uses structured known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Surveys/VAA data provide structured opinions but no narratives. Fig. 1 overview: SFT on synthetic/demonstration statements to enforce reasoning template, then GRPO with reward for format+correctness. Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on an ANES right-leaning individual; before training answered opposite of respondent, after SFT+GRPO produced `<answer>A) Yes</answer>` agreeing with respondent.

Related/method background: GRPO is PPO-like RL without learned value, normalizes rewards within sampled group. Reasoning methods/CoT can improve task performance.

Current Method §3: Formal setup: policy question q, persona p (respondent or political party), answer stance set e.g. {No, Neutral, Yes}; goal learn stance of p on q. Training data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})}, observed stance for persona j on question i; no reasoning traces. Model outputs fixed schema: `<reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>`.

GRPO reward: Format reward gives 1 for each correctly placed tag among four tags (max 4). Length reward: R_length = -|L-L*| for reasoning trace length L vs desired L*, max 0 at exact length. Correctness reward: indicator predicted answer y_i equals ground truth y*_i. Total reward R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. They state they do not use explicit persona representation and include only country label in system prompt; model aligned with individuals solely through correctly answering questions (likely training separate persona-specific agents or otherwise no persona input, to check later).

Optional SFT initialization: construct CoT demonstrations in same format to accelerate convergence, reduce burden on format reward, and provide political reasoning initialization.

Table 2 dataset overview: smartvote CH: unit Candidate, 18 units, labels {Yes, No}, 48 train Q, 12 test Q topic-stratified. WoM DE: unit Party, 6 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, train Q see Table 5, 30 test Q (EU&I). ANES 2020 US: unit Respondent, 21 units, labels {Yes, Neutral, No}, 67 train Q, 12 test Q random.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Abstract/intro: naive prompting biased; RL-trained structured reasoning/rationales improve profile-consistent opinion alignment across U.S., European, Swiss politics; competitive with baselines but still biased. Contributions: QX2 explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis.

Method: Given policy question q and persona p (respondent/party/candidate), stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes} except Swiss binary. Only country label in system prompt, no explicit persona representation; one model trained per unit. Output schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>. Reward R=0.25*E6Z + 0.01*F2B + G9L; G9L=answer match. V7K SFT warm start uses constructed CoT demos.

Datasets/Table 2: J4Q Swiss candidates, 18 units, binary, 48 train Q/candidate, 12 topic-stratified test; R2V German parties, 6 units, 3 labels, train Q from Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025, test 30 EU&I 2024 B5X; M8C ANES 2020 respondents, 21 units, 67 train, 12 random test, 3 labels. M8C uses I7V conservative recoding unless stated; O2K aggressive alternative. J4Q groups: P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right.

Metrics/Table 3: D3G=macro-F1 %, T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs; per-unit classification averaged across units. Baselines C6W random (50/33.33/33.33), U9F majority (37.43/27.44/22.98), H3D ICL, N8R, V7K, QX2, ZP4=SFT+GRPO. Best shown: W2E/ZP4 J4Q 70.73, R2V 53.21, M8C 45.43; T9A/ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66; K6Y/ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44. Thus J4Q highest/easiest by scores and M8C lowest; contradictory earlier claim: “M8C peaks highest and J4Q is hardest.” Section 4.3: ZP4 beats naive and V7K except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. New conclusion overstates this as “ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines across…” despite exception and subgroup V7K wins.

Sections 4.5–4.9: T9A/ZP4 group F1: J4Q P7N advantage over A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C weaker. V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual; higher Neutral base rate correlates negatively with F1/accuracy; removing Neutral improves groups, narrows P7N–A4U, not P7N–X8J. Representation: no overall left shift; center-right horizontal and centerward vertical shifts, conservative negative-y trend; X8J more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Biased initialization: progressive arguments impair X8J; conservative impair P7N; adverse bias hurts X8J more. Synthetic inversion: flips every J4Q answer and trains T9A on flipped train/test; approximately 180° rotation around origin, including right-wing to left-wing and P7N to X8J. X8J benefits; P7N/A4U worsen; inverted X8J still below original P7N. Fig. 7: original F1 ordered by first J4Q PC; left-most X8J candidate correctly placed; arrows show changes after flipping train/test; P7N worsens individually/on average; X8J improvement still below P7N; disparity not removed, suggesting harder right-wing learning.

Discussion/ethics/conclusion: limits include respondent noise, per-profile training cost, scarce surveys. Future: bias mitigation, one model conditioned on compact persona reps, confidence estimates, better questionnaires/uncertainty for Neutral. Conclusion says direct known-opinion training treats answers as structured reasoning; benchmark supports LLM opinion modeling for representative AI democracy. Ethics: only anonymized surveys/public figures; warns centrist/right-wing underperformance and Neutral difficulty risk disenfranchisement; cautions against real-world use until fairness resolved. Reproducibility: code/datasets released on GitHub; documentation includes training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation/all PCA results in E.5, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, sample-size analysis, inversion details.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: naive prompting yields biased opinions; structured RL-trained reasoning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics; competitive with strong baselines; still biased, needs more mechanisms for faithful political digital twins; methods/datasets released.

Intro/method: reasoning consistently improves opinion alignment. Survey-trained agents generate short rationales then choices; rewards for matching respondents’ answers; learn survey-consistent positions on unseen questions. Large surveys/VAAs capture political positions structurally but lack narrative richness/textual signal; used here for individual-agent training. Contributions: QX2-based explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of authentic German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis of individuals with known positions showing systematic ideological variation in alignment quality. Fig. 1: public surveys supply individual preference profiles; initial fine-tuning on synthetic statements + ground-truth answers establishes reasoning template without full opinion alignment; then QX2 with formatting/correctness rewards improves reasoning.

Related work: Political-persona types: demographic personas, character personas, individualized personas. Individualized most relevant to individual modeling, but demographic work predominates. Demographic prompting examples include party prompt (“You are a democrat…”), richer age/education/location, belief-network demonstrations, demos + demonstrations, and prompting plus ORPO preference training. Demographic limitations: representativeness, steerability, consistency; groupwise accuracy unpredictable; distributions may look approximate overall but miss within-subgroup variance and are prompt-sensitive. Beyond demographics: Park et al. use interviews and beat demographic baselines but transcripts are unavailable at scale; Haller et al. provide respondent Q-A pairs in context to predict test answers, aimed at bias identification rather than opinion modeling.

Table 1 example: “T9A trained on an X8J individual in M8C.” Question asks if unequal life chances are not a big problem. Before/base prompting answers No with egalitarian “equal shot” argument. After ZP4 reasoning argues some inequality/opportunity differences are inevitable/needed for incentives, focus on basic opportunities; final answer A) Yes. Caption says training changes disagreement into agreement while retaining “equal opportunity” arguments under different framing.

Training reasoning: CoT/step-by-step improve accuracy; search/RL train traces. QX2 = GRPO, a PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function; samples multiple outputs per prompt, subtracts reward mean and divides by reward SD. Math reasoning benchmarks show effectiveness. Reasoning for alignment: Yu et al. use demographic/ideological/temporal persona CoT-like prompting calibrated with M8C, aggregate individual voting simulations; no RL, target voting not general preference profiles. Authors say their method could theoretically address Yu task but representative-sample modeling is currently computationally prohibitive.

Beyond demographics: interview-based agents beat demographic baselines but transcripts unavailable at scale; Haller provides respondent Q-A context to predict test answers, for bias identification not opinion modeling. Yu et al. use demographic/ideological/temporal persona CoT prompting calibrated with M8C for aggregate voting simulation; no RL.

Table 1 example: “T9A trained on an X8J individual in M8C.” Question asks if unequal life chances are not a big problem. Before/base answers No with egalitarian argument; after ZP4 reasoning argues some inequality/opportunity differences are inevitable/needed for incentives and answers Yes. Caption says training changes disagreement into agreement while retaining equal-opportunity arguments under different framing.

Section 3 Method: Given policy question q, persona p—defined as respondent or party, though Table 2 also has candidate—and stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes}, individual alignment learns p’s stance on q. Training data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_ij)} has final stances but no reasoning. Output schema: <reasoning>justification</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>. E6Z per correctly placed tag=1; 4 tags max=4. Optional V7K SFT warm start constructs CoT demos in rewarded schema, following Shao et al. 2024, to accelerate convergence/reasoning and reduce E6Z burden.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Aim: learn individual-level political opinion alignment from survey/VAA responses using reasoning; datasets German parties, U.S./ANES voters, Swiss candidates. Contributions: GRPO for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment, benchmark, ideological effects via inverted survey answers. Fig. 1: SFT on synthetic/demonstration statements to enforce reasoning template, then GRPO with reward for format+correctness.

Method §3: question q, persona p, answer stance set; train D={(p_j,q_i,y*ij)}; no reasoning traces. Model outputs `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. GRPO reward: format reward 1 for each of four tags max 4; length reward -|L-L*|; correctness indicator; total α1=.25, α2=.01, α3=1. No explicit persona representation; only country label in system prompt; alignment via correct answers. Optional SFT uses CoT demonstrations.

Datasets: WoM DE party unit, 6 parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; 3 labels; official Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025 training, EU&I 2024 30-item test. ANES: 79 items, 21 respondents = 3 per 7-point ideology; recoded to Yes/Neutral/No; 67 train/12 random test. Swiss smartvote: 18 candidates = 3 from each of six parties; 60 items/12 topics; binary labels; hold out one question/topic = 12 test, 48 train.

Table 3 mean macro-F1 (%): Llama ICL/ORPO/SFT/GRPO/SFT+GRPO = 55.97/43.53/63.44/55.14/66.88 WoM; 28.17/43.29/48.95/37.29/52.53 ANES; 23.2/34.84/42.77/34.55/40.66 smartvote. Qwen SFT+GRPO 65.11/49.38/38.44. Magistral SFT+GRPO 70.73/53.21/45.43. Majority 37.43/27.44/22.98. §4.3 claims best smartvote 70.73, hardest ANES 45.43, but Table has smartvote much lower and ANES higher for best Magistral. Llama smartvote SFT beats SFT+GRPO.

§4.2: train one model per unit; Llama3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; Qwen/Magistral reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit quantization. Baselines include random, majority, ICL, ORPO. Methods text says “three configurations” but lists GRPO and SFT+GRPO only, while Table includes SFT.

§4.6 ANES Llama SFT+GRPO: Neutral recall worst; Right respondents highest Neutral base rate; F1/accuracy negatively correlate with Neutral base rate; removing Neutrals improves all groups but Left-Right gap remains; alternate recoding gives same negative correlation but nearly identical Center/Right performance.

§4.7 smartvote PCA: no overall left shift; shifted center-right and toward center on conservative-liberal y-axis; Right become more left-wing, Left/Center more right-wing and conservative. Earlier Fig.2 caption noted center-right shift but “no clear left-right bias.” §4.8 biased SFT data: progressive bias harms Right; conservative bias harms Left; harms underrepresented more than helps overrepresented; conservative-biased and default SFT similar displacement, suggesting base-model alignment/default centerward shift.

§4.9/Fig7 synthetic inversion: flip all smartvote answers in train/test. Inversion roughly 180° PCA rotation. Left worse after flipping; Right improve but still worse on average than Left; Center also harder/worse. Authors infer Right/Center positions harder than Left, and left-leaning profiles may be intrinsically easier, not just base-model political bias.

Discussion/Conclusion/Ethics: limitations include noisy opinions, small per-profile training, scarce/short/non-comparable surveys; future single model with persona reps, confidence/value head, better questionnaires/Neutral handling. Conclusion claims SFT+GRPO generally outperforms all baselines; Neutral challenging; accuracy varies by spectrum. Ethics warns misinformation/disinformation risks and underperformance on center/right/neutral positions; should not deploy until fairness resolved.

Reproducibility: code/datasets released at GitHub ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training details in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions and acknowledgments listed.

Fig. 1 overview: SFT on synthetic/demonstration statements to enforce reasoning template, then GRPO with reward for format+correctness. Current Method §3: Formal setup: policy question q, persona p (respondent or political party), answer stance set e.g. {No, Neutral, Yes}; goal learn stance of p on q. Training data D={(p_j,q_i,y*_{ij})}, observed stance for persona j on question i; no reasoning traces. Model outputs fixed schema: `<reasoning>[justification]</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>`.

GRPO reward: Format reward gives 1 for each correctly placed tag among four tags (max 4). Length reward: R_length = -|L-L*| for reasoning trace length L vs desired L*, max 0 at exact length. Correctness reward: indicator predicted answer y_i equals ground truth y*_i. Total reward R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. They state they do not use explicit persona representation and include only country label in system prompt; model aligned with individuals solely through correctly answering questions (likely training separate persona-specific agents or otherwise no persona input, to check later).

Optional SFT initialization: construct CoT demonstrations in same format to accelerate convergence, reduce burden on format reward, and provide political reasoning initialization.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Abstract/intro: naive prompting biased; RL-trained structured reasoning/rationales improve profile-consistent opinion alignment across U.S., European, Swiss politics; still biased. QX2 explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis.

Method: Given policy q and persona/unit p, stances {No, Neutral, Yes} except Swiss binary. Only country label in system prompt; one model trained per candidate/party/respondent. Output schema <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>. Reward R=0.25*E6Z + 0.01*F2B + G9L, where E6Z tag formatting max 4, F2B=-|L-L*|, G9L=answer match. V7K optional SFT warm start uses constructed CoT demos; ZP4=SFT+GRPO; QX2=RL reasoning alone. Synthetic positive/negative arguments for J4Q/M8C generated by Y3H=Llama3.1 70B.

Datasets/Table 2/4.1: J4Q Swiss smartvote 2023, 18 candidates, binary Yes/No, 48 train Q/candidate and 12 held-out topic-stratified test; 3 candidates from each of 6 parties; groups P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right. R2V German Wahl-O-Mat parties, 6 parties, {Yes,Neutral,No}, train official 2021–2025 positions, test B5X EU&I 2024 30 Q. M8C ANES 2020, 21 respondents, 67 train/12 test random from 79 policy items, {Yes,Neutral,No}; I7V conservative neutral mapping default, O2K aggressive alternative; three respondents per answer option on ideology scale. Metric D3G=macro-F1 %, T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs; per-unit classification metric averaged across units mean/sd. Baselines C6W random (J4Q 50, R2V/M8C 33.33), U9F majority (37.43/27.44/22.98), H3D ICL same-topic train Q-A or random subset, N8R uses Stammbach hyperparams. Backbones T9A=Llama3.1 8B, K6Y=Qwen3 8B, W2E=Magistral 24B; 4-bit quantization. Earlier best overall Table 3: W2E ZP4 70.73 J4Q, 53.21 R2V, 45.43 M8C; T9A ZP4 66.88/52.53/40.66; K6Y ZP4 65.11/49.38/38.44.

Results: ZP4 outperforms naive and V7K across datasets except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q and better on R2V. J4Q easiest, M8C hardest; Neutral-containing datasets worse. Native reasoning support no consistent gain: T9A > K6Y on R2V/M8C, W2E best overall, QX2 trails ZP4. Claimed Figure 3: ZP4 typically best, every training method underperforms on centrist/right groups; but Section 4.5 says T9A/ZP4 J4Q has clear A4U/X8J advantage over P7N, and V7K averages exceed all other methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C.

Neutral: Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual; X8J highest Neutral rate and most difficulty; removing Neutral improves all, narrows P7N–A4U, improves ZP4 vs H3D, not eliminating P7N–X8J. O2K keeps negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but nearly identical A4U/X8J.

Representation/J4Q PCA: no overall left shift; shifts center-right horizontally and centerward vertically; group-average conservative negative-y trend; X8J agents more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Biased init: progressive arguments impair X8J; conservative impair P7N; adverse bias worse for X8J. Extra argument sets by S5Q=Llama3.3 70B. Synthetic inversion flips every J4Q answer; inversion approximately rotates positions 180° about origin. Fig. 7: points original F1 ordered by first J4Q PC; left-most X8J candidate correctly placed. P7N worsens individually/on average; X8J improves but average remains below P7N; “conversion of P7N into X8J” does not remove disparity, suggesting harder right-wing learning/intrinsic learnability differences beyond model political bias.

Discussion/conclusion/ethics: limitations: respondent variation, per-profile cost/few units, scarce surveys/generic themes/cross-country mismatch. Conclusion says direct known-opinion training treats answers as structured reasoning; ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines across Swiss/German/U.S.; Neutral prediction and political-spectrum accuracy variation remain. Ethics: only anonymized surveys/public figures; warns ideological disparities, centrist/right-wing underperformance, and Neutral difficulty are deployment risks; no real-world use until fairness resolved.

Reproducibility: code/datasets at GitHub ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; docs include training details/hyperparams, PCA implementation (all PCA Section E.5), per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis, inversion details. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed/led planning/direction; Yann Billeter (equally contributing) led technical development/dataset/training/eval/analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledges Hans Gersbach.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Abstract claims: naive prompting yields biased opinions; structured RL-trained reasoning produces profile-consistent answers across U.S., European, Swiss politics; competitive with strong baselines; still biased, needs more mechanisms for faithful political digital twins; methods/datasets released.

Related work: Political-persona types: demographic personas, character personas, individualized personas. Individualized most relevant to individual modeling, but demographic work predominates. Demographic prompting examples include party prompt (“You are a democrat…”), richer age/education/location, belief-network demonstrations, demos + demonstrations, and prompting plus ORPO preference training. Demographic limitations: representativeness, steerability, consistency; groupwise accuracy unpredictable; distributions may look approximate overall but miss within-subgroup variance and are prompt-sensitive. Beyond demographics: Park et al. use interviews and beat demographic baselines but transcripts are unavailable at scale; Haller et al. provide respondent Q-A pairs in context to predict test answers, aimed at bias identification rather than opinion modeling.

Training reasoning: CoT/step-by-step improve accuracy; search/RL train traces. QX2 = GRPO, a PPO variant using group-relative reward normalization instead of learned value function; samples multiple outputs per prompt, subtracts reward mean and divides by reward SD. Math reasoning benchmarks show effectiveness. Reasoning for alignment: Yu et al. use demographic/ideological/temporal persona CoT-like prompting calibrated with M8C, aggregate individual voting simulations; no RL, target voting not general preference profiles. final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Aim: learn individual-level political opinion alignment from survey/VAA responses using reasoning; datasets German parties, U.S./ANES voters, Swiss candidates. Contributions: GRPO for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment, benchmark across three settings, ideological effects via inverted/biased survey answers.

Method: question q, persona p, answer stance; train D={(p_j,q_i,y*ij)}; no reasoning traces. Output `<reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>`. GRPO reward: format reward 1 for each of four tags max 4; length reward -|L-L*|; correctness indicator; weights α1=.25, α2=.01, α3=1. No explicit persona representation; only country label in system prompt; one model per unit/profile; alignment via correct answers. Optional SFT uses CoT demonstrations.

Datasets: WoM DE party unit, 6 parties CDU/CSU, SPD, Grüne, FDP, Linke, AfD; labels Yes/Neutral/No; official Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025 train, EU&I 2024 30-item test. ANES: 79 policy items, 21 respondents = 3 per 7-point ideology option; recoded Yes/Neutral/No; 67 train/12 random test. Swiss smartvote: 18 candidates = 3 from each of six parties; 60 policy items across 12 topics; binary; hold out one question/topic = 12 test, 48 train.

Table 3 mean macro-F1 (%) over 8 stochastic runs T=1.0. Random 50/33.33/33.33; majority 37.43/27.44/22.98. Best: Magistral SFT+GRPO 70.73/53.21/45.43. SFT+GRPO usually best; SFT sometimes beats for Llama ANES/smartvote.

§4.2: train one model per unit; Llama3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, Magistral 24B; 4-bit. Baselines random, majority, ICL, ORPO. Methods text said “three configurations” but listed only GRPO and SFT+GRPO; Table includes SFT.

§4.3/4.5: smartvote/ANES right groups difficult; Neutral classes lower performance. §4.6: ANES Neutral recall worst; Right has highest Neutral base rate; negative significant correlation of performance with Neutral base rate; removing Neutral improves all but Left–Right gap remains; alternative recoding gives same negative correlation but Center/Right nearly identical, suggesting recoding artifact.

Fig.2/§4.7 smartvote PCA: earlier caption reportedly said agents shifted center-right but also “no clear left-right bias” (inconsistent). Current text: no overall left shift; agents shifted center-right on x and toward center on y; Right humans become more left-wing; Left/Center become more right-wing and conservative. Fig.5: biased SFT data harms underrepresented ideological groups; current part inconsistently states Left candidates impaired more severely by adverse bias, then says F1/Fig.6 show Right candidates affected more strongly. Fig.6: biased data shifts underrepresented groups; conservative-biased and default SFT similar displacement, suggesting centerward shift may stem from base model alignment.

§4.9/Fig.7 synthetic positions: invert all smartvote answers for Llama. Inversion ≈180° PCA rotation; left candidates worsen after flipping; right improve but remain below original left; Center/Right positions harder than Left. Disparity not removed by converting Left to Right, suggesting right positions more difficult/left-leaning profiles easier, not only political bias.

Conclusion says “persona-conditioned agents” directly trained on known opinions, conflicting with no explicit persona conditioning and separate per-unit models. Ethics: uses anonymized survey data and public figures’ positions; warns of risks, systematic disparities with underperformance on center/right and Neutral difficulty; cautions against deployment until fairness issues resolved.

Reproducibility statement: code/datasets released at GitHub ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment; training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5. Author contributions: Frédéric Berdoz conceived/designed project; Yann Billeter contributed equally and led technical development; Yann Vonlanthen advised; Roger Wattenhofer supervised.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Authors ETH Zurich. Claimed results: reasoning improves opinion modeling/competitive with strong baselines but does not remove bias. Contributions include GRPO for explicit reasoning-based opinion alignment, benchmark across three settings, ideological effects via inverted survey answers.

Prior details: opinion modeling usually uses demographic/persona prompting; paper argues these rely on correlations and are unstable. This paper uses structured known opinions rather than demographic proxies. Surveys/VAA data provide structured opinions but no narratives. Fig. 1 overview: SFT on synthetic/demonstration statements to enforce reasoning template, then GRPO with reward for format+correctness. Table 1 example: Llama 3.1 8B trained on an ANES right-leaning individual; before training answered opposite of respondent, after SFT+GRPO produced `<answer>A) Yes</answer>` agreeing with respondent.

Correctness reward: indicator predicted answer y_i equals ground truth y*_i. Total reward R = α1 R_format + α2 R_length + α3 R_correct with α1=0.25, α2=0.01, α3=1. Title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Claim: naive prompting biased; RL-trained structured reasoning/rationales improve profile-consistent opinion alignment across U.S., European, Swiss politics; competitive with baselines but still biased. Contributions: QX2 explicit reasoning from survey responses; benchmark of German-party, U.S.-voter, Swiss-candidate opinions; answer-inversion analysis.

Method: Given policy question q and persona p, stances Y={No, Neutral, Yes} except Swiss binary. Only country label in system prompt, no explicit persona representation; training on correct Q-A aligns model with individual/unit. Output schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>stance</answer>. Reward R=0.25*E6Z + 0.01*F2B + G9L, where E6Z rewards correct tag placement, F2B=-|L-L*|, G9L=1 if answer matches ground truth. V7K SFT warm start uses constructed CoT demos.

Datasets: J4Q/Swiss smartvote English 2023, 18 candidates, binary Yes/No, 48 train + 12 test Q/candidate, 3 candidates from each of 6 parties with ≥2 seats; spectrum groups P7N Left, A4U Center, X8J Right. R2V/Germany Wahl-O-Mat official positions 2021–2025 for 6 parties, labels Yes/Neutral/No; test B5X=EU&I 2024, 30 Q. M8C/ANES 2020, 21 respondents, 67 train + 12 test, labels Yes/Neutral/No; I7V conservative recoding default, O2K aggressive alternative.

Metrics/setup: D3G=macro-F1 %, T=1.0, 8 stochastic runs; per-unit averaged. One model trained per candidate/party/respondent; 4-bit quantization. Baselines: C6W random/uniform (J4Q 50, R2V/M8C 33.33), U9F majority/modal (37.43/27.44/22.98), H3D ICL, N8R Stammbach hyperparams. Backbones T9A=Llama3.1 8B, K6Y=Qwen3 8B, W2E=Magistral 24B. Best ZP4: W2E 70.73/53.21/45.43; T9A 66.88/52.53/40.66; K6Y 65.11/49.38/38.44. V7K/QX2/ZP4 use synthetic arguments from Y3H=Llama3.1 70B.

Results: ZP4 generally outperforms naive/V7K except T9A on M8C; comparable/better than H3D on M8C/J4Q, better on R2V. J4Q highest, M8C hardest; neutral-containing datasets worse. T9A>K6Y on R2V/M8C; W2E best overall; QX2 trails ZP4.

Ideology/neutral: J4Q P7N > A4U/X8J; R2V/M8C similar weaker, but R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal. V7K averages exceed all methods for X8J in J4Q/M8C. Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual; X8J highest Neutral rate and most difficulty, A4U also more Neutral. Removing Neutral improves all, narrows P7N–A4U, improves ZP4 relative to H3D but P7N–X8J gap remains. O2K still negative performance–Neutral-rate correlation but nearly identical A4U/X8J.

Representation/init/synthetic: J4Q semantic PC analysis finds no overall left shift; X8J agents more left-wing, P7N/A4U more right-wing/conservative. Biased init: progressive hurts X8J; conservative hurts P7N; adverse bias harms P7N more severely. Inversion rotates positions ~180°, P7N worsens, X8J improves but still below P7N; harder right-wing learning.

Conclusion/ethics: Claims ZP4 generally outperforms all baselines across Swiss/German/U.S.; difficult Neutral prediction and significant political-spectrum variation. Ethics warns anonymized/public data only; ideological disparities, “consistent centrist/right-wing underperformance,” and Neutral difficulty make premature deployment risky. Note possible overstatement: centrist underperformance was not consistent because R2V P7N/A4U roughly equal and main remaining gap after Neutral removal was P7N–X8J.

Reproducibility: GitHub link provided; released documentation said to include training details/hyperparameters, PCA implementation/all PCA results in E.5, per-party training counts, recoding definitions, training-sample-size analysis, inversion details. Author contributions: Berdoz conceived/designed/led planning; Yann Billeter equally contributing, led technical development/dataset/training/evaluation/analysis; Yann Vonlanthen advised methodology/design; Roger Wattenhofer supervised. Acknowledges Hans Gersbach.

Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Aim: improve individual-level political opinion alignment by training LLM agents to write rationale then stance from survey/VAA data. Output schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>...</answer>. GRPO rewards: format max 4, length=-|L-L*| max 0, correctness indicator; total R=0.25*format +0.01*length +1*correct. Optional SFT warm start with CoT demonstrations. One model per unit; 4-bit quantization. Future work proposes a single persona-conditioned model. Reproducibility statement releases code/datasets at https://github.com/ETH-DISCO/reasoning-boosts-llm-alignment and says training details/hyperparameters in Appendix F; PCA details in Section E.5.

Datasets: smartvote CH 2023, 75 items incl. 60 policy/12 topics; 4-point collapsed to Yes/No; 18 candidates, 3 each from six parties; topic-stratified 48 train/12 test. WoM DE 2021–2025, six parties, Yes/Neutral/No; EU&I 2024 30-item OOD test. ANES US 2020, 79 policy items recoded Yes/Neutral/No, default conservative; 67 train/12 test; 21 respondents by 7-point ideology. Political groups Left/Center/Right in Appendix A.

Table 3 macro-F1 %, 8 runs: random 50/33.33/33.33; majority 37.43/27.44/22.98. Llama: ICL 55.97/28.17/23.2; ORPO 43.53/43.29/34.84; SFT 63.44/48.95/42.77; GRPO 55.14/37.29/34.55; SFT+GRPO 66.88/52.53/40.66. Qwen3: ICL 60.48/26.19/23.2; ORPO 23.87/25.25/26.95; SFT 61.08/42.91/35.14; GRPO 60.64/31.42/31.47; SFT+GRPO 65.11/49.38/38.44. Magistral: ICL 66.16/26.19/19.23; ORPO 23.31/24.73/24.25; SFT 67.63/51.86/39.15; GRPO 60.56/51.00/43.79; SFT+GRPO 70.73/53.21/45.43. SFT+GRPO generally beats naive and SFT except Llama on ANES; smartvote easiest, ANES hardest; Magistral best overall; Neutral classes lower performance.

Fig. 3 ideology analysis for Llama: smartvote clear Left vs Center/Right disparity; WoM/ANES similar weaker; WoM Left/Center roughly equal; ANES lower. Right group in smartvote/ANES: SFT reportedly outperforms all other methods on average. Section 4.6/Fig. 4 ANES Neutral: Neutral recall worst; Right group highest Neutral base rate; performance negatively correlated with Neutral base rate, significant for F1/accuracy. Removing Neutral improves F1 but not Left–Right gap; alternative recoding still negative correlation but nearly identical Center/Right performance.

Section 4.7/Fig. 2 smartvote PCA: no overall left shift; agents shifted center-right on x and toward center on conservative-liberal y. Right humans become more left-wing; Left/Center more right-wing and conservative. Caption tension: shifted center-right but also “no clear left-right bias/overall more conservative.”

Section 4.8 biased SFT: progressive bias strongly impairs Right candidates; conservative bias impairs Left; effects on overrepresented groups inconsistent. Right impaired more severely by adverse bias. PCA shifts mainly underrepresented groups, Right more strongly. Conservative-biased and default SFT displacement patterns highly similar, suggesting default centerward shift may originate from base model alignment rather than SFT-data bias.

Section 4.9 synthetic inversion: invert every smartvote answer and train Llama. Inversion roughly 180° rotation, converting right-wing to left-wing. Right group benefits; Left/Center worse. Even after inversion, Right does not reach original Left F1; Left drops to roughly original Right level. Authors infer not purely base-model political bias; left-leaning profiles may be intrinsically easier.

Conclusion: SFT+GRPO generally outperforms baselines; Neutral remains challenging; performance varies across political spectrum. Ethics statement warns of risks, anonymized/public data, and says there is consistent underperformance on center and right-wing profiles plus difficulties with neutral positions; this overstates Center underperformance given WoM Left/Center roughly equal.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Reasoning Boosts Opinion Alignment in LLMs.” Main claim: structured reasoning via RL improves profile-consistent opinion alignment across U.S., German/European, and Swiss politics; still biased. Internal errors found: (1) abstract/intro said answer inversion improves P7N and harms X8J, but §4.9/Fig. 7 says P7N worsens and X8J improves under inversion. (2) §4.2 said “Three configurations” but named QX2 and ZP4 while Table 3 has H3D/N8R/V7K/QX2/ZP4. (3) conclusion calls current approach “persona-conditioned agents,” but earlier method trained one model per candidate/party/respondent, prompt includes country label only/no explicit persona representation, and §5 future work says replace per-agent training with one model conditioned on compact persona representations.

Methods: QX2 = GRPO/PPO variant with group-relative reward normalization, no learned value. One model trained per candidate/party/respondent. Output schema: <reasoning>...</reasoning><answer>[stance]</answer>. Rewards: R=.25*E6Z+.01*F2B+1*G9L; E6Z max 4 for tags; F2B=-|L-L*| max 0; G9L correctness. V7K = SFT warm start using synthetic CoT arguments in rewarded schema; positive/negative arguments for every J4Q/M8C question generated by Y3H=Llama 3.1 70B. Backbones: T9A=Llama 3.1 8B; K6Y=Qwen3 8B and W2E=Magistral 24B reasoning-pretrained; 4-bit training.

Data: J4Q Swiss smartvote English 2023: 18 candidates, 6 parties, binary, 48 train/12 test topic-stratified; P7N Left/A4U Center/X8J Right. R2V German Wahl-O-Mat 2021–2025 six parties, labels Yes/Neutral/No, B5X EU&I 2024 test 30. M8C ANES 2020, 21 respondents, 79 items after exclusions, 67 train/12 test random; recoding via conservative I7V or aggressive O2K.

Table 3 macro-F1 percent. Best ZP4: W2E 70.73/53.21/45.43; T9A 66.88/52.53/40.66; K6Y 65.11/49.38/38.44. ZP4 beats naive and V7K except T9A M8C; J4Q easiest, M8C hardest; W2E best; QX2 trails ZP4. Fig. 3: all methods underperform on centrist/right groups.

§4.5–4.9: T9A/ZP4 J4Q P7N ahead of A4U/X8J. Neutral recall worst for every M8C individual; X8J highest Neutral rate and hardest. No overall left shift; positions shift center-right/centerward; X8J more left-wing; P7N/A4U more right-wing. Progressive arguments impair X8J; conservative impair P7N; X8J more harmed. Inversion flips J4Q answers; P7N worsens, X8J improves but remains below P7N.

§5/Conclusion/Ethics: limitations: answer variation, per-profile training costly/few profiles, surveys scarce, question mismatch; future bias mitigation, persona-conditioned single model, confidence estimates/value head, better questionnaires. final_notes:
Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Core claim: IA2 aligns model activations to its own ICL activations before SFT, using same data, improving accuracy/performance and calibration vs SFT across 12 benchmarks, two model families, >13k models. SFT is CE on GT; ICL uses frozen model with demos. Activations are self-attention outputs per layer/token; asim is token-wise cosine similarity.

§3: SFT-only activations do not align with ICL; alignment better initial/final layers, poor middle. Fig.2 says IA2→SFT aligns more with ICL and performs much better. Fig.1 says ICL is more calibrated than SFT at similar/slightly better accuracy; SFT can use shortcuts.

§4 IA2: target SA([I∘X];W) ≈ SA(X;W~) at generated output positions. For each sample, generate ICL response Ŷ_i using prompt with demos; collect A_ICL at output positions. Feed query + ICL response [X_i∘Ŷ_i], collect unaligned A, train to match A to A_ICL (prose MSE, Eq.4 norm). Then continue standard SFT CE on GT Y until convergence.

§5 setup: 12 eval benchmarks. Qwen3-4B on every task; Llama-3.2 variants depending on task. LoRA rank 8 modifies W_Q,W_K,W_O. Multi-token N capped Llama 16, Qwen 8. Max generated tokens training G=200; IA2 tensor L×200×d; SFT G equals GT answer token count.

Table 1 Qwen N=4 single-token: caption “outperforms SFT across the board” contradicted by BBCN accuracy: SFT 31.8 vs IA2→SFT 27.9. Other rows IA2→SFT > SFT. Table 2 Qwen N=4 multi-token: IA2→SFT beats SFT all cases but sometimes below ICL.

§5.2: Fig.3 increasing asim lowers ECE; extreme ICL alignment can leave accuracy gains; IA2→SFT between IA2 and SFT in similarity with better accuracy/calibration. Fig.4: SFT updates almost orthogonal to IA2/IA2→SFT; IA2→SFT shares ~39% average spanned space with IA2-only.

§6: unified L_IA2 + β L_SFT using ICL responses/self-distillation due to token-length mismatch for G>1. Table3 Qwen N=4 trained on ICL responses: IA2+SFT > SFT-only on all listed multi-token. Table4 KD soft labels on Llama: KD better than SFT in multi-token nearly IA2+SFT, weaker single-token; IA2 training consistently high. Table5 Qwen math shots: prose says ICL exceeds all training methods incl. IA2 on GSM8K/HMathA, but GSM8K IA2-only exceeds ICL at N=4,8. Table6 (IA)3 adaptation Llama N=4: IA2→SFT beats SFT and ICL accuracy in all shown rows; calibration not always better than SFT/ICL.

§7 Related Work: claims prior verdict on ICL vs SFT unclear but this work found SFT performs worse than ICL. Positions IA2 as addressing SFT memorization/overfitting/forgetting, complementary to context distillation and distinct from activation steering.

§8 Conclusion: repeats that ICL and SFT adapt through different mechanisms, ICL often richer/generalizable; IA2 primes SFT to induce ICL-like internal behavior and moves models to more adaptable subspace. Claims extensive experiments show IA2 consistently improves accuracy and calibration of SFT, but this conflicts with BBCN Table 1 accuracy and non-uniform calibration in Table 6. Future work: diversity, catastrophic forgetting, post-trained/RL-tuned models.

Reproducibility statement: code for data download/processing, training, evaluation, analysis, plotting on GitHub; §5 + appendix + README and repeatable seeds claimed sufficient to reproduce. Funding/acknowledgments: ONR, Amazon Research Award, Open Philanthropy; thanks Andrea Wynn.

Paper title: “IA2: Alignment with ICL Activations Improves Supervised Fine-Tuning.” Abstract/introduction claims: SFT adapts LLMs by training weights/PEFT params on labeled samples for target responses; useful but often needs many labeled samples and can overfit/shortcut in few-shot settings. ICL adapts at inference via instructions/demonstrations in context; prior work and their experiments (§5) say ICL generalizes well in few-shot settings and is typically well calibrated, but costs context/inference compute.

Research question: Can information-rich ICL activations be used to improve SFT quality? They claim ICL and SFT may look similar in token/output behavior but produce disparate internal activation patterns (§3), indicating different functional mechanisms. Hypothesis: ICL activations encode rich information about extracting generalizable patterns from context, which SFT may lack in low-data settings.

Method: ICL Activation Alignment (IA2), a self-distillation/priming method before SFT. Pipeline per intro/Fig. 1: (1) collect ICL activations, (2) enforce functional alignment with ICL by matching the model’s own activations while performing ICL, (3) perform SFT on this primed model using the same data. It is intended to provide a training signal not available from output-only SFT or response-text distillation.

Claims/results to check later: IA2 before SFT “drastically/significantly” improves performance/accuracy and calibration across a variety of text classification and generation tasks; extensive experiments on 12 popular benchmarks and two model families; intro says trained over 13,000 models spanning 12 benchmarks. They claim IA2 improves SFT using the same data, and that IA2 training signal is not present in SFT-only training (§5). If Y_i has G tokens, generate G tokens ybar and minimize CE over generated tokens vs ground truth: L_SFT=sum_i sum_j CE(ybar_ij,Y_ij). Note possible wording suggests generated tokens, not teacher forcing, but no contradiction yet.
