Multiclass zero-one, decoder argmax, f^T1=0 cone, nonnegative Q7D surrogate satisfying limit phi(s,y)->0 as y-margin→∞. T4K, unique population maximizer. Examples: multiclass logistic log(sum_j exp(s_j-s_y)) and pairwise sums with convex nonincreasing phi, phi'(0)<0, inf=0. Zhang gives consistency over full centered measurable class.

Sec4.3: finite-dim multiclass. Prop5 k>=3 Gaussian, logistic derivative invertibility; small misspecification set T_epsilon measure<=epsilon yields normalized first-order/logistic solution not equal normalized theta*. Theorem3: if Theta*=U*T*, aggregation gives Theta_m=U*T_m, ||T_m||→∞ and normalized T_m→normalized T*. Model defines p_Theta via link sigma with ordering consistency (14); logistic link example; aggregated labels Y_i^+=A_m iid labels have distribution p_{Theta*,m} via T4K distribution rho_m preserving ordering.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Main claims from abstract/introduction: label cleaning/aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency (e.g. logistic vs task loss) where aggregated-label procedures can be consistent/optimal in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) finite-dimensional/statistical settings where aggregation yields consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Concrete examples promised in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators; theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; fully nonparametric results on how number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency; aggregation allows approximate linear comparison inequalities and consistency under weak surrogate-loss conditions, including restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 preliminaries: Standard setup: data (X_i,Y_i) iid P on X×Y; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk initially R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq. 1). Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn(s), ell(y,y')=1{yy'≤0}, so R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). They then allow task loss to depend on conditional distribution P(Y∈·|X): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq. 2), claiming minimizers frequently coincide with original task problem; multiclass example with ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} equals standard 0-1 error. Surrogate loss φ:R^d×Y→R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/classical all Borel functions and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified hypothesis classes. Main message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: Instead of Y, observe abstract Z∈Z. Example multiple labels: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)∈Y^m. Aggregation space A, aggregating function A:Z→A (e.g. majority vote), surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq. 3). Question: when minimizing (3) suffices to minimize task risk (2).

Example 1 majority vote/repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For 0-1 ell this is majority vote; general form allows abstract procedures.

Example 2 KNN aggregation: Given X with label Y plus iid additional sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m, Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_1^m). Order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X. For K≥0, aggregate K-nearest neighbors plus original point via A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will address single-sample KNN aggregation beyond population-level setup.

Section 3 surrogate consistency. Assumes Fisher/classical setting where F is all Borel measurable f:X→R^d. Defines conditional task risk R(s|x)=ell(d∘s, P(Y|X=x)) and conditional surrogate risk R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excess risks delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s∈R^d. Minimal risks R*=inf_F R(f), R_phi*=inf_F R_phi(f). Consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi with psi(eps)>0 for eps>0 and psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi* for all f. In binary classification with convex margin losses, these coincide. Calibration: psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi(eps)=inf_x psi(eps,x). Cor. 3.1: phi Fisher consistent iff psi(eps,x)>0 for all x, eps>0. Let psi be Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi; overline psi(eps)>0 iff psi(eps)>0, and comparison inequality holds for all measurable f.

They argue in general risk problem (2), one would like Fisher-consistent surrogate using single paired (X,Y), but this is generally impossible; motivates aggregation theory in Sec. 3.2.

Sec. 3.1 ranking example: k items, labels Y=(i,j), i≠j, indicating i ranked above j. For each x, p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define normalized transition matrix C_x with diagonal 0 and off-diagonal (C_x)_ij=p_ij / sum_{l≠j} p_lj, with 0/0=1/(k−1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank by vector C_x 1 (preference counts). Task loss (decoder incorporated) ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i−s_j)(e_i−e_j)^T C1 ≤0, (e_i−e_j)^T C1≠0}, penalizing misordered score pairs. Population task risk (4): R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X 1 order differently). Scores restricted to s∈R^k with s^T1=0 since only ordering matters. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4) (proof App. A.1).

Aggregation for ranking: collect m independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X. If m≥k, define counts m_ij (intended frequency of pair (i,j)) and m_j=sum_i m_ij. Aggregator A(Z)=star if any m_j=0; otherwise returns vector over i: (m_i1/m_1 + m_i2/m_2 + … + m_ik/m_k). Claim: regressing predicted scores f(x) directly on A(Z) when not star yields consistency; Proposition 2 begins next.

grade.reason: None of the reported errors addresses the planted claim that aggregation count changes the intrinsic noise condition number (kappa), so the reviewer list did not identify this specific contradiction.

errors.claim: “m_{ij}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y^m}1\{y=(i,j)\}”
errors.evidence: Immediately before, the paper says “For multiple independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m) conditional on X, put …” and then defines A(Z) using the quantities m_{ij} and m_j as empirical counts.
errors.explanation: As written, m_{ij} sums over all possible tuples y∈Y^m rather than over the observed comparisons in Z, so it does not count occurrences in Z and generally is not a function of Z. This conflicts with the stated purpose of defining an aggregation A(Z) from the observed multiple comparisons.

errors.claim: “\overline\psi_A(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)”
errors.evidence: The preceding analogous construction defines the uniform form as “\overline\psi(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{x\in\mathcal X}\psi(\epsilon,x).” Also, \overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x) has already minimized over s: “\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\{...\}.”
errors.explanation: The uniform calibration function should vary over x, as in the earlier definition. Taking an infimum over s of an expression still containing x is inconsistent with both the earlier pointwise/uniform construction and the just-given definition that already optimized over s.

errors.claim: “Low noise permits a comparison written as ψ(R(f)−R*) ≤ R_φ(f)−R* …”
errors.evidence: Definition 3.2 immediately below requires “ψ(R(f)−R*) ≤ R_{φ,A}(f)−R_{φ,A}*.” Earlier notes likewise record the standard comparison as “ψ(R(f)−R*)≤R_φ(f)−R_φ*.”
errors.explanation: The right-hand side should be surrogate excess risk, subtracting the surrogate optimum, not the task optimum R*. The claim as written mixes surrogate risk with task-risk optimum and contradicts the paper’s own comparison definitions.

errors.claim: “The crude bound κ(x)≤1/Δ(x), choosing M=1 for card(Y)=k=2 and optimizing M otherwise, lower bounds the promised ξ_{m,k} by setting …”
errors.evidence: Corollary 3.3 then states: “Under the theorem’s conditions, every f with R(f)−R*≥ξ_{m,k} satisfies …” Theorem 1 only applies when R(f)−R* is at least the theorem threshold ξ.
errors.explanation: For Corollary 3.3 to follow from Theorem 1, ξ_{m,k} must be an upper/conservative bound on the theorem’s required threshold, not merely a lower bound. A lower bound on the threshold would not ensure the theorem’s hypothesis is met.

errors.claim: “R(f)-R^\star\leq 16N\bigl(R_{\varphi,A_n}(f)-R_{\varphi,A_n}^\star\bigr).”
errors.evidence: The same displayed condition uses the repetition count “m”: “\frac{32\mathsf C_{\mathsf{MT}}^4}{m}…”, and earlier notes record Theorem 1 as giving bounds for aggregated surrogate excess with aggregation count m, i.e. A_m.
errors.explanation: The bound switches from A_m to A_n although the aggregation/repetition parameter in the statement is m. This conflicts with the paper’s own notation for aggregation count.

errors.claim: “every measurable f … satisfying [threshold without a leading factor 4] also satisfies …” in Lemma 3.3 structured prediction application
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record the coarse k≥3 threshold from Theorem 1 as “4*(32 C_MT^4/m log(...))^{α/[2(1−α^2)]}.” The immediately preceding matching application in this same part also includes the leading “4·”.
errors.explanation: The structured-prediction threshold omits the factor 4 required by the stated general coarse bound and used in the matching application.

errors.claim: “R(f)-R^\star\leq \frac8{\min_{\hat y\neq y}\ell(\hat y,y)}(R_{\varphi,A_m}(f)-R_{\varphi,A_m}^\star).”
errors.location: this part, Lemma 3.3 structured prediction application
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record Theorem 1 as: “R−R* ≤ 16/Cφ1 · aggregated surrogate excess.” Lemma 3.3 in this part states “C_{φ,1}=min_{\hat y\neq y}\ell(\hat y,y).”
errors.explanation: Applying the paper’s stated Theorem 1 with the lemma’s Cφ1 gives constant 16/min loss, not 8/min loss. No special improvement is stated here to justify the changed factor.

errors.claim: “As a corollary to Theorem 2 … the aggregated approximate minimizers satisfy … \(\cos\angle(\theta_m,\theta^\star)\to1\).”
errors.evidence: Theorem 2 states only that every sequence of aggregated approximate minimizers satisfies \(R(f_m)\to R^\star\). It does not state any convergence of parameters or angles.
errors.explanation: The advertised corollary includes a directional parameter-convergence conclusion that is not contained in Theorem 2 as stated. Risk consistency alone, especially for a cone where positive rescalings decode identically, does not imply \(\cos\angle\to1\).

errors.claim: “The conditional distribution on Y samples Y∼σ^lr(t) if t∈T_ε and uniformly otherwise.”
errors.evidence: Immediately preceding definition: “σ^ε(t)=σ^lr(t)1{t∉T_ε}+\frac1k1 1{t∈T_ε}.”
errors.explanation: The formula makes the distribution uniform on T_ε and logistic outside T_ε, but the prose states the reverse.

errors.claim: “plotted classification-rule error is \(\left\|\|T_m\|-T^\star/\|T^\star\|\right\|\) against label count.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Theorem 3 was recorded as: “for each \(m\) exists \(\Theta_m=U^\star T_m\) with \(\|T_m\|\to\infty\) and direction \(T_m/\|T_m\|\to T^\star/\|T^\star\|\).”
errors.explanation: The theoretical consistency is about the direction \(T_m/\|T_m\|\), not the norm \(\|T_m\|\). The plotted error formula uses \(\|T_m\|\) minus a normalized matrix/vector, which is dimensionally inconsistent and contradicts the earlier stated convergence target.

errors.claim: “binary problems trivially have κ(X)=1.”
errors.location: this part, Fundamental limits of B2Z
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Noise definitions Δ,Nα,Mβ; binary κ=1 if Δ>0 a.s.”
errors.explanation: The earlier result recorded a condition for binary κ=1, namely positive margin/no tie Δ>0 almost surely. This discussion states κ(X)=1 for binary problems unconditionally, which conflicts with that caveat.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Setup: iid (X,Y), scores f:X→R^d decoded by d, task risk, surrogate risk R_φ, aggregated surrogate R_{φ,A}. A_m repeated-label aggregator minimizes empirical task loss. Q7D calibration gives ψ(R−R*)≤surrogate excess; pair-only Q7D often impossible. Prop1 convex pairwise ranking fails Q7D for k≥3; Prop2 squared loss with aggregation can be Q7D. Prior issues: ranking aggregation formula sums over y∈Y^m instead of observed indices; Eq (5) overlineψ_A uses wrong inf/pointwise form.

Aggregation consistency: Prop3 aggregated Q7D iff pointwise aggregated calibration positive; Cor3.2 m(n)→∞ and W3C φ + small aggregated surrogate excess implies task excess→0. W3C constants C1,C2 via (6a)(6b); hinge W3C (1,2). Theorem1: W3C+J9P+bounded loss+Nα gives linear comparison R−R*≤16/C1 aggregated surrogate excess above threshold involving P(κ>M), e_m(M), ξ_m. Coarse ξ_{m,k}; text wrongly says “lower bounds” threshold. U6A level-(ξ,ζ) has erroneous unaggregated comparison. Noise definitions Δ,Nα,Mβ; binary κ=1 if Δ>0 a.s. Final discussion incorrectly states binary κ(X)=1 unconditionally.

Examples: binary margin convex φ Lemma3.1 C1=φ(0)−φ(δ), C2=φ(−δ). Matching: k=N!, d=N^2, loss 1/(2N)||v1−v2||_1=1/(2N)||·||_2^2; surrogate W3C C1=1/N,C2=2; threshold displayed; bound constant 16N but displayed with A_n despite m. Structured hinge Lemma3.3 W3C C1=min loss, C2=max τ+1; binary embeddings ℓ=1/(2d)||·||_1 give τ=1,C2=2. Structured app omits factor 4 in threshold and gives 8/min loss vs Theorem’s 16/C1.

Section4: Restricted classes. Prop4: for any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, some binary distribution satisfies K7M along θ*, yet every unaggregated surrogate minimizer has higher task risk than θ* and |cos angle|≤ε. Cor4.1 claims from Theorem2 risk→R(fθ*) and cos angle→1; flagged because Theorem2 only states risk consistency.

Theorem2: cone F satisfying K7M and P(Δ>0)=1, ε_m→0 aggregated approximate minimizers of R_{φ,A_m} have R(f_m)→R*. Multiclass: labels [k], zero-one, argmax, f^T1=0 cone; nonnegative Q7D φ with limiting condition. Unique population maximizer; T4K aggregation. Examples logistic and pairwise convex losses.

Section4.3 finite-dimensional multiclass. Prop5 k≥3, Σ=I, invertibility of DM for logistic link; small perturbation set T_ε measure ≤ε yields Θ_1(ε) direction not equal Θ*/norm. Theorem3: if Θ*=U*T* with U orthogonal, T* nonsingular, then for each m exists Θ_m=U*T_m with ||T_m||→∞ and direction T_m/||T_m||→T*/||T*||. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract claims:
- Learning procedures relying on aggregated labels / cleaned labels distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties impossible without data cleaning.
- In risk consistency setting (minimizing surrogate loss instead of task loss like 0-1 error), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than possible using raw labels.
- Classical perfectly specified statistical modeling suggests incorporating all information / modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified.
- Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers, suggesting robustness from considering the full data pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) and refining noisy signals.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract/introduction main claims:
- Modern supervised datasets often involve data cleaning/filtering/crowdsourcing multiple labels and denoising/aggregating them into “gold standard” labels.
- Paper argues label cleaning / label aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation.
- Two robustness aspects: (1) improved consistency when minimizing surrogate loss (e.g. multiclass logistic) instead of task loss (e.g. zero-one error): aggregated-label procedures can achieve consistent/optimal prediction in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard methods fail.
- Classical surrogate risk consistency literature usually assumes standard pairs (X,Y) and does not address modern aggregation machinery.
- Motivating questions: whether aggregation is needed for surrogate consistency; whether/how aggregation helps.
- Paper will give concrete examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where estimators using only pairs (X,Y) necessarily fail, but label aggregation methods are consistent.
- Paper develops new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation.
- In fully nonparametric scenarios, paper claims to show how number of samples aggregated and noise conditions improve consistency.
- Aggregation supposedly allows surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions on the surrogate loss; losses using aggregated labels admit approximate linear comparison inequalities.
- Unlike conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F to be all measurable functions, paper will show classification results where aggregation guarantees consistency over restricted hypothesis classes, which may fail without aggregation.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Main claims from abstract/introduction: label cleaning/aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency (e.g. logistic vs task loss) where aggregated-label procedures can be consistent/optimal in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) finite-dimensional/statistical settings where aggregation yields consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Concrete examples promised in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators; theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; fully nonparametric results on how number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency; aggregation allows approximate linear comparison inequalities and consistency under weak surrogate-loss conditions, including restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 preliminaries: Standard setup: data (X_i,Y_i) iid P on X×Y; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk initially R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq. 1). Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn(s), ell(y,y')=1{yy'≤0}, so R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). They then allow task loss to depend on conditional distribution P(Y∈·|X): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq. 2), claiming minimizers frequently coincide with original task problem; multiclass example with ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} equals standard 0-1 error. Surrogate loss φ:R^d×Y→R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/classical all Borel functions and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified hypothesis classes. Main message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: Instead of Y, observe abstract Z∈Z. Example multiple labels: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)∈Y^m. Aggregation space A, aggregating function A:Z→A (e.g. majority vote), surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq. 3). Question: when minimizing (3) suffices to minimize task risk (2).

Example 1 majority vote/repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For 0-1 ell this is majority vote; general form allows abstract procedures.

Example 2 KNN aggregation: Given X with label Y plus iid additional sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m, Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_1^m). Order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X. For K≥0, aggregate K-nearest neighbors plus original point via A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will address single-sample KNN aggregation beyond population-level setup.

Section 3 surrogate consistency. Assumes Fisher/classical setting where F is all Borel measurable f:X→R^d. Defines conditional task risk R(s|x)=ell(d∘s, P(Y|X=x)) and conditional surrogate risk R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excess risks delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s∈R^d. Minimal risks R*=inf_F R(f), R_phi*=inf_F R_phi(f). Consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi with psi(eps)>0 for eps>0 and psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi* for all f. In binary classification with convex margin losses, these coincide. Calibration: psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi(eps)=inf_x psi(eps,x). Cor. 3.1: phi Fisher consistent iff psi(eps,x)>0 for all x, eps>0. Let psi be Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi; overline psi(eps)>0 iff psi(eps)>0, and comparison inequality holds for all measurable f.

They argue in general risk problem (2), one would like Fisher-consistent surrogate using single paired (X,Y), but this is generally impossible; motivates aggregation theory in Sec. 3.2.

Sec. 3.1 ranking example: k items, labels Y=(i,j), i≠j, indicating i ranked above j. For each x, p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define normalized transition matrix C_x with diagonal 0 and off-diagonal (C_x)_ij=p_ij / sum_{l≠j} p_lj, with 0/0=1/(k−1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank by vector C_x 1 (preference counts). Task loss (decoder incorporated) ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i−s_j)(e_i−e_j)^T C1 ≤0, (e_i−e_j)^T C1≠0}, penalizing misordered score pairs. Population task risk (4): R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X 1 order differently). Scores restricted to s∈R^k with s^T1=0 since only ordering matters. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4) (proof App. A.1).

Aggregation for ranking: collect m independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X. If m≥k, define counts m_ij (intended frequency of pair (i,j)) and m_j=sum_i m_ij. Aggregator A(Z)=star if any m_j=0; otherwise returns vector over i: (m_i1/m_1 + m_i2/m_2 + … + m_ik/m_k). Claim: regressing predicted scores f(x) directly on A(Z) when not star yields consistency; Proposition 2 begins next.

errors.claim: “m_{ij}=\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y^m}1\{y=(i,j)\}”
errors.evidence: Immediately before, the paper says “For multiple independent comparisons Z=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_m) conditional on X, put …” and then defines A(Z) using the quantities m_{ij} and m_j as empirical counts.
errors.explanation: As written, m_{ij} sums over all possible tuples y∈Y^m rather than over the observed comparisons in Z, so it does not count occurrences in Z and generally is not a function of Z. errors.claim: “\overline\psi_A(\epsilon)\coloneqq \inf_{s\in\mathbb R^d}\overline\psi_A(\epsilon,x)”

errors.explanation: The uniform calibration function should vary over x, as in the earlier definition. Taking an infimum over s of an expression still containing x is inconsistent with both the earlier pointwise/uniform construction and the just-given definition that already optimized over s.

errors.claim: “Low noise permits a comparison written as ψ(R(f)−R*) ≤ R_φ(f)−R* …”

errors.explanation: For Corollary 3.3 to follow from Theorem 1, ξ_{m,k} must be an upper/conservative bound on the theorem’s required threshold, not merely a lower bound. A lower bound on the threshold would not ensure the theorem’s hypothesis is met.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract claims:
- Aggregated/cleaned labels distilled from noisy responses provide robustness not available without cleaning.
- Minimizing a typically convex surrogate loss with cleaned/aggregated labels yields stronger task-risk consistency guarantees than procedures using raw labels.

- Aggregation/label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers.
- Overall theme: collection, fitting, and prediction can be jointly robust through noisy-signal refinement.

Introduction claims:

- Linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures.
- Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, permit approximately linear comparison inequalities under weak surrogate conditions, and extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable hypothesis classes.
- Conventional supervised pipeline collects (X_i,Y_i), fits a model, and suppresses cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising used in modern datasets.
- Work on crowdsourced “gold standard” labels is related, but this paper focuses on fundamental, necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency.
- The paper frames its questions as: whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and in what sense aggregation improves consistency.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Earlier abstract/introduction claims:
- Cleaned/aggregated labels from noisy responses provide robustness/consistency not available without cleaning.
- Minimizing convex-ish surrogate losses with cleaned labels gives stronger task-risk consistency than raw-label procedures.
- Finite-dimensional/parametric classifiers remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats uncertainty-modeling approaches; perfectly specified models using all info may be more efficient, but slight misspecification destroys standard consistency.
- Linear-estimator examples in ranking, binary, multiclass separate pair-based procedures from aggregation.
- Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions, weak surrogate assumptions, and extend beyond unrestricted measurable classes.

Section 2 preliminaries:
- Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency.
- Data: iid (X_i,Y_i)~P on X×Y. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y, prediction d∘f(x).
- Distribution-dependent task criterion defined as R(f)=E_P[ ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X)) ] (eq. 2). For multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y}, yielding standard 0-1 error.
- Instantaneous formulation for ell:Y×Y→R_+ minimizes R(f)=E_P[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] over f∈F (eq. 1). Binary: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ell(y,y')=1{yy'≤0}, so R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Task losses nonsmooth/nonconvex/flat; surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R gives R_φ(f)=E φ(f(X),Y). Need consistency with task.

Section 2.1 label aggregation:
- Aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq. 3), assessed against actual task-risk minimization. Z∈Z, aggregation space A, map A:Z→A, φ:R^d×A→R_+.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m), Y_i|X=x iid~P_{Y|X=x}. Aggregator A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l); for 0-1 loss this is majority vote. General ell allows abstract aggregation.
- Rough KNN aggregation: observe X,Y plus independent sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m iid~P; Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)). Order neighbors by dist(X,X_(1))≤…≤dist(X,X_(m)), set X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Population repeated-sampling treatment extends to one-sample aggregation in Appendix C.

Section 3 surrogate consistency: Fisher/classical setting; pointwise calibration; Prop.3 aggregation ψ_A(task excess)≤surrogate excess. Ranking example: no convex surrogate on pairwise labels Fisher consistent for k≥3; aggregation via vector sums/squared loss Fisher consistent if m≥k; discussion says Sec.3.1 has explicit finite-m consistency guarantees and asks whether higher-order comparisons C_x^p need increasing m.

Identifying surrogate Def.3.1: finite |Y|=k, constants Cφ1,Cφ2 with witnesses a_y,s_y and decoder d(s_y)=y; wrong-decoder gap ≥Cφ1 and cross-label value within Cφ2 of inf. Majority vote A_m returns empirical task risk minimizer. Cor.3.2: if m(n)→∞ and aggregated surrogate excess→0 then task excess→0. Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency and noise Nα/Mβ; Theorem 1 gives linear comparison above threshold; Cor.3.3 explicit ξ; α=1 with large m gives ξ=0. Discussion emphasizes many consistency results rely on m→∞; future work finite-m theory depending on (ell,φ) and m. Noise condition number κ(X) (eq.9) used for multiclass comparison; discussion says κ=1 in binary but can be large even with low Mammen-Tsybakov noise α≈1.

§3.3 examples. Binary margin surrogate Lemma 3.1: Cφ1=φ(0)−φ(δ)>0, Cφ2=φ(−δ). Bipartite matching structured hinge: Cφ1=1/N,Cφ2=2; comparison should be 16N (text wrote A_n). §4 restricted/model classes. Binary linear F={x↦<θ,x>}; “optimally predictable along θ*” means sign(<θ*,x>)=sign(P(Y=1|x)−1/2), so fθ* is Bayes. Prop.4: for any ε>0, nonzero θ*, exists distribution optimally predictable along θ* such that every surrogate-risk minimizer θφ has higher task risk than θ* and |cos angle(θφ,θ*)|≤ε. Aggregation majority vote: Cor.4.1/Thm2 says if ε_m→0 and P optimally predictable along θ*, then R(fθm)→R(fθ*) and cos angle→1.

§4.2 multiclass: Theorem 2 says for cone F, Fisher-consistent surrogate with limiting loss, if F cone optimally predicts P and P(Δ(X)>0)=1, then ε_m-argmin aggregated majority-vote surrogate risk has R(f_m)→R*.

§4.3 finite-dimensional multiclass: link condition (14): t_y=max_i t_i iff σ_y=max_i σ_i. Logistic minimizer gradient condition. For k=2 Gaussian, misspecified link still classification consistent. Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract claims:
- Learning procedures relying on aggregated labels / cleaned labels distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties impossible without data cleaning.
- In risk consistency setting (minimizing surrogate loss instead of task loss like 0-1 error), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than possible using raw labels.
- Classical perfectly specified statistical modeling suggests incorporating all information / modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when the minimized loss is even slightly misspecified.
- Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers, suggesting robustness from considering the full data pipeline (collection, fitting, prediction) and refining noisy signals.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract/introduction main claims:
- Modern supervised datasets often involve data cleaning/filtering/crowdsourcing multiple labels and denoising/aggregating them into “gold standard” labels.
- Paper argues label cleaning / label aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation.
- Two robustness aspects: (1) improved consistency when minimizing surrogate loss (e.g. multiclass logistic) instead of task loss (e.g. zero-one error): aggregated-label procedures can achieve consistent/optimal prediction in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard methods fail.
- Classical surrogate risk consistency literature usually assumes standard pairs (X,Y) and does not address modern aggregation machinery.
- Motivating questions: whether aggregation is needed for surrogate consistency; whether/how aggregation helps.
- Paper will give concrete examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where estimators using only pairs (X,Y) necessarily fail, but label aggregation methods are consistent.
- Paper develops new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation.
- In fully nonparametric scenarios, paper claims to show how number of samples aggregated and noise conditions improve consistency.
- Aggregation supposedly allows surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions on the surrogate loss; losses using aggregated labels admit approximate linear comparison inequalities.
- Unlike conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F to be all measurable functions, paper will show classification results where aggregation guarantees consistency over restricted hypothesis classes, which may fail without aggregation.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Main claims from abstract/introduction: label cleaning/aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency (e.g. logistic vs task loss) where aggregated-label procedures can be consistent/optimal in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) finite-dimensional/statistical settings where aggregation yields consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Concrete examples promised in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators; theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; fully nonparametric results on how number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency; aggregation allows approximate linear comparison inequalities and consistency under weak surrogate-loss conditions, including restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 preliminaries: Standard setup: data (X_i,Y_i) iid P on X×Y; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk initially R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq. 1). Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn(s), ell(y,y')=1{yy'≤0}, so R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). They then allow task loss to depend on conditional distribution P(Y∈·|X): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq. 2), claiming minimizers frequently coincide with original task problem; multiclass example with ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} equals standard 0-1 error. Surrogate loss φ:R^d×Y→R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/classical all Borel functions and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified hypothesis classes. Main message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: Instead of Y, observe abstract Z∈Z. Example multiple labels: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)∈Y^m. Aggregation space A, aggregating function A:Z→A (e.g. majority vote), surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq. 3). Question: when minimizing (3) suffices to minimize task risk (2).

Example 1 majority vote/repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For 0-1 ell this is majority vote; general form allows abstract procedures.

Example 2 KNN aggregation: Given X with label Y plus iid additional sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m, Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_1^m). Order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X. For K≥0, aggregate K-nearest neighbors plus original point via A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will address single-sample KNN aggregation beyond population-level setup.

Section 3 surrogate consistency. Assumes Fisher/classical setting where F is all Borel measurable f:X→R^d. Defines conditional task risk R(s|x)=ell(d∘s, P(Y|X=x)) and conditional surrogate risk R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excess risks delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s∈R^d. Minimal risks R*=inf_F R(f), R_phi*=inf_F R_phi(f). Consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi with psi(eps)>0 for eps>0 and psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi* for all f. In binary classification with convex margin losses, these coincide. Calibration: psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi(eps)=inf_x psi(eps,x). Cor. 3.1: phi Fisher consistent iff psi(eps,x)>0 for all x, eps>0. Let psi be Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi; overline psi(eps)>0 iff psi(eps)>0, and comparison inequality holds for all measurable f.

They argue in general risk problem (2), one would like Fisher-consistent surrogate using single paired (X,Y), but this is generally impossible; motivates aggregation theory in Sec. 3.2.

Sec. 3.1 ranking example: k items, labels Y=(i,j), i≠j, indicating i ranked above j. For each x, p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define normalized transition matrix C_x with diagonal 0 and off-diagonal (C_x)_ij=p_ij / sum_{l≠j} p_lj, with 0/0=1/(k−1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank by vector C_x 1 (preference counts). Task loss (decoder incorporated) ell(s,C)=max_{i<j} 1{(s_i−s_j)(e_i−e_j)^T C1 ≤0, (e_i−e_j)^T C1≠0}, penalizing misordered score pairs. Population task risk (4): R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X 1 order differently). Scores restricted to s∈R^k with s^T1=0 since only ordering matters. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4) (proof App. A.1).

Aggregation for ranking: collect m independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X. If m≥k, define counts m_ij (intended frequency of pair (i,j)) and m_j=sum_i m_ij. Aggregator A(Z)=star if any m_j=0; otherwise returns vector over i: (m_i1/m_1 + m_i2/m_2 + … + m_ik/m_k). Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Pair-only Q7D generally impossible. Ranking Prop1 convex pairwise fails Q7D for k≥3; Prop2 squared loss with aggregation Q7D. Prop3 aggregated Q7D iff pointwise aggregated calibration positive; Cor3.2 m(n)→∞ + W3C + small aggregated surrogate excess implies task excess→0. W3C constants Cφ1,Cφ2 via (6a,b); hinge W3C (1,2). Theorem1: W3C+J9P+bounded loss+Nα gives linear bound R−R* ≤16/Cφ1 aggregated surrogate excess above threshold involving κ,e_m; coarse ξ_{m,k}; text may wrongly say lower bounds. U6A level-(ξ,ζ) has erroneous unaggregated comparison R_φ(f)−R* instead of surrogate excess. Noise Δ,Nα,Mβ; binary κ=1 if Δ>0 a.s. Lemma3.1 binary margin convex constants. Structured/matching: matching C1=1/N,C2=2, threshold; some A_n/m inconsistency. Structured hinge Lemma3.3 C1=min loss, C2=max τ+1; structured application omits factor 4 and uses 8/min loss vs Theorem 16/C1.

Section 4 restricted/parametric F. Binary Y={±1}, zero-one ℓ=1{ys≤0}, margin surrogate φ(sy), linear fθ=⟨θ,x⟩. K7M/optimal predictability: sign(f(x))=sign(P(Y=1|X=x)−1/2); θ* realizing it has Bayes risk. Prop4: for any ε>0 and nonzero θ*, some P with K7M along θ* such that every unaggregated surrogate minimizer has larger risk than θ* and |cos angle(θφ,θ*)|≤ε, for any nonnegative φ. Cor4.1 claims from Theorem2 aggregated approximate minimizers have R→R(fθ*) and cos→1; issue: Theorem2 only states risk convergence and K7M is sign/order only, so cosine claim not implied.

Theorem2: cone F satisfying K7M, P(Δ>0)=1, ε_m→0; any ε_m-argmin over F of aggregated surrogate E[varphi(f(X),A_m(labels))] has R(f_m)→R*. Section 3 surrogate consistency: Fisher/classical; pointwise calibration; Prop.3 aggregation ψ_A(task excess)≤surrogate excess. Ranking example: no convex surrogate on pairwise labels Fisher consistent for k≥3; aggregation via vector sums/squared loss Fisher consistent if m≥k.

Identifying surrogate Def.3.1: finite |Y|=k, constants Cφ1,Cφ2 with witnesses a_y,s_y, decoder d(s_y)=y; wrong-decoder gap ≥Cφ1 and cross-label value within Cφ2 of inf. Majority vote A_m returns empirical task-risk minimizer. Cor.3.2: m(n)→∞ and aggregated surrogate excess→0 imply task excess→0. Level-(ξ,ζ) consistency: Theorem 1 gives linear comparison beyond threshold; Cor.3.3 explicit ξ; α=1 with sufficient m gives ξ=0. Examples: binary margin Cφ1=φ(0)−φ(δ), Cφ2=φ(−δ); structured hinge Cφ1=min loss, Cφ2=max τ+1; earlier text had possible constants inconsistencies (16N/8 vs theorem).

§4 restricted/model classes. Binary linear F={x↦<θ,x>}; zero-one 1{ys≤0}; convex margin surrogate. For all measurable functions Fisher/uniform iff φ′(0)<0. “Optimally predictable along θ*”: sign(<θ*,x>)=sign(η(x)−1/2), so fθ* minimizes task risk over all measurable. Prop.4: for any ε>0/nonzero θ*, exists distribution optimally predictable along θ* such that every surrogate-risk minimizer θφ has higher task risk than θ* and |cos angle(θφ,θ*)|≤ε. Aggregation with independent labels and majority vote: Cor.4.1/Thm2 imply if ε_m→0 and P optimally predictable along θ*, then R(fθm)→R(fθ*) and cos angle→1.

§4.2 multiclass: Y=[k], zero-one, argmax decoder, F linear cone with f^T1=0, closed under positive scaling. Surrogate Fisher consistent and limiting loss condition φ(s,y)→0 as correct margin grows; examples logistic and sum of binary margins. Zhang consistency for full measurable zero-sum class under convex nonincreasing binary φ with φ′(0)<0 and inf φ=0; binary case embedded as (g,−g). Defines multiclass optimal predictability: some f∈F has argmax included in argmax conditional class probabilities for all x. Theorem 2: if F cone optimally predicts P, P(Δ(X)>0)=1, ε_m→0, and f_m ε_m-minimizes aggregated surrogate risk with majority vote A_m over m labels, then R(f_m)→R*.

§4.3 finite-dimensional multiclass: X=R^d, Y=[k], linear Θ=[θ1…θ{k−1}], θ_k=0 convention. Link σ maps t∈R^{k−1} to first k−1 probabilities, kth residual; condition (14): coordinate maxima of t (with t_k=0) exactly match probability maxima. Logistic link example. Abstract claims:
- Learning procedures relying on aggregated labels / cleaned labels distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties impossible without data cleaning.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract/introduction main claims:
- Modern supervised datasets often involve data cleaning/filtering/crowdsourcing multiple labels and denoising/aggregating them into “gold standard” labels.
- Paper argues label cleaning / label aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation.
- Two robustness aspects: (1) improved consistency when minimizing surrogate loss (e.g. multiclass logistic) instead of task loss (e.g. zero-one error): aggregated-label procedures can achieve consistent/optimal prediction in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can yield consistent classifiers when standard methods fail.
- Classical surrogate risk consistency literature usually assumes standard pairs (X,Y) and does not address modern aggregation machinery.
- Motivating questions: whether aggregation is needed for surrogate consistency; whether/how aggregation helps.
- Paper will give concrete examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where estimators using only pairs (X,Y) necessarily fail, but label aggregation methods are consistent.
- Paper develops new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation.
- In fully nonparametric scenarios, paper claims to show how number of samples aggregated and noise conditions improve consistency.
- Aggregation supposedly allows surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions on the surrogate loss; losses using aggregated labels admit approximate linear comparison inequalities.
- Unlike conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F to be all measurable functions, paper will show classification results where aggregation guarantees consistency over restricted hypothesis classes, which may fail without aggregation.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Main claims from abstract/introduction: label cleaning/aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency (e.g. logistic vs task loss) where aggregated-label procedures can be consistent/optimal in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) finite-dimensional/statistical settings where aggregation yields consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Concrete examples promised in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators; theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; fully nonparametric results on how number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency; aggregation allows approximate linear comparison inequalities and consistency under weak surrogate-loss conditions, including restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 preliminaries: Standard setup: data (X_i,Y_i) iid P on X×Y; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk initially R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq. 1). Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn(s), ell(y,y')=1{yy'≤0}, so R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). They then allow task loss to depend on conditional distribution P(Y∈·|X): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq. 2), claiming minimizers frequently coincide with original task problem; multiclass example with ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} equals standard 0-1 error. Surrogate loss φ:R^d×Y→R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/classical all Borel functions and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified hypothesis classes. Main message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: Instead of Y, observe abstract Z∈Z. Example multiple labels: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)∈Y^m. Aggregation space A, aggregating function A:Z→A (e.g. majority vote), surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq. 3). Abstract claims:

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Main claims from abstract/introduction: label cleaning/aggregation provides robustness impossible without aggregation. Two aspects: (1) improved surrogate-risk consistency (e.g. logistic vs task loss) where aggregated-label procedures can be consistent/optimal in limits where raw (X,Y) procedures cannot; (2) finite-dimensional/statistical settings where aggregation yields consistent classifiers when standard methods fail. Concrete examples promised in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators; theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation; fully nonparametric results on how number of aggregated samples and noise conditions improve consistency; aggregation allows approximate linear comparison inequalities and consistency under weak surrogate-loss conditions, including restricted hypothesis classes where non-aggregated methods may fail.

Section 2 preliminaries: Standard setup: data (X_i,Y_i) iid P on X×Y; scoring f:X→R^d, decoder d:R^d→Y. Task risk initially R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq. 1). Binary example: d=1, decoder sgn(s), ell(y,y')=1{yy'≤0}, so R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). They then allow task loss to depend on conditional distribution P(Y∈·|X): R(f)=E[ell(d∘f(X),P(·|X))] (eq. 2), claiming minimizers frequently coincide with original task problem; multiclass example with ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y} equals standard 0-1 error. Surrogate loss φ:R^d×Y→R, surrogate risk R_φ(f)=E[φ(f(X),Y)]. They study consistency in (i) Fisher/classical all Borel functions and (ii) parametric possibly misspecified hypothesis classes. Main message: label aggregation improves consistency in both.

Section 2.1 label aggregation: Instead of Y, observe abstract Z∈Z. Example multiple labels: Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)∈Y^m. Aggregation space A, aggregating function A:Z→A (e.g. majority vote), surrogate φ:R^d×A→R_+, aggregated surrogate risk R_{φ,A}(f)=E[φ(f(X),A(Z))] (eq. 3). Question: when minimizing (3) suffices to minimize task risk (2).

Example 1 majority vote/repeated sampling: Y_i|X=x iid P_{Y|X=x}; A_m(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For 0-1 ell this is majority vote; general form allows abstract procedures.

Example 2 KNN aggregation: Given X with label Y plus iid additional sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m, Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_1^m). Order X_i by distance to X, set X_(0)=X. For K≥0, aggregate K-nearest neighbors plus original point via A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_{y∈Y} Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Appendix C will address single-sample KNN aggregation beyond population-level setup.

Section 3 surrogate consistency. Assumes Fisher/classical setting where F is all Borel measurable f:X→R^d. Defines conditional task risk R(s|x)=ell(d∘s, P(Y|X=x)) and conditional surrogate risk R_phi(s|x)=E[phi(s,Y)|X=x]. Pointwise excess risks delta_ell, delta_phi subtract inf over s∈R^d. Minimal risks R*=inf_F R(f), R_phi*=inf_F R_phi(f). Consistency notions: (i) Fisher consistency: for all P, R_phi(f_n)→R_phi* implies R(f_n)→R*. (ii) uniform comparison: nondecreasing psi with psi(eps)>0 for eps>0 and psi(R(f)-R*)≤R_phi(f)-R_phi* for all f. In binary classification with convex margin losses, these coincide. Calibration: psi(eps,x)=inf{delta_phi(s,x): delta_ell(s,x)≥eps}; overline psi(eps)=inf_x psi(eps,x). Cor. 3.1: phi Fisher consistent iff psi(eps,x)>0 for all x, eps>0. Let psi be Fenchel biconjugate of overline psi; overline psi(eps)>0 iff psi(eps)>0, and comparison inequality holds for all measurable f.

They argue in general risk problem (2), one would like Fisher-consistent surrogate using single paired (X,Y), but this is generally impossible; motivates aggregation theory in Sec. 3.2.

Sec. 3.1 ranking example: k items, labels Y=(i,j), i≠j, indicating i ranked above j. For each x, p_ij=P(Y=(i,j)|x). Define normalized transition matrix C_x with diagonal 0 and off-diagonal (C_x)_ij=p_ij / sum_{l≠j} p_lj, with 0/0=1/(k−1), so C_x^T 1=1. Rank by vector C_x 1 (preference counts). Population task risk (4): R(f)=P(f(X) and C_X 1 order differently). Scores restricted to s∈R^k with s^T1=0 since only ordering matters. Proposition 1: for k≥3, no convex surrogate phi:R^k×Y→R is Fisher consistent for ranking risk (4) (proof App. A.1).

Aggregation for ranking: collect m independent pairwise comparisons Z=(Y_1,…,Y_m)|X. If m≥k, define counts m_ij (intended frequency of pair (i,j)) and m_j=sum_i m_ij. Aggregator A(Z)=star if any m_j=0; otherwise returns vector over i: (m_i1/m_1 + m_i2/m_2 + … + m_ik/m_k). Claim: regressing predicted scores f(x) directly on A(Z) when not star yields consistency; Proposition 2 begins next.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Setup/results: iid (X,Y); scores f:X→R^d decoded by d. Surrogate/aggregated risks R_{φ,A}; repeated-label aggregator A_m minimizes empirical task loss. Q7D/calibration: ψ(R−R*)≤surrogate excess. Pair-only Q7D generally impossible; convex pairwise ranking fails for k≥3; squared loss with aggregation can be Q7D. Prop3: aggregated Q7D iff pointwise aggregated calibration positive; Cor3.2: m(n)→∞ and W3C φ + small aggregated surrogate excess imply task excess→0. W3C constants Cφ1,Cφ2 via (6a,b); hinge example (1,2). Theorem1: W3C+J9P+bounded loss+Nα gives comparison R−R* ≤16/Cφ1·aggregated surrogate excess above threshold 2P(κ>M)+(4 C_MT e_m(M))^{1/(1−α)}. Earlier possible errors: ranking aggregation sum over y∈Y^m instead of observed indices; Eq(5) overlineψ_A pointwise/inf issue; text called ξ lower bounds though used as sufficient threshold; U6A level-(ξ,ζ) had erroneous unaggregated comparison.

Noise: Δ=min wrong excess; binary |2η−1|. Nα: P(d∘f≠d∘f*)≤C_MT(R−R*)^α. κ=max/min wrong excess; binary κ=1 if Δ>0 a.s. Lemma3.1 binary margin convex φ with ∂φ(0)<0, lim∞φ=0 gives W3C constants Cφ1=φ(0)−φ(δ), Cφ2=φ(−δ).

Structured/matching: perfect bipartite matching, k=N!, embedding v∈R^{N^2}, loss ℓ=(1/(2N))||v1−v2||_1=(1/(2N))||·||_2^2. It stated contradictory Cφ2=1 then Cφ2=2, Cφ1=1/N. Matching bound threshold uses m but conclusion uses A_n. Structured hinge φ=max_yhat(ℓ(yhat,y)+<v(yhat)−v(y),s>). Lemma3.3: Cφ1=min wrong ℓ, Cφ2=max_y τ(y)+1; for binary embeddings with ℓ=1/(2d)||·||_1, τ=1 and Cφ2=2. Displayed consequence used threshold without leading 4 and constant 8/minℓ, conflicting with Theorem1 constants.

Sec4 restricted models: Prop4 claims for every ε and nonzero θ*, some P satisfies K7M along θ*, yet every unaggregated surrogate minimizer has higher risk and |cos|≤ε for any nonnegative φ; internal issue: constant-zero φ contradicts universal claim. Cor4.1 says from Theorem2, aggregated binary approximate minimizers θ_m have R→R(θ*) and cos angle→1; but Theorem2 only states risk consistency R(f_m)→R*. Theorem2: cone F satisfying K7M, P(Δ>0)=1, ε_m→0; any ε_m-argmin of aggregated R_{φ,A_m} has R(f_m)→R*. Section 2 preliminaries:
- Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with classical Fisher consistency; parametric/misspecified F where aggregation improves consistency.
- Data: iid (X_i,Y_i)~P on X×Y. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y, prediction d∘f(x).
- Distribution-dependent task criterion defined as R(f)=E_P[ ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X)) ] (eq. 2). For multiclass Y={1,…,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y}, yielding standard 0-1 error.
- Instantaneous formulation for ell:Y×Y→R_+ minimizes R(f)=E_P[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] over f∈F (eq. 1). Binary: d=1, d(s)=sgn(s), ell(y,y')=1{yy'≤0}, so R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0). Task losses nonsmooth/nonconvex/flat; surrogate φ:R^d×Y→R gives R_φ(f)=E φ(f(X),Y). Need consistency with task.

For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Population repeated-sampling treatment extends to one-sample aggregation in Appendix C.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract claims:
- Learning procedures relying on aggregated labels / cleaned labels distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties impossible without data cleaning.
- In risk consistency setting (minimizing surrogate loss instead of task loss like 0-1 error), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than possible using raw labels.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Abstract claims:
- Learning procedures relying on aggregated/cleaned labels distilled from noisy responses have robustness properties impossible without data cleaning.
- In risk consistency setting (minimizing surrogate loss instead of task loss like 0-1 error), procedures using label aggregation obtain stronger consistency guarantees than possible using raw labels.
- Classical perfectly specified statistical modeling suggests incorporating all information/modeling label uncertainty is statistically efficient, but consistency fails for “standard” approaches when minimized loss is even slightly misspecified.
- Procedures leveraging aggregated information still converge to optimal classifiers, suggesting robustness from considering full data pipeline.

Intro claims:
- Modern datasets often require cleaning/filtering/crowdsourcing multiple labels and denoising; paper studies how aggregation improves consistency.
- Two robustness aspects: (1) improved consistency of estimation: minimizing surrogate loss (e.g. multiclass logistic) rather than task loss (e.g. 0-1), aggregated labels can achieve consistent optimal prediction in limit when impossible without aggregation; (2) in finite-dimensional statistical problems, aggregation can provide consistent classifiers when standard methods fail.
- Existing surrogate risk consistency literature generally assumes standard supervised pairs (X,Y) and does not address data aggregation machinery.
- Main questions: whether aggregation is needed; whether/how it helps consistency.
- Paper proposes concrete examples in ranking and binary/multiclass classification with linear estimators where estimators using only pairs (X,Y) necessarily fail, but label aggregation methods yield consistency.
- Develops new notions/theory for surrogate consistency with data aggregation.
- Fully nonparametric scenarios: shows how number of samples aggregated combines with noise conditions to improve consistency.
- Claims aggregation allows surrogate risk consistency under weak conditions on surrogate loss; losses using aggregated labels admit approximate linear comparison inequalities, with multiclass threshold O(m^{-1}) at alpha=1/2.
- Unlike conventional risk consistency theory requiring hypothesis class F of all measurable functions, paper will show classification results where aggregation guarantees consistency even over restricted hypothesis classes, which may fail without aggregation.

U6A level-(ξ,ζ): ∃ψ with ψ(ε)≥ζε for ε≥ξ and ψ(task excess)≤ aggregated surrogate excess; earlier paragraph mistakenly wrote Rφ(f)−R*. Introduction part 1 claims:
- Aggregation permits consistent optimal prediction under surrogate rather than task loss when unaggregated estimation cannot, including finite-dimensional statistical problems.
- Linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary classification, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures.

- Conventional supervised pipeline collects (X_i,Y_i), fits a model, and suppresses cleaning/filtering/repeated crowdsourced labeling/denoising required by modern datasets.
- Paper’s concern is that such label-cleaning machinery gives a fundamental, necessary improvement of fitted-model consistency.
- Literature review: surrogate-risk consistency from 2000s; Bartlett et al. characterize convex-surrogate consistency for binary zero-one classification; later work covers multi-label, ranking, structured prediction, ordinal regression, restricted classes, general theory.
- Pair-based analyses admit empirical-process theory, but not aggregation machinery. The paper asks whether aggregation is needed, whether pair-based surrogate consistency suffices, and how aggregation improves consistency.

Paper title: “Some Robustness Properties of Label Cleaning” by Chen Cheng and John Duchi.

Core claims from abstract/introduction:
- Cleaned/aggregated labels distilled from noisy responses give robustness not available without cleaning.
- Minimizing typically convex surrogate losses with cleaned/aggregated labels yields stronger task-risk consistency than procedures using raw labels.
- Finite-dimensional classifiers can remain consistent under loss misspecification that defeats standard uncertainty-modeling approaches.
- If statistical models are perfectly specified, using all information is more efficient, but slight loss misspecification can destroy standard consistency; label cleaning retains convergence to optimal classifiers.
- Linear-estimator constructions in ranking, binary, and multiclass classification separate procedures restricted to raw (X,Y) pairs from aggregation procedures.
- Nonparametric results combine aggregation count and noise conditions; multiclass threshold O(m^{-1}) at alpha=1/2; extend consistency beyond unrestricted measurable classes.

Preliminaries:
- Two regimes: unrestricted Borel F with Fisher consistency; parametric/potentially misspecified F, where aggregation improves consistency.
- Data: iid (X_i,Y_i)~P on X×Y. Scores f:X→R^d decoded by d:R^d→Y.
- Distribution-dependent task criterion: R(f)=E_P[ ell(d∘f(X), P(.|X)) ] (eq. 2). For multiclass Y={1,...,k}, ell(yhat,P)=Σ_y P(Y=y)1{yhat≠y}, yielding standard zero-one error.
- Instantaneous task risk: R(f)=E_P[ell(d∘f(X),Y)] (eq. 1). Binary classification: d=1, decoder sign, ell(y,y’)=1{yy’≤0}, R(f)=P(Y f(X)≤0).
- Surrogate risk with raw labels: R_phi(f)=E_P[phi(f(X),Y)]. Consistency with task criterion is required.

Label aggregation:
- Aggregated surrogate risk: R_{phi,A}(f)=E[phi(f(X),A(Z))] (eq. 3), assessed against true task-risk minimization. Components: replacement response Z∈Z, aggregation space A, map A:Z→A, nonnegative surrogate phi:R^d×A→R_+.
- Repeated labeling: Z=(Y_1,...,Y_m), iid conditional on X=x from P_{Y|X=x}; aggregation A_m(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=1}^m ell(y,Y_l). For zero-one loss this is majority vote. General ell allows abstract aggregation.
- Rough KNN aggregation: for X with Y plus independent sample (X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^m, let Z=(Y,(X_i,Y_i)_i). Order neighbors by distance to X with X_(0)=X. For K≥0, A_{m,K}(Z)=argmin_y Σ_{l=0}^K ell(y,Y_(l)). Population repeated-sampling also extends to aggregation from one sample in Appendix C.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Goal: VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in T2V via event-based prompts and VLM-inferred actor attributes across frames. Aligned models = preference/reward optimized; unaligned = likelihood/base. Conclusion claims VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics and that reward-model alignment often inherits/amplifies biases from preference data.

Prompt setup: actual conditions Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts); no gender-specific prompt condition despite claims of four gender categories/seven ethnicities. Verbs list has 42. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” VLM gender labels binary {man,woman}. Issue: gender categories/systematic gender variation conflict with no gender prompts.

Eval: 10 videos/prompt/model, 16 frames/video. VLMs Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Frame predictions majority-voted to video labels, then fused across VLMs. TAS=% frames matching final majority-voted video attribute label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male. RDS_e=P_e−1/7. SDI=1−ΣP_e². Δ compares aligned to unaligned.

Sec 4/Table 2: ModelScope avg PBSG 0.4815, White RDS 0.7690, SDI 0.0538; InstructVideo 0.5295, 0.7833, 0.0267; VideoCrafter-V2 0.7581, 0.6905, 0.1252; T2V-Turbo 0.8306, 0.6381, 0.1119. Issues: text says InstructVideo PBSG increase 0.04 vs table 0.0480; “ModelScope strongest imbalance” conflicts with InstructVideo; caption says missing “—” means zero recognizable under person-only though PBSG missing entries are ethnicity+person. Human eval SDI 0.745/0.761 conflicts with Table 2 SDI ~0.0267–0.1252 unless different setting.

Sec 5 preference datasets: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Gender valid verbs: HPDv2 26/42, Pick-a-Pic 18/42. Issue: figures/text say distributions “across 42 verbs” despite fewer covered/valid verbs. Image reward benchmark Table 4 reward PBSG: CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.0 0.6039, HPSv2.1 -0.0984, PickScore -0.1157; SDI all ~0.847–0.849. Issue: says shifts align with training data while HPSv2.1 training data undisclosed.

Sec 6/Table 5: VCM-VC2 PBSG 0.8034, White RDS 0.6405, SDI 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 PBSG 0.9116, White RDS 0.3667, SDI 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 PBSG 0.2267, White RDS 0.4286, SDI 0.0976; +PickScore PBSG 0.3714, White RDS 0.6833, SDI 0.1467. Issues: “ethnicity-only” conflicts with person-only; HPSv2.1 Latino RDS=-0.4352 misreads Δ Latino PBSG; says HPSv2.0 reinforces White preference though White RDS decreases.

Sec 7 controllable preference modeling: Table 7 reward PBSG RMM avg 1.5280 all positive; RMW avg -0.7448 all negative. Table 8 video alignment: base avg PBSG 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584 all positive/increased; +RMW 0.3082 all still positive though reduced. Thus RMW counteracts male bias but does not create woman preference or balance. Current part repeats overstatement: says RMW corrects skew and produces balanced/socially representative generations. Fig. 6 claims: RMM amplifies male portrayals for exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred bake/sleep/sweep; normalized sensitivity ranks sleep/stretch/read most sensitive under both.

Limitations: acknowledges focus on gender/ethnicity predefined categories; VLM evaluators validated against humans but may have biases/inaccuracies; mainly assesses specific training strategy and limited reward models; controllable preference modeling limited to synthetic gender preference manipulations; VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 socially associated actions. Main result claimed: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: VideoBiasEval uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames and aggregates them for bias quantification (Section 3.3). Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Introduction definitions/claims: “aligned models” are video diffusion models with post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline described as base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” are trained solely with likelihood-based objectives and serve as controlled baselines for isolating alignment effects. Existing bias evaluation frameworks are said to have three limitations: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack of comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, and no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/intro claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation grounded in established bias taxonomies. Uses event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts/events) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and temporal/attribute persistence within videos. VLMs infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames and aggregate for bias quantification.

Definitions: “aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly with reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style procedures using learned preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. “Unaligned counterparts” are likelihood-trained baselines for isolating alignment effects. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Stated limitations of existing bias eval: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. VideoBiasEval focuses on gender and ethnicity as dimensions with comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries, controlling verb/event type and actor identity attributes.

Planned/claimed analyses: Section 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Section 5.2 investigates inheritance by image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Section 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models to compare video outputs before/after alignment. Section 7 examines intentionally controllable image reward datasets by manipulating social-attribute distributions and tests whether reward models trained on curated datasets enable controllable bias representations in video diffusion outputs.

Main results/conclusions claimed so far: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models trained on them inherit and amplify biases, propagated through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models shifts gender portrayals; ethnic representation remains uneven. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) indicates alignment improves consistency of social-attribute portrayals over time but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Alignment tuning enhances video quality/coherence while reinforcing/stabilizing social biases; produces smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Also claims comprehensive analysis across 42 events of reward model preference changes and resulting video model bias shifts.

Contributions stated: (1) VideoBiasEval with event-based prompting and multi-granular metrics for ethnicity bias, gender conditioned on ethnicity, and temporal stability. (2) First end-to-end analysis connecting human preference datasets, reward models, and alignment-tuned video diffusion models, showing biases inherited/amplified/stabilized. (3) Experiments show preference alignment improves perceptual quality/temporal coherence but reshapes/reinforces social composition; guidance via controllable preference modeling, targeted data composition, and counter-biased reward design to steer toward more equitable behavior.
