Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates T2V social bias via event prompts and VLM-inferred actor attributes across frames. Aligned models = preference/reward optimized; unaligned = likelihood/base. Conclusion/broader impact: VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics; alignment/reward models often inherit/amplify human-preference biases; alignment can stabilize/polish biased representations; controllable preference modeling is dual-use; preference dataset curation/auditing is urged.

Prompt/metrics: actual video conditions seen: Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors+person, 294 prompts); earlier claimed gender categories but no gender-specific video prompt condition. VLM gender labels binary {man,woman}. TAS = % frames matching final video majority attribute. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; SDI=1−ΣP_e². Δ compares aligned to unaligned.

Sec 4 Table 2: ModelScope PBSG 0.4815, White RDS 0.7690, SDI 0.0538. InstructVideo 0.5295, 0.7833, 0.0267. VideoCrafter-V2 0.7581, 0.6905, 0.1252. T2V-Turbo 0.8306, 0.6381, 0.1119. Prior errors: text said InstructVideo PBSG increase 0.04 vs table 0.0480; “ModelScope strongest imbalance” conflicts with InstructVideo.

Human eval: 400 videos/3 annotators. VLM ensemble Pearson 0.89 gender/0.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ 0.91/0.78; Fleiss κ 0.92/0.82. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG 0.846→0.863 p=0.68; SDI 0.745→0.761. Prior issue: annotation verifies prompted demographic attribute conflicts with no gender prompts; SDI scale conflicts with Table 2 unless different setting.

Sec 5 image reward datasets: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Prior issues: captions claimed 42 verbs despite 29/19; Pick-a-Pic women preference “51.11% (11/18)” should be 61.11%; Sec 5.2 used Ethnicity+Gender prompts conflicting with earlier no gender-specific video templates. Ethnicity pref: White 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic.

Image reward benchmark: Table 3 Ethnicity+Person 294 and Ethnicity+Gender 1176; example East Asian woman. Fig 5 only binary genders, count issue: 1176=7×42×4, but binary would be 588. Table 4 image reward: HPSv2.0 male PBSG 0.6039; CLIP -0.0726, HPSv2.1 -0.0984, PickScore -0.1157 female preference. Ethnicity reward: CLIP White RDS 0.0182 highest SDI 0.8495; HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern 0.0315; HPSv2.1 Latino 0.0382; PickScore East Asian 0.0352; fine-tuned models reduced SDI.

Sec 6 Table 5: VCM avg PBSG 0.8034, White RDS 0.6405, SDI 0.1433. +HPSv2.0 avg PBSG 0.9116, White RDS 0.3667, SDI 0.1257. +HPSv2.1 avg PBSG 0.2267, White RDS 0.4286, most RDS missing, SDI 0.0976. +PickScore avg PBSG 0.3714, White RDS 0.6833, SDI 0.1467. Prior errors: HPSv2.1 improves Black balance despite missing/zero recognizable; Latino RDS=-0.4352 was PBSG Δ; HPSv2.0 “reinforces White” though White RDS decreases.

Sec 7: man-preferred/woman-preferred reward datasets: claims 2.94M pairs from Ethnicity+Gender plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7 reward scores: CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280; RMW avg -0.7448. Error: text calls these PBSG despite caption “average scores” and RMM >1. Table 8 video PBSG: VCM 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082, all ethnicity values still positive. Error: claims RMW shift to woman-preference bias, but positive PBSG means remaining male bias. Fig 6: RMM amplifies male-preferred portrayals in exercise,row,cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions bake,sleep,sweep. Sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; top actions sleep, stretch, read under both.

Limitations: focuses on gender and ethnicity using predefined categories; VLM evaluators image-level and may be biased/inaccurate despite ensemble/human validation; alignment impacts mainly under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable preference experiments limited to synthetic gender preference; VideoBiasEval benchmark fixed to 42 socially associated actions.

Introduction definitions/claims: “aligned models” are video diffusion models with post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline described as base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” are trained solely with likelihood-based objectives and serve as controlled baselines for isolating alignment effects. Existing bias evaluation frameworks are said to have three limitations: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack of comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, and no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/intro claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation grounded in established bias taxonomies. Uses event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts/events) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and temporal/attribute persistence within videos. VLMs infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames and aggregate for bias quantification.

Definitions: “aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly with reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style procedures using learned preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. “Unaligned counterparts” are likelihood-trained baselines for isolating alignment effects. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Stated limitations of existing bias eval: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. VideoBiasEval focuses on gender and ethnicity as dimensions with comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries, controlling verb/event type and actor identity attributes.

Planned/claimed analyses: Section 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Section 5.2 investigates inheritance by image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Section 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models to compare video outputs before/after alignment. Section 7 examines intentionally controllable image reward datasets by manipulating social-attribute distributions and tests whether reward models trained on curated datasets enable controllable bias representations in video diffusion outputs.

Main results/conclusions claimed so far: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models trained on them inherit and amplify biases, propagated through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models shifts gender portrayals; ethnic representation remains uneven. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) indicates alignment improves consistency of social-attribute portrayals over time but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Alignment tuning enhances video quality/coherence while reinforcing/stabilizing social biases; produces smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Also claims comprehensive analysis across 42 events of reward model preference changes and resulting video model bias shifts.

Contributions stated: (1) VideoBiasEval with event-based prompting and multi-granular metrics for ethnicity bias, gender conditioned on ethnicity, and temporal stability. (2) First end-to-end analysis connecting human preference datasets, reward models, and alignment-tuned video diffusion models, showing biases inherited/amplified/stabilized. (3) Experiments show preference alignment improves perceptual quality/temporal coherence but reshapes/reinforces social composition; guidance via controllable preference modeling, targeted data composition, and counter-biased reward design to steer toward more equitable behavior.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core claim: alignment tuning improves quality/coherence but can increase/stabilize social bias. Aligned = post-likelihood video diffusion optimized with learned preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood-only. Broader Impact reiterates alignment/RLHF can stabilize/entrench bias by making stereotypes polished/coherent; preference data can be used for bias mitigation or harmful exclusion; recommends continual event-centric audits like QX2 and diverse/equitable preference curation.

QX2/VideoBiasEval: actor/verb/context. J7K = 42 person-only prompts, one per verb, for ethnic balance; V9R = 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities, explicit ethnicity, for gender. Earlier inconsistency: text said demographic attributes not introduced despite ethnicity descriptors. Gender labels included man/woman/neutral/non-binary, but metrics use binary G={man,woman}. Attribute extraction: 3 VLM judges classify 16 frames/video; frame majority → video label → fused. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final video label.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias, negative=female bias. F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7, P_e=N_e/N_total over identifiable ethnicity; min should be −1/7≈−.1429. Repeated issue: Tables 2 and 5 report F6N below −1/7 and use em dash for zero ethnicity instances, though formula would give −1/7 if P_e=0.

Part 4 Table 2: D8P/ModelScope→K5X/InstructVideo/A3J avg L2V .4815→.5295 (Δ+.0480), White F6N .7690→.7833, W3H .0538→.0267. B7Q/VideoCrafter-2→H4M/T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D rewards avg L2V .7581→.8306, White F6N .6905→.6381, W3H .1252→.1119. Added table said K5X L2V increase 0.04, not .0480 unless truncated.

Human verification: 400 gender/400 ethnicity videos; Pearson .89/.73; κ .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82; human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%. Full-pool→perfect-agreement subset: L2V .846→.863, W3H .745→.761; L2V p=.68.

Preference datasets: R9C=HPDv2: 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs, 26 valid man-woman verbs, men preferred 69.23% (18/26), White 43.34%. N6T=Pick-a-Pic: 14,958 tuples, 19 verbs, 18 valid, women “51.11% (11/18)” arithmetic conflict; White 40.08%. Reward identities: Y2F=CLIP base; A3J=HPSv2.0/R9C; U8D=HPSv2.1/X7H; E5W=PickScore/N6T. Image benchmark count conflict: C4Z=1176 ethnicity+gender prompts, but if 294×{man,woman}=588.

Table 4: Y2F avg L2V −.0726 W3H .8495; A3J .6039/.8492; U8D −.0984/.8470; E5W −.1157/.8483. Narrative conflict: E5W East Asian F6N said .0352 vs table .0316.

Part 9 Table 5: G4S baseline avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J .9116, White F6N .3667, W3H .1257. +U8D .2267, White F6N .4286, W3H .0976. +E5W .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. Errors: added table says U8D Latino F6N −.4352, but Table 5 has Latino F6N em dash and −.4352 is Δ Latino L2V; claims U8D decreases Latino representation and A3J reinforces White tendency conflict with Table 5. Table 6 temporal: all reward alignments improve stability.

Part 10 controllable gender preference. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg −.0726; Z6B man-preferred avg 1.5280; P3L woman-preferred avg −.7448. Error: Table 7 deltas for Z6B are vs Y2F, but P3L deltas are vs Z6B, not Y2F. Table 8 G4S avg .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082. Error: text says P3L shifts toward woman preference, but all +P3L L2V values remain positive, hence still male-biased by metric.

Conclusion/limitations: calls for bias auditing/mitigation throughout generation; predefined categories socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level and potentially biased; experiments mainly single-step latent consistency distillation with limited rewards; synthetic gender manipulation limited and not full responsible-deployment solution; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization. Supplement inventory lists per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses, WebVid effects, reward implementation/training, video post-training/inference, and numbered gender/ethnicity plots for four-model, reward-model, reward-aligned, and controllable-preference analyses.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice…” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in T2V via event prompts and VLM-inferred actor attributes. Aligned = post-trained for human preferences; unaligned = likelihood-trained/base.

Prompt setup: Earlier claimed four gender categories/seven ethnicities, but actual VideoBiasEval conditions are Person-only (actor “person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts). No gender-specific prompt condition in VideoBiasEval; VLM gender labels binary {man,woman}; demographics unconstrained and analyzed post hoc. Prompts “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Errors already noted: claims about systematic gender variation/gender categories conflict with no gender prompt condition and binary labels; “Person-only removes contextual and identity cues” wrong because verb/context remain; human-eval claim about “prompted demographic attribute” for gender conflicts with no gender-prompted condition.

Generation/eval: Models: ModelScope (u), InstructVideo (a, based on ModelScope, HPSv2.0), VideoCrafter-2/V2 (u), T2V-Turbo-V1 (a, based on VideoCrafter-2; aligned with HPSv2.1/InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP wording). 10 videos/prompt/model. VLMs Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; 16 frames/video; majority/fusion. Human eval: Pearson .89 gender/.73 ethnicity; kappas .91/.78; consensus 99.0%/83.3%.

Metrics: TAS = % frames matching final majority video attribute. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male; 0.5 means 3x men. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; if P_e=0 then −1/7, so claims that zero instances make RDS missing contradict definition. SDI=1−ΣP_e². Δ=aligned−unaligned.

Prior errors: Table 2 text says InstructVideo PBSG increase .1480 but table Δ +.0480; text says ModelScope strongest imbalance though InstructVideo has higher White RDS/lower SDI. Sec. 5 Fig. 3/4 captions “across 42 verbs” despite reward data coverage lower (HPDv2 26 gender verbs, Pick-a-Pic 18). Sec. 5.2 Ethnicity+Gender references Sec. 3.2 templates though no gender prompt condition. HPSv2.1 training data called undisclosed but shifts claimed to align with each model’s training data.

T2I reward benchmark: FLUX; Table 3 counts Ethnicity+Person 294, Ethnicity+Gender 1176, gender {man,woman}; 100 images/prompt apparently. Reward metrics: adapted PBSG = male avg standardized score minus female; ethnicity scores softmaxed for RDS/SDI. Reported CLIP −0.0726, HPSv2.0 +0.6039, PickScore −0.1157, HPSv2.1 −0.0984.

Fine-tunes VCM-VC2 with HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5: VCM PBSG .8034 SDI .1433; +HPS2.0 PBSG .9116 SDI .1257; +HPS2.1 PBSG .2267 SDI .0976; +PickScore PBSG .3714 SDI .1467. Prior errors: Table 5 caption says missing RDS due to zero instances/person-only; paragraph says “ethnicity-only”; text says HPSv2.1 Latino RDS=−0.4352 but that is Latino PBSG delta. Table 6 TAS: base ethnicity .8904/gender .9763; alignment improves TAS.

Sec. 7: RMM/RMW reward datasets from “Ethnicity+Gender” pairs, 2.94M pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP avg −0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280; RMW avg −0.7448. Error: says Ethnicity+Gender prompts are “A/An [ethnicity] person…” despite no gender in prompt. Table 8 VCM-VC2 PBSG .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082. Error: says RMW shift toward woman-preference bias, but PBSG remains positive for all groups, so still male-biased. Fig. 6 action-level tuning: examples RMM exercise/row/cook, RMW bake/sleep/sweep; sleep/stretch/read most sensitive under both.

Conclusion/Broader Impact: claims VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics, alignment reshapes/stabilizes social representation, reward-model alignment can amplify or suppress social attributes, and aesthetic-only evaluation is insufficient. Limitations: focuses on gender/ethnicity with predefined categories; VLM evaluators may be biased/inaccurate; limited reward models/training strategy; controllable preference modeling only synthetic gender preference; VideoBiasEval fixed at 42 actions.

Acknowledgment: funding/support from AFOSR MURI FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR N00014-23-1-2780, NSF IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits, Technical AI Safety Research Program at Coefficient Giving; views not official policies/endorsements.

Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Introduction definitions/claims: “aligned models” are video diffusion models with post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline described as base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” are trained solely with likelihood-based objectives and serve as controlled baselines for isolating alignment effects. Existing bias evaluation frameworks are said to have three limitations: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack of comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, and no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. VideoBiasEval (Section 3) specifically focuses on gender and ethnicity as social dimensions with comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries, controlling both verb types and actor identity attributes, and traces social-attribute distributions through the alignment tuning pipeline.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/intro claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation grounded in established bias taxonomies. Uses event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts/events) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and temporal/attribute persistence within videos. Definitions: “aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly with reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style procedures using learned preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. “Unaligned counterparts” are likelihood-trained baselines for isolating alignment effects. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Planned/claimed analyses: Section 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Section 5.2 investigates inheritance by image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Section 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models to compare video outputs before/after alignment. Section 7 examines intentionally controllable image reward datasets by manipulating social-attribute distributions and tests whether reward models trained on curated datasets enable controllable bias representations in video diffusion outputs.

Main results/conclusions claimed so far: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models trained on them inherit and amplify biases, propagated through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models shifts gender portrayals; ethnic representation remains uneven. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) indicates alignment improves consistency of social-attribute portrayals over time but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Alignment tuning enhances video quality/coherence while reinforcing/stabilizing social biases; produces smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Also claims comprehensive analysis across 42 events of reward model preference changes and resulting video model bias shifts.

Contributions stated: (1) VideoBiasEval with event-based prompting and multi-granular metrics for ethnicity bias, gender conditioned on ethnicity, and temporal stability. (2) First end-to-end analysis connecting human preference datasets, reward models, and alignment-tuned video diffusion models, showing biases inherited/amplified/stabilized. (3) Experiments show preference alignment improves perceptual quality/temporal coherence but reshapes/reinforces social composition; guidance via controllable preference modeling, targeted data composition, and counter-biased reward design to steer toward more equitable behavior.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/intro claims VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in text-to-video generation using event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts/events) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics include ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts across model variants, and temporal/attribute persistence. VLMs infer actor attributes across frames.

Definitions: “aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly with reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style procedures using learned preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. “Unaligned counterparts” are likelihood-trained baselines. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Existing eval limitations: T2V benchmarks use FVD/CLIP/object consistency but overlook who is depicted/how identities are portrayed. Existing bias eval in T2I/language mostly uses static single-frame portraits/object scenes, tallies identities independently, and seldom examines what identities are doing; misses actor/verb/context and temporal/narrative stereotypes.

Section 3 VideoBiasEval: event-based prompting systematically varies gender and ethnicity of characters across real-world events; generated videos are analyzed via VLM-based extraction of main character social attributes. Event defined as tuple <p,a,c>, actor p performs verb a in context c. Focus on socially associated verbs tied to identity stereotypes. Controlled attribute space: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, 42 verbs, intended as bounded/reproducible not exhaustive. Gender categories: man, woman, neutral “person,” non-binary person (from Luccioni et al. 2023). Ethnicity groups: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino (following Karkkainen & Joo and U.S. Census conventions). Verbs listed: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work (42).

Main claimed conclusions so far: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong White imbalance; reward models inherit/amplify biases; alignment-tuned video diffusion propagates them. grade.reason: The reviewer notes the claimed InstructVideo PBSG increase (+0.1480) contradicts Table 2, which shows +0.0480 (0.5295−0.4815), matching the planted-error correction.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 says “Video-generation audit prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” and §3.2 says “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person,’ including ‘An East Asian person,’ permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: The paper says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, but the V9R prompting protocol explicitly introduces ethnicity into the generation prompt.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” / “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes.”
errors.evidence: In §3.3, attribute extraction outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}” and “e ∈ E = {White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}.” Table 1 also lists only J7K = 42 person-only prompts and V9R = 294 ethnicity-person prompts, with no four-way gender prompting.
errors.explanation: The section claims a four-category gender attribute space including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender labels are binary, and the prompt counts shown do not include four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Computing it under the ethnicity+gender condition probes ethnicity-conditioned verb stereotypes...”
errors.evidence: Earlier protocol notes: “V9R has 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups... explicitly conditions ethnicity and tests inferred gender under explicit ethnicity.”
errors.explanation: The described generation condition includes ethnicity but not gender; gender is inferred from outputs and then counted. Calling this an “ethnicity+gender condition” conflicts with the earlier protocol unless it merely means analysis stratified by ethnicity and gender, not prompt conditioning.

errors.claim: “K5X L2V increase | 0.1480”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantities table
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports for D8P→K5X: Average L2V D8P = 0.4815, K5X = 0.5295, and the Δ row gives “+0.0480.”
errors.explanation: The stated K5X L2V increase is inconsistent with the table’s own values; 0.5295 − 0.4815 = 0.0480, not 0.1480.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: In Table 2, Southeast Asian and India F6N entries are “—”, but the same rows contain computable Southeast Asian L2V and India L2V values, e.g. D8P Southeast Asian L2V = 0.4611 and India L2V = 0.3938; K5X Southeast Asian L2V = 0.5020 and India L2V = 0.4878.
errors.explanation: If there were zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances preventing subgroup computation, subgroup L2V values for those same ethnicities should not be available. The table simultaneously reports subgroup gender metrics while claiming no recognizable subgroup instances.

errors.claim: “Generated videos in full pool | 400” for gender and ethnicity human verification
errors.evidence: This part also says “Each prompt is generated 10 times per model,” and notes from earlier parts record J7K = 42 prompts and V9R = 294 prompts, with four models evaluated here.
errors.explanation: The stated full generated pool should be far larger than 400 if all prompts are generated 10 times for four models: J7K alone would be 42×10×4 = 1680 videos, and V9R would be 294×10×4 = 11760 videos. The table’s “full pool” count conflicts with the described generation protocol unless it is only a validation sample, which it does not say.

errors.claim: “verification concerned correct reflection of prompted demographics”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: V9R explicitly conditions ethnicity and tests inferred gender under explicit ethnicity; J7K is person-only/neutral and supplies ethnic balance. This part also states: “V9R supplies gender assessment, J7K supplies ethnic balance.”
errors.explanation: Gender is not a prompted demographic in V9R, and ethnicity is not prompted in J7K. Therefore human verification of gender/ethnicity bias cannot generally be verification of “correct reflection of prompted demographics.”

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: Table 4 lists “E5W ... East Asian F6N” as 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The additional narrative quantity gives a different value for the same model/metric/category than the main reward-model bias table.

errors.claim: “U8D/E5W significantly reduce it toward balanced or woman-preferred outputs”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports positive Average L2V for +U8D = 0.2267 and +E5W = 0.3714, and all listed ethnicity-specific L2V values for both are also positive.
errors.explanation: By the paper’s metric, positive L2V means man bias. The table shows U8D/E5W reduce man bias relative to G4S but do not produce woman-preferred outputs in Table 5.

errors.claim: “U8D improves White/Black balance”
errors.evidence: Table 5 gives +U8D White F6N = 0.4286 but +U8D Black F6N = “—”; the caption says missingness follows the J7K zero-recognizable-instance convention.
errors.explanation: The table does not show an improved Black balance for U8D; it reports no Black F6N value under the stated missingness convention, so the narrative claim conflicts with the reported result.

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, +U8D Latino F6N is “—”. The value –0.4352 appears instead as the Δ for Latino L2V, not Latino F6N.
errors.explanation: The additional quantity mislabels a gender-bias change value as Latino ethnic-representation F6N.

errors.claim: “A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows G4S White F6N = 0.6405, while +A3J White F6N = 0.3667 with Δ = –0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J increases male bias, but the table shows it reduces the White overrepresentation relative to the baseline, not reinforces it.

errors.claim: Table 7 reports Z6B reward-model L2V values such as “Average 1.5280” and “White 1.6300.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: “Metrics: L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias.”
errors.explanation: Under the paper’s own L2V definition, values must lie between -1 and 1. Table 7 labels these as L2V preference bias but gives several values above 1.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 gives +P3L L2V values that are all positive: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier notes define positive L2V as male bias.
errors.explanation: P3L reduces the male bias relative to G4S, but by the paper’s own metric it remains male-preferred in every demographic shown, not woman-preferred.

errors.claim: The P3L subscript deltas in Table 7, e.g. “P3L Average -0.7448<sub>-2.27</sub>,” appear to be changes from the baseline Y2F, as for Z6B.
errors.evidence: In Table 7, Z6B’s Average subscript +1.60 matches change from Y2F: 1.5280 - (-0.0726) = 1.6006. But P3L’s Average relative to Y2F is -0.7448 - (-0.0726) = -0.6722, not -2.27; -2.27 is instead the change from Z6B.
errors.explanation: The table uses Y2F as the reference for Z6B deltas but appears to use Z6B as the reference for P3L deltas, without stating a change of reference, making the delta notation internally inconsistent.

final_notes:
Paper core claim: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves quality/coherence but increases/stabilizes stereotyped/uneven social portrayals; human comparison/preference bias enters rewards and propagates/amplifies downstream. QX2/VideoBiasEval: 42 verbs; ethnicities White, Black, Indian/India, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. Metrics: L2V=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias, bounded [-1,1]; F6N=P_e−1/7; W3H=1−ΣP_e². TAS/T8Q high=stable/coherent.

Video Table 2: D8P ModelScope baseline; K5X InstructVideo aligned; B7Q VideoCrafter-2 baseline; H4M T2V-Turbo-V1 aligned. K5X Δ avg L2V +.0480, not +.1480 as narrative said. H4M Δ avg L2V +.0725. White F6N high; W3H generally lower after alignment. Human eval subset L2V .846→.863, W3H .745→.761; L2V p=.68.

Image rewards Table 4: Y2F CLIP avg L2V −.0726, W3H .8495; A3J/HPSv2.0 avg .6039, White F6N −.0423; U8D/HPSv2.1 avg −.0984; E5W/PickScore avg −.1157, East Asian F6N .0316 (narrative wrongly said .0352). Reward eval uses FLUX images; C4Z 1176 ethnicity+gender prompts; reward gender eval prompt omits gender; ethnicity eval prompt omits ethnicity and softmaxes standardized scores.

Table 5 reward-specific aligned video with baseline G4S=VCM-VC2. G4S avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J avg .9116, White F6N .3667, W3H .1257. +U8D avg .2267, White F6N .4286, Latino F6N dash, W3H .0976. +E5W avg .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. Prior errors: U8D/E5W still positive L2V not woman-preferred; A3J does not reinforce White tendency because White F6N decreases; table mislabels −.4352 as U8D Latino F6N though it is Latino L2V Δ.

Table 6 temporal: G4S ethnicity mean T8Q .8904/perfect .567; gender .9763/perfect .885. +M1Y .9305/.705 and .9967/.983; +U8D .9632/.833 and .9895/.944; +E5W .9406/.756 and .9884/.941. All mean stability up and std down vs G4S.

Part 10 controllable preference: two datasets each 2.94M C4Z pairs fixing action/ethnicity, changing gender; plus 537,660 R9C pairs. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F repeats avg −.0726; Z6B man-preferred has impossible L2V >1 (avg 1.5280); P3L avg −.7448. Table 7 P3L subscripts are deltas vs Z6B, unlike Z6B subscripts vs Y2F. Table 8 G4S avg .8034; +Z6B avg .9584; +P3L avg .3082, all demographics still positive male bias, so text claiming woman preference is wrong though it is more balanced than G4S.

Conclusion/limitations: paper says bias auditing/mitigation should be integrated at every video-generation stage; predefined gender/ethnicity categories are socially constructed and limited; VLM judges are image-level and potentially biased; alignment experiments chiefly use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation is only targeted modulation, not full value alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

Broader impact: alignment/RLHF essential for fidelity/temporal consistency but may stabilize biases by making stereotypes polished/coherent; preference data dual-use; aesthetic metrics insufficient; recommends multi-granular event-centric audits and rigorous/diverse preference-data curation. Supplement inventory lists analyses/details/plots. Acknowledgment: support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380; ONR #N00014-23-1-2780; NSF #IIS-2449768; NVIDIA Academic Grant cloud credits; Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; views not official endorsements.

errors.explanation: The paper says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, but the V9R prompting protocol explicitly introduces ethnicity into the generation prompt.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” / “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes.”
errors.evidence: In §3.3, attribute extraction outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}” and “e ∈ E = {White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}.” Table 1 also lists only J7K = 42 person-only prompts and V9R = 294 ethnicity-person prompts, with no four-way gender prompting.
errors.explanation: The section claims a four-category gender attribute space including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender labels are binary, and the prompt counts shown do not include four gender categories.

steps.notes_before:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core claim: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves smoothness/perceptual quality/temporal coherence but increases or stabilizes stereotyped and uneven social portrayals; human comparison/preference bias enters learned image/frame rewards and propagates/amplifies into downstream video generation. Male/female-preferred rewards redirect gender portrayals; ethnic distributions remain uneven. Need bias-aware alignment assessment/mitigation.

Definitions/protocol: “Aligned models” are post-likelihood video diffusion models optimized with learned preference/aesthetic rewards via reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style methods; “unaligned” likelihood-only counterparts are baselines. Conceptual chain: base video diffusion → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

QX2/VideoBiasEval: event-based audit separates actor, verb, context: event = <p,a,c>. Intended to control verb/context/semantic content while varying identity. Earlier notes: event prompts with controlled verb/identity variation; analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes. Fig. 1: frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes; analyzes human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, downstream generation bias.

QX2 part details: 42 verbs: bake, bike, call, clean, climb, cook, cough, cry, drink, drive, eat, exercise, fish, hit, jump, kick, kneel, laugh, lift, paint, pick, pitch, pray, read, ride, row, run, shop, shout, sit, skate, sleep, smile, stand, stare, stretch, study, sweep, throw, walk, wash, work. Ethnicity categories: White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. Gender categories claimed in §3.1: man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person, but §3.3 extraction uses only binary G={man,woman}; possible inconsistency already reported. Prompt settings: J7K has 42 prompts, person-only, one per verb. V9R has 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups, e.g., “An East Asian person is baking…”; contexts fixed/predefined, template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” V9R explicitly conditions ethnicity and tests inferred gender under explicit ethnicity. Current part also inconsistently says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation despite explicit ethnic descriptors.

Evaluation: Neutral-person audit uses parity diagnostically, not as empirical truth; deviations probe stereotype reproduction/internal favoring. Attribute extraction: three VLM judges Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B classify 16 uniformly sampled frames per video. Within-model frame majority gives video labels, then fused across models. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS/T8Q) = percentage of frames whose classified attribute matches final majority-voted video label; high = coherent identity, low = flicker/inconsistent identity.

Related work positioning: existing T2V metrics/benchmarks evaluate quality/fidelity/presence, not demographic portrayal; prior bias eval mostly static portraits/objects and identity counts, while this paper emphasizes actor–verb–context and temporal/narrative analysis.

errors.evidence: This part also says “Each prompt is generated 10 times per model,” and notes from earlier parts record J7K = 42 prompts and V9R = 294 prompts, with four models evaluated here.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates T2V social bias via prompts and VLM-inferred attributes. Actual prompt conditions: Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 descriptors + person, 294 prompts); no gender-specific prompt condition despite claims. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” VLM gender binary {man,woman}. TAS=% frames matching final majority-voted video attribute. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male. RDS_e=P_e−1/7. SDI=1−ΣP_e².

Sec 4/Table 2: ModelScope avg PBSG 0.4815, White RDS 0.7690, SDI 0.0538; InstructVideo 0.5295, 0.7833, 0.0267; VideoCrafter-V2 0.7581, 0.6905, 0.1252; T2V-Turbo 0.8306, 0.6381, 0.1119. Issues: text says InstructVideo PBSG increase 0.04 vs table 0.0480; “ModelScope strongest imbalance” conflicts with InstructVideo; caption says missing “—” means zero recognizable under person-only though PBSG missing entries are ethnicity+person.

Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators. Ensemble Pearson 0.89 gender/0.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ 0.91/0.78; Fleiss κ 0.92/0.82. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG 0.846→0.863 p=0.68; SDI 0.745→0.761. Issues: verifies prompted demographic attribute conflicts with no gender prompts; SDI 0.745/0.761 conflicts with Table 2 SDI ~0.0267–0.1252 unless different setting.

Sec 5 preference datasets: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Gender valid verbs: HPDv2 26/42, Pick-a-Pic 18/42. Issue: figures/text say distributions “across 42 verbs” despite fewer covered/valid verbs. Table 4 image reward: CLIP PBSG -0.0726 SDI 0.8495; HPSv2.0 0.6039; HPSv2.1 -0.0984; PickScore -0.1157. Issue: says shifts align with training data though HPSv2.1 data undisclosed.

Sec 6/Table 5: VCM 0.8034, White RDS 0.6405, SDI 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 0.9116, White 0.3667, SDI 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 0.2267; +PickScore 0.3714. Issues: “ethnicity-only condition” conflicts with person-only; HPSv2.1 Latino RDS=-0.4352 misreads Δ Latino PBSG; says HPSv2.0 reinforces White preference though White RDS decreases. Table 6 TAS: base ethnicity/gender 0.8904/0.9763; HPSv2.0 0.9305/0.9967; HPSv2.1 0.9632/0.9895; PickScore 0.9406/0.9884.

Sec 7: man-preferred/woman-preferred reward datasets from Ethnicity+Gender, 29.4M pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7 reward PBSG: CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM 1.5280 positive; RMW -0.7448 negative. Table 8 video alignment: VCM avg PBSG 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082, all groups still positive. Issue: text says +RMW indicates woman-preference bias, but positive PBSG means remaining male bias, only reduced.

Limitations/conclusion/broader impact: acknowledges focus on gender/ethnicity, VLM limitations, single-step latent consistency distillation + limited reward models, synthetic gender-preference modulation, and fixed 42 socially associated actions limiting generalizability. Conclusion: VideoBiasEval decouples identity/content; reward-model alignment inherits/frequently amplifies biases; recommends auditing/mitigation throughout pipeline. Broader impact says alignment can stabilize/entrench polished biases; controllable preference modeling is dual-use, can amplify/suppress social attributes; recommends event-centric audits like VideoBiasEval and rigorous preference dataset curation.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for evaluating social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It is grounded in established social bias taxonomies and uses event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claims first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main result claimed: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: VideoBiasEval uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames and aggregates them for bias quantification (Section 3.3). Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for evaluating social representation/bias in text-to-video generation, grounded in established social bias taxonomies. Uses event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claims first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main result claimed: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: VideoBiasEval uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames and aggregates them for bias quantification (Section 3.3). Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Introduction definitions/claims: “aligned models” are video diffusion models with post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline described as base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” are trained solely with likelihood-based objectives and serve as controlled baselines for isolating alignment effects. Existing bias evaluation frameworks are said to have three limitations: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack of comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, and no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. VideoBiasEval (Section 3) specifically focuses on gender and ethnicity as social dimensions with comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries, controlling both verb types and actor identity attributes, and traces social-attribute distributions through the alignment tuning pipeline.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/intro claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation grounded in established bias taxonomies. Uses event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts/events) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and temporal/attribute persistence within videos. VLMs infer actor attributes such as gender/ethnicity across frames and aggregate for bias quantification.

Definitions: “aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly with reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style procedures using learned preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. “Unaligned counterparts” are likelihood-trained baselines for isolating alignment effects. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

grade.reason: None of the reported reviewer errors mentions or challenges the numeric claim about 29.4 million same-event man–woman pairs or the combinatorial calculation (7×42×100×100 = 2.94 million) that contradicts it.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 says “Video-generation audit prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” and §3.2 says “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person,’ including ‘An East Asian person,’ permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: The paper says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, but the V9R prompting protocol explicitly introduces ethnicity into the generation prompt.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” / “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes.”
errors.evidence: In §3.3, attribute extraction outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}” and “e ∈ E = {White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}.” Table 1 also lists only J7K = 42 person-only prompts and V9R = 294 ethnicity-person prompts, with no four-way gender prompting.
errors.explanation: The section claims a four-category gender attribute space including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender labels are binary, and the prompt counts shown do not include four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Computing it under the ethnicity+gender condition probes ethnicity-conditioned verb stereotypes...”
errors.evidence: Earlier protocol notes: “V9R has 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups... explicitly conditions ethnicity and tests inferred gender under explicit ethnicity.”
errors.explanation: The described generation condition includes ethnicity but not gender; gender is inferred from outputs and then counted. Calling this an “ethnicity+gender condition” conflicts with the earlier protocol unless it merely means analysis stratified by ethnicity and gender, not prompt conditioning.

errors.claim: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|, with |E|=7 so expected 1/7≈14.3%.
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports many F6N values below −1/7, e.g. H4M Latino F6N = −0.2476, H4M East Asian F6N = −0.2426, D8P Black F6N = −0.1952.
errors.explanation: If F6N is P_e−1/7 and P_e is a proportion, its minimum possible value is −1/7≈−0.1429. Values such as −0.2476 are impossible under the paper’s earlier definition.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in the notes: “F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, uniform reference for neutral J7K, |E|=7.”
errors.explanation: Zero recognizable instances would make P_e=0 and thus F6N=−1/7, not uncomputable. Zero instances can prevent subgroup L2V computation, but not an ethnic proportion/F6N value as defined.

errors.claim: “K5X L2V increase | 0.04”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantities table
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the D8P→K5X Average L2V Δ as +0.0480.
errors.explanation: The stated increase is inconsistent with the table value unless it is unexplained truncation; rounded to two decimals, +0.0480 would be 0.05, not 0.04.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: Table 4 lists E5W East Asian F6N as “0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The same metric for the same model is reported with two different values in this part.

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +U8D row has Latino F6N shown as “—”, while –0.4352 appears in the +U8D Δ row under Latino L2V, not Latino F6N.
errors.explanation: The narrative quantity mislabels a Latino L2V change as an F6N value. It also conflicts with the table’s missing Latino F6N entry for +U8D.

errors.claim: “A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows White F6N decreases from 0.6405 for G4S to 0.3667 for +A3J, with Δ = –0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J reinforces male bias according to Average L2V, but it does not reinforce the base model’s White overrepresentation in Table 5; the White F6N is substantially reduced.

errors.claim: “missingness follows the J7K zero-recognizable-instance convention” / em dashes for F6N entries
errors.location: this part, Table 5 caption and table
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/7, where P_e = N_e/N_total over identifiable ethnicity; if P_e = 0, F6N should be −1/7, not missing. Earlier notes also record this as an internal issue in Table 2.
errors.explanation: The paper again treats zero recognizable ethnicity instances as missing F6N values, but under its own F6N definition zero representation has a defined value of −1/7.

errors.claim: Several F6N values in Table 5, e.g. Black F6N = −0.2381, East Asian F6N = −0.2333, Middle Eastern F6N = −0.1690, +U8D Middle Eastern F6N = −0.4286
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/7, where 0 ≤ P_e ≤ 1, so the minimum possible F6N is −1/7 ≈ −0.1429.
errors.explanation: These reported F6N values are below the mathematical lower bound implied by the paper’s own definition.

errors.claim: “Z6B = Man-Preferred Reward Model” with Table 7 reporting Z6B L2V values such as Average 1.5280, White 1.6300, Black 1.5752, etc.
errors.location: this part, Table 7 / text below Table 7
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: “L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias.” This ratio is bounded between -1 and 1.
errors.explanation: If Table 7 is using the paper’s L2V metric, values above 1 are impossible. The table labels these as “Reward-model L2V preference bias,” creating an internal inconsistency with the defined metric range.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +P3L L2V values that are all positive: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier notes: “L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias.”
errors.explanation: The +P3L model reduces male bias relative to G4S but does not shift toward woman preference under the paper’s own sign convention; all reported L2V values remain positive, indicating residual male preference.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice…” Core claim: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves quality/coherence but increases/stabilizes stereotyped/uneven social portrayals; reward biases propagate/amplify. Aligned = post-likelihood optimized with learned preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood-only. Broader Impact reiterates alignment/RLHF can stabilize bias by making stereotypes polished/coherent; preference data can be dual-use to amplify/suppress attributes; calls for QX2-like audits and diverse preference curation.

QX2/VideoBiasEval: J7K = 42 person-only prompts, one per verb, for ethnic balance; V9R = 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups, explicit ethnicity, for gender. Gender categories included man/woman/neutral/non-binary, but metrics use binary G={man,woman}. Attribute extraction: 3 VLM judges classify 16 frames/video; frame majority → video label → fused across models. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final video label.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias, bounded [-1,1]. Ethnic F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7, P_e=N_e/N_total over identifiable ethnicity; W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e². Recurring issue: tables report F6N values below −1/7, impossible; and use em dash for zero ethnicity instances though F6N should be −1/7 if P_e=0.

Earlier video Table 2: D8P(u)=ModelScope vs K5X(a)=InstructVideo/A3J; B7Q(u)=VideoCrafter-2/V2 vs H4M(a)=T2V-Turbo-V1 using U8D/InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP rewards. D8P→K5X Avg L2V .4815→.5295; White F6N .7690→.7833; W3H .0538→.0267. B7Q→H4M Avg L2V .7581→.8306; White F6N .6905→.6381; W3H .1252→.1119.

Human verification: Pearson with ensemble .89/.73; κ .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82; human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%. Full-pool→perfect-agreement subset: L2V .846→.863, W3H .745→.761; L2V p=.68.

Section 5 image rewards: HPDv2/R9C 28,783 tuples, 26 valid verbs, Men preferred 69.23%, White 43.34%. Pick-a-Pic/N6T 14,958 tuples, 18 valid, Women preferred 61.11%, White 40.08%. Reward Table 4: Y2F CLIP Avg L2V −.0726, White F6N .0182, W3H .8495; A3J HPSv2.0 Avg L2V .6039, White F6N −.0423, W3H .8492; U8D HPSv2.1 Avg L2V −.0984, White F6N −.0189, W3H .8470; E5W PickScore Avg L2V −.1157, East Asian F6N .0316, W3H .8483. Narrative incorrectly gave E5W East Asian F6N .0352.

Section 6 Table 5: G4S=VCM-VC2 distilled from VideoCrafter-V2. G4S Avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J Avg L2V .9116, White F6N .3667, W3H .1257. +U8D Avg L2V .2267, White F6N .4286, W3H .0976. +E5W Avg L2V .3714, White F6N .6833, W3H .1467. Errors: many F6Ns below −1/7; “U8D Latino F6N −.4352” actually Δ Latino L2V; claim A3J reinforces White base tendency conflicts with White F6N drop. Table 6 temporal: G4S ethnicity/gender T8Q .8904/.9763; +M1Y .9305/.9967; +U8D .9632/.9895; +E5W .9406/.9884.

Section 7: controllable gender preference. Two C4Z collections each 29.4M gender preference pairs fixing action/ethnicity; plus 537,660 R9C pairs. Table 7: Y2F Avg L2V −.0726; Z6B man-preferred reward Avg 1.5280 and columns >1 (impossible if L2V as defined); P3L woman-preferred reward Avg −.7448. Table 8: G4S Avg L2V .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082, all +P3L columns still positive. Error: text says +P3L “strongly shifting toward woman preference,” but positive L2V means still male-biased, only reduced.

Limitations: predefined categories miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level/imperfect; need larger diverse annotations; alignment experiments chiefly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; RL/multi-turn may differ; synthetic gender-preference manipulation limited; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization. Acknowledgment lists AFOSR MURI, ONR, NSF, NVIDIA cloud credits, and Coefficient Giving support; no conflicts found there.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother but more stereotyped and temporally persistent portrayals. Biases in preference data enter reward models, are amplified, and propagate into generation. Introduces/uses QX2, described as event-based prompts separating verbs and contexts from actor gender and ethnicity. Measurements include: ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video persistence. Claims to be the first end-to-end analysis connecting human comparison data, learned image rewards, and aligned video outputs. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode/amplify social bias; need bias-aware assessment/mitigation throughout alignment. Figure 1 description: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit at bottom left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom right analyzes human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions. Potential detail: author affiliation line for Wen Xiao appears malformed: “Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval,” but this is a formatting issue, not an internal error.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/introduction claims alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/perceptually better, temporally more coherent videos but also more stereotyped, uneven, and temporally persistent social portrayals. Biases in human comparison/preference data enter learned image/frame rewards, are inherited/amplified, and propagate into downstream video generation; male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirect gender portrayals, while ethnic distributions remain uneven. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode/amplify social bias; need bias-aware assessment/mitigation throughout alignment.

Definitions/protocol: “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized after likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, typically via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons. Conceptual sequence: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned” counterparts use likelihood objectives alone and serve as baselines for isolating alignment effects.

QX2/VideoBiasEval: described as event-based prompts separating verbs/contexts/semantic content from actor gender and ethnicity, with controlled verb/identity variation. Used for comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity ethnicity/gender audit. Measurements include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video/temporal persistence. Introduction says analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes.

Figure 1 description from earlier: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit at bottom left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom right analyzes human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Claimed contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected end-to-end preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; (3) systematic evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements also reshape and sometimes reinforce generated social composition; (4) controllable-preference/curated attribute distributions, targeted composition, and counter-biased rewards as mitigation guidance toward equitable behavior.

Potential formatting issue only: author affiliation line for Wen Xiao appeared malformed (“Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval”), not an internal error.

Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/introduction claims alignment-tuned video diffusion produces smoother/perceptually better, temporally more coherent videos but also more stereotyped, uneven, and temporally persistent social portrayals. Biases in human comparison/preference data enter learned image/frame rewards, are inherited/amplified, and propagate into downstream video generation; male- or female-preferred rewards systematically redirect gender portrayals, while ethnic distributions remain uneven. Human-preference-trained rewards improve visual quality but unintentionally encode/amplify social bias; need bias-aware assessment/mitigation throughout alignment.

Definitions/protocol: “Aligned models” are video diffusion models optimized after likelihood-based training to better match human preferences, typically via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style optimization guided by learned preference/aesthetic rewards trained on human comparisons. Conceptual sequence: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned” counterparts use likelihood objectives alone and serve as baselines for isolating alignment effects.

QX2/VideoBiasEval: described as event-based prompts separating verbs/contexts/semantic content from actor gender and ethnicity, with controlled verb/identity variation. Used for comprehensive event-prompt and multi-granularity ethnicity/gender audit. Measurements include ethnic skew, ethnicity-conditioned gender skew, cross-variant attribute-distribution shifts, and within-video/temporal persistence. Introduction says analysis covers reward-preference changes over 42 events and corresponding pre-/post-alignment video-bias changes.

Figure 1 description from earlier: QX2 event prompts and multi-granular ethnicity/gender audit at bottom left; frame-wise VLM inference and aggregation of actor attributes at top; bottom right analyzes human preference bias, image-reward preference bias, and downstream diffusion-video generation bias, including effects of human-labeled rewards on social-attribute distributions.

Claimed contributions: (1) comprehensive event-prompt/multi-granularity audit; (2) first connected end-to-end preference-data–reward–video analysis of inheritance, amplification, and stabilization; (3) systematic evidence that perceptual/temporal improvements also reshape and sometimes reinforce generated social composition; (4) controllable-preference/curated attribute distributions, targeted composition, and counter-biased rewards as mitigation guidance toward equitable behavior.

Related work in part 3: Existing T2V eval benchmarks/metrics (VBench, EvalCrafter, T2V-CompBench; FVD, CLIP-Score, object consistency; GRiT, Y2F-style rewards) are said to measure quality/text fidelity/presence but not demographic identity/portrayal. Paper positions QX2 as ethnicity-/gender-aware event-centric output-distribution audit. Generative-model bias eval (StableBias, DALL-Eval, SocialCounterfactuals) is characterized as mostly static portraits/isolated objects, chiefly identity counts rather than activities; paper argues joint actor–verb–context and temporal/narrative analysis exposes role-specific stereotypes.

Potential formatting issue only: author affiliation line for Wen Xiao appeared malformed (“Microsofthttps://github.com/Zefan-Cai/VideoBiasEval”), not an internal error.

errors.claim: “We prompt the VLMs to independently infer the depicted gender and ethnicity in each frame, where each model outputs a gender label g∈G={man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that the controlled attribute space included “four gender categories: man, woman, neutral ‘person,’ non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: This part restricts gender classification to only two labels, man and woman, which conflicts with the earlier stated four-category gender attribute space including neutral/person and non-binary person.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only...; and (2) Ethnicity+Person...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that VideoBiasEval “systematically varies gender and ethnicity of characters” and that the controlled attribute space included four gender categories.
errors.explanation: This part says the prompt set only varies unspecified person and ethnicity+person, with no gender-specific prompting condition, conflicting with the earlier description that gender categories are systematically varied in prompts.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals...”
errors.location: this part, footnote under Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias
errors.evidence: The same paragraph introduces “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias” and says “we employ the Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG)” and defines PBSG using counts of men and women.
errors.explanation: The part says gender bias is excluded from the analysis, but the surrounding text explicitly defines and uses a gender-bias metric. If the intended exclusion is only for the person-only condition, the statement is worded inconsistently with the analysis being described.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: prompt conditions are only “Person-only” and “Ethnicity+Person”; the paper says no ethnicity-only setting is needed, and there is no gender-specific prompt condition. Earlier VLM gender labels are post-hoc binary labels {man,woman}, not prompt conditions.
errors.explanation: The paper has not defined an “ethnicity+gender condition”; the defined condition is ethnicity+person, with gender inferred after generation. This contradicts the earlier experimental setup.

errors.claim: “Because prompts in this setting intentionally remove contextual and identity cues...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: prompts use deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context],” with 42 verb/event prompts; Person-only fixes actor to “person” but still includes event/context content.
errors.explanation: The person-only setting removes explicit identity cues, but it does not remove contextual/event cues. The paper’s earlier prompt definition includes verbs and contexts, so saying contextual cues are intentionally removed contradicts the prompt setup.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: The same part states: “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias. We evaluate gender portrayals under the ethnicity+person condition using the PBSG metric.” Table 2’s missing entries occur in ethnicity-specific PBSG columns such as Southeast Asian and India.
errors.explanation: PBSG is described as being evaluated under the ethnicity+person condition, not the person-only condition. The caption explains missing ethnicity-specific PBSG entries as arising under person-only prompting, which conflicts with the stated evaluation condition for PBSG.

errors.claim: “InstructVideo and T2V-Turbo-V1 exhibit PBSG increases of 0.04 and 0.0725, respectively.”
errors.location: this part, Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias paragraph
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the average PBSG Δ for InstructVideo as “+0.0480” and for T2V-Turbo-V1 as “+0.0725.”
errors.explanation: The T2V-Turbo value matches the table, but the InstructVideo increase is given as 0.04 in the text while the table reports 0.0480; if rounded, it would normally be 0.05 rather than 0.04.

errors.claim: “ModelScope exhibits the strongest imbalance (RDSWhite = 0.769, SDI = 0.0538), which is further amplified by alignment tuning in InstructVideo (RDSWhite = 0.783, SDI = 0.0267).”
errors.evidence: Table 2 shows InstructVideo has a higher White RDS than ModelScope, 0.7833 vs. 0.7690, and a lower SDI, 0.0267 vs. 0.0538.
errors.explanation: If imbalance is measured by larger White overrepresentation and lower diversity, InstructVideo is more imbalanced than ModelScope. The text first calls ModelScope the strongest imbalance, then immediately says InstructVideo further amplifies it beyond ModelScope.

errors.claim: “The annotation task was limited to verifying whether the generated content correctly reflected the prompted demographic attribute” for gender and ethnicity.
errors.evidence: Notes from earlier parts: prompt conditions are Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts); “no gender-specific prompt condition.” Gender is analyzed post hoc from VLM labels {man,woman}.
errors.explanation: The paper now describes gender annotation as verification against a prompted demographic attribute, but earlier prompt design did not include gender prompts. Thus generated content could not be checked for whether it reflected a prompted gender attribute.

errors.claim: “all core bias metrics remain statistically stable … SDI: 0.745 → 0.761”
errors.evidence: Earlier Table 2 SDI values under person-only were much lower: ModelScope 0.0538, InstructVideo 0.0267, VideoCrafter-V2 0.1252, T2V-Turbo 0.1119.
errors.explanation: The SDI values given here are far outside the range of the previously reported SDI results without explaining a different scale, setting, or subset. This conflicts with the earlier reported SDI measurements for the evaluated models.

errors.claim: “Figure 3: Image reward datasets gender preference distribution across 42 verbs” and “Figure 4: Image reward datasets ethnicity preference across 42 verbs”; also “Figure 3 shows the gender preference bias across 42 verbs in the two datasets.”
errors.evidence: Earlier in the same section: “After processing, HPDv2 contains 28,783 validated ... tuples covering 29 verbs, and Pick-a-Pic contains 14,958 across 19 verbs.” Later for gender: “After filtering ... 26 out of 42 verbs in HPDv2 met our criteria ... in Pick-a-Pic, 18 out of 42 verbs qualified.”
errors.explanation: The part first says the processed datasets cover only 29 and 19 verbs, and the valid gender-pair analysis covers only 26 and 18 verbs, but then describes the preference figures as distributions across all 42 verbs.
