errors.claim: “Using the event prompting templates introduced in Section 3.2 ... [the benchmark varies] systematically across gender, ethnicity, and verb dimensions” and includes “Ethnicity+Gender, where both gender and ethnicity are explicitly indicated.”
errors.evidence: Notes from earlier parts: the actual Section 3 prompt conditions seen were Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts); there was no gender-specific prompt condition, despite earlier broad claims about gender categories.
errors.explanation: This part says the Section 3.2 event prompting templates are used for a benchmark that explicitly varies gender and ethnicity, but the earlier prompt setup did not include a gender-explicit prompt condition. That makes the reference to previously introduced templates inconsistent with the earlier described template conditions.

errors.claim: “Ethnicity + Gender” prompt setting with 1176 prompts, e.g. “An East Asian woman is baking…”
errors.evidence: Earlier VideoBiasEval prompt setup recorded in notes had only Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts), with “no gender-specific prompt condition.”
errors.explanation: This part introduces a systematic Ethnicity+Gender prompt condition, while the earlier benchmark description/notes indicated the paper’s prompt conditions did not include gender-specific prompts. If Table 3 is meant to describe the same benchmark construction framework, this contradicts the earlier stated prompt setup.

errors.claim: “The base model, CLIP, slightly favors White individuals (RDS = 0.0182) and achieves the lowest SDI score (0.8495), indicating relatively balanced ethnic representation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes for Table 4: “CLIP avg PBSG -0.0726 SDI 0.8495; HPSv2.0 avg PBSG 0.6039 SDI 0.8492; HPSv2.1 avg -0.0984 SDI 0.8470; PickScore avg -0.1157 SDI 0.8483.” This part also says “A higher SDI score corresponds to more balanced and diverse outputs” and “All show reduced SDI” after fine-tuning.
errors.explanation: CLIP’s SDI 0.8495 is the highest among the listed models, not the lowest. The claim also conflicts with the part’s own statement that higher SDI is more balanced and that fine-tuned models have reduced SDI relative to CLIP.

errors.claim: “Under the ethnicity-only condition, we analyze models’ representation balance using the previously defined RDSe and SDI metrics.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “actual VideoBiasEval conditions were Person-only (‘person,’ 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts)” and no ethnicity-only condition was described.
errors.explanation: This part refers to an “ethnicity-only condition,” but the paper’s earlier evaluation conditions were Person-only and Ethnicity+Person. This is inconsistent with the previously defined setup.

errors.claim: “Alignment with HPSv2.1 … significantly decreases Latino representation (RDS = –0.4352)”
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +HPSv2.1 row has Latino RDS marked “—”. The value –0.4352 appears in the Δ row under Latino PBSG, not Latino RDS.
errors.explanation: The text attributes –0.4352 to Latino ethnicity representation disparity, but the table shows no Latino RDS value for HPSv2.1; –0.4352 is a change in Latino PBSG.

errors.claim: “Missing values … indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Table 5 contains missing values in ethnicity-specific PBSG/RDS columns, while the text says PBSG is evaluated “under the ethnicity+person condition.” Earlier notes also record that the same caption logic conflicted with Table 2 because PBSG missing entries are for ethnicity+person, not person-only.
errors.explanation: The caption explains missing subgroup entries as arising under the person-only condition, but ethnicity-specific gender PBSG is computed under ethnicity+person prompts, so this explanation does not match the table’s metrics.

errors.claim: “HPSv2.0 reinforces the base model’s male- and White-preferred tendencies”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes/Table 5: VCM White RDS = 0.6405, while +HPSv2.0 White RDS = 0.3667; HPSv2.0 PBSG rises from 0.8034 to 0.9116.
errors.explanation: HPSv2.0 does reinforce/amplify the male preference, but its White RDS is lower than the baseline, so it mitigates rather than reinforces the base model’s White-preferred tendency.

errors.claim: “Each dataset includes 2.94 million preference pairs from the Ethnicity+Gender set”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Actual conditions: Person-only (‘person,’ 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts); no gender-specific prompt condition despite earlier claims.”
errors.explanation: This part refers to an “Ethnicity+Gender set,” but the recorded experimental setup had only Person-only and Ethnicity+Person prompt conditions, with no gender-specific condition.

errors.claim: “As shown in Table 7, RMM consistently assigns higher PBSG scores…” / Table 7 reports RMM PBSG values such as 1.5280, 1.6300, etc.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes define PBSG as “PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total,” which is bounded between -1 and 1.
errors.explanation: Table 7 labels these as PBSG scores, but RMM values above 1 are impossible under the paper’s own PBSG definition.

errors.claim: “alignment with RMW substantially reduces these scores, indicating a strong shift toward woman-preference bias.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +RMW PBSG values that remain positive for every group: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Earlier notes define positive PBSG as more men than women: “PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total.”
errors.explanation: The RMW-aligned model is less male-biased than VCM-VC2, but its positive PBSG values still indicate man-preference rather than woman-preference bias.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates T2V bias using event prompts and VLM-inferred actor attributes across frames. Actual prompt conditions: Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts); no gender-specific prompt condition despite earlier claims. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” VLM gender binary {man,woman}. Metrics: TAS=% frames matching final video attribute label; PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; SDI=1−ΣP_e²; Δ aligned−base.

Sec 4/Table 2 video results: ModelScope avg PBSG 0.4815, White RDS 0.7690, SDI 0.0538; InstructVideo 0.5295, 0.7833, 0.0267; VideoCrafter-V2 0.7581, 0.6905, 0.1252; T2V-Turbo 0.8306, 0.6381, 0.1119. Issues: text says InstructVideo PBSG increase 0.04 vs table 0.0480; “ModelScope strongest imbalance” conflicts with InstructVideo; caption says “—” means zero recognizable under person-only though PBSG missing entries are ethnicity+person.

Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators. Ensemble Pearson 0.89 gender/0.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ 0.91/0.78; Fleiss κ 0.92/0.82. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG 0.846→0.863 p=0.68; SDI 0.745→0.761. Issues: verifying prompted demographic attribute conflicts with no gender prompts; SDI 0.745/0.761 conflicts with Table 2 SDI ~0.0267–0.1252 unless different setting.

grade.reason: Yes — review item 13 flags the planted claim: Table 4 shows CLIP's SDI (0.8495) is higher than HPSv2.0 (0.8492) and HPSv2.1 (0.8470), so CLIP does not have the lowest SDI.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 says “Video-generation audit prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” and §3.2 says “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person,’ including ‘An East Asian person,’ permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: The paper says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, but the V9R prompting protocol explicitly introduces ethnicity into the generation prompt.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” / “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes.”
errors.evidence: In §3.3, attribute extraction outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}” and “e ∈ E = {White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}.” Table 1 also lists only J7K = 42 person-only prompts and V9R = 294 ethnicity-person prompts, with no four-way gender prompting.
errors.explanation: The section claims a four-category gender attribute space including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender labels are binary, and the prompt counts shown do not include four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Computing it under the ethnicity+gender condition probes ethnicity-conditioned verb stereotypes...”
errors.evidence: Earlier protocol notes: “V9R has 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups... explicitly conditions ethnicity and tests inferred gender under explicit ethnicity.”
errors.explanation: The described generation condition includes ethnicity but not gender; gender is inferred from outputs and then counted. Calling this an “ethnicity+gender condition” conflicts with the earlier protocol unless it merely means analysis stratified by ethnicity and gender, not prompt conditioning.

errors.claim: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|, with |E|=7 so expected 1/7≈14.3%.
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports many F6N values below −1/7, e.g. H4M Latino F6N = −0.2476, H4M East Asian F6N = −0.2426, D8P Black F6N = −0.1952.
errors.explanation: If F6N is P_e−1/7 and P_e is a proportion, its minimum possible value is −1/7≈−0.1429. Values such as −0.2476 are impossible under the paper’s earlier definition.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in the notes: “F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, uniform reference for neutral J7K, |E|=7.”
errors.explanation: Zero recognizable instances would make P_e=0 and thus F6N=−1/7, not uncomputable. Zero instances can prevent subgroup L2V computation, but not an ethnic proportion/F6N value as defined.

errors.claim: “K5X L2V increase | 0.04”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantities table
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the D8P→K5X Average L2V Δ as +0.0480.
errors.explanation: The stated increase is inconsistent with the table value unless it is unexplained truncation; rounded to two decimals, +0.0480 would be 0.05, not 0.04.

errors.claim: “Y2F ... has the lowest diversity”
errors.evidence: Table 4 Overall W3H values are Y2F 0.8495, A3J 0.8492, U8D 0.8470, E5W 0.8483; earlier metric definition says W3H/SDI = 1−ΣP_e², so higher means more diversity.
errors.explanation: Y2F has the highest W3H among the listed reward models, not the lowest. U8D has the lowest W3H/diversity.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 4, the E5W row lists East Asian F6N as 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The additional narrative quantity gives a different value for the same metric/model than Table 4.

errors.claim: “U8D = HPSv2.1”
errors.location: this part, Reward identities and scoring
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that the B7Q→H4M aligned video model used “U8D/InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP rewards.”
errors.explanation: The same identifier U8D is used for two different reward identities: InternVid2-S2/ViCLIP earlier and HPSv2.1 here.

errors.claim: Table 5 reports multiple F6N values such as Black F6N = -0.2381, East Asian F6N = -0.2333, Middle Eastern F6N = -0.3667, and U8D Middle Eastern F6N = -0.4286.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition in notes: "Ethnic F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7 over identifiable ethnicity" with 7 ethnic groups.
errors.explanation: If F6N = P_e − 1/7 and P_e is a proportion between 0 and 1, the minimum possible F6N is −1/7 ≈ −0.1429. Values below −0.1429 are impossible under the paper’s own metric definition.

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +U8D row has Latino F6N shown as “—”, while −0.4352 appears in the Δ row under Latino L2V, not Latino F6N.
errors.explanation: The added narrative quantity labels −0.4352 as Latino F6N, but the table shows it is the change in Latino L2V. The reported quantity is therefore mislabeled and contradicts Table 5.

errors.claim: “U8D improves White/Black balance”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows U8D White F6N changes from 0.6405 to 0.4286, but Black F6N for +U8D is “—” and its Δ is also “—”.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core claim: alignment tuning improves quality/coherence but increases/stabilizes stereotyped and uneven social portrayals; reward biases propagate/amplify. Definitions: aligned = post-likelihood optimized with learned preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood-only. L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), range [-1,1], positive=male bias. Ethnic F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7, range [-1/7,6/7]; W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e², higher=more diversity.

Benchmarks: J7K=42 person-only prompts, V9R=294 prompts, C4Z=1176 prompts. Gender categories earlier included man/woman/neutral/non-binary but metrics binary. Extraction uses 3 VLM judges over 16 frames, majority/fusion; TAS/T8Q=% frames matching final video label.

Earlier Table 2: D8P→K5X avg L2V .4815→.5295; White F6N .7690→.7833; W3H .0538→.0267. B7Q→H4M avg L2V .7581→.8306; White F6N .6905→.6381; W3H .1252→.1119. All male-biased; aligned increases average imbalance. H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity. Prior issues: impossible F6N below −1/7; K5X increase described .04 vs actual .0480.

Human verification: 400 gender/400 ethnicity; Pearson .89/.73; κ .91/.78; Fleiss .92/.82; human-majority/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%. Full-pool→perfect-agreement: L2V .846→.863, W3H .745→.761; L2V p=.68.

Reward data: HPDv2/R9C 28,783 tuples, 26 valid man-woman-pair verbs, men preferred 69.23%, White 43.34%. Pick-a-Pic/N6T 14,958 tuples, 18 valid, women preferred 61.11%, White 40.08%. Table 4 reward models: Y2F avg L2V −.0726, White F6N .0182, W3H .8495; A3J avg L2V .6039; U8D −.0984; E5W −.1157. Prior errors: narrative said Y2F lowest diversity though highest W3H; E5W East Asian F6N mismatch; U8D label conflict.

Table 5: G4S baseline avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J avg .9116, W3H .1257; +U8D avg .2267, W3H .0976; +E5W avg .3714, W3H .1467. Table 6 T8Q: G4S ethnicity/gender .8904/.9763; +M1Y .9305/.9967; +U8D .9632/.9895; +E5W .9406/.9884. Prior errors: impossible F6N values; U8D Latino F6N actually Δ Latino L2V; Black F6N missing; +M1Y/+A3J label conflict.

Part 7: two 2.94M C4Z gender preference-pair datasets plus 537,660 R9C image pairs. Z6B=Man-Preferred/RMM; P3L=Woman-Preferred/RMW, fine-tuned from Y2F. Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg −.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280 and all groups >1, impossible under definition; P3L avg −.7448. Table 8 video L2V: G4S avg .8034; +Z6B avg .9584; +P3L avg .3082, all still positive despite text saying shifted to woman preference. Action sensitivity uses ΔL2V divided by reward baseline L2V; sensitive actions include sleep/stretch/read both directions.

Conclusion/limitations: auditing/mitigation needed at every stage, not preference alignment alone. Limitations: predefined categories miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level and can be biased/inaccurate; larger diverse video annotation needed. Alignment experiments chiefly use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; RL-based/multi-turn instruction alignment may differ. Synthetic gender-preference manipulation targeted only. Fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

Broader impact: alignment incl. RLHF can stabilize/entrench polished biases; preference data can be used for mitigation or harmful exclusion/propaganda; developers should monitor with multi-granular event-centric audits such as QX2 and curate preference data for equity. Supplement inventory lists per-verb gender/ethnicity analyses, WebVid training-data effects, reward dataset ethnicity distributions, reward/video training details, and plot numbers for four-model, reward-model, reward-aligned, and controllable-preference analyses.

grade.reason: Yes — review item 6 correctly flags that the paper's claim that Y2F has the lowest diversity contradicts Table 4, which shows Y2F with the highest W3H/SDI among the listed reward models.

errors.claim: “We prompt the VLMs to independently infer the depicted gender and ethnicity in each frame, where each model outputs a gender label g∈G={man, woman}.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that the controlled attribute space included “four gender categories: man, woman, neutral ‘person,’ non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: This part restricts gender classification to only two labels, man and woman, which conflicts with the earlier stated four-category gender attribute space including neutral/person and non-binary person.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only...; and (2) Ethnicity+Person...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record that VideoBiasEval “systematically varies gender and ethnicity of characters” and that the controlled attribute space included four gender categories.
errors.explanation: This part says the prompt set only varies unspecified person and ethnicity+person, with no gender-specific prompting condition, conflicting with the earlier description that gender categories are systematically varied in prompts.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals...”
errors.location: this part, footnote under Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias
errors.evidence: The same paragraph introduces “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias” and says “we employ the Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG)” and defines PBSG using counts of men and women.
errors.explanation: The part says gender bias is excluded from the analysis, but the surrounding text explicitly defines and uses a gender-bias metric. If the intended exclusion is only for the person-only condition, the statement is worded inconsistently with the analysis being described.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: prompt conditions are only “Person-only” and “Ethnicity+Person”; the paper says no ethnicity-only setting is needed, and there is no gender-specific prompt condition. Earlier VLM gender labels are post-hoc binary labels {man,woman}, not prompt conditions.
errors.explanation: The paper has not defined an “ethnicity+gender condition”; the defined condition is ethnicity+person, with gender inferred after generation. This contradicts the earlier experimental setup.

errors.claim: “Because prompts in this setting intentionally remove contextual and identity cues...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: prompts use deterministic template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context],” with 42 verb/event prompts; Person-only fixes actor to “person” but still includes event/context content.
errors.explanation: The person-only setting removes explicit identity cues, but it does not remove contextual/event cues. The paper’s earlier prompt definition includes verbs and contexts, so saying contextual cues are intentionally removed contradicts the prompt setup.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: The same caption and following text distinguish PBSG from person-only RDSe/SDI: “For PBSG…” and later “We evaluate gender portrayals under the ethnicity+person condition using the PBSG metric.” Yet Table 2 contains ‘—’ entries in PBSG columns as well as RDS columns.
errors.explanation: The explanation for missing values cannot apply to all ‘—’ entries: PBSG is computed under the ethnicity+person condition, not the person-only condition, so missing PBSG values cannot be explained solely by zero recognizable instances under person-only prompts.

errors.claim: “Overall, reducing White overrepresentation directly causes demographic diversity to fall, establishing an unavoidable trade-off between ethnic bias reduction and representational variety.”
errors.evidence: Table 2 shows VideoCrafter-V2 has lower White overrepresentation than ModelScope but higher diversity: ModelScope RDSWhite = 0.7690, SDI = 0.0538; Video-Crafter-V2 RDSWhite = 0.6905, SDI = 0.1252.
errors.explanation: This directly contradicts the claimed unavoidable trade-off: in this comparison, White overrepresentation falls while SDI diversity rises.

errors.claim: “The annotation task was limited to verifying whether the generated content correctly reflected the prompted demographic attribute” for “gender and ethnicity.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Prompt setup: ... actual prompt conditions defined are Person-only (actor ‘person,’ 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts). No gender-specific prompt condition was defined; VLM gender labels binary {man,woman}. Demographics unconstrained; analyzed post hoc.”
errors.explanation: This part implies gender was a prompted demographic attribute that annotators could verify against the prompt, but earlier methodology defined no gender-prompt condition; gender was inferred post hoc from unconstrained generations.

final_notes:
Paper: VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in T2V using event prompts; VLMs infer actor attributes across 16 frames, majority vote per model and fusion across Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. Prompts: Person-only 42; Ethnicity+Person 7×42=294. No gender-specific video prompt condition defined; VLM gender labels binary {man,woman}. Metrics: TAS; PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive male, range [-1,1]; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; SDI=1−ΣP_e²; Δ aligned vs unaligned.

Initial T2V/Table 2: ModelScope PBSG .4815, White PBSG .5683, RDSWhite .7690, SDI .0538. InstructVideo PBSG .5295, RDSWhite .7833, SDI .0267; ΔPBSG +.0480, ΔRDSWhite +.0143, ΔSDI −.0271. Video-Crafter-V2 PBSG .7581, RDSWhite .6905, SDI .1252. T2V-Turbo-V1 PBSG .8306, RDSWhite .6381, SDI .1119; ΔPBSG +.0725, ΔRDSWhite −.0524, ΔSDI −.0133. Prior errors: ‘—’ caption overgeneralized; “prompted gender” despite no gender prompts; claim reducing White lowers diversity contradicted by data.

Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators. VLM-human Pearson .89 gender/.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ .91/.78; Fleiss κ .92/.82. High-agreement subset consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG .846→.863 p=.68; SDI .745→.761.

Image reward analysis: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Gender pair: HPDv2 26 valid verbs, 18/26 male-preferred; Pick-a-Pic 18 valid, 11/18 woman-preferred. Ethnicity preference: White 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic. Reward benchmark FLUX, 100 images/prompt. Table 3 inconsistent Ethnicity+Gender count 1176 vs binary gender×7×42=588. Table 4: CLIP avg PBSG −.0726 SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 PBSG .6039 SDI .8492; HPSv2.1 PBSG −.0984 SDI .8470; PickScore PBSG −.1157 SDI .8483.

Section 6 fine-tunes VCM-VC2 using HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, PickScore. Table 5: VCM PBSG .8034, White RDS .6405, SDI .1433. +HPSv2.0 PBSG .9116, White RDS .3667, Middle Eastern RDS −.3667, SDI .1257. +HPSv2.1 PBSG .2267, White RDS .4286, Middle Eastern RDS −.4286, SDI .0976; Latino RDS ‘—’ and Δ Latino PBSG −.4352. +PickScore PBSG .3714, White RDS .6833, SDI .1467. Errors: says two metrics though lists three; undefined “ethnicity-only”; says HPSv2.1 decreases Latino representation RDS=−.4352 but table shows ΔPBSG; Table 6 says +HPSv2 not +HPSv2.0; HPSv2.0 not reinforce White preference because White RDS drops .6405→.3667.

Table 6 TAS: VCM ethnicity mean .8904/gender .9763; +HPSv2.0 ethnicity .9305 gender .9967; +HPSv2.1 ethnicity .9632 gender .9895; +PickScore ethnicity .9406 gender .9884. Claims: HPSv2.1 ethnicity perfect stability .5670→.8330, gender perfect .9440; HPSv2.0 gender TAS .9967/perfect .9830.

Section 7 controllable gender preference: constructs man/woman-preferred reward datasets: 2.94M gender-paired images from Ethnicity+Gender plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7 labels reward model “PBSG scores”: CLIP avg −.0726; RMM avg 1.5280 and all >1; RMW avg −.7448. Error: PBSG >1 impossible. Table 8 video alignment: VCM PBSG .8034; +RMM avg .9584; +RMW avg .3082, all groups positive. Error: text says RMW shifts to woman-preference bias, but positive PBSG means still male-preferred, only reduced. Action-level Fig.6 claims RMM amplifies male portrayals in exercise/row/cook; RMW shifts toward women-preferred bake/sleep/sweep; normalized sensitivity = ΔPBSG divided by each reward model’s baseline PBSG; sleep/stretch/read most sensitive under both.

Conclusion/broader impact: VideoBiasEval decouples identity attributes from content semantics; reward-model-based alignment frequently amplifies/stabilizes biases in human preference data; alignment can polish biases and make them harder to detect; controllable preference modeling can amplify or suppress social attributes, with dual-use risks. Limitations: gender/ethnicity only, predefined U.S. Census/prior categories; limited intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM biases; limited alignment/reward setups; synthetic gender manipulations; 42 actions limit generalizability. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for evaluating social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. Introduction definitions/claims: “aligned models” are video diffusion models with post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Main claim: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves quality/smoothness but can amplify/stabilize stereotypes; bias in human comparison data enters reward models and propagates to aligned video outputs. Broader Impact repeats: alignment/RLHF improves fidelity/temporal consistency but can stabilize bias; polished stereotypes become harder to detect; preference data can be dual-use for mitigation or intentional exclusion/propaganda; aesthetic metrics insufficient, need multi-granular event-centric audits like QX2 and careful preference-data curation.

Definitions: “Aligned” = optimized after likelihood training via reward/preference/aesthetic models from human comparisons; “unaligned” = likelihood-only. Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive = male bias; F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7; W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e²; TAS/T8Q temporal consistency.

Internal errors found earlier: §3.2 said demographic attributes not introduced/constrained/inferred during generation, but V9R introduces ethnicity. Claim J7K removes contextual cues despite retaining verb/context. Table 2 narrative says D8P strongest imbalance/B7Q more balanced, contradicted by Avg L2V. Table 2 caption says dash means zero recognizable ethnicity preventing subgroup computation, yet L2V shown where F6N dash. Table 4 vs additional table: E5W East Asian F6N .0316 vs .0352. Figure 5 caption says all images use [ethnicity][gender], contradicting V9R/ethnicity eval. In §6 Table 5, –0.4352 mislabeled as U8D Latino F6N though it is Δ Latino L2V; claims U8D decreasing Latino representation unsupported; U8D/E5W aligned outputs not woman-preferred because L2V remains positive; A3J does not reinforce White tendency because White F6N falls. Table 7 subscripts use inconsistent delta baselines: Z6B deltas match vs Y2F; P3L deltas match vs Z6B, not vs Y2F. Table 8 text says P3L shifts toward woman preference/corrects imbalance/equilibrium/equitable representation, but L2V remains positive in every subgroup, so only mitigates male bias.

Key results: Table 4 reward models: Y2F Avg L2V -0.0726; A3J Avg .6039; U8D Avg -.0984; E5W Avg -.1157. Table 5 G4S baseline Avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433; +A3J Avg .9116; +U8D Avg .2267; +E5W Avg .3714. Table 6 temporal all aligned variants have higher T8Q than G4S. §7: C4Z gender preference-pair collections, 2.94M pairs each; prompts omit gender; labels man-preferred male=1/female=0, woman-preferred reverse; plus 537,660 R9C pairs; fine-tunes Y2F encoders into Z6B/RMM and P3L/RMW. Table 7 reward-model L2V: Z6B Avg 1.5280; P3L Avg -0.7448. Table 8 aligned-video L2V: G4S Avg .8034; +Z6B Avg .9584; +P3L Avg .3082 all subgroups positive.

§8 limitations: predefined U.S. Census/prior-literature gender/ethnicity categories miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges image-level and may be biased/inaccurate; experiments mainly single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation only targeted modulation, not full value alignment; fixed socially associated action taxonomy limits generalization.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in T2V with event prompts and VLM-inferred attributes. Aligned = preference/reward optimized; unaligned = likelihood/base. Actual video conditions earlier: Person-only (42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts), no gender-specific or ethnicity-only condition despite some claims. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” VLM gender labels binary {man,woman}. Metrics: TAS = % frames matching final majority-voted video attribute label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male and bounded [-1,1]. RDS_e=P_e−1/7. SDI=1−ΣP_e². Δ compares aligned to base.

Sec 4/Table 2: ModelScope avg PBSG 0.4815, White RDS 0.7690, SDI 0.0538; InstructVideo 0.5295, 0.7833, 0.0267; VideoCrafter-V2 0.7581, 0.6905, 0.1252; T2V-Turbo 0.8306, 0.6381, 0.1119. Issues: text says InstructVideo PBSG increase 0.04 vs table 0.0480; “ModelScope strongest imbalance” conflicts with InstructVideo; caption says missing “—” means zero recognizable under person-only though PBSG missing entries are ethnicity+person.

Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators. Ensemble Pearson 0.89 gender/0.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ 0.91/0.78; Fleiss κ 0.92/0.82. High-agreement consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG 0.846→0.863 p=0.68; SDI 0.745→0.761. Issues: “prompted demographic attribute” conflicts with no gender prompts; SDI 0.745/0.761 conflicts with Table 2 SDI ~0.0267–0.1252 unless different setting.

Sec 5 datasets: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Gender pair valid verbs: HPDv2 26/42, 18/26 male-preferred; Pick-a-Pic 18/42, 11/18 female-preferred. Ethnicity prefs: White 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic. Issue: figures/text say “across 42 verbs” despite fewer covered/valid verbs. Image reward/Table 4: CLIP avg PBSG -0.0726 SDI 0.8495; HPSv2.0 0.6039; HPSv2.1 -0.0984; PickScore -0.1157. Error: text says CLIP man-preference +0.0726.

Sec 6/Table 5 VCM-VC2: base avg PBSG 0.8034 SDI 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 0.9116 SDI 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 0.2267 SDI 0.0976; +PickScore 0.3714 SDI 0.1467. Errors: HPSv2.1/PickScore called woman-preferred despite positive PBSG; ethnicity-only condition claimed; Latino RDS=-0.4352 misread from Δ Latino PBSG. Also HPSv2.0 said to reinforce White preference though HPSv2.0 reward ethnicity preference was Middle Eastern.

Sec 7: Constructs RMM/RMW gender preference reward datasets. Table 7: CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM avg 1.5280+1.60; RMW avg -0.7448-2.27. Errors: RMM “PBSG” values exceed PBSG bound; Table 7 deltas inconsistent (RMM vs CLIP, RMW vs RMM). Table 8: VCM avg PBSG 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082, all +RMW ethnic PBSGs positive. Error: text says +RMW shifts to woman-preference bias, but positive PBSG means still male-preferred, just reduced.

Limitations/Broader impact/Conclusion: claims focus on gender/ethnicity with predefined categories; VLM evaluators validated but may be biased; alignment impacts assessed mainly under single-step latent consistency distillation and limited reward models; controllable experiments limited to synthetic gender manipulation; VideoBiasEval fixed to 42 actions. Conclusion says reward-model alignment inherits/frequently amplifies biases; controllable/social-attribute-aware rewards can direct/counter bias. Acknowledgment only funding/support; no contradictions.

Main result claimed: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Introduction definitions/claims: “aligned models” are video diffusion models with post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline described as base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” are trained solely with likelihood-based objectives and serve as controlled baselines for isolating alignment effects. Existing bias evaluation frameworks are said to have three limitations: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack of comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, and no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. VideoBiasEval (Section 3) specifically focuses on gender and ethnicity as social dimensions with comparatively well-defined evaluative boundaries, controlling both verb types and actor identity attributes, and traces social-attribute distributions through the alignment tuning pipeline.

Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Planned/claimed analyses: Section 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Section 5.2 investigates inheritance by image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Section 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models to compare video outputs before/after alignment. Section 7 examines intentionally controllable image reward datasets by manipulating social-attribute distributions and tests whether reward models trained on curated datasets enable controllable bias representations in video diffusion outputs.

Main results/conclusions claimed so far: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Reward models trained on them inherit and amplify biases, propagated through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models shifts gender portrayals; ethnic representation remains uneven. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) indicates alignment improves consistency of social-attribute portrayals over time but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Alignment tuning enhances video quality/coherence while reinforcing/stabilizing social biases; produces smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Also claims comprehensive analysis across 42 events of reward model preference changes and resulting video model bias shifts.

Contributions stated: (1) VideoBiasEval with event-based prompting and multi-granular metrics for ethnicity bias, gender conditioned on ethnicity, and temporal stability. (2) First end-to-end analysis connecting human preference datasets, reward models, and alignment-tuned video diffusion models, showing biases inherited/amplified/stabilized. (3) Experiments show preference alignment improves perceptual quality/temporal coherence but reshapes/reinforces social composition; guidance via controllable preference modeling, targeted data composition, and counter-biased reward design to steer toward more equitable behavior.

grade.reason: Reviewer item 13 points out the sign error: Table 4 gives CLIP avg PBSG = -0.0726 (woman-preference), contradicting the paper's claim of +0.0726 male-preference and thus invalidating the follow-on claim that HPSv2.0 strengthened an inherited male preference.

sol_grade.reason: The reviewer identifies the reversed CLIP PBSG sign: Table 4 reports −0.0726, indicating woman-preference rather than the claimed man-preference.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 says “Video-generation audit prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” and §3.2 says “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person,’ including ‘An East Asian person,’ permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: The paper says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, but the V9R prompting protocol explicitly introduces ethnicity into the generation prompt.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” / “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes.”
errors.evidence: In §3.3, attribute extraction outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}” and “e ∈ E = {White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}.” Table 1 also lists only J7K = 42 person-only prompts and V9R = 294 ethnicity-person prompts, with no four-way gender prompting.
errors.explanation: The section claims a four-category gender attribute space including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender labels are binary, and the prompt counts shown do not include four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Computing it under the ethnicity+gender condition probes ethnicity-conditioned verb stereotypes...”
errors.evidence: Earlier protocol notes: “V9R has 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups... explicitly conditions ethnicity and tests inferred gender under explicit ethnicity.”
errors.explanation: The described generation condition includes ethnicity but not gender; gender is inferred from outputs and then counted. Calling this an “ethnicity+gender condition” conflicts with the earlier protocol unless it merely means analysis stratified by ethnicity and gender, not prompt conditioning.

errors.claim: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|, with |E|=7 so expected 1/7≈14.3%.
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports many F6N values below −1/7, e.g. H4M Latino F6N = −0.2476, H4M East Asian F6N = −0.2426, D8P Black F6N = −0.1952.
errors.explanation: If F6N is P_e−1/7 and P_e is a proportion, its minimum possible value is −1/7≈−0.1429. Values such as −0.2476 are impossible under the paper’s earlier definition.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in the notes: “F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, uniform reference for neutral J7K, |E|=7.”
errors.explanation: Zero recognizable instances would make P_e=0 and thus F6N=−1/7, not uncomputable. Zero instances can prevent subgroup L2V computation, but not an ethnic proportion/F6N value as defined.

errors.claim: “K5X L2V increase | 0.04”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantities table
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the D8P→K5X Average L2V Δ as +0.0480.
errors.explanation: The stated increase is inconsistent with the table value unless it is unexplained truncation; rounded to two decimals, +0.0480 would be 0.05, not 0.04.

errors.claim: “Y2F slightly favors men …”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports Y2F Average L2V = -0.0726. Earlier metric definition: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias.
errors.explanation: A negative L2V indicates woman preference/bias, not man preference. Thus the narrative reverses the direction shown by the table and the paper’s metric definition.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.evidence: Table 4 reports E5W East Asian F6N = 0.0316.
errors.explanation: The same quantity is given two different values in this part.

errors.claim: “Constructed-benchmark images use ‘A/An [ethnicity][gender] is baking [context].’ Only [gender]∈{man,woman} appears.”
errors.evidence: This part’s Table 3 lists V9R prompts as ethnicity-only, e.g. “An East Asian person is baking cookies…,” and later says for ethnicity evaluation generation uses “A/An [ethnicity] person is [verb]-ing [context]” with ethnicity and verb explicit.
errors.explanation: The Figure 5 caption appears to describe all constructed-benchmark images as containing explicit gender, but the same part says V9R/ethnicity-evaluation images use “person” and omit gender.

errors.claim: "U8D/E5W significantly reduce it toward balanced or woman-preferred outputs"
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows all U8D and E5W output L2V values remain positive: +U8D Average L2V 0.2267 and all ethnicity-specific L2V values positive; +E5W Average L2V 0.3714 and all ethnicity-specific L2V values positive.
errors.explanation: Under the paper’s definition, positive L2V means male bias. These aligned outputs are less male-biased than G4S, but the reported values do not become woman-preferred.

errors.claim: "U8D improves White/Black balance"
errors.evidence: Table 5 gives +U8D White F6N = 0.4286 but Black F6N is shown as an em dash, not a numeric value. The baseline Black F6N is -0.2381, but no +U8D Black F6N is reported.
errors.explanation: The table supports a reduction in White overrepresentation, but it does not report a U8D Black F6N value, so the claim that Black balance improves is not supported by the part’s own data.

errors.claim: "U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352"
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, +U8D Latino F6N is an em dash. The value -0.4352 appears in the Δ row under Latino L2V, not under Latino F6N.
errors.explanation: The additional narrative quantity mislabels a gender-bias delta as an ethnicity-representation F6N value.

errors.claim: "A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies"
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows White F6N decreases from G4S 0.6405 to +A3J 0.3667, with Δ = -0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J reinforces male bias in Table 5, but it reduces rather than reinforces the baseline’s White overrepresentation according to the reported White F6N.

errors.claim: Table 5 reports F6N values such as Middle Eastern F6N = -0.3667 for +A3J and -0.4286 for +U8D, Latino F6N = -0.1929 for +E5W, and East Asian F6N = -0.1952 for +E5W.
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: F6N/RDS_e = P_e - 1/7, where P_e is a proportion over identifiable ethnicity; therefore the minimum possible value is -1/7 ≈ -0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several reported F6N values are below the metric’s possible lower bound, contradicting the paper’s own definition of F6N.

errors.claim: Table 7 reports Z6B reward-model L2V values such as Average = 1.5280, White = 1.6300, Black = 1.5752, etc.
errors.evidence: Notes: “L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias.” This metric is bounded between -1 and +1.
errors.explanation: The reported Z6B L2V values exceed the maximum possible value of 1 under the paper’s own L2V definition.

errors.claim: “Prompts are ‘A/An [ethnicity] person is [action]-ing [context].’” while the dataset “fixes action and ethnicity while changing gender, including M-1 versus W-1.”
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says each pair changes gender, including male-vs-female images, but gives a prompt template using only “[ethnicity] person” with no gender term.
errors.explanation: If pairs are constructed by changing gender, the stated prompt template omits the gender variable needed to distinguish the paired male and female conditions.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 reports +P3L L2V values that remain positive for every group: Average 0.3082, White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894. Notes: positive L2V = male bias.
errors.explanation: Although P3L reduces male bias, the aligned-video outputs remain male-biased by the paper’s own metric, so the claim that it shifts the generator toward woman preference overstates/contradicts the table.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice...” Core claim: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves quality/coherence but increases/stabilizes stereotyped social portrayals; preference/reward biases propagate/amplify. aligned = post-likelihood video diffusion optimized with learned preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood-only.

QX2/VideoBiasEval: J7K = 42 person-only prompts, one per verb, used for ethnic balance; V9R = 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups, explicit ethnicity, used for gender assessment. Gender categories included man/woman/neutral/non-binary, but metrics use binary G={man,woman}. Extraction: 3 VLM judges classify 16 frames/video; frame majority → video label → fused; TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final video label.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias, bounded [-1,1]. Ethnic F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7, min −1/7≈−0.1429; W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e². Repeated issue: F6N tables report below −1/7 and use dash for zero recognizable/zero ethnicity cases despite definition.

Video Table 2: D8P ModelScope→K5X InstructVideo/A3J Avg L2V .4815→.5295 Δ+.0480; White F6N .7690→.7833; W3H .0538→.0267. B7Q VideoCrafter-2→H4M T2V-Turbo-V1/U8D Avg L2V .7581→.8306 Δ+.0725; White F6N .6905→.6381; W3H .1252→.1119. All male-biased; aligned increases avg gender imbalance; all overrepresent White; H4M reduces White dominance while lowering diversity.

Human verification: 400 gender/400 ethnicity; Pearson .89/.73; Cohen κ .91/.78; Fleiss κ .92/.82; human/VLM consensus 99.0%/83.3%; full→perfect subset L2V .846→.863, W3H .745→.761; L2V p=.68.

Reward datasets: HPDv2/R9C 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs, 26 valid man-woman, men preferred 69.23%, White 43.34%. Pick-a-Pic/N6T 14,958 tuples, 19 verbs, 18 valid, women preferred 61.11%, White 40.08%. Reward Table 4: Y2F Avg L2V −.0726; A3J .6039; U8D −.0984; E5W −.1157. Errors: narrative says Y2F favors men despite negative L2V; E5W East Asian mismatch.

Part 9 Table 5: G4S baseline Avg L2V .8034, White F6N .6405, W3H .1433. +A3J .9116; +U8D .2267; +E5W .3714; all positive male-biased despite claims of woman-preferred outputs. Table 6 temporal: all reward alignments improve T8Q vs G4S.

Part 10 controllable gender rewards: §7.1 says two C4Z collections each 2.94M gender-changing preference pairs plus 537,660 R9C pairs; prompt template given as “[ethnicity] person” (inconsistent with gender-changing pairs). Table 7 reward L2V: Y2F avg −.0726; Z6B avg 1.5280 and group values >1 (impossible for L2V); P3L avg −.7448. Table 8 G4S .8034; +Z6B .9584; +P3L .3082, still positive for all groups. Error: text says +P3L shifts toward woman preference though Table 8 remains male-biased.

Part 11 conclusion/limitations: calls for auditing/mitigation rather than treating preference alignment as sufficient. Limitations: predefined categories socially constructed; VLM classifiers may be biased; limited single-step latent consistency/rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation not full responsible alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits generalization.

Part 12 broader impact: claims alignment/RLHF essential for fidelity/temporal consistency but can stabilize bias by making stereotypes polished/coherent; preference-data engineering is dual-use; aesthetic metrics insufficient and QX2-like event-centric audits needed. Supplement inventory lists analyses/plots.

Part 13 acknowledgments: funding/support from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA Academic Grant Program cloud credits, Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; standard disclaimer that views do not represent funder/government policies or endorsements.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice…” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in T2V with event prompts and VLM-inferred attributes. Actual conditions Person-only (“person,” 42 prompts) and Ethnicity+Person (7 ethnic descriptors + person, 294 prompts); no gender-specific prompt condition despite claims about four gender categories/seven ethnicities. 42 verbs. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” VLM gender binary {man,woman}. Metrics: TAS=% frames matching final majority video label; PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male; RDS_e=P_e−1/7; SDI=1−ΣP_e²; Δ aligned−base.

Sec4/Table2: ModelScope avg PBSG 0.4815, White RDS 0.7690, SDI 0.0538; InstructVideo 0.5295, 0.7833, 0.0267; VideoCrafter 0.7581, 0.6905, 0.1252; T2V-Turbo 0.8306, 0.6381, 0.1119. Issues: text says InstructVideo PBSG increase 0.04 vs table 0.0480; “ModelScope strongest imbalance” conflicts with InstructVideo; caption says missing “—” means zero recognizable under person-only though PBSG missing entries are ethnicity+person. Human eval: 400 videos/3 annotators; ensemble Pearson 0.89 gender/0.73 ethnicity; Cohen κ 0.91/0.78; Fleiss κ 0.92/0.82. Consensus 99.0% gender, 83.3% ethnicity; PBSG 0.846→0.863 p=0.68; SDI 0.745→0.761. Issues: verifying prompted demographic attribute conflicts with no gender prompts; SDI 0.745/0.761 conflicts with Table2 SDI ~0.03–0.13 unless different setting.

Sec5: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Gender valid verbs: HPDv2 26/42, Pick-a-Pic 18/42. Issue: figures/text say distributions “across 42 verbs” despite fewer valid verbs. Image reward benchmark: Ethnicity+Person 294; Ethnicity+Gender 1176. Table4 reward PBSG/SDI: CLIP -0.0726/0.8495; HPSv2.0 0.6039/0.8492; HPSv2.1 -0.0984/0.8470; PickScore -0.1157/0.8483. Reward PBSG can exceed 1. Ethnicity softmax: CLIP White RDS 0.0182; HPSv2.0 Middle Eastern 0.0315; HPSv2.1 Latino 0.0382; PickScore East Asian 0.0352. Issue: says shifts align with training data while HPSv2.1 data undisclosed.

Sec6/Table5 VCM PBSG 0.8034, White RDS 0.6405, SDI 0.1433; +HPSv2.0 0.9116, White 0.3667, SDI 0.1257; +HPSv2.1 0.2267, White 0.4286, SDI 0.0976; +PickScore 0.3714, White 0.6833, SDI 0.1467. Issues: “ethnicity-only” conflicts with person-only; HPSv2.1 Latino RDS=-0.4352 misreads Δ Latino PBSG; says HPSv2.0 reinforces White though White RDS decreases. Table6 TAS: base ethnicity/gender 0.8904/0.9763; HPSv2.0 0.9305/0.9967; HPSv2.1 0.9632/0.9895; PickScore 0.9406/0.9884.

Sec7: RMM/RMW from CLIP using 2.94M gender-differing pairs + 537,660 HPDv2. Table7 PBSG: CLIP avg -0.0726; RMM 1.5280; RMW -0.7448. Error: says RMW matches RMM absolute magnitude, but magnitudes differ. Table8 VCM 0.8034; +RMM 0.9584; +RMW 0.3082, all group PBSG positive; text calling +RMW woman-preference/balanced conflicts with positive male bias. Part17 repeats: RMW can correct skewed portrayals producing balanced/socially representative generations; RMW shifts toward women-preferred actions (bake/sleep/sweep); top sensitive actions sleep/stretch/read under both; sensitivity across 42 actions.

Sec8 conclusion/limitations/broader impact: claims VideoBiasEval decouples identity from content and alignment tuning reshapes representations; reward-model alignment inherits/frequently amplifies preference-data biases. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories; VLM evaluator bias risk; alignment mainly single-step latent consistency distillation/limited reward models; controllable preference modeling only synthetic gender manipulation; fixed 42 actions. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for evaluating social representation/bias in text-to-video generation. It is grounded in established social bias taxonomies and uses event-based prompting to disentangle semantic content (verbs/contexts) from actor attributes (gender/ethnicity). Metrics evaluate: (1) overall ethnicity bias, (2) gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, (3) distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and (4) temporal persistence of bias within videos. Claims first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main result claimed: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Figure 1 overview: VideoBiasEval uses VLMs to infer actor attributes such as gender and ethnicity across frames and aggregates them for bias quantification (Section 3.3). Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

grade.reason: Reviewer item 18 directly points out that Table 7 reports Average PBSG RMM = 1.5280 and RMW = -0.7448, so the magnitudes are not matched and the claim of equal absolute bias magnitude is false.

errors.claim: “Demographic attributes are not introduced, constrained, or inferred during generation.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 says “Video-generation audit prompts explicitly contain ethnicity when specified,” and §3.2 says “Deterministically prepending a predefined ethnic descriptor to ‘person,’ including ‘An East Asian person,’ permutes the verbs across ethnic groups.”
errors.explanation: The paper says demographic attributes are not introduced during generation, but the V9R prompting protocol explicitly introduces ethnicity into the generation prompt.

errors.claim: “The bounded attribute space balances coverage against control: four gender categories, seven ethnic groups, and 42 verbs…” / “Each actor carries gender and ethnicity attributes.”
errors.evidence: In §3.3, attribute extraction outputs are defined as “g ∈ G = {man,woman}” and “e ∈ E = {White,Black,Indian,East Asian,Southeast Asian,Middle Eastern,Latino}.” Table 1 also lists only J7K = 42 person-only prompts and V9R = 294 ethnicity-person prompts, with no four-way gender prompting.
errors.explanation: The section claims a four-category gender attribute space including neutral person and non-binary person, but the actual extraction/evaluation gender labels are binary, and the prompt counts shown do not include four gender categories.

errors.claim: “Computing it under the ethnicity+gender condition probes ethnicity-conditioned verb stereotypes...”
errors.evidence: Earlier protocol notes: “V9R has 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups... explicitly conditions ethnicity and tests inferred gender under explicit ethnicity.”
errors.explanation: The described generation condition includes ethnicity but not gender; gender is inferred from outputs and then counted. Calling this an “ethnicity+gender condition” conflicts with the earlier protocol unless it merely means analysis stratified by ethnicity and gender, not prompt conditioning.

errors.claim: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E|, with |E|=7 so expected 1/7≈14.3%.
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports many F6N values below −1/7, e.g. H4M Latino F6N = −0.2476, H4M East Asian F6N = −0.2426, D8P Black F6N = −0.1952.
errors.explanation: If F6N is P_e−1/7 and P_e is a proportion, its minimum possible value is −1/7≈−0.1429. Values such as −0.2476 are impossible under the paper’s earlier definition.

errors.claim: “Throughout the video-distribution tables, ‘—’ denotes zero recognizable corresponding-ethnicity instances under J7K, severe diversity absence preventing subgroup computation.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in the notes: “F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/|E|, uniform reference for neutral J7K, |E|=7.”
errors.explanation: Zero recognizable instances would make P_e=0 and thus F6N=−1/7, not uncomputable. Zero instances can prevent subgroup L2V computation, but not an ethnic proportion/F6N value as defined.

errors.claim: “K5X L2V increase | 0.04”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantities table
errors.evidence: Table 2 reports the D8P→K5X Average L2V Δ as +0.0480.
errors.explanation: The stated increase is inconsistent with the table value unless it is unexplained truncation; rounded to two decimals, +0.0480 would be 0.05, not 0.04.

errors.claim: “E5W East Asian F6N | 0.0352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: Table 4 lists E5W East Asian F6N as “0.0316.”
errors.explanation: The same metric for the same model is reported with two different values in this part.

errors.claim: “U8D-aligned Latino representation F6N | –0.4352”
errors.location: this part, Additional narrative quantity table
errors.evidence: In Table 5, the +U8D row has Latino F6N shown as “—”, while –0.4352 appears in the +U8D Δ row under Latino L2V, not Latino F6N.
errors.explanation: The narrative quantity mislabels a Latino L2V change as an F6N value. It also conflicts with the table’s missing Latino F6N entry for +U8D.

errors.claim: “A3J reinforces male- and White-preferred base tendencies”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows White F6N decreases from 0.6405 for G4S to 0.3667 for +A3J, with Δ = –0.2738.
errors.explanation: A3J reinforces male bias according to Average L2V, but it does not reinforce the base model’s White overrepresentation in Table 5; the White F6N is substantially reduced.

errors.claim: “missingness follows the J7K zero-recognizable-instance convention” / em dashes for F6N entries
errors.location: this part, Table 5 caption and table
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/7, where P_e = N_e/N_total over identifiable ethnicity; if P_e = 0, F6N should be −1/7, not missing. Earlier notes also record this as an internal issue in Table 2.
errors.explanation: The paper again treats zero recognizable ethnicity instances as missing F6N values, but under its own F6N definition zero representation has a defined value of −1/7.

errors.claim: Several F6N values in Table 5, e.g. Black F6N = −0.2381, East Asian F6N = −0.2333, Middle Eastern F6N = −0.1690, +U8D Middle Eastern F6N = −0.4286
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: F6N/RDS_e = P_e − 1/7, where 0 ≤ P_e ≤ 1, so the minimum possible F6N is −1/7 ≈ −0.1429.
errors.explanation: These reported F6N values are below the mathematical lower bound implied by the paper’s own definition.

errors.claim: “P3L equally strongly favors women, matching Z6B’s absolute bias magnitude” / “Magnitude-matched reward tuning establishes direction alone, rather than strength, as the corrective mechanism.”
errors.location: this part, Section 7.2 text after Table 7
errors.evidence: Table 7 reports Z6B Average L2V = 1.5280, while P3L Average L2V = -0.7448; the deltas from Y2F are +1.60 and -2.27 respectively.
errors.explanation: The absolute L2V magnitudes are not matched: |1.5280| is about twice |−0.7448|, and the reported changes are also not equal in magnitude. Thus the text’s claim that the reward biases are magnitude-matched conflicts with its own table.

errors.claim: “P3L substantially lowers them, strongly shifting toward woman preference.”
errors.evidence: Earlier metric definition in notes: L2V/PBSG = (N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive = male bias. Table 8 reports +P3L Average L2V = 0.3082, with all demographic values positive: White 0.3341, Black 0.3913, Latino 0.3314, East Asian 0.1008, Southeast Asian 0.2639, India 0.3446, Middle Eastern 0.3894.
errors.explanation: P3L reduces male bias relative to G4S, but the resulting L2V values remain positive for every group, which indicates continued male preference rather than a shift toward woman preference.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice…” Core claim: alignment-tuned video diffusion improves quality/coherence but increases/stabilizes stereotyped/uneven social portrayals; reward biases propagate/amplify. Aligned = post-likelihood optimized with learned preference/aesthetic rewards; unaligned = likelihood-only. Broader Impact reiterates alignment/RLHF improves fidelity/temporal consistency but stabilizes polished bias; preference data can be used for mitigation or malicious amplification; recommends continuous QX2-style audits and diverse/equitable preference curation. Acknowledgment: thanks reviewers; funding from AFOSR MURI #FA9550-22-1-0380, ONR #N00014-23-1-2780, NSF #IIS-2449768, NVIDIA cloud credits, Coefficient Giving Technical AI Safety Research Program; disclaimer that views do not represent funders/government.

QX2/VideoBiasEval: event audit separates actor/verb/context. J7K = 42 person-only prompts, one per verb, used for ethnic balance; V9R = 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic groups, explicit ethnicity, used for gender. Earlier inconsistency: said demographic attributes not introduced despite ethnic descriptors. Gender categories included man/woman/neutral/non-binary, but metrics use binary G={man,woman}. Attribute extraction: 3 VLM judges classify 16 frames/video; frame majority → video label → fused across models. TAS/T8Q = % frames matching final video label.

Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/(N_man+N_woman), positive=male bias. Ethnic F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7, P_e=N_e/N_total over identifiable ethnicity; uniform reference for neutral J7K; W3H/SDI=1−ΣP_e². grade.reason: Entry 11 points out that Table 7 reports Z6B Average L2V = 1.5280 and P3L Average L2V = -0.7448, so the claimed magnitude-matching is contradicted by the paper's own numbers.

errors.claim: “we define two prompting conditions: (1) Person-only ...; and (2) Ethnicity+Person ... yielding 294 prompts”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “event-based prompting systematically varies gender and ethnicity of characters”; “Controlled attribute space: four gender categories ... Gender categories: man, woman, neutral ‘person,’ non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: This part defines only person-only and ethnicity+person prompt conditions, with no gender-specific or non-binary prompt conditions, contradicting the earlier stated design that systematically varies gender using four gender categories.

errors.claim: “each model outputs a gender label g ∈ G = {man, woman}”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Controlled attribute space: four gender categories ... Gender categories: man, woman, neutral ‘person,’ non-binary person.”
errors.explanation: The current evaluation label space is binary gender only, conflicting with the earlier described four-category gender attribute space.

errors.claim: “By computing PBSG under the ethnicity+gender condition, we capture how gender portrayals vary within each ethnic group”
errors.evidence: Earlier methodology defined only two prompt conditions: Person-only and Ethnicity+Person. It explicitly described Ethnicity+Person prompts as ethnic descriptor + “person,” with 42 verbs × 7 ethnicities = 294 prompts, and did not define an “ethnicity+gender condition.”
errors.explanation: The paper’s stated prompt design has no ethnicity+gender condition, so this metric description refers to an experimental condition that contradicts the previously defined setup.

errors.claim: “We exclude gender bias from this analysis because, in the absence of explicit ethnicity specifications, generative models predominantly produce representations of White individuals...”
errors.location: this part, footnote attached to Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias
errors.evidence: The surrounding section says it is assessing gender bias: “Ethnicity-Aware Gender Bias. To assess how video generation models portray gender across different ethnic groups, we employ the Proportion Bias Score for Gender (PBSG)...”
errors.explanation: The footnote says gender bias is excluded from the analysis, but the section is explicitly defining and using a gender-bias metric. This is internally inconsistent within the part.

errors.claim: “Because prompts in this setting intentionally remove contextual and identity cues...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Person-only prompts use the template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context]” with 42 verbs and fixed contexts, e.g. “A person is baking cookies...”. They remove explicit identity cues by using “person,” but still include verbs and contexts.
errors.explanation: The person-only setting removes actor identity descriptors, but it does not remove contextual cues; the prompts explicitly retain action and context.

errors.claim: “For RDSe, positive values indicate overrepresentation of a given ethnicity, while negative values indicate underrepresentation” with table entries such as RDS = -0.1952 and -0.2476.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E| with seven ethnic groups, balanced probability 1/7≈14.3%.” Since P_e cannot be below 0, the minimum possible RDS_e is −1/7≈−0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several RDSe values in Table 2 are below the mathematically possible minimum under the paper’s own definition, so the reported values conflict with the metric definition.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E| with seven ethnic groups.” If a model generated zero recognizable instances of an ethnicity, then P_e=0 and RDS_e should be computable as −1/7≈−0.1429.
errors.explanation: Zero instances would prevent PBSG computation for that subgroup, but not RDSe computation under the stated formula. The caption’s explanation for missing RDSe values conflicts with the metric definition.

errors.claim: “We apply our proposed evaluation framework to four state-of-the-art video diffusion models…” followed by “the aligned models include InstructVideo … as well as T2V-Turbo-V1 … InternVid2-S2 … and ViCLIP.”
errors.location: this part, opening paragraph of Section 4
errors.evidence: The same paragraph says the unaligned counterparts are “ModelScope and VideoCrafter-2,” and Table 2 reports only four evaluated video diffusion models: ModelScope, InstructVideo, Video-Crafter-V2, and T2V-Turbo-V1.
errors.explanation: The text first says four video diffusion models are evaluated, but then appears to list four aligned models plus two unaligned counterparts. This conflicts with the four-model evaluation and with Table 2, unless InternVid2-S2 and ViCLIP are intended as alignment/reward components rather than evaluated aligned video models.

errors.claim: “The annotation task was limited to verifying whether the generated content correctly reflected the prompted demographic attribute” for “gender and ethnicity.”
errors.evidence: Notes: prompt conditions were Person-only (“person”) and Ethnicity+Person; “Demographics not constrained during generation; analyzed post hoc. No ethnicity+gender prompt condition defined. Gender label space for VLMs is only {man,woman}.”
errors.explanation: Gender was not a prompted demographic attribute in the described prompt design, so human gender annotation cannot be limited to verifying whether generated content reflected a prompted gender attribute.

errors.claim: “Our ensemble ... shows strong alignment with human judgments, achieving Pearson correlations of 0.89 (gender) and 0.73 (ethnicity)” and “residual disagreement”; also “human majority votes perfectly align with VLM predictions” only on a subset, with consensus rates “99.0% for gender and 83.3% for ethnicity.”
errors.evidence: Notes from earlier parts: “Paper claims human verification exact agreement with ensemble for every gender/ethnicity label and Section 4 gives human–model correlations.”
errors.explanation: Earlier content reportedly claimed exact agreement for every gender and ethnicity label, but this part reports imperfect correlations, residual disagreement, and perfect alignment only on a subset.

errors.claim: “all core bias metrics remain statistically stable when restricting to this subset (e.g., PBS_G: 0.846 → 0.863, p=0.68; SDI: 0.745 → 0.761).”
errors.evidence: Notes: Table 2 SDI values for the evaluated video models were ModelScope .0538, InstructVideo .0267, VideoCrafter-2 .1252, and T2V-Turbo-V1 .1119.

errors.claim: “this capability offers a powerful mechanism for correcting historical underrepresentation and mitigating bias”

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in T2V via event prompts; VLMs infer actor attributes across frames. Aligned models = post-trained to match human preferences; unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines. Conclusion/Broader Impact: alignment tuning may stabilize/entrench biases; aesthetic metrics insufficient; preference curation should be audited. Broader Impact also claims controllable preference modeling can correct underrepresentation/mitigate bias, but Sec. 7 only reduced male bias, not parity.

Prompt design inconsistency: early paper claimed controlled attribute space included four gender categories, seven ethnicities, 42 verbs, systematic gender/ethnicity variation. Actual Sec. 3.2 video prompts only Person-only: 42 prompts; Ethnicity+Person: 42×7=294. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” No ethnicity+gender video prompt condition; gender analyzed post hoc. Gender VLM labels only {man,woman}; ethnicity seven groups. Sec. 5.2 reward benchmark separately uses Ethnicity+Person 294 and Ethnicity+Gender 1176 image prompts. Sec. 7.1 again says Ethnicity+Gender pairs differ by gender, but gives prompt format “A/An [ethnicity] person…” with no gender.

VLM evaluation: Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B; 16 frames/video; majority vote within model then across models. Human eval: 400 videos, 3 annotators, Pearson 0.89 gender/0.73 ethnicity, Cohen kappa 0.91/0.78, Fleiss 0.92/0.82; high-agreement consensus 99.0% gender/83.3% ethnicity. Limitation falsely claims ensemble achieved exact human agreement/error-free. Human task reportedly verified prompted demographic attribute, conflicting with no prompted gender.

Metrics: TAS=% frames matching final majority video label. PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, range [-1,1], positive male bias. RDS_e=P_e−1/7; balanced≈14.3%; min −0.1429, so lower values impossible. SDI=1−ΣP_e^2.

Sec. 4 Table 2: ModelScope/InstructVideo and VideoCrafter-2/T2V-Turbo-V1, 10 generations/prompt. Alignment increases avg PBSG +0.0480/+0.0725. White overrepresented; SDI .0538, .0267, .1252, .1119. Sensitivity example SDI .745→.761 appears inconsistent unless different data/metric.

Sec. 5 preferences: HPDv2 28,783 tuples/29 verbs; Pick-a-Pic 14,958/19 verbs. Captions say across 42 verbs; after filtering HPDv2 26/42 verbs, 18 male-preferred; Pick-a-Pic 18/42, 11 female-preferred. Ethnicity prefs: White 43.34% HPDv2, 40.08% Pick-a-Pic.

Sec. 5.2 reward benchmark: FLUX, 100 images/prompt. Table 4: CLIP PBSG −.0726 SDI .8495; HPSv2.0 .6039 Δ+.6765; HPSv2.1 −.0984; PickScore −.1157. HPSv2.0 male preference; HPSv2.1/PickScore female preference.

Sec. 6 fine-tunes VCM-VC2 with HPSv2.0/2.1/PickScore. Table 5 has impossible RDS values below −1/7 and text misreads HPSv2.1 Latino ΔPBSG −0.4352 as RDS. Table 6 TAS: base ethnicity .8904/gender .9763; HPSv2.0 .9305/.9967; HPSv2.1 .9632/.9895; PickScore .9406/.9884.

Sec. 7: man-preferred/woman-preferred reward datasets, 2.94M pairs plus 537,660 HPDv2 pairs. Table 7 calls values PBSG but RMM values exceed PBSG range (avg 1.5280); CLIP row matches Table 4. Table 8 VCM-VC2 PBSG avg .8034; +RMM .9584; +RMW .3082; all groups still positive.

Claims first end-to-end analysis connecting biases in human preference datasets, amplification in reward models, and propagation through alignment-tuned video diffusion models. Main result claimed: alignment tuning strengthens representational biases and makes them temporally stable, producing smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Work analyzes how image-based reward models, shaped by human-labeled preferences, influence social-attribute distributions in diffusion-generated videos, disentangling human preference biases, reward preference biases, and downstream video generation biases (Sections 5.1, 5.2, 6).

Introduction definitions/claims: “aligned models” are video diffusion models with post-training optimization to better match human preferences beyond likelihood-based training, commonly via reward-weighted fine-tuning or RLHF-style procedures using a learned preference/aesthetic reward model trained on human comparisons. Pipeline described as base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization. “Unaligned counterparts” are trained solely with likelihood-based objectives and serve as controlled baselines for isolating alignment effects. Existing bias evaluation frameworks are said to have three limitations: inadequate prompts for diverse social identities, lack of comprehensive identity coverage/specific metrics, and no dedicated method to track social-attribute shifts before/after alignment. Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Abstract/intro claims: introduces VideoBiasEval, a diagnostic framework for social representation/bias in text-to-video generation grounded in established bias taxonomies. Metrics evaluate ethnicity bias, gender bias conditioned on ethnicity, distributional shifts in social attributes across model variants, and temporal/attribute persistence within videos. Definitions: “aligned models” are video diffusion models post-trained to match human preferences beyond likelihood training, commonly with reward-weighted fine-tuning/RLHF-style procedures using learned preference/aesthetic reward models trained on human comparisons. “Unaligned counterparts” are likelihood-trained baselines for isolating alignment effects. Pipeline: base video diffusion model → preference/reward model → post-training optimization.

Planned/claimed analyses: Section 5.1 examines demographic preferences in human preference datasets HPDv2 and Pick-a-Pic. Section 5.2 investigates inheritance by image reward models HPSv2.0, HPSv2.1, and PickScore. Section 6 fine-tunes a video consistency model distilled from VideoCrafter-2 using different image reward models to compare video outputs before/after alignment. Section 7 examines intentionally controllable image reward datasets by manipulating social-attribute distributions and tests whether reward models trained on curated datasets enable controllable bias representations in video diffusion outputs.

Main results/conclusions claimed so far: human preference datasets have non-neutral gender preferences and strong imbalance favoring White representations. Alignment with male- or female-preferred reward models shifts gender portrayals; ethnic representation remains uneven. Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS) indicates alignment improves consistency of social-attribute portrayals over time but can make biased representations more persistent/stable. Alignment tuning enhances video quality/coherence while reinforcing/stabilizing social biases; produces smoother yet more stereotyped portrayals. Also claims comprehensive analysis across 42 events of reward model preference changes and resulting video model bias shifts.

Contributions stated: (1) VideoBiasEval with event-based prompting and multi-granular metrics for ethnicity bias, gender conditioned on ethnicity, and temporal stability. (2) First end-to-end analysis connecting human preference datasets, reward models, and alignment-tuned video diffusion models, showing biases inherited/amplified/stabilized. (3) Experiments show preference alignment improves perceptual quality/temporal coherence but reshapes/reinforces social composition; guidance via controllable preference modeling, targeted data composition, and counter-biased reward design to steer toward more equitable behavior.
