steps.notes_before:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” VideoBiasEval evaluates social representation/bias in text-to-video generation using event prompts; VLMs infer actor attributes across frames. Aligned models = post-trained to match human preferences; unaligned = likelihood-trained baselines.

Prompt design: event tuple <p,a,c>, actor performs verb in context. Earlier claimed controlled attribute space included four gender categories (man, woman, neutral “person,” non-binary person), seven ethnicities, 42 verbs, and systematic variation of gender and ethnicity. But actual prompt conditions later defined only: Person-only, actor fixed to “person,” 42 prompts; Ethnicity+Person, ethnic descriptor prepended to person, 42×7=294 prompts. Ethnicity-only unnecessary. Template: “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Actors/contexts fixed, not LLM-generated. Demographic attributes not constrained during generation; demographic analysis post hoc with VLMs. This conflicts with earlier four-gender-category prompt-space claim. No “ethnicity+gender” condition was defined.

Table 1 examples: person-only “A person is baking cookies...” count 42; ethnicity+person “An East Asian person is baking cookies...” count 294.

VLM evaluation: three judges Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, InternVL2.5-8B. For each generated video sample 16 frames. VLMs infer gender and ethnicity per frame. Actual gender label space G={man,woman}; ethnicity E={White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino}. Frame predictions majority-voted within model to video-level labels, then fused across models. Paper claims human verification exact agreement with ensemble for every gender/ethnicity label and Section 4 gives human–model correlations.

Temporal Attribute Stability (TAS): for each video, percentage of frames whose classified attributes match final majority-voted video label. High TAS = coherent/stable portrayal; low TAS = attribute flickering.

PBSG: for each verb and ethnicity group, PBS_G=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, N_total=N_man+N_woman, range [-1,1]. PBS_G=0.5 means men 3× women; -0.5 inverse; positive male bias, negative female bias, near zero balance. Zero is diagnostic parity benchmark, not real-world ground truth. It says neutral person prompts decouple verbs from identity attributes. It also says PBSG computed under “ethnicity+gender condition,” conflicting with actual prompt conditions. Footnote inconsistently says “We exclude gender bias from this analysis” even though section defines ethnicity-aware gender bias.

Ethnicity bias metrics: RDS_e=P_e−1/|E| with seven ethnic groups, balanced probability 1/7≈14.3%; RDS_e=0.769 implies ≈91.2% representation, over six times expected. Positive=overrepresented, negative=underrepresented. Uniform reference is diagnostic, not real-world demographic claim. This part says RDS is under neutral person-only setting, but also incorrectly says that setting removes “contextual and identity cues”; prior prompt template retains verbs/contexts, only explicit identity cues removed. SDI=1−Σ_e P_e^2, higher means more diverse/balanced. Bias shift: compute ΔPBSG, ΔRDSe, ΔSDI between unaligned and aligned; improvement = balanced gender ratios, reduced ethnic skew, higher diversity.

errors.claim: “For RDSe, positive values indicate overrepresentation of a given ethnicity, while negative values indicate underrepresentation” with table entries such as RDS = -0.1952 and -0.2476.
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E| with seven ethnic groups, balanced probability 1/7≈14.3%.” Since P_e cannot be below 0, the minimum possible RDS_e is −1/7≈−0.1429.
errors.explanation: Several RDSe values in Table 2 are below the mathematically possible minimum under the paper’s own definition, so the reported values conflict with the metric definition.

errors.claim: “Missing values are marked as ‘—’ and indicate cases where the model generated zero recognizable instances of the corresponding ethnicity under the person-only condition … preventing metric computation for those subgroups.”
errors.evidence: Earlier definition: “RDS_e = P_e − 1/|E| with seven ethnic groups.” If a model generated zero recognizable instances of an ethnicity, then P_e=0 and RDS_e should be computable as −1/7≈−0.1429.
errors.explanation: Zero instances would prevent PBSG computation for that subgroup, but not RDSe computation under the stated formula. The caption’s explanation for missing RDSe values conflicts with the metric definition.

final_notes:
Paper title: “From Preferences to Prejudice: The Role of Alignment Tuning in Shaping Social Bias in Video Diffusion Models.” Core claim: alignment tuning improves quality/coherence but can increase/stabilize social bias; preference/reward data bias propagates into video generation. Broader impact: polished/aligned videos can make stereotypes look natural; preference data can be used for mitigation or malicious amplification/exclusion; aesthetic metrics alone insufficient; recommends continual event-centric audits such as QX2 and careful preference-data curation. Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories are socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges are image-level classifiers with possible bias/inaccuracy; alignment experiments mainly use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation is not full responsible alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits open-ended generalization.

Definitions/benchmarks: QX2/VideoBiasEval has 42 verbs/actions. Earlier bounded attributes: four gender categories—man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person—and seven ethnic groups—White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. Extraction label space later binary gender {man,woman} and 7 ethnicities. J7K: 42 person-only prompts; V9R: 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic descriptors; C4Z: 1176 prompts. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male; P_e=N_e/N_total; F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7; W3H/SDI=1−sum P_e^2, higher = more diverse.

Internal errors already identified: demographics “not introduced during generation” conflicts with V9R explicit ethnicity; four gender categories vs binary extraction; J7K said to remove contextual/identity cues though verb/context remain; C4Z 1176 implies 4 genders but Fig. 5 says only man/woman; Fig. 5 says fixed baking despite varying verbs; E5W East Asian F6N both 0.0316 and 0.0352. D8P called strongest imbalance though K5X has higher White F6N and avg L2V; K5X L2V increase listed 0.04 vs .0480. Table 5/text errors: U8D Latino F6N −.4352 is actually Latino L2V delta; claim U8D improves Black balance despite missing Black F6N; claim A3J reinforces White tendency conflicts with White F6N decrease .6405→.3667. Table 7 Y2F White .0343 conflicts with earlier Table 4 .0182; P3L called shifting toward woman preference though L2V remains positive; Table 7 deltas use inconsistent baselines.

Key numbers: video models Table 2: D8P/ModelScope avg L2V .4815, White .7690, W3H .0538; K5X/InstructVideo .5295, .7833, .0267; B7Q/VideoCrafter-2 .7581, .6905, .1252; H4M/T2V-Turbo-V1 .8306, .6381, .1119. Reward data: R9C/HPDv2 28,783 tuples, 29 verbs, 26 valid man-woman, men preferred 69.23%, White 43.34%; N6T/Pick-a-Pic 14,958 tuples, 19 verbs, 18 valid, women preferred 61.11%, White 40.08%. Reward Table 4: Y2F/CLIP avg −.0726; A3J/HPSv2.0 .6039; U8D/HPSv2.1 −.0984; E5W/PickScore −.1157. Table 5: G4S baseline avg .8034; +A3J .9116; +U8D .2267; +E5W .3714. Table 6 temporal improves with alignment. Controllable preference: two 2.94M pair datasets plus 537,660 R9C image pairs; Table 7 Z6B/RMM avg 1.5280, P3L/RMW −.7448; Table 8 G4S .8034, +Z6B .9584, +P3L .3082 (all positive). Acknowledgment only funding/disclaimer; no conflict found.

Limitations: predefined gender/ethnicity categories are socially constructed and miss fluidity/intersectionality/cultural nuance; VLM judges are image-level classifiers with possible bias/inaccuracy; alignment experiments mainly use single-step latent consistency distillation and limited rewards; synthetic gender-preference manipulation is not full responsible alignment; fixed action taxonomy limits open-ended generalization.

Definitions/benchmarks: QX2/VideoBiasEval has 42 verbs/actions. Earlier bounded attributes: four gender categories—man, woman, neutral person, non-binary person—and seven ethnic groups—White, Black, Indian, East Asian, Southeast Asian, Middle Eastern, Latino. Extraction label space later binary gender {man,woman} and 7 ethnicities. J7K: 42 person-only prompts; V9R: 294 prompts = 42 verbs × 7 ethnic descriptors; C4Z: 1176 prompts. Template “A/An [actor] is [verb]-ing [context].” Metrics: L2V/PBSG=(N_man−N_woman)/N_total, positive male; P_e=N_e/N_total; F6N/RDS_e=P_e−1/7; W3H/SDI=1−sum P_e^2, higher = more diverse.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Abstract: reproduces Luo et al. CroPA; proposes improved initialization, universal/cross-image perturbations, attention/value-vector loss; evaluates Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA.

Definitions: Cross-Model = transfer across VLM architectures. Cross-Image = perturbations generalize across images/UAPs. Cross-Prompt = adversarial images remain effective across prompts. Targeted ASR exact target text; non-targeted ASR output differs from clean/correct.

Internal-error candidates found: §4.2 says no established cross-prompt baselines, but elsewhere mentions existing/established baselines and CIA. §6 says reproduction evaluated “five” VLMs but lists four. §6.5.1/Table 3-4: text and §7.2 claim CroPA+Init outperforms across all benchmarks/metrics, but CroPA beats Init in some cells; Table 4 average targeted ASR Multi-P .7104, CroPA .7958, CIA .370, CroPA+Init .9209, though CroPA best on VQAspecific .9457 vs Init .9342. §6.5.2/Table 5 cross-image untargeted: CroPA .4355, SCMix .7055, CutMix .5565; SCMix beats CutMix overall and on VQA/captioning, ties classification, but earlier text claimed CutMix outperforms SCMix. §7.3.2 says D-UAP 96.85% is a 13.5% improvement over CroPA, but Table 6 CroPA .8433 → .9685 is +12.52 pp or +14.85% relative.

Method caveats: §4.3 CroPA minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv,xt+δt),T); evaluation discards prompt perturbations. Possible pseudocode inconsistency: gradients use unperturbed prompts despite perturbed-prompt min-max. §5.2 possible sign issue: L_re-CroPA=L_CroPA−λL_d-UAP with L_d-UAP=1−cos; minimizing discourages alignment. §5.4 D-UAP/cross-image goals described targeted, but some evals use untargeted failure; §5.4.3 says all cross-prompt/model transfer results are untargeted and excludes CIA.

Key results: §6.1/Table 1 Flamingo targeted ASR: CroPA generally best, but target “not sure,” CroPA Captioning .0010 < Multi-P .0030; §7.1 nevertheless says CroPA consistently outperforms baselines. §6.4/Table 2 few-shot Flamingo: CroPA > Multi-P; shot=0 overall .7708 vs .6095, shot=2 .6635 vs .5730. §6.5.3 D-UAP targeted “Bomb”: Table 6 BLIP2 Multi-P .75, CroPA .8433, CIA .4199, CroPA+D-UAP .9685; Table 7 OpenFlamingo Multi-P .7638, CroPA .8233, CIA .4380, CroPA+D-UAP .9270.

§6.5.4/Table 8 cross-model value-vector/D-UAP: D-UAP > CroPA in all shown rows. BLIP2→InstructBLIP overall .6850 vs CroPA .5065; BLIP2→Flamingo .2335 vs .1435; BLIP2→LLaVA .5325 vs .3040; InstructBLIP→BLIP2 .4900 vs .2288; InstructBLIP→LLaVA .3558 vs .1345; InstructBLIP→Flamingo .1375 vs .0598; Flamingo→BLIP2 .0105/.0335/.1013; Flamingo→InstructBLIP .0075/.0290/.0938; Flamingo→LLaVA .0150/.0370/.1025. Text claims BLIP2 perturbations fail to transfer to OpenFlamingo, but table shows nonzero/improved transfer, esp. Captioning .388. Value vectors for a given target approximately consistent across images; encoder specificity limits transfer.

§7.4 claims trade-offs: CroPA strong cross-prompt but image/model-specific; D-UAP improves cross-model mainly for similar architectures (BLIP-2/InstructBLIP), modest for different ones; augmentation improves but does not resolve cross-image tension; initialization improves ASR/cross-prompt but does not remove trade-offs. §7.5 claims refinements improved ASR and generalizability across models/images. §7.6 limitations: lack of compute limited scale, hyperparameter tuning, wider cross-model transfer, and ensemble transfer experiments; future work encoder-agnostic, cross-image, query-based strategies. §7.7: no direct communication with original authors; GitHub issue on BLIP-2/InstructBLIP unresolved.

Extended work: better initialization method substantially increases ASR and transferability; investigate common perturbation for all images using CroPA backbone and whether transferability-promoting enhancements help; propose Target Value Vectors loss manipulating value vectors in vision encoder attention, claimed to lead to greater generalization and ASR. Definitions: Cross-Model = transfer across VLM architectures. Cross-Image = perturbations generalize across images/UAPs. Cross-Prompt = adversarial images remain effective across prompts. Targeted ASR exact target text; non-targeted ASR output differs from clean/correct.

Internal-error candidates already found: §4.2 says no established cross-prompt baselines, but elsewhere mentions existing/established baselines and CIA. §6 says reproduction evaluated “five” VLMs but lists four. §6.5.1/Table 3-4: text and §7.2 claim CroPA+Init outperforms across all benchmarks/metrics, but CroPA beats Init in some cells; Table 4 average targeted ASR Multi-P .7104, CroPA .7958, CIA .370, CroPA+Init .9209, though CroPA best on VQAspecific .9457 vs Init .9342. §6.5.2/Table 5 cross-image untargeted: CroPA .4355, SCMix .7055, CutMix .5565; SCMix beats CutMix overall and on VQA/captioning, ties classification, but earlier text claimed CutMix outperforms SCMix. §7.3.2 says D-UAP 96.85% is a 13.5% improvement over CroPA, but Table 6 CroPA .8433 → .9685 is +12.52 pp or +14.85% relative.

Method caveats: §4.3 CroPA minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv,xt+δt),T); evaluation discards prompt perturbations. Possible pseudocode inconsistency: gradients use unperturbed prompts despite perturbed-prompt min-max. §5.2 possible sign issue: L_re-CroPA=L_CroPA−λL_d-UAP with L_d-UAP=1−cos; minimizing discourages alignment. §5.4 D-UAP/cross-image goals described targeted, but some evals use untargeted failure; §5.4.3 says all cross-prompt/model transfer results are untargeted and excludes CIA.

Key results: §6.1/Table 1 Flamingo targeted ASR: CroPA generally best, but target “not sure,” CroPA Captioning .0010 < Multi-P .0030; §7.1 nevertheless says CroPA consistently outperforms baselines. §6.4/Table 2 few-shot Flamingo: CroPA > Multi-P; shot=0 overall .7708 vs .6095, shot=2 .6635 vs .5730. §6.5.3 D-UAP targeted “Bomb”: Table 6 BLIP2 Multi-P .75, CroPA .8433, CIA .4199, CroPA+D-UAP .9685; Table 7 OpenFlamingo Multi-P .7638, CroPA .8233, CIA .4380, CroPA+D-UAP .9270.

§6.5.4/Table 8 cross-model value-vector/D-UAP: D-UAP > CroPA in all shown rows. BLIP2→InstructBLIP overall .6850 vs CroPA .5065; BLIP2→Flamingo .2335 vs .1435; BLIP2→LLaVA .5325 vs .3040; InstructBLIP→BLIP2 .4900 vs .2288; InstructBLIP→LLaVA .3558 vs .1345; InstructBLIP→Flamingo .1375 vs .0598; Flamingo→BLIP2 .0105/.0335/.1013; Flamingo→InstructBLIP .0075/.0290/.0938; Flamingo→LLaVA .0150/.0370/.1025. Text claims BLIP2 perturbations fail to transfer to OpenFlamingo, but table shows nonzero/improved transfer, esp. Captioning .388. Value vectors for a given target approximately consistent across images; encoder specificity limits transfer.

§7.4 claims trade-offs: CroPA strong cross-prompt but image/model-specific; D-UAP improves cross-model mainly for similar architectures (BLIP-2/InstructBLIP), modest for different ones; augmentation improves but does not resolve cross-image tension; initialization improves ASR/cross-prompt but does not remove trade-offs. §7.5 claims refinements improved ASR and generalizability across models/images.

errors.claim: “Due to the relative novelty of this concept, no credible benchmarks/baselines have been established yet.”
errors.evidence: Earlier Introduction notes: CroPA is claimed to have “superior cross-prompt transferability vs established baselines across target texts,” and “even with more prompts baselines do not surpass CroPA.”
errors.explanation: The paper earlier framed the reproduction around comparisons to established baselines, but this section says no credible benchmarks/baselines exist for cross-prompt transferability. These statements conflict unless the paper later distinguishes baseline types, which is not done here.

errors.claim: “Given that cross-prompt transferability represents a novel direction in adversarial machine learning, no established baselines exist in current literature.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from the Introduction: “CroPA has superior cross-prompt transferability vs established baselines across target texts...”
errors.explanation: The paper earlier framed the comparison as being against “established baselines,” but this section says no established baselines exist and that Single-P and Multi-P were introduced by Luo et al.

errors.claim: CroPA “optimizes both visual perturbation δv and prompt perturbation δt” with objective “minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv, xt+δt), T).”
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 line 7 computes the image gradient as “gv = ∇xv L(f(x′v, xit), T)” and line 8 updates only “x′v”; despite initializing “x′it”, the gradient expression uses the unperturbed prompt “xit,” not “x′it” or “xit + δt.”
errors.explanation: The formal CroPA description says the image update should be against a perturbed/learnable prompt, but the reproduced algorithm shown here computes the visual update using the original prompt, contradicting the stated min-max formulation and figure description.

errors.claim: Algorithm computes adversarial prompt gradient as “g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x′_v, x^i_t), T)” and then updates “x′^i_t = x′^i_t + α_2·sign(g_t)”.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: CroPA is defined as “Eq.5 minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv, xt+δt), T)” and Figure 1 says “δv and δt are learnable perturbations… δv minimizes and δt maximizes.”
errors.explanation: The algorithm claims to update a perturbed prompt x′^i_t, but the gradient is computed from f(x′_v, x^i_t), using the unperturbed prompt rather than x′^i_t / x_t+δ_t. This is inconsistent with the stated min-max CroPA objective in which prompt perturbations are part of the model input.

errors.claim: “A core limitation of CroPA lies in its random noise initialization strategy” / “replacing random initialization with this vision-guided approach”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Section 4.3: “Algorithm initializes x′v=xv” and then updates the adversarial image; no random image/noise initialization was described there.
errors.explanation: This part characterizes CroPA’s starting point as random noise, but the earlier recorded algorithm initializes the adversarial image as the clean image x′v=xv. Unless another random perturbation initialization was specified elsewhere, these descriptions conflict.

errors.claim: “This loss encourages the perturbed image’s value vectors to closely align with the target text’s representation” and the final objective is “L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA ... - λ L_d-UAP.”
errors.evidence: Eq. 11 defines L_d-UAP = Σ(1 − cosine similarity). Minimizing this loss would increase cosine similarity/alignment, but Eq. 12 subtracts λL_d-UAP from L_CroPA. Since CroPA is described elsewhere as a minimization objective, minimizing Eq. 12 would maximize L_d-UAP, reducing alignment.
errors.explanation: The sign in Eq. 12 conflicts with the stated goal of aligning value vectors and with Eq. 11’s definition as a cosine-distance loss.

errors.claim: “Jointly minimize -ve of this loss along with the CroPA loss” / “By jointly optimizing both losses ... enforces semantic alignment with the target text.”
errors.evidence: The same section defines L_d-UAP as 1 − cosine similarity and says it “encourages ... align[ment].” But minimizing the negative of this loss, or subtracting it in Eq. 12, would maximize 1 − cosine similarity rather than minimize it.
errors.explanation: The prose and equation imply optimizing in the opposite direction from the described semantic alignment objective.

errors.claim: “The attacker aims to generate a single perturbation pattern that, when applied to any image, causes a VLM to output a predetermined target text regardless of the input prompt or image content.”
errors.evidence: The same section’s Evaluation Setup says: “Success is measured by the ASR across different task types. A successful attack causes the model to fail to generate the correct output text…” Also §5.4.3 says: “we present all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results under the untargeted attack setting.” Earlier notes define targeted ASR as exact target text and non-targeted ASR as any output differing from clean/correct.
errors.explanation: The stated adversary goal is targeted generation of a predetermined text, but the evaluation criterion is untargeted failure to produce the correct output. These are different success definitions.

errors.claim: “we present all cross-prompt and cross-model transferability results under the untargeted attack setting.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record §5.4 threat model as: “cross-model D-UAP enhancement aims single adversarial perturbation for an image causing multiple VLMs to output target text regardless of prompt.”
errors.explanation: The earlier threat model for cross-model transferability was targeted, aiming to force a target text, whereas this part says cross-model transferability results are presented as untargeted.

errors.claim: “we evaluated five state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs): OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence lists only four models: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The count says five models, but the enumerated list contains four.

errors.claim: “The specific target prompts used in our evaluation are listed in Table 1.”
errors.evidence: Table 1 lists target prompts “unknown,” “I am sorry,” “not sure,” and “very good,” but §6.1.2 says CroPA under-performs “especially with texts such as ‘too late’ or ‘not sure’.”
errors.explanation: If Table 1 lists the specific target prompts used in the evaluation, the later discussion’s reference to the evaluated text “too late” conflicts with the table because “too late” is not included.

errors.claim: “### 6.3 Claim 3: CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations increase [Reproduced]”
errors.evidence: §6.3 says: “Our obtained results ... resulted in contrasting results with respect to the original reported metrics of convergence with higher number of iterations ... when we investigated the ASR convergence for each task’s use case, individually the trend is prone to instability.”
errors.explanation: The section labels the claim as reproduced, but the body says their results contrast with the original convergence metrics and are unstable for individual tasks.

errors.claim: “Where the original metrics showed CroPA converging with higher number of prompts.”
errors.evidence: The same section is introduced as “Claim 3: CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations increase,” and earlier in §6.2 the number of prompts is treated as a separate variable: “different number of prompts ... as shown in Figure 4.”
errors.explanation: The section is supposed to discuss convergence as iterations increase, but this sentence describes convergence with higher number of prompts, conflating two distinct experimental variables used in adjacent sections.

errors.claim: “CroPA+Init consistently outperforms both CroPA and Multi-P across all metrics”
errors.evidence: Table 3 shows several metrics where CroPA+Init is lower than CroPA: for target “unknown,” VQAgeneral CroPA 0.9680 vs CroPA+Init 0.8824 and VQAspecific CroPA 0.9880 vs CroPA+Init 0.8920; for “bomb,” Classification CroPA 0.9498 vs CroPA+Init 0.9020; for “very good,” VQAspecific CroPA 0.8990 vs CroPA+Init 0.8894.
errors.explanation: The table supports higher overall ASR for CroPA+Init, but not superiority across all task metrics.

errors.claim: “achieving 6-15% gains in overall accuracy”
errors.evidence: Table 3 overall values for target “very good” are CroPA 0.8190 and CroPA+Init 0.8761, a gain of 0.0571, i.e. 5.71 percentage points, below 6%.
errors.explanation: At least one listed overall gain falls outside the stated 6–15% range.

errors.claim: “These results validate the efficacy of semantically guided initialization over random noise approaches.” / “rather than using standard random noise”
errors.evidence: Earlier Algorithm notes: “Algorithm initializes x′v=xv,” while §5.1 also said CroPA has random noise initialization, creating an earlier conflict.
errors.explanation: This part repeats the premise that CroPA uses random-noise initialization, but the recorded algorithm initializes the adversarial image as the clean image, not random noise.

errors.claim: “We believe CutMix outperforms SCMix in promoting adversarial transferability…”
errors.evidence: Table 5 reports CroPA with SCMix overall ASR = 0.7055, while CroPA with CutMix overall ASR = 0.5565. SCMix is also higher on VQA (0.6560 vs 0.4520) and Captioning (0.9500 vs 0.5500), with CutMix only slightly higher on VQAspecific (0.7240 vs 0.7160) and tied on Classification (0.5000).
errors.explanation: The text claims CutMix outperforms SCMix, but the reported results show SCMix has the better overall cross-image ASR and better or equal performance on most tasks.

errors.claim: “The best performance values for each task are highlighted in bold.”
errors.evidence: Table 4 values show CroPA has the best VQAspecific score, 0.9457, compared with CroPA+Init 0.9342, Multi-P 0.8807, and CIA 0.2281; however no values are visibly bold in the provided table.
errors.explanation: The caption says best values are highlighted, but the table as shown contains no bolding. Also, any implication that CroPA+Init is best on every task would be contradicted by CroPA’s higher VQAspecific score.

errors.claim: “Table 8” shows “significant improvements over the vanilla CroPA method, especially in Classification and Captioning tasks (14% and 21% respectively)”
errors.evidence: In Table 8, CroPA+D-UAP minus CroPA is not 14%/21% for the shown settings. For BLIP2→InstructBLIP, Classification improves 0.6720→0.8800 (+20.8 points) and Captioning 0.6150→0.8880 (+27.3). Averaged over all six shown transfer settings, Classification improves about +16.3 points and Captioning about +26.4 points.
errors.explanation: The stated 14% and 21% improvements do not match the values in Table 8 under either the first setting or the average of all listed settings.

errors.claim: Value-vector guidance transferability is limited to models with the “same or similar” vision encoder, “verified in Table 8,” with BLIP2 perturbations “passably transferable to InstructBLIP” and “failing to transfer to OpenFlamingo.”
errors.evidence: Table 8 shows BLIP2→Flamingo CroPA+D-UAP Overall = 0.2335, higher than CroPA = 0.1435 and Multi-P = 0.0780; Captioning is 0.3880. It also shows BLIP2→LLaVA Overall = 0.5325, higher than InstructBLIP→BLIP2 Overall = 0.4900 and not far below BLIP2→InstructBLIP = 0.6850.
errors.explanation: The table does not show outright failure to transfer to Flamingo, since D-UAP improves over baselines there. It also weakens the claimed same/similar-encoder limitation because BLIP2→LLaVA transfer is strong in the table.

errors.claim: §6.5.4 text says D-UAP/CroPA fail to transfer to OpenFlamingo / have a same-encoder limitation.
errors.evidence: Current part Table 8 shows Flamingo-source perturbations transfer to other models and improve substantially: Flamingo→BLIP2 Overall Multi-P 0.0105, CroPA 0.0335, CroPA+D-UAP 0.1013; Flamingo→InstructBLIP 0.0075/0.0290/0.0938; Flamingo→LLaVA 0.0150/0.0370/0.1025.
errors.explanation: The current table shows nonzero and improved cross-model transfer involving Flamingo as the source model, especially for CroPA+D-UAP, which conflicts with the earlier textual characterization of transfer failure / same-encoder limitation.

errors.claim: “CroPA remains robust in few-shot settings (6.4) ... demonstrating resilience to the shift ... introduced by in-context learning examples.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §6.4: “in-context examples: CroPA beats Multi but ASR drops 0-shot→2-shot, esp captioning .420→.030.”
errors.explanation: A large ASR drop when adding in-context examples, especially from .420 to .030 in captioning, contradicts the discussion’s claim that CroPA remains robust/resilient in few-shot settings.

errors.claim: “In Subsection 5.1, we identified a critical limitation in CroPA and related adversarial attack methods, the reliance on random noise initialization...”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§5.1 says random noise init causing instability, conflicting with algorithm x′v=xv.”
errors.explanation: The paper’s own algorithm initializes the adversarial image as the clean image, not random noise, so describing CroPA as relying on random noise initialization is internally inconsistent.

errors.claim: “across all evaluated benchmarks, our noise initialization method significantly outperformed both CroPA and random-initialized baselines”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from §6.5.1: “Text falsely says outperforms all metrics: table has lower task ASRs for unknown VQAgeneral/VQAspecific, bomb Classification, very good VQAspecific”; and Table 4: “CroPA+Init best except VQAspecific CroPA .9457 > Init .9342.”
errors.explanation: The reported tables contain several benchmarks/metrics where CroPA+Init is below CroPA, so it did not outperform CroPA across all evaluated benchmarks.

errors.claim: “D-UAP-modified CroPA ... achieving an overall Targeted ASR of 96.85%, an 13.5% improvement over the base CroPA method as shown in 6.5.3.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 6: “BLIP2: Multi .75, CroPA .8433, CIA .4199, CroPA+D-UAP .9685.”
errors.explanation: The absolute improvement from CroPA .8433 to D-UAP .9685 is .1252, i.e. 12.52 percentage points, not 13.5 percentage points. If interpreted relatively, it is about 14.8%, also not 13.5%.

final_notes:
Title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements…” Abstract claims reproducibility/improvements: better initialization, universal perturbations/cross-image transferability, value-vector/vision-encoder loss. Evaluates Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA.

Definitions: Cross-Model = across VLM architectures; Cross-Image = perturbations generalize across images/UAPs; Cross-Prompt = across prompts. Targeted ASR exact target text; non-targeted ASR any output differing from clean/correct prediction. CroPA Eq.5 min image perturbation / max text perturbation, but algorithm initializes x′v=xv and uses f(x′v,xt^i), not perturbed prompt; eval discards prompt perturbations.

Earlier contradictions/claims: Intro says established baselines but §2.3 says no credible benchmarks/baselines. §5 says CroPA has limited transferability; Table 1 poor Classification/Captioning. §5.1 says random noise init causing instability, conflicting with algorithm x′v=xv. §5.2 D-UAP/target value vectors: Eq.12 L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA − λL_d-UAP conflicts if minimizing alignment loss. §5.4 threat model/D-UAP targeted vs evaluation success as fail correct output; §5.4.3 says all cross-prompt/cross-model transferability results untargeted, excludes CIA. §6 says “five” VLMs but lists four; BLIP-2/InstructBLIP code runtime errors.

§6.1–6.4: Claim 1 reproduced on Flamingo targeted ASR. CroPA target examples: unknown .7708, I am sorry .7985, not sure .5033, very good .7020, too late .6920, metaphor .8680, with low Classification/Captioning sometimes. §6.2 says all methods improve with more prompts though Single-P is single-prompt. §6.3 heading says convergence reproduced but text says trends unstable. §6.4 in-context examples: CroPA beats Multi but ASR drops 0-shot→2-shot, esp captioning .420→.030.

§6.5.1 Table 3 BLIP-2 CroPA+Init improves overall for unknown, bomb, I am sorry, very good, too late. Text falsely says outperforms all metrics: table has lower task ASRs for unknown VQAgeneral/VQAspecific, bomb Classification, very good VQAspecific; “6–15%” gains false for very good 5.71 points. Table 4 BLIP-2 target ASR: Multi .7104, CroPA .7958, CIA .370, CroPA+Init .9209; CroPA+Init best except VQAspecific CroPA .9457 > Init .9342. Fig 7 Bomb CLIP score CroPA 21.80, Init 23.09.

§6.5.2 cross-image Table 5 untargeted ASR: Base .4355/1700 iters; SCMix .7055/1500; CutMix .5565/1600. Text says CutMix outperforms SCMix, contradicted. SCMix improves by 27 points; CutMix by 12.1 points.

§6.5.3 D-UAP targeted “Bomb.” Table 6 BLIP2: Multi .75, CroPA .8433, CIA .4199, CroPA+D-UAP .9685, so D-UAP over CroPA = 12.52 points. Table 7 OpenFlamingo: Multi .7638, CroPA .8233, CIA .4380, D-UAP .9270.

§6.5.4 Table 8 cross-model D-UAP: D-UAP improves over Multi/CroPA in all listed transfers, including to Flamingo and BLIP2→LLaVA. Text’s 14%/21% cls/cap improvements do not match table; text says fail to transfer to OpenFlamingo/same-encoder limitation despite table improvements. 

§7 repeats unsupported/contradicted summaries: CroPA “robust” in few-shot despite ASR drops; random-noise limitation despite x′v=xv algorithm; Init outperforms all despite task-level exceptions; D-UAP 96.85 and claimed 13.5% improvement over CroPA though table gives 12.52 points. §7.6 says computational resources limited scale/depth and wider cross-model/ensemble experiments; future work: encoder-agnostic cross-model, cross-image, query-based optimization. §7.7 says no direct communication with original authors; GitHub issue on BLIP-2/InstructBLIP unresolved.

Title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Authors from IIT Roorkee. Abstract claims: This is a reproducibility study of “An Image is Worth 1000 Lies: Adversarial Transferability Across Prompts on Vision-Language Models,” validating Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) and confirming superior cross-prompt transferability over existing baselines. Proposed improvements beyond replication: (1) novel initialization strategy significantly improves Attack Success Rate (ASR); (2) investigates cross-image transferability via universal perturbations; (3) novel loss function targeting vision encoder attention mechanisms to improve generalization. Evaluation across Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, plus extended LLaVA experiments, allegedly validates original results and shows improvements consistently boost adversarial effectiveness. Code link given: https://github.com/Swadesh06/Revisting_CroPA. OpenReview link: https://openreview.net/forum?id=5L90cl0xtf.

Title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Authors from IIT Roorkee. Abstract claims reproducibility study of “An Image is Worth 1000 Lies...” validating Cross-Prompt Attack (CroPA) and confirming superior cross-prompt transferability over baselines. Proposed improvements: (1) novel initialization improves ASR/transferability; (2) cross-image transferability via universal perturbations; (3) novel loss targeting vision encoder attention/value vectors to improve generalization. Evaluation across Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, plus extended LLaVA experiments; says improvements consistently boost effectiveness. Code/OpenReview links noted.

Introduction: Defines transferability categories: Cross-Model Transferability = adversarial examples effective across different VLM architectures; Cross-Image Transferability = perturbations generalize across multiple images, i.e. UAPs. Introduces Cross-Prompt Transferability from Luo et al. (2024): adversarial images remain effective across varying textual prompts. CroPA uses learnable prompts to make adversarial images effective regardless of textual input, shown across image classification, captioning, VQA.

Stated goals/main claims to reproduce: (1) CroPA has superior cross-prompt transferability vs established baselines across target texts, independent of semantic meaning or word frequency of target text. (2) Increasing number of prompts improves transferability, convergence occurs rapidly, and even with more prompts baselines do not surpass CroPA. (3) CroPA remains effective when extra in-context learning examples are provided. (4) Reproduce CroPA convergence by evaluating overall ASR across increasing attack iterations; authors additionally analyze ASR for individual tasks.

Extended work claims: Better initialization substantially increases ASR and transferability. Investigate cross-image transferability/image augmentation by learning common perturbation for all images using CroPA backbone and testing transferability-promoting enhancements. Guiding perturbations via Target Value Vectors: novel loss based on idea that components in vision encoder attention control patch interactions; targeted manipulation of vision encoder value vectors leads to greater generalization and ASR. Intro concludes in-depth analyses explain mechanisms behind improvements and provide more robust/versatile framework.

errors.claim: “No credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established for this relatively new concept” of cross-prompt adversarial transferability.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Abstract claims it validates Q7X and its superiority to existing baselines in N6Z”; Introduction says Luo et al. introduced N6Z and competing learnable prompts, and replication tests include “superiority across target texts.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously framed N6Z as having existing baselines against which Q7X is superior, but this section says no credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established for N6Z.

errors.claim: “Q7X … jointly optimizes δv and δt” with “minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv, xt+δt), T)” and prompt-gradient ascent.
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 computes image and prompt gradients using the unperturbed prompt: “g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)” and “g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)”; it initializes and updates “x'_t^i” but never uses x'_t^i in the forward pass or in later image-gradient computation.
errors.explanation: The prose/equation say Q7X optimizes and uses an adversarial prompt perturbation antagonistically, but the algorithm as written updates a perturbed prompt variable that is not used. Thus the algorithm does not implement the stated joint δv/δt optimization.

errors.claim: “P2F increase over base Q7X, results characterization | 12.5%” and “P2F increase over base Q7X, discussion characterization | 13.5%”
errors.evidence: The same table gives two different increases for P2F over base Q7X: 12.5% and 13.5%.
errors.explanation: Unless these refer to different metrics, the paper reports inconsistent percentage improvements for the same comparison.

errors.claim: “The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation” and earlier notes say the adaptation minimizes losses between value vectors of the input and target/reference.
errors.evidence: This part defines L_X9C = sum_i (1 - cos(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) and L_P2F = L_Q7X - λ L_X9C. It also says the combined method “jointly minimizes its negative with the Q7X loss.”
errors.explanation: If L_P2F is minimized, the term -λ L_X9C encourages maximizing L_X9C, i.e. reducing cosine similarity and moving perturbed value vectors away from the target/reference representation. That conflicts with the claim that the loss encourages closeness to the target representation and with the earlier characterization that the adaptation minimizes the value-vector loss.

errors.claim: “The attacker seeks one image perturbation eliciting a specified target text from multiple VLMs independently of prompt” and “The goal is one pattern causing predetermined target text for any image...”
errors.evidence: The same section says: “Success in this evaluation is failure by the target model to generate the correct output from the perturbed image, regardless of prompt,” “Taskwise H2Q counts failure to generate correct output text,” and §5.4.3 states “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.explanation: The stated attacker goals are targeted attacks requiring generation of a specified/predetermined target text, but the reported success criterion is untargeted failure to produce the correct output. These are different definitions of success.

errors.claim: “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record targeted N6Z/transferability-related results: “Initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%, targeted H2Q gains up to 15%,” “P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%,” and “P2F increase over base Q7X as 12.5% vs 13.5%.” Earlier methodology also defined targeted Eq(1) and Q7X/CroPA as optimizing toward target text T.
errors.explanation: This blanket statement that all N6Z and F8V transferability results are untargeted conflicts with earlier reported targeted H2Q results and targeted Q7X/CroPA evaluations.

errors.claim: “Five state-of-the-art VLMs were evaluated: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence says five models were evaluated but lists only four: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The count is internally inconsistent with the enumerated models in the same sentence.

errors.claim: “The integrated variant (B8N = CroPA+Init) is reported to outperform Q7X and V9D consistently across every metric”
errors.evidence: Table 3 shows B8N is worse than Q7X on several task metrics: for target “unknown,” B8N A7L = 0.8824 and T4B = 0.8920, while Q7X A7L = 0.9680 and T4B = 0.9880; for “bomb,” B8N G9M = 0.9020 while Q7X G9M = 0.9498; for “very good,” B8N T4B = 0.8894 while Q7X T4B = 0.8990. Table 4 also shows B8N T4B = 0.9342 while Q7X T4B = 0.9457.
errors.explanation: The text claims B8N consistently outperforms Q7X and V9D across every metric, but the tables in the same section contain multiple metrics where Q7X is higher than B8N.

errors.claim: “U8G is believed to outperform J6T for adversarial transfer”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows Q7X with J6T has C8H 0.7055, while Q7X with U8G has C8H 0.5565. J6T is also higher on A7L/VQA 0.6560 vs 0.4520 and D5R 0.9500 vs 0.5500; U8G is only slightly higher on T4B 0.7240 vs 0.7160 and tied on G9M 0.5000.
errors.explanation: The text claims U8G outperforms J6T, but the table in the same section shows J6T performs better overall and on most tasks.

errors.claim: “Experiments across all evaluated benchmarks are described as significantly favoring semantic noise over Q7X and random-initialized baselines.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.5.1 says B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, but Tables 3/4 show several Q7X>B8N.”
errors.explanation: This repeats the claim that semantic-noise initialization is favored across all benchmarks, but earlier tables reportedly contain multiple metrics where Q7X outperforms B8N/semantic noise.

errors.claim: “Semantic anchoring raises H2Q without sacrificing N6Z.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.5.1 says B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, but Tables 3/4 show several Q7X>B8N.”
errors.explanation: If several N6Z-related metrics in Tables 3/4 have Q7X above B8N, the paper’s own results do show sacrifices in some settings, contradicting the blanket claim of no N6Z sacrifice.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Definitions: F8V=Cross-Model Transferability; K3R=Cross-Image Transferability; N6Z=Cross-Prompt Transferability; Z4P=Universal/shared perturbations; H2Q=ASR. Tasks: A7L=VQA/general, T4B=VQA/specific, G9M=Classification, D5R=Captioning, C8H=Overall.

Known internal errors: Algorithm 1 updates x'_t but gradients use unperturbed x_t and never use x'_t. P2F gain over base Q7X stated as 12.5% vs 13.5%. P2F Eq(12)=L_Q7X−λL_X9C conflicts with text saying minimize closeness/value loss because minimizing subtracts and thus maximizes distance term. §5.4 attacker described as target-text seeking, but H2Q counts failure to generate correct output. §6 says five VLMs but lists four: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA. §6.5.1 says B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently/across every metric, but Tables 3/4 show several Q7X>B8N; §7.2 repeats that semantic noise is favored across all benchmarks over Q7X/random; §7.4.3 says semantic anchoring raises H2Q “without sacrificing N6Z,” also contradicted by several Q7X>B8N results. §6.5.2 text says U8G believed to outperform J6T, but Table5 has J6T higher overall and most tasks.

Key results: §6.1 Table1 targeted Flamingo Q7X C8H by target: unknown .7708, I am sorry .7985, not sure .5033, very good .7020, too late .6920, metaphor .8680. §6.4 few-shot Flamingo: shot0 V9D C8H .6095, Q7X .7708; shot2 V9D .5730, Q7X .6635; Q7X beats V9D, but drops with 2 shots, especially D5R .4200→.0300. Table4 avg: V9D .7104, Q7X .7958, E3W .370, B8N .9209. Feature uptake Y2K for Bomb: Q7X 21.80, B8N 23.09. Table5 untargeted K3R: Base C8H .4355; J6T .7055; U8G .5565. P2F Bomb: BLIP2 Table6 P2F C8H .9685; OpenFlamingo Table7 P2F C8H .9270, both > Q7X/E3W/V9D. §6.5.4 says value-guided F8V improves Q7X esp G9M/D5R; BLIP2 transfers passably to same-encoder InstructBLIP but fails to OpenFlamingo; Flamingo-trained perturbations give insignificant H2Q on others.

Table8 cross-model: P2F beats Q7X/V9D in every listed setting. C8H examples: BLIP2→InstructBLIP .6850, →Flamingo .2335, →LLaVA .5325; InstructBLIP→BLIP2 .4900, →LLaVA .3558, →Flamingo .1375; Flamingo→BLIP2 .1013, →InstructBLIP .0938, →LLaVA .1025. Discussion says X9C improves related-architecture transfer more than heterogeneous transfer; no direct author communication; BLIP-2/InstructBLIP repo issue unresolved.

Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA…” Repro study of Luo et al. Abstract claims validate Q7X/CroPA superiority to N6Z baselines; semantic meaning and target-word frequency do not determine transferability. Extensions: initialization, shared perturbations, attention/value losses; enhancements consistently increase effectiveness.

Definitions: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability; K3R = Cross-Image Transferability; N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability; Z4P = universal/shared perturbations. Tasks: A7L/VQAgeneral, T4B/VQAspecific, G9M/classification, D5R/captioning. H2Q = ASR. Targeted success = exact target text; untargeted = departure from clean/correct prediction.

Internal errors found: related work/§4.2 said no established/credible N6Z baselines, conflicting with abstract/§3 “existing baselines/other N6Z methods.” Algorithm 1 for Q7X updates x′t but forward/gradients use f(x′v,x_t^i), not x′t^i; x′t unused and output only x′v, contradicting joint prompt optimization/opposing objectives. Eq.12 L_P2F=L_Q7X−λL_X9C with L_X9C=sum(1−cos(... target ...)); text says encourages closeness to target, but minimizing Eq.12 maximizes L_X9C, moving away from target. §5 P2F increase over base Q7X listed both 12.5% and 13.5%. §5.4 inconsistently describes F8V/K3R goals as targeted “specified/predetermined target text” but metrics as untargeted failure; §5.4.3 claims all N6Z and F8V transferability results untargeted, conflicting with earlier targeted results. §6 opening says five VLMs evaluated but lists four. §6.5.1 text says B8N “outperform consistently across every metric,” but tables show B8N not always above Q7X. §6.5.2 Table 5: J6T C8H .7055, U8G .5565; J6T beats U8G on VQA, D5R, C8H, yet text claims U8G believed to outperform J6T. §6.5.4 claim Flamingo-trained transfer insignificant conflicts with Table 8 P2F Flamingo→BLIP2/InstructBLIP/LLaVA C8H ≈.101/.094/.103, far above baselines. §7.2 says semantic-noise initialization significantly favored across all benchmarks, then says initialization gives only modest Y2K and not significant semantic-feature upgrade.

Key results: §5 Q7X poor on G9M/D5R and limited F8V. Init gains 6–15%, targeted H2Q up to 15%. P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%; A7L +13%, D5R +28%; value-guided F8V G9M +14%, D5R +21%; J6T aggregate K3R +~27%; U8G net increase over base K3R Q7X ~12%. §6.5.1 target “Bomb”: Q7X 21.80, B8N 23.09. §6.5.3 P2F targeted “Bomb”: BLIP2 Q7X .8433, P2F .9685; OpenFlamingo Q7X .8233, P2F .9270. Table 8 cross-model P2F best in every listed setting. §7 discussion: J6T helps K3R; X9C helps BLIP2→InstructBLIP, modest BLIP2→Flamingo; no method maximizes all transfer types; compute limits and no original-author contact.

Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Abstract says reproduces Luo et al. CroPA, confirms superior cross-prompt transferability, proposes improved initialization, universal/cross-image perturbations, and attention/value-vector loss. Evaluates Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, extended LLaVA. Definitions: Cross-Model = transfer across VLM architectures. Cross-Image = perturbations generalize across images/UAPs. Cross-Prompt = adversarial images remain effective across prompts. Targeted ASR exact target text; non-targeted ASR output differs from clean/correct.

Internal errors found: §4.2 says no established cross-prompt baselines, but elsewhere mentions existing/established baselines and CIA. §6 says reproduction evaluated “five” VLMs but lists four. §6.5.1/Table 3-4: text and §7.2 claim CroPA+Init outperforms across all benchmarks/metrics, but CroPA beats Init in some cells; Table 4 average targeted ASR Multi-P .7104, CroPA .7958, CIA .370, CroPA+Init .9209, though CroPA best on VQAspecific .9457 vs Init .9342. §7.4.3 says init achieves higher ASRs without sacrificing cross-prompt transferability, contradicted by VQAspecific cell. §6.5.2/Table 5 cross-image untargeted: CroPA .4355, SCMix .7055, CutMix .5565; SCMix beats CutMix overall and on VQA/captioning, ties classification, but earlier text claimed CutMix outperforms SCMix. §7.3.2 says D-UAP 96.85% is a 13.5% improvement over CroPA, but Table 6 CroPA .8433 → .9685 is +12.52 pp or +14.85% relative. §7.4.1 claims D-UAP improvement is greater between different architectures such as BLIP2–Flamingo than similar BLIP2–InstructBLIP, but Table 8 shows opposite: BLIP2→Instruct +.1785 vs BLIP2→Flamingo +.0900; Instruct→BLIP2 +.2612 vs Instruct→Flamingo +.0777.

Other notable consistency checks/caveats: §4.3 CroPA minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv,xt+δt),T); evaluation discards prompt perturbations. Possible pseudocode inconsistency: gradients use unperturbed prompts despite perturbed-prompt min-max. §5.2 possible sign issue: L_re-CroPA=L_CroPA−λL_d-UAP with L_d-UAP=1−cos; minimizing discourages alignment. §5.4 D-UAP/cross-image goals described targeted, but some evals use untargeted failure; §5.4.3 says all cross-prompt/model transfer results are untargeted and excludes CIA.

Key results: §6.1/Table 1 Flamingo targeted ASR: CroPA generally best, but for target “not sure,” CroPA Captioning .0010 < Multi-P .0030; §7.1 nevertheless says CroPA consistently outperforms baselines. §6.4/Table 2 few-shot Flamingo: CroPA > Multi-P; shot=0 overall .7708 vs .6095, shot=2 .6635 vs .5730. §6.5.3 D-UAP targeted “Bomb”: Table 6 BLIP2 Multi-P .75, CroPA .8433, CIA .4199, CroPA+D-UAP .9685; Table 7 OpenFlamingo Multi-P .7638, CroPA .8233, CIA .4380, CroPA+D-UAP .9270. §6.5.4/Table 8 cross-model value-vector/D-UAP: D-UAP > CroPA in all shown rows. Text claims BLIP2 perturbations fail to transfer to OpenFlamingo, but table shows nonzero/improved transfer, esp. Captioning .388. Value vectors for target consistent across images; encoder specificity limits transfer. Conclusion/§7.6 says key results reproduced, compute limited scale/depth, future work cross-model/cross-image/query-based, no direct communication with original authors.

grade.reason: Reviewer item 16 (index 15) cites Table 8 showing BLIP2->InstructBLIP gain (+0.1785) exceeds BLIP2->Flamingo gain (+0.0900), directly contradicting the paper's claim that the Flamingo transfer improvement is greater.

errors.claim: “No credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established for this relatively new concept” of cross-prompt adversarial transferability.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Abstract claims it validates Q7X and its superiority to existing baselines in N6Z”; Introduction says Luo et al. introduced N6Z and competing learnable prompts, and replication tests include “superiority across target texts.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously framed N6Z as having existing baselines against which Q7X is superior, but this section says no credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established for N6Z.

errors.claim: “Q7X … jointly optimizes δv and δt” with “minδv maxδt L(f(xv+δv, xt+δt), T)” and prompt-gradient ascent.
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 computes image and prompt gradients using the unperturbed prompt: “g_v = ∇_{x_v} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)” and “g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x'_v, x_t^i), T)”; it initializes and updates “x'_t^i” but never uses x'_t^i in the forward pass or in later image-gradient computation.
errors.explanation: The prose/equation say Q7X optimizes and uses an adversarial prompt perturbation antagonistically, but the algorithm as written updates a perturbed prompt variable that is not used. Thus the algorithm does not implement the stated joint δv/δt optimization.

errors.claim: “P2F increase over base Q7X, results characterization | 12.5%” and “P2F increase over base Q7X, discussion characterization | 13.5%”
errors.evidence: The same table gives two different increases for P2F over base Q7X: 12.5% and 13.5%.
errors.explanation: Unless these refer to different metrics, the paper reports inconsistent percentage improvements for the same comparison.

errors.claim: “The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation” and earlier notes say the adaptation minimizes losses between value vectors of the input and target/reference.
errors.evidence: This part defines L_X9C = sum_i (1 - cos(V_i(x+δ), V_t)) and L_P2F = L_Q7X - λ L_X9C. It also says the combined method “jointly minimizes its negative with the Q7X loss.”
errors.explanation: If L_P2F is minimized, the term -λ L_X9C encourages maximizing L_X9C, i.e. reducing cosine similarity and moving perturbed value vectors away from the target/reference representation. That conflicts with the claim that the loss encourages closeness to the target representation and with the earlier characterization that the adaptation minimizes the value-vector loss.

errors.claim: “The attacker seeks one image perturbation eliciting a specified target text from multiple VLMs independently of prompt” and “The goal is one pattern causing predetermined target text for any image...”
errors.evidence: The same section says: “Success in this evaluation is failure by the target model to generate the correct output from the perturbed image, regardless of prompt,” “Taskwise H2Q counts failure to generate correct output text,” and §5.4.3 states “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.explanation: The stated attacker goals are targeted attacks requiring generation of a specified/predetermined target text, but the reported success criterion is untargeted failure to produce the correct output. These are different definitions of success.

errors.claim: “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes record targeted N6Z/transferability-related results: “Initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%, targeted H2Q gains up to 15%,” “P2F aggregate targeted H2Q 96.85%,” and “P2F increase over base Q7X as 12.5% vs 13.5%.” Earlier methodology also defined targeted Eq(1) and Q7X/CroPA as optimizing toward target text T.

errors.claim: “Experiments across all evaluated benchmarks are described as significantly favoring semantic noise over Q7X and random-initialized baselines.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.5.1 says B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, but Tables 3/4 show several Q7X>B8N.”
errors.explanation: If semantic-noise initialization is B8N, the paper’s own tables do not support that it significantly favors semantic noise over Q7X across all evaluated benchmarks, because several reported metrics have Q7X higher than B8N.

errors.claim: “X9C ... improves related-architecture transfer, BLIP-2 to InstructBLIP, but offers greater aggregate gains across fundamentally different architectures, BLIP-2 to Flamingo.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes from Table 8: “BLIP2→InstructBLIP V9D .2270, Q7X .5065, P2F .6850; BLIP2→Flamingo .0780/.1435/.2335.”
errors.explanation: For the reported overall C8H values, P2F/X9C improves over Q7X by .1785 for BLIP-2→InstructBLIP, but only by .0900 for BLIP-2→Flamingo. This contradicts the claim that the greater gain is for the fundamentally different BLIP-2→Flamingo transfer.

errors.claim: “Semantic anchoring raises H2Q without sacrificing N6Z.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “§6.5.1 says B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, but Tables 3/4 show several Q7X>B8N.”
errors.explanation: The paper’s own earlier tables reportedly include several N6Z-related metrics where Q7X exceeds B8N, so the broad claim that semantic anchoring raises H2Q without sacrificing N6Z is not consistently supported.

grade.reason: The reviewer’s item about X9C (index 10) directly flags the claim that BLIP-2→Flamingo shows greater aggregate gains than BLIP-2→InstructBLIP, noting Table 8 reports gains .0900 vs .1785 (the opposite), which matches the planted-error contradiction.

errors.claim: “Due to the relative novelty of this concept, no credible benchmarks/baselines have been established yet.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: abstract says the study confirms CroPA’s “superior cross-prompt transferability versus existing baselines”; introduction says it reproduced the claim that “CroPA [has] superior cross-prompt transferability vs established baselines across target texts.”
errors.explanation: This part says no credible baselines have been established for cross-prompt transferability, but earlier sections described CroPA as being compared against existing/established baselines.

errors.claim: “Given that cross-prompt transferability represents a novel direction in adversarial machine learning, no established baselines exist in current literature.”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: Abstract claims CroPA confirms superior cross-prompt transferability “vs existing baselines”; Intro claims reproduced claim that CroPA is superior “vs established baselines” and that “baselines fail to surpass CroPA even with additional prompts.”
errors.explanation: This part says no established baselines exist, but earlier parts described comparisons against existing/established baselines. The paper uses both positions for the same evaluation context.

errors.claim: “Compute gradient for adversarial prompt: g_t = ∇_{x_t} L(f(x′_v, x^i_t), T)” followed by “Update with gradient ascent: x′^i_t = x′^i_t + α_2 · sign(g_t)”
errors.evidence: The gradient is stated as taken with respect to x_t and the loss is evaluated at f(x′_v, x^i_t), but the update is applied to x′^i_t, the adversarial prompt variable.
errors.explanation: Within this algorithm fragment, the variable used to compute the prompt gradient does not match the variable being updated. If the gradient is for the adversarial prompt, it should be computed with respect to the adversarial prompt/input used in the update, not the clean prompt notation shown.

errors.claim: “We integrate this loss with the CroPA loss ... L_re-CroPA = L_CroPA(...) - λ L_d-UAP(δ_v)” and “By jointly optimizing both losses ... enforces semantic alignment with the target text.”
errors.location: this part, Eq. 12 and following paragraph
errors.evidence: Just before Eq. 12, Eq. 11 defines “L_d-UAP = Σ(1 - cosine similarity)” and states: “This loss encourages the perturbed image’s value vectors to closely align with the target text’s representation.”
errors.explanation: If the final objective is minimized as CroPA’s targeted objective is, subtracting λL_d-UAP would maximize the distance loss 1−cosine, pushing value vectors away from the target representation, not aligning them. This conflicts with the stated purpose of jointly optimizing the losses for semantic alignment.

errors.claim: For cross-model transfer, “Success is measured by the target model failing to generate the correct output when given the perturbed image, regardless of input prompt.”
errors.location: this part, Evaluation Setup under cross-model transfer
errors.evidence: Earlier notes for 5.4 threat model: “goal single image perturbation causes multiple VLMs to output target text regardless prompt.”
errors.explanation: The earlier cross-model threat model defined success as a targeted attack causing a specified target text, but this part defines success as untargeted failure to generate the correct output.

errors.claim: For universal cross-image perturbations, “The attacker aims to generate a single perturbation pattern that, when applied to any image, causes a VLM to output a predetermined target text regardless of the input prompt or image content.”
errors.evidence: In the same subsection: “A successful attack causes the model to fail to generate the correct output text when presented with any previously unseen image, regardless of its content or the associated prompt.” Also 5.4.3 says transferability is evaluated through “non-targeted ASR.”
errors.explanation: The adversary goal is stated as targeted generation of a predetermined text, but the evaluation success criterion is untargeted failure to produce the correct output.

errors.claim: “we evaluated five state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs): OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence names only four models: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA. Earlier notes also record evaluation of “Flamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The count of five contradicts the four models actually listed in the same sentence and recorded earlier.

errors.claim: “Claim 3: CroPA converges towards higher ASR as number of iterations increase [Reproduced]”
errors.evidence: Section 6.3 says: “Our obtained results ... resulted in contrasting results with respect to the original reported metrics of convergence with higher number of iterations ... despite using the exact same parameters...” and “when we investigated the ASR convergence for each task’s use case, individually the trend is prone to instability.”
errors.explanation: The heading labels the claim as reproduced, but the text says the obtained results contrast with the original reported convergence metrics and are unstable by task. That is inconsistent with an unqualified '[Reproduced]' claim.

errors.claim: “Where the original metrics showed CroPA converging with higher number of prompts.”
errors.evidence: The section title and preceding sentence frame Claim 3 as convergence “as number of iterations increase” / “with higher number of iterations.”
errors.explanation: Within the same paragraph, the variable being tested switches from number of iterations to number of prompts, which conflicts with the stated claim and setup of Section 6.3.

errors.claim: “CroPA+Init consistently outperforms both CroPA and Multi-P across all metrics”
errors.evidence: Table 3 shows several metrics where CroPA+Init is lower than CroPA: for target “unknown,” VQAgeneral is 0.8824 vs CroPA 0.9680 and VQAspecific is 0.8920 vs CroPA 0.9880; for “bomb,” Classification is 0.9020 vs CroPA 0.9498; for “very good,” VQAspecific is 0.8894 vs CroPA 0.8990.
errors.explanation: The table supports higher Overall ASR for CroPA+Init in each listed target, but not consistent improvement across all individual task metrics.

errors.claim: “achieving 6-15% gains in overall accuracy”
errors.evidence: Table 3 Overall values vs Multi-P are much larger than 6–15 percentage-point gains for several targets: unknown 0.8977 vs 0.6095, I am sorry 0.9458 vs 0.7318, too late 0.9333 vs 0.7585. Against CroPA, very good is 0.8761 vs 0.8190, a 5.71 percentage-point gain, slightly below 6%.
errors.explanation: The stated 6–15% range does not match the table if compared to both named baselines; it only roughly fits CroPA for most targets, and even then one listed gain is below 6 percentage points.

errors.claim: “We believe CutMix outperforms SCMix in promoting adversarial transferability...”

Table 1 CroPA overall: unknown .7708, I am sorry .7985, not sure .5033, very good .7020, too late .6920, metaphor .8680. 6.3 heading says convergence reproduced, but text says original metrics contrasted and per-task trends unstable. 6.4 few-shot: Table 2 shot=0 Multi .6095, CroPA .7708; shot=2 Multi .5730, CroPA .6635, captioning collapses.

6.5.1/Table 3: CroPA+Init generally improves BLIP2, but Init lower than CroPA on unknown VQAgeneral/VQAspecific, bomb Classification, very good VQAspecific. 6.5.2 cross-image Table 5 untargeted ASR: Base .4355; SCMix .7055; CutMix .5565. Best iterations: base 1700, SCMix 1500, CutMix 1600. Discussion says SCMix +27 points, CutMix +12 points over base.

errors.claim: “No credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established for this relatively new concept” of cross-prompt adversarial transferability.
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: “Abstract claims it validates Q7X and its superiority to existing baselines in N6Z”; Introduction says Luo et al. introduced N6Z and competing learnable prompts, and replication tests include “superiority across target texts.”
errors.explanation: The paper previously framed N6Z as having existing baselines against which Q7X is superior, but this section says no credible benchmarks or baselines have yet been established for N6Z.

errors.claim: “absent established N6Z baselines”
errors.evidence: Earlier notes: abstract/introduction/scope claim Q7X’s “superiority to existing baselines,” “outperforms baselines,” and includes “comparison to other N6Z methods.”
errors.explanation: The paper cannot both frame the area as lacking established N6Z baselines and claim superiority/outperformance against existing baselines without clarifying that these are only newly constructed/reference baselines rather than established ones.

errors.claim: “Q7X … jointly optimizes δv and δt” and uses antagonistic image/prompt optimization
errors.location: this part, §4.3 Cross Prompt Attack and Algorithm 1
errors.evidence: Algorithm 1 initializes and updates x′_t^i, but the image gradient is computed as ∇_{x_v} L(f(x′_v, x_t^i), T) and the prompt gradient as ∇_{x_t} L(f(x′_v, x_t^i), T); neither uses x′_t^i or x_t+δ_t in the forward pass. Equation (5), by contrast, defines min_{δv} max_{δt} L(f(x_v+δ_v, x_t+δ_t),T).
errors.explanation: The textual/formal claim says prompt perturbations are part of the adversarial input during optimization, but the algorithm as written never feeds the updated adversarial prompt into the model, so δt cannot affect the optimized image perturbation.

errors.claim: P2F increase over base Q7X is characterized as 12.5% in results and 13.5% in discussion.
errors.evidence: The same table lists both: “P2F increase over base Q7X, results characterization | 12.5%” and “P2F increase over base Q7X, discussion characterization | 13.5%”.
errors.explanation: These appear to be two different reported values for the same P2F increase over base Q7X, creating an internal numerical inconsistency unless later clarified as different metrics or settings.

errors.claim: “The loss is described as encouraging closeness to the target representation” and the method “jointly minimizes its negative with the Q7X loss.”
errors.evidence: Eq. 11 defines L_X9C = Σ(1 - cosine similarity between V_i(x+δ) and V_t). Eq. 12 defines L_P2F = L_Q7X − λ L_X9C.
errors.explanation: If L_P2F is minimized, subtracting λL_X9C encourages L_X9C to become large, i.e. lowers cosine similarity and moves the perturbed value vectors away from the target representation. That conflicts with the textual claim that the loss encourages closeness to the target representation.

errors.claim: “The attacker seeks one image perturbation eliciting a specified target text from multiple VLMs independently of prompt”
errors.evidence: The same subsection says: “Success in this evaluation is failure by the target model to generate the correct output from the perturbed image, regardless of prompt.” §5.4.3 also says: “All N6Z and F8V transferability results are presented under untargeted attacks.”
errors.explanation: Eliciting a specified target text is a targeted attack objective, but the evaluation is described as untargeted failure to produce the correct output. The section gives incompatible definitions of the F8V attack goal.

errors.claim: “The goal is one pattern causing predetermined target text for any image, regardless of image content and prompt”
errors.evidence: The same subsection says: “Taskwise H2Q counts failure to generate correct output text on previously unseen images independently of content or prompt.” §5.4.3 says: “Non-targeted H2Q is also the chosen robust, fair, comparable assessment of between-model and between-image transfer.”
errors.explanation: A pattern causing predetermined target text is targeted K3R, while failure to generate the correct output is untargeted. The stated goal and the stated metric/threat model conflict.

errors.claim: “Five state-of-the-art VLMs were evaluated: OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.evidence: The sentence says five VLMs were evaluated but names only four: “OpenFlamingo, BLIP-2, InstructBLIP, and LLaVA.”
errors.explanation: The stated count conflicts with the enumerated list in the same sentence.

errors.claim: “B8N = CroPA+Init is reported to outperform Q7X and V9D consistently across every metric”
errors.evidence: Table 3 shows several metrics where B8N is lower than Q7X or V9D: for target “unknown,” B8N A7L=0.8824 and T4B=0.8920, below Q7X A7L=0.9680 and T4B=0.9880; for “bomb,” B8N G9M=0.9020, below Q7X=0.9498 and V9D=0.9050; for “very good,” B8N T4B=0.8894, below Q7X=0.8990.
errors.explanation: The table does not support consistent outperformance across every metric; B8N loses on multiple task/target entries.

errors.claim: Earlier discussion reported initialization targeted H2Q gains “up to 15%.”
errors.evidence: In this part, Table 3 reports much larger B8N-over-Q7X gains, e.g. target “unknown” D5R rises from Q7X 0.4200 to B8N 0.9306, a +0.5106 gain; Table 4 average D5R rises from Q7X 0.6138 to B8N 0.9464, a +0.3326 gain.
errors.explanation: If the earlier “up to 15%” claim referred to the same initialization targeted H2Q results, the current reported gains exceed that maximum by a large margin.

errors.claim: “U8G is believed to outperform J6T for adversarial transfer”
errors.evidence: Table 5 shows J6T higher than U8G on VQA/A7L (0.6560 vs 0.4520), D5R (0.9500 vs 0.5500), and C8H (0.7055 vs 0.5565), tied on G9M (0.5000), with U8G higher only on T4B (0.7240 vs 0.7160). Earlier notes also record §5.3: “J6T=SCMix selected because superior K3R.”
errors.explanation: The text says U8G should outperform J6T, but the reported K3R results show J6T is clearly better overall and on most tasks.

errors.claim: “Experiments across all evaluated benchmarks are described as significantly favoring semantic noise over Q7X and random-initialized baselines.”
errors.evidence: Notes from §6.5.1: “claims B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, contradicted by Tables 3–4”; earlier notes also say “Added initialization time 20–25s/image. Initialization aggregate accuracy gains 6–15%; targeted H2Q gains up to 15%—conflicts with §6.5 tables showing larger B8N gains.”
errors.explanation: The discussion repeats/strengthens a universal performance claim for semantic-noise initialization, but the recorded results did not consistently favor B8N/Q7X-initialization across every benchmark/metric.

errors.claim: “Semantic anchoring raises H2Q without sacrificing N6Z”
errors.evidence: Notes from §6.5.1: “claims B8N outperforms Q7X/V9D consistently across every metric, contradicted by Tables 3–4.”
errors.explanation: If Tables 3–4 contain metrics where B8N does not outperform Q7X/V9D, the categorical claim that initialization raises attack success without any N6Z sacrifice is not supported by the paper’s own reported results.

final_notes:
Paper title: “Revisiting CroPA: A Reproducibility Study and Enhancements for Cross-Prompt Adversarial Transferability in Vision-Language Models.” Definitions: F8V = Cross-Model Transferability; K3R = Cross-Image Transferability; N6Z = Cross-Prompt Transferability; Z4P = Universal/shared perturbations, associated with cross-image. Tasks: A7L/VQAgeneral, T4B/VQAspecific, G9M/classification, D5R/captioning, C8H/overall. H2Q = ASR. Q7X/CroPA uses image perturbation at eval; prompt perturbations optimized but discarded. Algorithm 1 inconsistency: initializes/updates x′t but gradients/forward passes use clean xt, so prompt perturbation has no effect as written.

Scope inconsistencies: Intro claimed superiority to baselines/comparison to other N6Z methods, while related work/methodology say no established N6Z baselines; Luo attacks R4K=Single-P and V9D=Multi-P are called baselines. §6 says “Five” VLMs but lists four. §5.4 describes F8V/K3R goals as targeted specified text but evaluation as untargeted failure; §5.4.3 says all N6Z and F8V transfer results are untargeted; E3W excluded from transfer due negligible transfer.

§5 says Q7X poor on G9M/D5R and limited F8V; S3D raises single-model H2Q but constrains transferability. Transfer not core to Luo et al. Training on 50 images >6h on 48GB L40S, 95% VRAM. Initialization adds 20–25s/image. Earlier text says initialization aggregate gains 6–15% and targeted H2Q up to 15%, conflicting with §6.5 tables showing larger B8N gains.
